Workspace.Name: BlindEqLms
Workspace.Description:
Blind Equalisation Example - LMS

 

This example implements a blind equaliser. The adaptive filter LMS core block is used as the adaptive algorithm. Note that in this case the desired signal is the output of the non linearity block. This means that no training sequence is required.

 

The input signal to the system is a set of random symbols. Theseare produced with the combination the IID Uniforn Noise Waveform and the Unifrom Quantizer parts. These symbols are mapped using the modulation mapping in the symbol modulator part. These complex symbols are then sent through the channel, which is represented as a complex FIR filters.

 

The blind equaliser is implemented with a complex LMS adaptive filter core and a non linearity part. The non linearity is used to operate at the output of the LMS part in order to produce the desired signal. This in turn is used to generate the error signal required by the LMS adaptive filter core block.

 

The complex error filter block performs a Gaussian filtering operation on the norm (square of the modulus) of the error signal. The effect is a smoothing of the norm of the norm of the error.

Workspace.Name: EqualiserCoreRLS
Workspace.Description:
Complex RLS Adaptive Filter Core

 

This example shows the use of the Complex RLS Adaptive Filter Core block in an inverse system identification scenario. An equivalent implementation using the Complex RLS Adaptive Filter is also provided. Note that the Complex RLS Adaptive Filter Core block only implementes the complex FIR filter with variable coefficients and the adaptive RLS algorithm controlling them. Therefore the subtractor and error feedback loop need to be implemented externally when using the Complex RLS Adaptive Filter Core block.

 

After running the simulation observe that the channel frequency response is equalised, i.e. the frequency response of the equaliser is the inverse of the frequency response of the channel. Note also the error signal for both the Complex RLS Adaptive Filter Core and the Complex RLS Adaptive Filter are the same, showning that the two implementations are equivalent.

Workspace.Name: SysIdAPA
Workspace.Description:
System Identification Example - APA

 

In this example a system identification configuration has been setup, where the adaptive filter attempts to identify the impulse response of a complex arithmetic unknown system.  Both the unknown system and the adaptive filter are excited with white noise. The unknown system is represented here by a complex FIR filter. Its output is used as the desired signal input of the adaptive filter as shown.

 

During the simulation the adaptive filter block updates the coefficient values of the adaptive filter to the data set.   If the adaptive filter can successfully adapt; the value of the coefficients should the match the coefficients of the complex filter representing the unknown system.  A plot of the real and imaginary components of the unknown system and the adaptive filter is provided on the right.

 

Note that this example also uses the complex error filter block. This block performs a Gaussian filtering operation on the norm (square of the modulus) of the error signal. The effect is a smoothing of the norm of the norm of the error. It also provides a floor or minimum representable level for the output.

Workspace.Name: SysIdLMSCore
Workspace.Description:
LMS Adaptive Filter Core

 

This example shows the functionality of the LMS_AdaptFltCore part. This block contains the core functionality of the adaptive filter, i.e. the FIR filter with variable weights and the adaptive algorithm which controls them. Therefore it does not contain the calculation of the error signal and the feedback loop required to pass this signal back into the adaptive filter.

 

The two structures shown here are equivalent, therefore they should produce the same error signal and adapt to the same solution in terms of final filter weights.

Workspace.Name: Beam_wADAR1000
Workspace.Description:
STK Cosim with ADAR1000 Phased Array Design

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

The Analytical Graphics Inc. (AGI) System Tool Kit (STK) product is a physics based software geometry engine that accurately displays and analyzes land, sea, air, and space assets in real or simulated time.

 

Objective:

Use SystemVue Phased Array Design with comercial of the shelve (COTS) beamformer ADAR1000 part from Analog Devices. The Phased Array antenna beam pattern is then exported to STK. Once the beam pattern is exported and loaded into the STK scenario perform a signal to noise (SNR) analysis will be performed.

 

Workspace Description:

The equation a0_RunSims block controls all the simulations and the user should always run the analyses by executing this script.

The script runs the phased array analysis twice, in Rx and Tx mode, exports the beam pattern data to the corresponding STK antenna pattern file. In the script an STK command is created to use the external antenna patterns for the radar antennas in the STK scenario.

Radar_SNR design executes the STK command and runs STK to obtain SNR data.

 

Note: You have to start STK and load the scenario Radar_drone before running this example.

 

Things to try:

1. Observe the 3D antenna pattern  view loaded in the STK scenario (make sure you are zoomed on to the drone to see it).

 

2. Modify  the anetnna design by moving the atype slider on the PhasedArrayDesign schematic. Observe the SNR results and 3D antenna beam pattern.

 

3. Change the theta (elevation) angle of the array with the sch_th.

 

4. Set atype = 2. The input power to the array is 0 dBm increase to +15 dBm. You should see a warning that BF1 is past it's 1 dB compression point. This is correct you have exceed the ADAR1000 Tx 1dB at this frequency. Observe the Tx Phi Cut and SNR changes.

Workspace.Name: LFM_EW_STK_Scenario
Workspace.Description:
LFM_PDW_EW_STK_Scenario

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

The Analytical Graphics Inc. (AGI) System Tool Kit (STK) product is a physics based software geometry engine that accurately displays and analyzes land, sea, air, and space assets in real or simulated time. The STK_Interface controls STK in the background and runs the STK scenario, extracts multiple STK scenario report parameter values vs time and makes those values available to the Channel design.

 

In this example, the STK_Interface extracts propagation loss, delay and noise temperature between two STK objects and feeds those values to the channel model. You can select different STK scenario objects and observe the radar signal in real environment.

 

The scenario includes three radars, two on the coast and one on a ship. There is an EW receiver mounted on an Airplane that approaches the coast, turns and follows the coast line for a while and then turns away.

 

Note: You have to start STK and load the scenario EW_Radar_2018 before running this example.

 

Things to try

1. In the Design1 schematic move the Select Transmitter slider and observe how the Tx/Rx signals change.

2. Open the STK Interface and change the start time to 14 May 2018 16:05:00.000. This change moves the Airplane in STK five minutes in time. Try other times but remember that in the STK scenario the airplane only flies for 15 minutes.

3. So far you have been observing the received pulse from one transmitter. Create a new schematic and replicate the transmitter setup so you can analyze all three transmitters simultaneously. You will have to also replicate the STK interface and channel.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_3DScan
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar Library 3D scan

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

 

This workspace provides Automotive Radar 3D scan solution under lower cost constraint, consisting of FMCW signal generation, transmitter antenna, target, receiver antenna, beat frequency extracting, constant false alarm rate (CFAR) processing. The workspace can be used as templates for Automotive Radar scenario information perceiving.

 

System Structure

 

1.Signal generation

The AutomotiveRadar_CW model is used to generate FMCW signal which is a function of pulse repeat frequency (PRF), power, and pulse width. 

 

2. Transmitter Antenna

The transmitting antenna is a vertical array scanning in the elevation region. The transmitting array aperture size can be specified. The transmitting beam is controlled by the MATLAB script (TxBeamControl).

 

3. Target Echoes

According to the radar platform, target position and target RCS input, echo generator model generates multiple target echoes with corresponding delay and RCS.

 

4. Receiver Antenna

The receiving antenna is a horizontal array scanning in the azimuth region, the receiving array aperture size can be specified. The receiving beam is controlled by the MATLAB script (RxBeamControl).

 

5. Range Information Extracting

The echo signal and local transmitting signal are mixed; the simulation obtains the beat frequency which is proportional to the target range. With FFT spectrum analysis, the target range information can be extracted. 

 

Simulation Results

The target space distribution is showed in 3D coordinate system, where 3 points in the figure stands for 3 targets.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_MultiTargetsDetection
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar Multi-Target Detection

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

Simulation Task

This workspace illustrates an Automotive Radar multi-target detection system using diversified frequency modulated continuous wave (FMCW) transmit signal waveforms.

  • Design1 is for linear FMCW signal.
  • Design2 is for MFSK signal.
  • Design3 is for Fast Chirp signal.
  • DS1_1 is for PRBS signal.

Workspace Description

  • Top level design

The workspace consists of four parts.

·         Transmit Signal Generation

In this part, the baseband transmit signal is generated. And then a CxToEnv model is used to change the signal to envelope signal with carrier frequency.

·         In Design1, the AutomotiveRadar_CW model is used to generate the pure linear FMCW signal and its frequency vs. time is trapezoidal in each period. It consists of up-chirp segment, single tone segment and down-chirp segment.

·         In Design2, the AutomotiveRadar_FSK model is used to generate the MFSK modulated FMCW signal. The MFSK consists of two sequence (A and B), these two sequence will be transmitted in an intertwined sequence (ABABAB...). The frequency increment in every step of each sequence of A and B is called Fincr and the sequence B is shifted from sequence A in frequency with Fshift. 

·         In Design3, the AutomotiveRadar_CW model is used to generating the fast chirp signal. Its frequency vs. time is sawtooth in each period.

·         In DS1_1, the Gold model is used to generating binary phase coded signal. Its bandwidth is the reciprocal of bit duration.

·         Target Echo Generation

In this part, several AutomotiveRadar_Target models are used to generate each target's echo. Every target may have different range, velocity and RCS. And one Add model is used to generate the combined echoes from them all.

·         Beat Frequency Generation

In this part, the mixer is used to get the beat frequencies. The input of the mixer is the combined echoes from targets and the LO is the transmit signal. 

·         In Designs numbered 1-3, two mixers are used to do IQ down conversion. A PhaseShifter model with 90-degree phase shift is used to generate the quadrature signal of LO. Then a RectToCx model is used to converting the data type to complex for the following digital signal processing parts.

·       In Design DS1_1, the envelop signal is firstly transformed to complex then the traditional Pulse Compression part is applied instead of IQ down conversion before digital signal processing.

·         Signal Processing

In this part, multi-targets detection algorithm is applied here and results are displayed in figures.

·         In Design1, we set the ADC sample rate in the actual automotive radar hardware system is 1MHz. However, the simulation time step is a tiny value such as 1e-9 second in this example for high resolution simulation, so a down sampler is used to decrease the sample rate first. And then a FFT processor is applied to get the frequency domain of the beat frequencies. A Constant false alarm rate (CFAR) model and several other models are used to cancel the clutter. And then a MATLAB script model named 'AmbiguityResolution' is used to measure the multiple targets' range and velocity. In this MATLAB script model, the beat frequencies in each period of up-chirp, single tone and down-chirp are processed respectively to get the lines in the R-v-diagram [1] and then the interception points are detected to measure the real targets' range and velocity. Finally, all real targets' range and speed are displayed in the figure 'Targets Plot1' by the equations in 'TargetsPlot1'.

·         In Design2, we assume that there is only one sample point in the time interval of every step of the MFSK signal. In this case, the time interval is 10e-6 s then the sample rate of the ADC should be 100K Hz. So, the down sampler is used to change the data rate from 1e9 Hz to 100K Hz. And the phase of down sampler should be set as half of its factor, otherwise the phase of the signal will not be correct. Then after IQ, the complex signal is generated by one RecToCx model. One Distributor model is used to split the sequence A and sequence B. Then each of the sequences is applied to FFT processor to get the beat frequencies. Then the FFT results of each sequence are applied to CFAR and BinaryDetector. At the same time, the phase difference between sequence A and is calculated using combination of Conjugation, Mpy and CxtoPolar. All these data, beat frequencies of sequence A and B after CFAR and BinaryDetector and phase difference between sequence A and B, is applied to a MATLAB script model named 'AmbiguityResolution'. Then every target's range and velocity is measured. Finally, all real targets' range and speed are displayed in the figure 'Targets Plot2' by the equations in 'TargetsPlot2'.

·         In Design3, the down sampler is used to change the data rate from 3.2e9 Hz to 32e6 Hz, which is real ADC sample rate. Then after IQ, the complex signal is generated by one RecToCx model. First, one FFT processor is used to get the range dimension FFT in each period of fast chirp. And then the other FFT processor is used to get the Doppler dimension FFT. Then the FFT results are applied to CFAR and BinaryDetector. And then all data is applied to a MATLAB script model named 'RVMeasurement'. Then every target's range and velocity is measured. Finally, all real targets' range and speed are displayed in the figure 'Targets Plot3' by the equations in 'TargetsPlot3'.

·         In DS1_1, the signal processing adopts pulse compressing to realize code correlation processing, AutomotiveRadar_MatchedSrc model is waveform frequency domain template. In the receiver, the target echoes is changed into frequency domain data, the local template is matched with target echoes to achieve the target range information. And in the slow time dimension the FFT is applied for the Doppler processing to achieve target velocity information, the data gets through the CFAR to detect the target, the RVMeasurement MATLAB script is used to output the target range and velocity information.

  • Note

Please refer to section III in the reference [1] for the algorithm of Design1 in details. This paper used two triangular linear FMCW signal with different slope but we use one trapezoidal linear FMCW signal here. However, the concept is the same.

Please refer to section IV in the reference [1] or section III in the reference [2] for the algorithm of Design2 in details.

And also, please refer to section 7.2.5 in reference [3] for the algorithm of Design3 in details.

For the Radar_PhasedArrayTx / Radar_PhasedArrayRx model, the spacing of elements can either be uniform or non-uniform. The value of the spacing will be multiples of wavelength when the spacing is uniform, otherwise the spacing values can be set arbitrarily by using an array where the unit is meter.

The parameter mask_array provide the capability to enable or disable the elements to simulate the arbitrary linear array or 2-D planar array. The size of mask_array should be the same as the maximum element number of the array. If the value in the mask_array is set to 1, it means the element at the corresponding position is enabled. Otherwise the elements at the corresponding position are disabled or not installed.

The final 2-D antenna pattern is plotted using Dynamic3D model or MATLAB Script equations.

To scan the antenna pattern, the theta range is [0:180] and the phi range is [0:360], same as the setting of EMPro antenna pattern file or HFSS antenna pattern file or CST antenna pattern file.

1. One Element

In this design, one CST antenna pattern file is read to draw its pattern.

2. Horizontal Linear Array

In this design, 16 antenna elements are placed on horizontal orientation. And Radar_Tx_DBS_2D model is used to set the beam radiation direction as [30,0].

3. Vertical Linear Array

In this design, 16 antenna elements are placed on vertical orientation. And Radar_Tx_DBS_2D model is used to set the beam radiation direction as [30,90].

4. Planar Array

In this design, 16*16 antenna elements are placed on planar. And Radar_Tx_DBS_2D model is used to set the beam radiation direction as [30,60].

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_SignalGeneration
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar Signal Generation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

Simulation Task

This workspace shows how to generate different Automotive Radar transmit signal.

  • Design1 is for linear FMCW and Fast Chirp basic signal generation.
  • Design2 is for MFSK signal generation.
  • Design3 is for FMCW signal analysis in Keysight 89600 VSA.
  • Design4 is for linear FMCW sawtooth pulse train signal generation.
  • Design5 is for linear FMCW and Fast Chirp flexible signal generation using chop part.
  • Design6 is for Nonlinear FMCW signal generation using NLFM part.

Workspace Description

  • The AutomotiveRadar_CW model is used in Design1. It can generate sawtooth, triangle or trapezoidal FMCW signal. When the parameter DeltaFreq of AutomotiveRadar_CW model is set to zero, the FMCW signal will be simple Sine/Cosine waveform.
  • The AutomotiveRadar_FSK model is used in Design2. In this case, one continuous wave called FSK-LFMCW signal is generated. It is combined with the combination of Frequency Shift Keying (FSK) and Linear Frequency Modulated (LFM). This waveform could offer the possibility of an unambiguous target range and velocity measurement simultaneously. Please refer to reference [1] for this kind of MFSK signal.
  • One kind of triangle FMCW is generated in Design3 and VSA_89600B_Sink model is used to call Keysight 89600 VSA software and then analyze this triangle FMCW signal. The setup file 'FMCW_VSA.setx' is used to configure VSA as 'FMCW Radar' analysis mode. This mode also can be set by clicking 'MeasSetup – Measurement Type – Radar Analysis – FMCW Radar' in VSA.
  • The AutomotiveRadar_LFM model is used in Design4. In this case, three consecutive LFMCW pulse trains are generated, with one long pulse followed by two short pulses. This waveform offers the user flexible LFMCW signal pulse configurations, with chirp BW, pulse length, pulse combinations all open for user settings.
  • The AutomotiveRadar_CW, Waveform, Chop, ChopVarOffset models are used in Design5. In this case, a flexible fixed frequency signal is combined with triangular FMCW signal. Using the ChopVarOffset & Chop models, the original FMCW signals could be reorganized with flexible timing controls to form variable FMCW waveforms.
  • The AutomotiveRadar_NLFM model is used in Design6. In this case, four types of nonlinear FMCW generation modes could be selected, and nonlinear frequency modulation distortions can be modeled at transmitter.

Reference

[1] H. Rohling and M.-M. Meinecke, ‘‘Waveform design principles for Automotive Radar systems’’, in CIE International Conference on Radar, pp. 1--4, Beijing, China, October 2001.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_FMCW_Interference
Workspace.Description:
FMCW RADAR Simulation with Interference Impacts

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace provides an example of a FMCW Radar simulation platform with interference impacts.

The design is more advanced with 3-layer architecure and basic TRx modeling

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Example Highlights:

  • Generate FMCW signals with triangle or Saw tooth or custom waveform frequency sweep in 77 GHz Band.
  • Target models can be set according to user interests in the Trajectory Layer. 
  • FMCW chirp waveform is applied in Tx.
  • Antenna modeling and multi-target echo generations are realized.
  • Beat frequency IQ mixing & sampling, range and doppler FFT and CFAR are realized in Rx.
  • More advanced multi-target range & velocity detection algorithms based on CFAR results are realized by MultiTarDetect model. AoA results are shown as NaN since 1Rx cannot measure AoA.
  • FMCW radar generic detection performance evaluations are provided in FMCW_Perf equation file (range, velocity and AoA detection performance calculations are provided).
  • Two interference sources are added before the Receiver to model interference impacts. User could modify Interference_Equations file together with IntSrc_Modeling subnet.
  • The interference sources with propagation loss and single-trip delay (Range/C) are modelled in the subnet.
  • If the two interference sources are disabled, only the two true targets are detected. The presented workspace has enabled these two sources, and the two near-range targets (with true ranges of 10m and 16m) are replaced with 15 false targets.
  • The SIR (Signal to Interference Ratio in dB) is provided for the user to control the output power of interference sources before the Receiver.

All the models in this example can be used as templates for custom models. 

Users can open these models and modify them as needed to create custom models for their own system simulation.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_GroundClutter_Guardrail
Workspace.Description:
Automotive radar Ground Clutter + Guardrail Simulation

 

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example workspace demonstrates how to perform target + ground clutter + uninterested targets (guardrail as example) simulations using SystemVue automotive radar library models.

 

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

The ground clutter indirect generation with complex environment scenario example (inside folder "Target+Clutter with Guardrail Modeling").

 

This example is designed with the classical 3-layer architecture. The main signal path is designed with 2 targets, 2 guardbelts, and ground clutter modeling.

  • The clutter modeling method is the area clutter superposition algorithm, designed in M6 MATLAB part. The area clutter echo is generated in each range-bin of the unambiguous range, and clutter gain is calculated considering TRx antenna gains and free-space propagation loss attenuations.
  • Simulation procedures:
    • 1st step: run the System_Equation to set basic system-design parameters,
    • 2nd step: run the Clutter_Modeling equation to set clutter modeling parameters;
    • 3rd step: run the DA2 simulation, then use Range-Doppler Spectrum Plot equation to generate 3-D plot (target + clutter + guardbelt). The MathLang plot function is built-in in automotive radar library, and calling method is demonstrated.

NOTE: surface clutter modeling is slow, therefore we intentionally add two additional Sink parts (S2 & S3) to improve user’s understanding of the simulation progress.


Reference:

Bassem R. Mahafza, 'Radar Systems Analaysis and Design Using MATLAB (3rd Edition)', Chapter.9.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_GroundClutter_ManholeCover
Workspace.Description:
Automotive radar Ground Clutter

+ Manhole Cover Simulation

 

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example workspace demonstrates how to use ClutterGen model and Mathlang based surface clutter modeling to generate the ground clutter + target + Manhole Cover complex environmental scenario and realize radar detection analysis.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

 

1, the functions folder:

 

This folder contains three functions written in MATHLang:

  • CirTarGen: this is the function to generate circular target in the XOZ plane, to transform radar & manhole parameters into valid parameters to be input in "TargetScatterLocation" model(s) in the Trajectory Layer. 
  • RCS_CirFlatPlate: this is the function to calculate RCS values for circular flat plate, and the approximation method is valid for traditional A/D radar frequency ranges (generally lower than K-band) ONLY.
  • RCS_RectFlatPlate: this is the function to calculate RCS values for rectangular flat plate, and the approximation method is valid for traditional A/D radar frequency ranges (generally lower than K-band) ONLY.

2, the ground clutter + target + manhole cover environment scenario example (inside folder "Target + Clutter + Manhole Cover").

 

This example is designed with classical 3-layer architecture. The main signal path is designed with 2 targets, 1 manhole cover, and ground clutter is generated by the surface clutter modeling method:

  • The surface clutter modeling method is applied (See AutomotiveRadar_GroundClutter_Guardrail for more details);
  • Simulation procedures:
    • 1st step: run the Manhole_Cover_Modeling equation to obtain manhole modeling parameters,
    • 2nd step: run the System_Equation equation to set system-level simulation parameters for Design3 schematic;
    • 3rd step: run the Clutter_Modeling equation to set clutter modeling parameters;
      • If no errors are shown in the Errors column, pls move forward to the 4th step.
    • 4th step: run the "DA1/2 (for No Clutter/With Clutter cases)" dataflow analysis;
    • 5th step: run the Range-Doppler Spectrum Plot equation to generate 3-D plot (target + clutter + Manhole Cover).

In the calculated 2D FFT results, for the CPINum = 64 (NO Clutter) figure, marker m95 refers to the manhole (actually contains two peaks), and peaks (No.96 & 97) are the two targets; for the CPINum = 64 (With Clutter) figure, marker m105 refers to the manhole (actually contains two peaks), and two other peaks (No.103 & 104) refer to the two targets.

 

The Step05 equation file is provided as a template for using the range-doppler spectrum plotting function. This range-doppler spectrum plotting function is built-in for automotive radar library.

 

Notes:

1, "No Clutter" case

If the user would like to reproduce "NO clutter" conditions, please refer to the DA1 Analysis and Design1 schematic for more understanding.

 

2, Clutter impacts on range-doppler plot

The impact of clutter on range-doppler plot is generally determined by the Sigma0 setting. Under generic road surface conditions, the Sigma0 parameter is usually -50~-30 dB ground clutter is NOT the decisive factor for reliable target detection.

 

3, Simulation time

Manhole clutter requires high range resolution, and consequently high bandwidth LFM signal. Therefore, the sampling rate is high, which results in huge size for range-doppler spectrum matrix.

 

The presented surface clutter modeling method requires range related weighting in each range bin, hence the simulation speed is dragged down a lot because of the huge size of range-doppler spectrum matrix. For instance, the CPINum = 16 case runs for 20 min on HP Z440 workstation. The CPINum = 64 cases are provided to the user by figures.


Reference:

Bassem R. Mahafza, 'Radar Systems Analysis and Design Using MATLAB (3rd Edition)', Chapter.14 (circular & rectangular plate RCS calculations for traditional  aerospace/defense radar frequency bands).

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_MicroDopplerEffect
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar Library Micro-Doppler Effect Simulation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace as a template shows how to set up micro-Doppler target effect simulation based on the generalized framework and how to generate the echoes from the multiple scatters of the pedestrian target.

This workspace as a template shows how to set up the arbitrary type radar simulation based on the generalized framework and how to generate the echoes from the scatters of targets.

The example includes two layers: trajectory layer and signal layer.

a. The Trajectory Layer with pink color is to set Tx and Rx platform property. The pedestrian target moving properties with initial velocity, position is set here. In the trajectory layer, the AutomotiveRadar_Platform model and AutomotiveRadar_TargetScatterLocation model are used to generate the trajectories of transmitter, receiver, and scatters of target. The output is at the SimpleXYZ frame (x, y, z).

b. The Signal layer with green color is the multi scatters pedestrian echoes generation for setting the position of Tx and Rx platform position.  the input signal is fed to the AutomotiveRadar_EchoGenerator model and echoes from different scatters of pedestrian target are generated per the scatter locations.

Pedestrian 

1. The echoes mixed with local signal to achieve beat frequency, the beat frequency changes from 20MHz to 5MHz through down sampling. The down sampling beat frequency is analyzed by FFT to get the target range information. 

2. The transmit waveform is the fast chip FMCW, the PRI is 51.2us. The band width is 20MHz. The pedestrian is slow target, in order to extracting the target micro Doppler information, the coherent processing interval (CPI) pulse number is 1024, the coherent processing time is about 52.4ms. Every 52.4ms the simulation outputs range-Doppler spectrum of pedestrian target one time. The simulation needs multiple CPI data to observe the micro Doppler periodic variation. The simulation CPI number (RangeSample) is 40, the 40 RangeSample Doppler data is showed in one graph. The graph is the micro-Doppler changing with the time.

 UserDefined

1.  The echoes mixed with local signal to achieve beat frequency, the beat frequency changes from 50MHz to 5MHz through down sampling. The down sampling beat frequency is analyzed by FFT to get the target range information. 

2. The transmit waveform is the fast chip FMCW, the PRI is 12.8us. The band width is 50MHz. The coherent processing interval (CPI) pulse number is 128, the coherent processing time is about 1.6384ms. Every 1.6384ms the simulation outputs range-Doppler spectrum of pedestrian target one time. The simulation needs multiple CPI data to observe the micro Doppler periodic variation. The simulation CPI number (RangeSample) is 20, the 20 RangeSample Doppler data is showed in one graph. The graph is the micro-Doppler changing with the time.

  DynamicDisplay

     In this folder, two examples are provided to dynamically display 3D Micro-Doppler target trajectory.

1.     In PedestrianDisplay design, the scatter positions generated from AutomotiveRadar_MicroDopplerTarget model are directly sent to dynamic display model (Dynamic3D) with necessary data processing.

2.     In UserDefinedDisplay design, a custom MATLAB script model is provided to input user-defined trajectory file as well as antenna array positions ([X Y Z]), and finally Dynamic3D model will show both antenna array and target trajectory.

Note that for User-Defined mode, users can also follow the same process defined in PedestrianDisplay design to get target trajectory (i.e. directly get trajectory from AutomotiveRadar_MicroDopplerTarget model instead of using this custom MATLAB script model).

Note that input file name in the custom MATLAB script model needs a full path. So please make sure the path is set correctly.

Note: Trajectory file description

The file format supports two modes.

Mode 1: Each line is the position values and RCS values of all the scatters at each time step, like  x0 y0 z0 RCS0; x1 y1 z1 RCS1; …; xn yn zn RCSn in the SimpleXYZ frame.  For example, here are two-line examples for two scatters.  In this mode, the time step defined in Parameter TimeStep will be used.

 

20.0000 0.0000 0.0000 1.0000; 120.2000 0.0000 0.0000 0.2000
40.0000 0.0000 0.0000 4.0000; 120.2000 0.0000 0.0000 0.2000

 

Mode 2: The first lines starts with "TimeStep =" and then specifies the actual time step used when the data are generated. From the second line, it is the same as Mode 1. For example, here are two-line examples for two scatters with first line of TimeStep definition.

 

TimeStep = 2e-9
20.0000 0.0000 0.0000 1.0000; 120.2000 0.0000 0.0000 0.2000
40.0000 0.0000 0.0000 4.0000; 120.2000 0.0000 0.0000 0.2000

 

Note that when simulation reaches last line of the file, the output from this model will remain the data at last line.

 

Two sample files are provided.

 

1. The first sample file (Trajectory_UserDefined.txt) is provided with Mode 2. This file is in Trajectory_UserDefined.zip, please unzip this Trajectory_UserDefined.zip file in the workspace the directory. The trajectory file is 2 scatters motion coordinate and RCS. One scatter initial position is [20 0 0], the RCS is 1 m2, the scatter velocity is 40m/s. the other scatter initial position is [20 0 0], the RCS is 0.2 m2, the scatter motion is superposition of translation and rotation, which is same as car and rolling wheel. The wheel radius is 0.2m. So, the file is the 2 scatters coordinate every time sample. The sample rate is consistent with the simulated SampleRate. The file format is (x0 y0 z0 RCS0; x1 y1 z1 RCS1; …; xn yn zn RCSn) in the SimpleXYZ frame. For example, the first sample date is (20.0000 0.0000 0.0000 1.0000; 20.2000 0.0000 0.0000 0.2000).

2. The second sample file (Trajectory_Pedestrian.txt) is provided with Mode 1. This file defines the same moving trajectory defined when MicroDopplerMode = Pedestrian with 17 scatters.

 

 Built-in MathLang Function Note

 

There is one function named "AutomotiveRadar_DisplayDopplerVsTime()" to help user plot the adjacent CPI slice based doppler variation with time delay. Please see the note below and refer to the MicroDoppler plot equations for application details.

 

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
%% Function Note
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
% Plot Doppler Amplitude Distribution Versus Time
%
% [USAGE]
% AutomotiveRadar_DisplayDopplerVsTime(GraphName, RawData, PRI, ADCFs, DopplerFFTSize, PulseNum_Total, OverlapPulseNum, Limit_dB)
%
% [INPUTS]
% GraphName: Output Graph Name;
% RawData: Complex Echo Data Matrix for DopplerVSTime Display(Size PRISampleNum*PulseNum)
% PRI: Pulse Repetition Interval (in sec)
% ADCFs: ADC Sample Rate (in Sample/Sec)
% DopplerFFTSize: Doppler FFT Size (eg 1024, unitless)
% PulseNum_Total: Total Pulse Number (CPI_Num*DopplerFFTSize, unitless)

% OverlapPulseNum: Overlapping Number of Pulses between consecutive CPIs (unitless)
%% Working Theory:
%% Suppose we have one CPI of 1024 pulses, then we need to look at doppler variations between adjacent CPIs.
%% If the OverlapPulseNum is set to 100, the 2nd CPI we are looking at would be 101 to 1124 pulses.
%% The reason we are doing this is to avoid abrupt Micro-Doppler variations between "real" consecutive adjacent CPIs.

% Limit_dB: Amplitude lower from the maximum value (in dB)
%
% [OUTPUTS]
% Micro-Doppler Slicing VS Time Plot, New Figure created automatically

 

Reference

[1] Victor C. Chen, ''The Micro-Doppler Effect in Radar'', Artech House Radar Library, pp.157-194

[2] Peter Sorowka, Hermann Rohling, ‘‘Pedestrian Classification with 24 GHz Chirp Sequence Radar'', in Radar Symposium (IRS), pp. 1--4, 24-26 June 2015.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_PropagationLoss
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar Propagation Loss Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

Simulation Task

This workspace illustrates an Automotive Radar Propagation Loss simulation example

with measurement-based propagation loss models from 77 GHz radar rainfall tests with pencil beam antennas.

 

Workspace Description

 

The example is divided into two folders:

 

1, The basic example is in "Basic-Range VS PropLoss" folder with basic propagation loss model, and MATLAB script is applied to control range sweep (in this example from 1m to 100m).

 

2, The advanced example is in "Advanced-PropLoss Integrated into EchoGen" folder, with typical three-layer radar simulation architectures. The propagation loss models are integrated into EchoGen model, and one propagation channel is set to be without propagation loss, the other is set to with. Then the received signals are fed into identical receivers to demonstrate loss effects by FFT magnitude plots.

 

Propagation Loss Modeling Method Descriptions

 

For propagation loss model, three general modeling methods are provided: generic rain loss, generic snow loss, and specific 77 GHz radar rain loss. The propagation loss is ONLY applicable to outSignal port. Generally, it is not recommended to use multiple propagation loss modeling within one wave propagation channel (from radar AntennaTx to AntennaRx).

 

For generic rain/snow loss, the rainfall/snowfall rates can be set as input parameter. The calculation methods are inherited from previous models.

 

For specific 77 GHz radar rain loss, three modeling methods are available. Also, please note that near/mid-range loss modeling is based on pencil-beam 77 GHz radar only, with road clutter already taken into consideration.

 

(1) Near range rain loss:

This is the sophisticated method based on measured backscattering coefficients determined by different rainfall rates.

The operating frequency, antenna parameters, radar bandwidth and target RCS are required as input parameters. It is recommended to use this method to obtain rain loss in the near range (typically < 50m).

 

(2) Mid-range rain loss:

This is the simpler rain loss modeling method similar with generic rain loss, which is based on measured SNR loss at medium range with fixed RCS.

The rainfall rate is the only input parameters required. It is recommended to use this method to obtain rain loss in the medium/far range (typically from 50m to 200m).

 

(3) Antenna radome water layer loss:

This is the loss modeling for water covered antenna radome.

The operating frequency, temperature, and water layer thickness are required. Thickness is generally between 0-1 mm.

NOTE: This radome water loss is NOT related to any propagation/target parameters such as range, RCS, etc.

 

Special Note: If you are not familiar with the three-layer radar simulation architectures, please refer to other radar/automotive radar examples for more information.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_VehicleScenarios
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar Practical Vehicle RCS Modeling Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace provides an example of a FMCW Radar simulation platform. The design is more advanced with 3-layer architecture. 4 typical vehicle + VRU (Vulnerable Road User) scenarios from experimental results reported by world-class enterprises/research institutes are extracted for system-level simulation .

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Example Highlights:

  • 4-Scenarios from 3 world-class enterprises/research institutes to cover typical anechoic chamber and indoor RCS measurement setups;
  • Various types of vehicular and VRU RCS data available;
  • Range-doppler spectrum plots for before and after CFAR are demonstrated.

RCS Data Notes:

 

The RCS data are extracted from the reference papers, with value selection options provided for each scenario as:

  • Scenario-01: minimum, mean and maximum;
  • Scenario-02 & 03: back/front peak, oblique peak (if any), side peak, minimum;
  • Scenario-04: mean, back/front peak, oblique peak (if any), side peak, minimum.

Generic simulation procedures:

 

1, Define the RCS extraction parameters in the equation: Step01-ScenarioX_RCS_Main,

2, Modify the system-level simulation parameters in the equation: Step02-System_Equations;

3, Modify the AdvFMCW-Sce0X schematic for correct target scatter parameters (scatter numbers, ranges, velocities);

4, Run the analysis DFA_AdvFMCW with correct setups of schematic and output datasets;

5, Run Step03-Results_RDPlot for Range-Doppler spectrum plots with proper plotting configurations.

 

The desired ranges, velocities are also provided in the equation tab of each schematic, and demonstrated in Scenario-01 schematic for their extraction methods.

 

Further Notes:

 

1, RCS VS Range issue

 

According to publicized research results, automotive radar target RCS values are sensitive to the measurement ranges. Also, the designed scenarios, chamber setups and range gating filtering implementations also impact the results.

 

Due to detection limitations, the targets are NOT placed at their test ranges, but at near ranges. The Before-CFAR and After-CFAR range-doppler spectrum plots for each scenario are provided for user evaluations.

 

2, Possible false detections

Besides the RCS uncertainties, the target detection results are influenced by the signal processing methods and the corresponding parameters (2D-FFT, CFAR, etc.).

3, Built-in Function Note

There is one built-in MathLang function named "AutomotiveRadar_DisplayRangeDopplerSpectrum()" to help user plot the range-doppler spectrum mappling with one CPI radar complex echo data. Please see the note below and refer to the "Step02" equation for application details.

      %%%%%%%%%%%%%%
%% Function Note
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

        % Range-Doppler Map Spectrum Plot for FMCW Radar 1-Rx Complex Echo Data
%
% [USAGE]
% DisplayRangeDopplerSpectrum(echo,Fcarrier,PRI,RangeFFTSize,DopplerFFTSize,RangeMax,ADCFs,ChirpDuration,Bandwidth,Name, DisplayUnit, Norm, DispLimit)
%
% [INPUTS]
% echo: Complex Rx Echo Data (complex data in linear scale after dechirp);
% Fcarrier: Carrier Frequency (in Hz);
% PRI: Pulse Repetition Interval (in sec)；
% Range/DopplerFFTSize: FFT Size in Range/Doppler domain;
% RangeMax: Range Display Control Struct:
%% RangeMax.Switch controls the OFF/ON of Range Display Range switch (bool, 0 for OFF, 1 for ON),
%% RangeMax.Limit sets the number of range values to be displayed (in number of points, unitless);
% ADCFs: Sample Rate for ADC output data (sample rate after down chirp, in Samp/sec);
% ChirpDuration: Chirp Pulse Duration (in sec);
% Bandwidth: Baseband Bandwidth (in Hz);
% Name: Figure Name to be displayed;
% DisplayUnit: Range-Doppler Map Spectrum Display Unit Setting (bool, 0 for linear, 1 for dB)
% Norm： Range-Doppler Output Normalization (bool, 0 for No, 1 for Yes (normalized to maximum value))
% DispLimit: Display Limiting Control Struct:
%% DispLimit.Switch: Amplitude Display Limit Switch (bool, 0 for OFF, 1 for ON)
%% DispLimit.Upper: Upper Limit for Amplitude Display (linear or dB, unitless)
%% DispLimit.Lower: Lower Limit for Amplitude Display (linear or dB, unitless)
%
% [OUTPUTS]
% Range/Doppler Spectrum Mapping Plot, New Figure created automatically

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_VRU_Modeling
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar VRU RCS Modeling and Detection Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace provides an example of a FMCW Radar simulation platform. The design is more advanced with 3-layer architecture and basic TRx modeling, which forms the basis for VRU (Vulnerable Road Users) modeling.

 

The VRU RCS modeling method is presented in this example, with bicyclist and pedestrian RCS measurement data provided. The reference RCS value (in square meters) is output to Scatter model No.1 & No.2, respectively.

 

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Bicyclist RCS Modeling:

 

As detection range is proved to be the dominant factor for VRU RCS measured values, three modeling modes are provided:

 

1, Mode 01-Near Range RCS:

 

This mode applies anechoic chamber dummy bicyclist RCS measurement data from JRC report published by the European Commission. Extensive dummy RCS experimental verification results are provided in the document for both 23-28 GHz and 76-81 GHz automotive radar bands.

 

The experiments were conducted in anechoic chamber under near range conditions (distance between antenna pairs and dummy targets is approx.. 3.4 meters). The measurement polarization is VV (Vertical to Vertical). As the published dummy bicyclist RCS curves in polar plots do not exhibit distinctive patterns as compared to Mode 03 (Long Range anechoic chamber cases), only the average RCS values are provided for 23-25 GHz and 76-81 GHz.

 

2, Mode 02- Medium Range RCS

 

This mode takes advantages of reference dummy bicyclist radar reflectivity measurement results published by the 4Active Systems Corporation as the bicyclist dummy product specifications. Extensive dummy RCS experimental verification results is conducted by the BOSCH MRR-SGU 77 GHz automotive radar sensor and compared with average real bicyclist RCS measurement results.

 

As the RCS values are governed by the ranges and AoAs, we provide upper and lower RCS boundary values for ranges of 1m, 5m, 20m, 40m and 50m, and for front or oblique (0 deg, 45 deg, 135 deg, 180 deg) case and side (90 deg) case.

 

3, Mode 03 – Long Range (Anechoic Chamber) RCS

 

This mode utilizes published data from The ElectroScience Lab of The Ohio State University, USA. The authors gave extensive RCS experimental verification results under the compact range condition, with 8 real bicycle riders as samples.

 

The experiments were conducted using HH (Horizontal to Horizontal) polarization, and the results were proposed in 360 deg with max, min and mean curves. Like the medium range RCS mode, we presented the results by the azimuth angle and the upper/lower limit for RCS values.

 

Pedestrian RCS Modeling:

 

Pedestrian RCS modeling methods are similar with bicyclists, and the measured RCS data are also provided by three modes:

 

1, Mode 01-Near Range RCS:

 

This mode applies anechoic chamber pedestrian/dummy RCS measurement data from JRC report published by the European Commission. Extensive dummy RCS experimental verification results are provided in the document for both 23-28 GHz and 76-81 GHz automotive radar bands.

 

The experiments were conducted in anechoic chamber under near range conditions (distance between antenna pairs and dummy targets is approx.. 3.4 meters). The measurement polarization is VV (Vertical to Vertical).

 

For this mode, the averaged RCS values for different measurement groups are provided: Group-01 for adult dummy, group-02 for dummy gait average, group-03 for child dummy average, group-04 for real pedestrian averaged RCS.

 

2, Mode 02- Medium Range RCS

 

This mode takes advantages of reference dummy pedestrian radar reflectivity measurement results published by the EAMA (European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association)-ACEA as the articulated pedestrian dummy target specifications. Extensive dummy RCS experimental verification results is conducted by the BOSCH MRR-SGU 77 GHz automotive radar sensor and compared with average real bicyclist RCS measurement results.

 

As the measured RCS value ranges are governed by ranges, we provide upper and lower RCS boundary values for radial ranges of 2.5m, 5m, 10m, 20m, 30m, 40m and 50m.

 

3, Mode 03- Long Range (Anechoic Chamber) RCS

 

This mode utilizes published data from The ElectroScience Lab of The Ohio State University, USA. The authors gave solid RCS verification results firstly by full-wave RCS simulations, then conducted measurements under the compact range condition for 10 real humans and 3 mannequins.

 

The experiments were performed by using HH (Horizontal to Horizontal) polarization, and the results were proposed in 360 deg or categorized by BSP (Body Shape Parameter). Like the medium range RCS mode, we presented the results by the azimuth angle modes and the upper/lower limit for RCS values.

 

Further Notes on VRU detection analysis methods:

 

From the VRU target detection analysis perspective, two generic methodology exist: FT (Fast Time) and ST (Slow Time). FT refers to the traditional pulse and CPI based range-doppler signal processing, the time line is usually under 1 second; ST refers to the Micro-Doppler effect modeling (automotive radar library has shipping examples) whose analysis time range is several seconds.

 

The VRU RCS modeling method presented in this example belongs to the FT method. Therefore, the doppler spreading effect across the long time line CANNOT be simulated. Interested users are recommended to investigate the micro-doppler example for ST analysis.

 

Note for target detection results:

 

 

Target detection results can be affected by a lot of factors, including echo signal magnitude (determined by target range and RCS in this example) and signal processing methods (CFAR, detector) and parameter setups.

 

Generic Example Introduction:

  • Generate FMCW signals with triangle or Saw tooth or custom waveform frequency sweep in 77 GHz Band.
  • Target models can be set according to user interests in the Trajectory Layer. 
  • FMCW chirp waveform is applied in Tx.
  • Antenna modeling and multi-target echo generations are realized.
  • Beat frequency IQ mixing & sampling, range and doppler FFT and CFAR are realized in Rx.
  • More advanced multi-target range & velocity detection algorithms based on CFAR results are realized by MultiTarDetect model. AoA results are shown as NaN since with only 1-Rx the AoA value cannot be determined.
  • FMCW radar generic detection performance evaluations are provided in FMCW_Perf equation file (range, velocity and AoA detection performance calculations are provided).

References:

 

1, Joaquim Fortuny-Guasch and Jean-Marc Chareau, Radar Cross Section Measurements of Pedestrian Dummies and Humans in the 24/77 GHz Frequency Bands (Establishment of a Library of RCS Signatures of Pedestrian Dummies in the Automotive Radar Bands), JRC Scientific and Policy Reports, European Commission, 2013.

 

2, Eugen Schubert, Martin Kunert, etc., Human RCS measurements and dummy requirements for the assessment of radar based active pedestrian safety systems. In: The 14th International Radar Symposium, 2013.  

 

3, CATS D3.4 – Specifications Bicyclist and Bike Target v1.1, 4Active Systems Corporation, 2016.

 

4, Articulated Pedestrian Target Specifications – V 1.0, EAMA (European Automobile Manufacturers’ Assiciation) – ACEA, 2016.

 

5, Belgiovane, Domenic; Chen, Chi-Chih, Bicycles and human riders backscattering at 77 GHz for automotive radar. In: Antennas and Propagation (EuCAP), 2016 10th European Conference on. IEEE, 2016. p. 1-5.

 

6, Belgiovane, Domenic; Chen, Chi-Chih, etc. 77 GHz radar scattering properties of pedestrians. In: IEEE Radar Conference, 2014. P. 0735-0738.

 

7, Chen, Ming and Chen, Chi-Chih. RCS patterns of pedestrians at 76-77 GHz. In IEEE Antennas and Propagation Magazine (Vol.56, Issue: 4, Aug.2014).

 

8, BOSCH MRR-SGU product datasheet: https://www.bosch-mobility-solutions.com/media/global/products-and-services/passenger-cars-and-light-commercial-vehicles/driver-assistance-systems/predictive-emergency-braking-system/mid-range-radar-sensor-(mrr)/product-data-sheet-mid-range-radar-sensor-(mrr)-2.pdf

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_CDM-FMCW_MIMO_SNR-FOV-Enhan
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar CDM-MIMO (Hadamard Coding) Example Note

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

Simulation Task

This workspace illustrates an Automotive Radar MIMO Radar FMCW-based CDMA (Hadamard Coding) example with 4*4 MIMO radar architectures. The range, velocity and AoA measurements are presented.

 

Workspace Description

 

This example is based on typical 3-layer radar simulation architecture.

 

The baseband waveform design is based on FMCW, with 4 Tx channels modulated by different codes defined by Hadamard coding. The aim is to realize a much wider FOV (Field of View or azimuth angular coverage), especially in the near-range.

 

With 4 Rx channels, the radial range, radial velocity and AoA measurements are conducted, with results compared with preset values in textboxes. To lower the calculation burden, only the I channel baseband signal is applied for 2D-FFT signal processing.

 

The SNR enhancement and wide FOV demonstrations are proposed in the Graphs folder. Please look at graph note for detailed descriptions.

 

To simplify the main schematic, the Tx & Rx subnets are created for easier understanding of system-level radar signal processing architecture.   

 

Special Note: If you are not familiar with the three-layer radar simulation architectures, please refer to other radar/automotive radar examples for more information.

 

Reference

[1] Hongbo Sun, Frederic Brigui, Marc Lesturgie "Analysis and Comparison of MIMO Radar Waveforms," 2014 International Radar Conference.

[2] http://www.ti.com/lit/an/swra554/swra554.pdf (Texas Instrument Inc. Application Note on MIMO architecture based Automotive Radar Design).

         Automotive Radar CDM-MIMO (Hadamard Coding) Graph Note

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

1, This result is obtained through data acquisitions in the Subnet named Rx_CDM_MIMO_SigAddition.

 

2, SNR Enhancement Result explanations:

 

1) The aim of this figure is to show SNR enhancement capabilities of CDM-MIMO radar architecture. The user could reproduce the result by changing TxEleNum = 1, disable the Tx channels 2-4, and rename dataset for 1Tx4Rx.

2) The red curve refers to RangeFFT amplitude for beat-freq signal in dB for 4Tx4Rx case. Target detection SNR is 11.94 dB better than blue curve@ boresight. 

(The theoretical SNR enhancement is 20*log10(4/1) = 12.04 dB, which is very close to the simulated result of 11.94 dB).

It is observed that noise level remains almost the same for the two curves.

3) The blue curve refers to RangeFFT amplitude for beat-freq signal in dB for 1Tx4Rx case. Target detection SNR is poor @ boresight.  

4) The measured target angles, ranges and velocities are presented in the "Results" folder.

 

3, WideFOV Result explanations:

 

1) The aim of this figure is to show Wide FOV capabilities of CDM-MIMO Hadamard Coding radar architecture. The target No.1 are intentionally set to possess approx. 80 deg. of AoA, while No.2 & 3 targets are with 0 & 45 deg AoA. The desired ranges are 30.4m, 25m & 42.4m respectively.

2) The red curve refers to RangeFFT amplitude for beat-freq signal in dB WITH CDM MIMO processing.

Target No.1 is detected (approx. 80 deg AoA.) with 19.4 dB amplitude enhancement.

This feature is significant in mid-range and short-range (MRR & SRR) designs.

3) The blue curve refers to RangeFFT amplitude for beat-freq signal in dB WITHOUT CDM MIMO processing.

Target No.1 is NOT detected and submerged in noise floor.

4) The measured target angles, ranges and velocities are presented in the "Results" folder.

Automotive Radar TDM-FMCW MIMO Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

Simulation Task 

This workspace illustrates an Automotive Radar MIMO Radar FMCW-based (the transmit waveform in different slot time) example with 4*4 MIMO radar architectures. The range, velocity and AoA measurements are presented.

Workspace Description 

This example is based on typical 3-layer radar simulation architecture. The baseband waveform design is based on TDM-FMCW, with 4 Tx channels transmit the FMCW waveform in different slot time.

With 4 Rx channels, the radial range, radial velocity and AoA measurements are conducted, with results compared with preset values.

The aim is to improve automotive radar angle measurement accuracy. The AoA measurement accuracy variations across different Rx SNR values are presented using sweeps. The user is recommended to change TxNum_H (in System_Equations) between 1 or 4 and reproduce the swept AoA error results.

The red curve is the 4Tx-4Rx TDM MIMO AoA angular accuracy, while the blue one is for 1Tx-4Rx case. The AoA accuracy is improved, especially for low SNR cases (< 0 dB).

The actual Rx power after LNA is measured using CCDF model to setup SNR sweep. This Rx power is manually input as Rx_Pwr parameter in DS3 schematic parameter table.

Note:

If you are not familiar with the three-layer radar simulation architectures, please refer to other radar/automotive radar examples for more information.

Reference

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

Simulation Task 

This workspace illustrates an Automotive Radar MIMO Radar FMCW-based (the transmit waveform in different slot time) example with 2 Tx ABwave signal generation capabilities.

Workspace Description

This example is from a typical customer requirement that the two Tx antennas transmit two distinct FMCW profiles alternatively as TDM MIMO radar. That is, antenna A transmits wave profile A for a certain CPI number (in this example is 4 pulses) and then transmit wave profile B for the same CPI number; antenna B transmits wave profile A and B in the antenna A wave idle times.

Note:

Please run the simulation and refer to the figures for a clearer understanding of ABwave signal generation theories.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_TDM-PRBS_MIMO
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar TDM-PRBS

MIMO Radar Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

Simulation Task

This workspace illustrates an Automotive Radar MIMO Radar measurement system with following system configurations:

 

Transmit signal: use PRBS signal (GoldCode) with PRBS sequence length defined in the PRBS_Length parameter. Note that if users like to change the sequence length, they also need to update the parameters in GoldCode to ensure the sequence with expected length is generated. Also, users need to ensure that the PRBS sequence length is less than one PRI duration.

 

Transmit and Receive antennas: the transmit antennas could be one single antenna or multiple antennas. For multiple antennas case, four antennas could be supported following Chapter 3 (Principle of the MIMO Radar) of [2] to create a virtual horizontal antenna array of (4 (NumTxAntennas) * 4 (NumRxAntennas)) with the following parameters:

          TxNum_H = 4;

          TxNum_V = 1;

    TxD_H = 2;

    TxD_V = 2; %useless

          RxNum_H = 4;

          RxNum_V = 1;

    RxD_H = 0.5;

    RxD_V = 0.5; %useless

 

Note: for other antenna configurations, the TxD_H parameter needs to be equal to RxD_H* RxNum_H to maintain the equal antennal distance for all adjacent antenna elements for the virtual horizontal antenna array.

Note: The current example uses TDM-MIMO with time division multiplexing (TDM) method in transmit side. However binary phase modulation (BPM) method is also possible with further modification in both transmit and receiver sides.

 

Workspace Description

  • Top level design

The workspace consists of three layers.

·        Trajectory Layer

In this layer, the Tx radar platform and Rx radar platform is defined using AutomotiveRadar_Platform model. In this scenario, Tx radar and Rx radar is both at origin point of cartesian coordinates. And two targets' position is defined using AutomotiveRadar_TargetScatterLocation model. One target is at (0,0,30) and the other is at (-20/sqrt(2),0,20/sqrt(2)). 

·        Antenna Layer

In this layer, AutomotiveRadar_LocInAntennaFrame model is used to calculate the targets' antenna theta and phi degree.

In this scenario, XY-Plane antenna frame is used. It means that, the antenna array is positioned at XY-Plane. X axis is along horizontal orientation and Y axis is along vertical orientation. And the beam radiates along +Z axis.

So, in this XY-Plane,

·        The antenna theta of target (0, 0, 30) is 0 degree and its AoA is 0 degree also.

·        The antenna theta of target (-20/sqrt(2), 0, 20/sqrt(2)) is 45 degrees and its AoA is -45 degrees.

·        Signal Processing Layer

In this layer,  

·        Transmit Signal Generation: GoldCode model is used to generate one kind of PRBS signal with period of 20us defined by the PRI parameter, carrier frequency of 77GHz and power of 13dBmW.

·        Tx Antenna: AutomotiveRadar_PhasedArrayTx is used to setup the transmitter antenna. In this scenario, one or more Tx element antennas could be used, by the parameters of TxNum_H and TxNum_V. All Targets' antenna theta and phi from Antenna Layer are as input of the Tx antenna model.

·        Target Echo Generation: AutomotiveRadar_EchoGenerator model is used to generate all targets' echo. The position of all targets and radar platform from Trajectory Layer is as its input.

·        Rx Antenna: AutomotiveRadar_PhasedArrayRx is used to setup the receiver antenna. In this scenario, four antenna elements in horizontal orientation are used, so RxNum_H is set as 4 RxNum_V is set as 1. All Targets' antenna theta and phi from Antenna Layer are as input of the Rx antenna model.

·        For each receiver channel, one Receiver model is used to measure the signal with the input and output ports:

·        Input ports:

·        MatchedSrc: Matched PRBS signal for each PRI generated from AutomotiveRadar_MatchedSrc model. It is the frequency data of conjugate transmit PRBS signal.

·        SigIn: the received signal.

·        Output ports:

·        FFTBinBeforeCFAR: 2D FFT output before CFAR for this receiver channel. One 2D FFT output contains RangeFFTSize*DopplerFFTSize samples. The output is arranged in the order of Range-dimension first.

·        FFTBinAfterCFAR: 2D FFT output after CFAR for this receiver channel. One 2D FFT output contains RangeFFTSize*DopplerFFTSize samples. The output is arranged in the order of Range-dimension first.

·        Inside the Receiver model, the following steps are included:

·        AutomotiveRadar_PC model does pulse compression with local Matched PRBS signal from MatchedSrc port and generate correlation peaks.

·        Select the first RangeFFTSize samples as range-dimension data, and then perform Doppler FFT to achieve Doppler information.

·        Note that for TDM-MIMO, each receiver channel will get NumTxAntennas 2D FFT data consuming NumTxAntennas PRI data, where NumTxAntennas = TxNum_H* TxNum_V.

·        Then AutomotiveRadar_Detector, AutomotiveRadar_CFAR and AutomotiveRadar_BinaryDetector are used to cancel the noise. Note that two CFAR models are needed for Doppler and range dimensions respectively.

·        AoA measurement: One MATLAB script model used to all targets' range, velocity and angle. Note that in current implementation for angle estimation, we use phase difference at each receiver antenna element to calculate the angle of each target. Users can also use angle-FFT as [2]. 

Reference

[1] HH. C. Chen, T. H. Lin, H. T. Kung, C. K. Lin and Y. Gwon, "Determining RF angle of arrival using COTS antenna arrays: A field evaluation," MILCOM 2012 - 2012 IEEE Military Communications Conference, Orlando, FL, 2012, pp. 1-6.

[2] MIMO Radar, http://www.ti.com/lit/an/swra554/swra554.pdf

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_CompressSensing
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar CS Algorithm Simulation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace as a template shows how to apply Compressed Sensing (CS) algorithm in the automotive radar. The automotive radar system is a low-cost equipment. So, the memory of the radar signal processing chip is limited. Automotive radar system can recover the target's distance and velocity information by compress sensing algorithm with less data storage. In this workspace the target velocity estimation is realized by the compressed sensing algorithm. For example, If the number of pulses is N, compressed sensing recovers the target velocity needs only store N / 2 or less in some constrain conditions. Incidentally, radar systems in the range bin can utilize ‘wavegate’ technology to reduce data storage.

Workspace Description 

1. Transmit waveform parameters: wave type as user defined (Fast chirp), pulse repeating interval is 51.2us + 8.8us (off time), bandwidth 100MHz, Samplerate 200MHz. 

2. In the simulation set two different range and velocity target.

3. Signal processing section gives the pulse Doppler processing and compressed sensing of the results of the comparison.

 CS algorithm description

1.  Compressive sensing algorithm is mainly applied to the target speed estimation. So, the echo goes through the 1D FFT to achieve the range information, the range data go through the SampleMatrix (MATLAB script) to achieve the Doppler domain under sampled data, the SampleData and SampleMatrix enters the next CSReconstruct (MATLAB script) model to estimate the target velocity. 

2. The CSReconstruct model adopts OMP (orthogonal matched pursuit) algorithm to reconstruct the signal, SystemVue provides orthogonal matching pursuit function AutomotiveRadar_CSOMP. The built-in MathLang function usage note is given below.

  [USAGE]

 A = AutomotiveRadar_CSOMP (D, X, L, eps)

 [INPUTS]

 D M x K overcomplete dictionary

 X Data vector or matrix. Must be of size M x P, where P is number of signals to code

 L Maximum number of coefficients for each signal

eps Stopping criterion (stop when l2 norm of residual is less than eps)

[OUTPUTS]

A Sparse coefficient matrix of size K x P

Reference

[1] Steffen Lutz, Daniel Ellenrieder, Thomas Walter, Robert Weigel, “On fast chirp Modulations and Compressed Sensing for Automotive Radar Applications”, Radar Symposium (IRS), 2014 15th International, pp.1-6

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_FFTAveraging
Workspace.Description:
FMCW RADAR FFT Averaging Modeling

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace provides an example of a FMCW Radar simulation platform. The design is more advanced with 3-layer architecture and basic TRx modeling, aimed to demonstrate two types of FFT averaging modeling commonly encountered in automotive radar signal processing.

 

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Example Highlights:

  • Generate FMCW signals with triangle or Saw tooth or custom waveform frequency sweep in 77 GHz Band.
  • Target models can be set according to user interests in the Trajectory Layer. 
  • FMCW chirp waveform is applied in Tx.
  • Antenna modeling and multi-target echo generations are realized.
  • Beat frequency IQ mixing & sampling, range and doppler FFT and CFAR are realized in Rx.
  • More advanced multi-target range & velocity detection algorithms based on CFAR results are realized by MultiTarDetect model. AoA results are shown as NaN since 1Rx cannot measure AoA.
  • FMCW radar generic detection performance evaluations are provided in FMCW_Perf equation file (range, velocity and AoA detection performance calculations are provided).

The FFT averaging is divided to two types: 1, the coherent averaging (CohAvg, time domain averaging); 2, the incoherent averaging (InCohAvg, frequency domain averaging). Both types of averaging are realized with data gathering after the BeatFreq generation subnet, and the after the RangeFFT subnet, respectively.

 

CohAvg means performing averaging for the beat frequency complex echo data, whereas InCohAvg averaging refers to frequency domain amplitude averaging using multiple RangeFFT echo results. The detailed calculation after data gathering is realized in the FFT_PostProc equation file.

 

Pros and Cons:

Compared with single pulse FFT results (same for the two types of FFT averaging), CohAvg lowers the noise floor but smears the target peaks at the same time, whereas InCohAvg enhances the power estimation accuracy.

 

Sometimes, the FFT averaging method is applied to address transmit waveform nonideal issues (nonlinearities, phase noise impacts, etc.).

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_MUSICAOA
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar Library MUSIC AOA Simulation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

Simulation Task

This workspace illustrates an Automotive Radar MUSIC AoA (Angle of Arrival) measurement system using 1*4 phase array.

 

Workspace Description

  • Top level design

The workspace consists of three layers.

·        Trajectory Layer

In this layer, the Tx radar platform and Rx radar platform is defined using AutomotiveRadar_Platform model. In this scenario, Tx radar and Rx radar is both at origin point of cartesian coordinates. And two targets' position is defined using AutomotiveRadar_TargetScatterLocation model. The workspace set up 4 targets. 

·        Antenna Layer

In this layer, AutomotiveRadar_LocInAntennaFrame model is used to calculate the targets' antenna theta and phi degree.

In this scenario, XY-Plane antenna frame is used. It means that, the antenna array is positioned at XY-Plane. X axis is along horizontal orientation and Y axis is along vertical orientation. And the beam radiates along +Z axis.

·        Signal Processing Layer

In this layer,  

·        Transmit Signal Generation: AutomotiveRadar_CW model is used to generate fast chirp FMCW signal with period of 51.2us, bandwidth of 200MHz, carrier frequency of 77GHz.

·        Tx Antenna: AutomotiveRadar_PhasedArrayTx is used to setup the transmit antenna. In this scenario, only one Tx element antenna is used.

·        Target Echo Generation: AutomotiveRadar_EchoGenerator model is used to generate all targets' echo. The position of all targets and radar platform from Trajectory Layer is as its input.

·        Rx Antenna: AutomotiveRadar_PhasedArrayRx is used to setup the transmit antenna. In this scenario, 6*6 antenna elements in horizontal orientation are used, so RxNum_H is set as 6 RxNum_V is set as 6. All Targets' antenna theta and phi from Antenna Layer are as input of the Rx antenna model.

·        Beat Frequency: In this scenario, each Rx element is connected to transmitting waveform and then Mixer to get the multi-channel beat frequencies.

·        FFT: FFT_Cx processor is used to get the frequency domain data of beat frequencies.

·        CFAR: AutomotiveRadar_Detector, AutomotiveRadar_CFAR and AutomotiveRadar_BinaryDetector are used to noise suppression. By CFAR processing, the targets bin is marked. 

·        MUSIC: The 4 reciever channels data after range and Doppler processing and CFAR, the worksapce extract the target peak data to do the MUSIC processing. The simulation achieves target angles in one range bin and doppler bin.

·        MUSIC AoA measurement is in the MATLAB script RVAMes model.

NOTE: The 2D-FFT range-doppler plot function is built-in in Automotive Radar Library,   and the user could call it directly as shown in the "Range-Doppler Plot" equation file.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_PhaseDifferenceAoA
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar Phase Difference AoA

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

Simulation Task

This workspace illustrates an Automotive Radar Phase Difference AoA (Angle of Arrival) measurement system using three receive antenna elements.

 

Workspace Description

  • Top level design

The workspace consists of three layers.

·         Trajectory Layer

In this layer, the Tx radar platform and Rx radar platform is defined using AutomotiveRadar_Platform model. In this scenario, Tx radar and Rx radar is both at origin point of cartesian coordinates. And two targets' position is defined using AutomotiveRadar_TargetScatterLocation model. One target is at (0,0,100) and the other is at (-20/sqrt(2),0,20/sqrt(2)). 

·         Antenna Layer

In this layer, AutomotiveRadar_LocInAntennaFrame model is used to calculate the targets' antenna theta and phi degree.

In this scenario, XY-Plane antenna frame is used. It means that, the antenna array is positioned at XY-Plane. X axis is along horizontal orientation and Y axis is along vertical orientation. And the beam radiates along +Z axis.

So, in this XY-Plane,

·         The antenna theta of target (0, 0, 100) is 0 degree and its AoA is 0 degree also.

·         The antenna theta of target (-20/sqrt(2), 0, 20/sqrt(2)) is 45 degrees and its AoA is -45 degrees.

·         Signal Processing Layer

In this layer,  

·         Transmit Signal Generation: AutomotiveRadar_CW model is used to generate one kind of linear FMCW signal with period of 100us, bandwidth of 300MHz, carrier frequency of 24GHz and power of 13dBmW. In the design2 the Gold model is used to generate binary coded waveform. The waveform bandwidth is bit duration reciprocal.

·         Tx Antenna: AutomotiveRadar_PhasedArrayTx is used to setup the transmitter antenna. In this scenario, only one Tx element antenna is used, so the parameter of TxNum_H and TxNum_V is set as 1 both. All Targets' antenna theta and phi from Antenna Layer are as input of the Tx antenna model.

·         Target Echo Generation: AutomotiveRadar_EchoGenerator model is used to generate all targets' echo. The position of all targets and radar platform from Trajectory Layer is as its input.

·         Rx Antenna:AutomotiveRadar_PhasedArrayRx is used to setup the receiver antenna. In this scenario, three antenna elements in horizontal orientation are used, so RxNum_H is set as 3 RxNum_V is set as 1. All Targets' antenna theta and phi from Antenna Layer are as input of the Rx antenna model.

·         Beat Frequency: In this scenario, each Rx element is connected to Amplifier and then IQ Mixer to get the beat frequencies.

·         ADC: The SampleRate of this design is set as 1GHz, DownSampler is used to get real ADC sampling rate. In this scenario, the ADCFs is set as 10MHz.

·         FFT: FFT_Cx processor is used to get the frequency domain data of beat frequencies.

·         CFAR: AutomotiveRadar_Detector, AutomotiveRadar_CFAR and AutomotiveRadar_BinaryDetector are used to cancel the noise.

·         Phase Difference: The phase difference between every two adjacent antenna elements are calculated and then the average result is got.

·         AoA measurement: One MATLAB script model AoAMeasurement is used to calculate all targets’' AoA.

  • Note

The design2 adopt PRBS waveform to achieve the target AOA using phase difference algorithm.

User can change the number of targets and every target's position and re-run the design and get different results.

Please refer to section III. PHASE DIFFERENCE OF ARRIVAL in reference [1] for basic concept.

Reference

[1] HH. C. Chen, T. H. Lin, H. T. Kung, C. K. Lin and Y. Gwon, "Determining RF angle of arrival using COTS antenna arrays: A field evaluation," MILCOM 2012 - 2012 IEEE Military Communications Conference, Orlando, FL, 2012, pp. 1-6.

Workspace.Name: AutomotiveRadar_FMCW_SISO
Workspace.Description:
Automotive Radar FMCW SISO Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

Simulation Task 

This workspace illustrates an Automotive Radar FMCW-based example with single Tx and single Rx radar architecture. The range and velocity measurements are presented.

Workspace Description

 

This example is based on typical 3-layer radar simulation architecture. The baseband waveform design is based on FMCW, with single Tx transmits the FMCW waveform.

With single Rx, the radial range and radial velocity measurements are conducted. To run the simulation, just run the Step01-System_Equations to setup basic parameters, then run the Step02-Simulation_and_Results_Demo where the analysis and result demos are performed.

All the parameters are defined in the Step01-System_Equations Equation, including:

1.      System parameters

2.      Antenna array parameters

3.      FMCW chirp parameters

4.      ADC/FFT/LNA parameters for receiver

5.      Phase Noise Parameters

6.      Target Parameter (for this example, only one target is placed)

Also, this equation will display Range-Doppler Spectrum and Target diagrams after the simulation and get range and velocity measurement.

In the schematic design, users can tune some of parameters defined in the Step01-System_Equations Equation as follows to easily observe the different results with different settings

1.      Enable FFT window in Range-Doppler FFT or not

2.      Set RF transmit power

3.      Set transmit antenna setting mode with a fixed antenna gain or reading a custom antenna pattern file

4.      Enable phase noise simulation or not (The actual phase noise data is defined in PN_Data variable in the Step01-System_Equations Equation)

5.      Enable thermal noise or not

6.   Target range

7.   Target velocity

After the simulation is finished, the following results are shown in the text windows:

1.      Target Range True Value

2.      Target Range Measured Value

3.      Target Velocity True Value

4.      Target Velocity Measured Value

Note

1.      If you are not familiar with the three-layer radar simulation architectures, please refer to other radar/automotive radar examples for more information.

2.   In current Rx design, there is no filter added before DownSample model to reduce the noise output of signal bandwidth. This is not the same as generic RF design noise floor changing and will decrease input noise level. To compensate the noise level, the noise added in AddNDensity model is set with an offset of (-10*log10(ADC_DS_Ratio)).  If users want to add a filter to reduce the noise out of signal bandwidth, then they need to adjust measured range result by removing the filter delay introduced by the filter.

3.   There is one built-in MathLang function named "AutomotiveRadar_DisplayRangeDopplerSpectrum()" to help user plot the range-doppler spectrum mappling with one CPI radar complex echo data. Please see the note below and refer to the "Step02" equation for application details.
