Workspace.Name: RF_Beamforming_ElementFailure
Workspace.Description:
RF Beamforming Element Failure

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

 

Design1

This design shows how to simulate element failures over time using a random binary matrix, which is used as a mask of the transmitted signal.

The masking is implemented usign a MATLAB_Script model.

The MATLAB_Script model has a parameter RunsToFail, which is set to a vector of 64 random numbers uniformly distributed between 0 and 1e5.

It represents the number of runs (simulation samples) at which each of the 64 elements of the array will fail.

It uses a persistent variable to keep track of the number of times it is called.

Using this number and the parameter RunsToFail it forms a mask of 0s and 1s to zero out (over time) elements that should fail.

 

Design2

This design shows how to simulate element failures with custom failure specification, which can be tied to MonteCarlo to preform Monte Carlo evaluation of element failures.

The MonteCarlo1 is set up such that 10% of the element fails in each run. The failed elements are different across each MonteCarlo run.

The graph MonteCarlo1_ElementFailure shows 10 Phi cuts of the beam pattern across 10 Monte Carlo runs with 10% element failure.

Workspace.Name: SearchQAM
Workspace.Description:
QAM Search - Applied Beamforming

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This interactive demo example builds a simple TX/RX beamforming example, from the point of the of the Receiver.

 

Imagine you are at the RX array.  When you see an incoming signal, it is one signal, but because it originates from a particular direction, the actual signal arrives at different teims (phases) across the elements of the array.  Therefore, the TX beamforming eleemnts are not about the TX beamforming...just assume that has already be done.  Instead, the TX beamforming simply distributes the incoming signals across the face of the array, from different directions.  When the RX beamforming "tunes" to a different direction, then it may or not receive the one or more of the incident signals, depending on the originating direction. 

 

In each schematic, the relevant variables have been packaged as "run-time tuning" sliders.  The only slider that is not fully tunable is the array size itself.  To change from a 4x4 to 8x8 array, for example, please stop the simulation, make the adjustment, and re-start the simulation.

 

Folders in this workspace:

  • 1. Basic Modulation
    • start with a known signal, Radar or Comms.  Get a basic physical layer link to work. 
    • We use QAM16 & EVM because they are easy, and provide dynamic feedback about signal quality.
    • The link is at 28 GHz but the actual frequencies and bandwidths are not critical for now.
  • 2. Using Beams
    • Explore the beamforming components, and basic impairments.  Explore the subnetworks.
  • 3. Interference
    • Explore a typical application of beamforming: to avoid interference from a blocking signal
    • Explore how much margin exists for power levels, offsets, and the Array size (ie - narrow beamwidth)

 

Atmospheric attenuation reference - "Recommendation  ITU-R  P.676-10, Attenuation by atmospheric gases" (9/2013)

Workspace.Name: Squint
Workspace.Description:
Squint

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates beam squinting. There are two design folders:

 

PhaseShiftBeamforming

 

In Design1, beamforming is done using phase shifters. The phases shifts are computed based on frequency fc. The same phase shifts are used for all three paths (frequencies f_min, fc, f_max). The rest of the design is set up to simulate a wavefront at different scanning angles and compute the beam patterns. Run the Equation PlotPhaseShiftPattern to plot the three beam patterns. In addition to the beam patterns having different shapes, you can observe that the beam peak has squinted from the desired theta direction of 20 degrees for the beams at f_min and f_max.

 

TimeDelayBeamforming

 

In Design2, beamforming is done using time delays. The delays are computed based on frequency fc. The same delays are used for all three paths (frequencies f_min, fc, f_max). The rest of the design is set up to simulate a wavefront at different scanning angles and compute the beam patterns. Run the Equation PlotTimeDelayPattern to plot the three beam patterns. In this case, although the beam patterns have different shapes, you can observe that the beam peak is at the same direction for all three frequencies.

Workspace.Name: TrackingMode_Scenario
Workspace.Description:
Simulation Template for Moving Platform Based on the Generalized Framework

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

 

To design your own system, you don't have to start from scratch.  SystemVue provides uniform processes for designing and testing Radar systems using preconfigured simulation templates.  Users can begin by modifying a similar template to their system based on their system spec.  Additionally, your legacy IP in m co de or C/C++ code can be imported to SystemVue as SystemVue models, or save it in your own library and use it in conjunction with existing SystemVue models. 

 

This workspace as a template shows how to set up the phased array type radar simulation based on the generalized framework and how to generate the echoes from the scatters of targets.

The example includes three layers: trajectory layer, antenna layer and signal layer.

In the trajectory layer, the RADAR_Platform model and RADAR_TargetScatterLocation model are used to generate the trajectories of transmitter, receiver, and scatters of target. The output is at the ECI frame(x, y, z).

In antenna layer, the transmit antenna gains and the receive antenna gains to the scatters of targets can be computed according to the locations of transmit platforms and receive platforms and scatters of targets. The locations are at the ECI frame.

In the signal layer, the input signal will be changed to the echoes from different scatters of targets according to the locations at ECI frame at each sampling time and the antenna gains from antenna layer.

Workspace.Name: TrackingMode_Scenario_Jammer
Workspace.Description:
Simulation Template for Phased Array Doppler Radar
with EW Jammer

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace has been saved without simulation data to reduce its size. Please run the simulation to see the data in the graphs.

This example uses simulation models from the W1905 Radar library, and also the W1720 Phased Array Beamforming Kit, which is included with the Radar library.  There are several things for you to explore:

  1. Vary the Pulsed Doppler Radar architecture in terms of its signaling parameters
        Pulse Width, PRF, Carrier frequency, Sample Rate, Pulse compression ratio
  2. Explore the phased array architecture:  
        Number of Elements, Geometry of the elements, spacing between the elements
  3. Study the effect of the EW jammer, noise and clutter (in future).

 

Simple tests to do out of box.

  1. Run the script "Scenario_Simulation" from the workspace (right-click on the workspace icon, then "Run Equations").  Observe the plots of Tx beam, Rx beam, Jammer beam and Doppler plot. Note the agreement of the computed and set ranges.
  2. Vary the parameters in the tune window (make sure you hit enter after changing the values) and run the above script again.
  3. Find the angles and power of jammer at which the radar can be immune or susceptible.

Workspace.Name: V5G_DL_Tx_MultiBeam_VSA_EVM
Workspace.Description:
V5G_DL_Tx_MultiBeam_EVM

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example uses two V5G_DL_Src in this workspace to generate two Verizon pre-5G signals. Each signal is modulated to 28GHz. There are two 8x8 RF beamformers to steer the two signals to two different directions. The two RF beamformers use shared array architecture to share 8x8 antenna array. The AntennaArrayTx takes the 8x8 beamformed envelope matrix and generates two far-field signals at the directions that the two beams pointing to. Two VSA sinks are used to measure EVM at the two far-field directions. 

 

The V5G_DL_Src in this workspace is a special version that generates only 2 subframes and the corresponding VSA setx files demod 2 subframes.

 

The requried VSA version is 22.2 or newer.

 

Initially UE1 direction is set to Theta = 25 degree and Phi = 250 degree and UE2 direction is set to Theta = 30 degree and Phi = 120 degree. Under this condition, the side lobes of two beams interfere with the main lobes of the other beams. The EVM is about 10% under this condition. If you turn on tapers for UE2 beam (set TurnOnTaper2.Value = 1 in the Tune Window), you can observe UE1 EVM improved to about 7% to 8%. If you change UE2 beam direction to Phi = 30 degree, the side lobes of the two beams will not interfere with the main lobes, and you can observe EVM improvement in VSA.

Workspace.Name: XParameter Matrix
Workspace.Description:
Modeling PA Compression

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example models a 2140MHz basestation amplifier designed in ADS using a Freescale FET.  The ADS microstrip circuit was extracted to an X-parameter file, as well as various power-dependent parameters exported from DataDisplay to a CSV file.  There are a few ways to import the data and model amplifiers.  The X-parameter case is then used in a RFLINK beamforming situation.

  • X-parameter amplifier extracted from ADS
    • use Spectrasys, which can then be used in RF LINK.  Direct method.
  • Absolute power curves from ADS -->CSV file--> workspace variables
    • using interpolated math Lookup table.  Flexible, but slow.
  • AMAM/AMPM compression curves from ADS --> CSV file
    • using "Amplifier" distortion model.  The fastest execution.
  • Methods not shown:
    • direct co-sim with ADS Ptolemy/CktEnvelope
    • export an FCE model from GoldenGate
    • measure an X-parameter on a PNA-X analyzer
    • capture power-dependent AMAM, AMPM using a modulated
      signal on the VSG/VSA, and the 89600 VSA software.
    • SystemVue's own W1716 DPD, a more professional tool
      for linearization that can correct for memory effects.

Here, since you are modeling a PA using a power compression curve, you are only a couple steps away from having a simple DPD correction model.  This workspace provides a couple possible ways to approximate that.

Workspace.Name: CodeGen_CIC_filter
Workspace.Description:
CIC Filter Code Gen Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue 

Tutorial Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how you can use built-in SystemVue parts, to implement a Cascaded integrator-comb (CIC) filter that can be targeted to the SystemVue C++ Code Generator. 

 

This example is a companion to the "Discovering - C++ Code Generation" video. To view this video before using this example, go to :

Help > Tutorial Videos ... > Additional Videos on the Web > Introduction to C++ Code Generation from SystemVue Schematic

 

C++ Code generation in SystemVue supports creation of stand-alone, compiled .dlls that can be used by SystemVue, ADS, or any 3rd party 64-bit application that supports .dll import.  

 

Creation of compiled .dll requires Microsoft Visual Studio to be installed on your machine.   SystemVue support Microsoft Visual Studio Express Edition, which is a free version of Microsoft Visual Studio. 

 

Any base SystemVue product support C++ Code generation with the following limitations:

 

- Generated .dlls will require a SystemVue license to run

- Only .h files are visible after code generation

- Only .dll generation is supported

 

NOTE:  For "unlicensed" .dll generation you must first be licensed to use W1718 C++ Code Generation.   This add-on feature will also give you access to generated C++ code for editing and inclusion into other source code programs.

 

Workspace Overview

 

CIC_filter Design

 

This design contains the top level CIC filter, built from basic signal processing building blocks.   These blocks are also part of the "C++ Code Generation" category in the "algorithm" library, supporting C++ code gen.

 

CIC_Filter Model

 

This is a sub-network model of the same top level CIC filter design.   This sub-network is useful for targeting a complete schematic based model to C++ Code Generator which will effectively "encrypt" this model in a .dll once compiled.

 

Note:  C++ Code Generation supports generation of multiple models from any given top level design.   All selected models will be compiled into a single .dll which can serve as a portable SystemVue library

 

Validate Model Design

 

This design contains both the CIC_Filter model subnetwork as well as the top level CIC filter design for comparison.  

 

You can use this design with the CPP1 C++ Code Generator controller to export the sub-network model for code generation.   Once the code is generated and compiled, this same schematic can be used to validate the new compiled model using the model view switch in the sub-network properties.

Workspace.Name: AGC_4Stage_DistributedVGA
Workspace.Description:
Automatic Gain Control, 4-Stage Distributed VGA

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace demonstrates a methodology for building a simple receive AGC model, then scaling the topology up to include an n-stage digitally controlled VGA to allow for filtering, frequency conversion, or switched networks as necessary within the signal path.  Even though an analog loop is shown, the 4-stage VGA design embedded within this workspace includes individual level-shifting to accommodate unique OEM bus ratings and control as necessary for a baseband controlled application. 

 

A 5-bit bus is used to control the 4 individual stages of the VGA; each wire represents a binary (ON/OFF) toggle for the respective stage with the exception of DVGA-1 which is controlled by 2 bits representing 4 gain steps rather than 2.  This implementation could be linked to a register, and over-written by a baseband algorithm to tune the total signal path gain in order to maintain an optimum drive level into an ADC.  The 5-bit configuration here represents a total of 32 gain states, from 0 to 31dB.

  • TimeDelay, Quantization, VGA, and AGC designs are the initial building blocks that will be used as performance "reference" to the scalable design. 
  • DigVGAx1, DigVGAx4, and DigAGC designs are the level-shift and bus-controlled versions of the reference blocks defined above.

The "top-level" design is DigAGC, all of the other designs may need to be simulated in order to fully populate the corresponding top-level presentation graphs.

 

The datasets are not saved with this workspace, you need to Run All Analyses to see the results.

Workspace.Name: Bluetooth
Workspace.Description:
Bluetooth Hopping

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates simple hopping and demdulation of a Bluetooth-like signal, but not modulated to the actual RF frequency, using a lower frequency instead to speed simulation. 

  • Data sequence is at a 1MHz rate, with signal level -1 to 1, shaped by Gaussian filter
  • Hopping generator produced hopping symbols at 1600Hz rate, value from 0 to 79, with a 200MHz sample rate (125Ks samples per symbol).
  • Modulator part is configured as an FM modulator, producing a signal from 1MHz to 80MHz using the sum of hopping level and data value.
  • TDD control is applied to the output with a multiplier to examine the effect of carrier switching.
  • The dehopping signal is offset by 10.7MHz to look at IF filtering effects.
  • A simple PLL model is used to demodulate.
  • The Bluetooth Frequency Hopping graph shows frequency hopping spectrum over different time stamps in 3D graph.

Workspace.Name: Costas
Workspace.Description:
Second-Order Costas Loop

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates a second-order Costas Loop for demodulation of a BPSK waveform.  The Costas Loop is a specialized form of PLL that regenerates the carrier from a bi-phase modulated signal using quadrature mixer.

 

BPSK Generator

  • A Data Pattern bit source generates pseudo-random (PN9) binary data at a 4Hz symbol rate, generating 40 samples per symbol.
  • The bits drive a Modulator which is configured as a phase modulator, creating a BPSK signal on a 1000.75Hz carrier.

VCO for the loop is a Modulator part configured as an FM modulator.  Both in-phase and quadrature outputs are used to drive the loop mixers

 

Loop

  • Quadrature mixers (M2 and M3) produce I/Q baseband data.  I/Q are filtered to remove second harmonic.  Note that the actual data sequence can appear on either the I or Q, with the other remaining near zero.
  • I & Q are multiplied by M1, producing carrier phase drift.  An integrator in the loop filter creates the frequency offset to drive the VCO.
  • Note that there is a one sample Delay in the feedback loop that is required by the simulator to prevent deadlock.

The output graph compares the original data, demodulated I & Q baseband, and the frequency offset which shows the loop lock.

Workspace.Name: DFT-S-OFDM_TxRX
Workspace.Description:
DFT-S-OFDM Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Template Workspace

 

This example is to demo to create a DFT-S-OFDM source and receiver.

 

DFT-S-OFDM

 

This folder includes an example to demo DFT-S-OFDM generator. 100 mapping signals (QPSK, 16-QAM and etc) in ntime-domain are transftered into frequency domain by DFT. These 100 frequency domain signals are loaded into a 128 point IFFT (50 signals are loaded into the positive frequency part, other 50 are loaded into minus frequency part) and center 28 oints are filled with 0. Then, these signals (100 frequency domain siganl+zeros) are transftered into time domain by using IFFT. The mapping siganl is interpolated after above procedure. The constellation has four points (QPSK) if the mapping signal is QPSK. 

 

DFT-S-OFDM-BER-Sim

 

This folder includes an example to demo BER of DFT-S-OFDM source and receiver. In DFT-S-OFDM source, 25 DFT-S-OFDM symbols consist of one frame, each symbol consists of 32 point cyclic prefix and 128 points IFFT. In the receiver, the basic function includes timing and frequency synchronization, channel estimation and equalizer.

 

DFT-S-OFDM-BER_CS

 

This folder includes an example to demo BER of DFT-S-OFDM with Keysight instruments (MXG/PXA).

Workspace.Name: DQPSK Encoder Modeling
Workspace.Description:
Simple Differential Encoding theory:

 

In differential encoding information is modulated into the change of a modulation envelope vector rather than the instantaneous amplitude or phase.  Thus a means is needed for mapping this information given memory of the previous envelope state and information on where the new state needs to be.

 

For standard PSK modulation, information is mapped into the absolute phase of the modulating envelope with constant amplitude.   For 4 level PSK, or QPSK, the  information is encoded into one of four possible phase points, namely:

 

State 0 - 0

State 1 - pi/2

State 2 - pi

State 3 - 3pi/2 or -pi/2

 

Additionally, coding can be applied to this signal to improve the ability of a detector to distinguish between states.  For Grey coding (maximize Cartesian distance between states), binary data can be encoded as follows:

 

0,0 - State 0

0,1 - State 1

1,0 - State 3

1,1 - State 2

 

In discrete form, each state is represented by a sample value of,

 

in = Sin (Ωn) and qn = Cos(Ωn) , where Ωn= one of the above phase states

 Obviously such a modulation format requires a “coherent” detector at the receiver to phase synchronize the envelope to a reference, otherwise these states can be anywhere in the envelop phase given channel and filter delays. 

 

To combat this information can be encoded in the change in phase, rather than the absolute phase.   This will simplify receiver archecture considerably, but will give up some performance, which in many cases is a simple trade-off.

 

A simply algorithm can be used to create the differentially encoded signal given the discrete form of “I” and “q” shown above.

 

Qn= qn*qn-1 -in*in-1 

In  = qn* in-1 + in * qn-1

In the remainder of this example we will create a simulation of this algorithm, starting with MATLAB Script then finally in fixed point form. The performance will be analyzed using Keysight Glacier VSA.

DQPSK Encoder/Modulator Design

 

This workspace contains a simple top level design (design1) that illustrates how to utilize different modeling types to create a DQPSK modulator.   The different models available in this workspace are:

 

- MATLAB Script based DQPSK

- Schematic based Floating Point DQPSK

- Schamatic based Fixed Point  DQPSK

- Schematic based Digital Upconverter Design (DUC)

 

Three configurations are created for the top level design to use different flavors of DQPSK. These configurations can be selected at "Design1 Analysis".

 

The top level design also utilizes a link to Keysight 89601B VSA for dynamic demodulation of the DQPSK waveform. 89601B needs to be installed and licensed seperately from SystemVue.

Workspace.Name: DQPSK Modem
Workspace.Description:
DQPSK MODEM Example

 

DQPSK Modem illustrates the simple design of a typical SATCOM or MILCOM PHY using DQPSK modulation. There are two main designs in this workspace:

 

DQPSK_Baseband:  This design implements a purely baseband digital DQPSK modem, with sub-systems that implement differential encoding, modulation, filtering, differential decoding, symbol/bit slicing, and Grey decoding.  

 

DQPSK_RF:  This design builds upon DQPSK_Baseband and adds RF modulation/demodulation.   Noise can be added to the channel to further impair SNR and produce bit errors.   Also available in this design is a link to Keysight's 89601B VSA SW.  For this link to work Keysight's 89601B SW must be installed on your computer.  

 

For illustration purposes, there is also a model implemented for a fixed point DQPSK decoder to explore fixed point impairements during demod.   This model can be simply activated through the model pull down menu in the Decoder block.

 

An Eval copy of 89601B can be downloaded by cutting and pasting the following link into your web browser:

http://www.keysight.com/find/89600vsa


This workspace also contains a number of graphs that can be used to visualize the system.

Workspace.Name: DynamicPlots
Workspace.Description:
Dynamic Plots

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

 

This example workspace demonstrates some of the dynamic sinks in SystemVue. The dynamic sinks create dynamic graphs where the displayed data is updated throughout the simulation.

 

The design in this workspace creates a modulated signal, which is then amplified through a non-linear amplifier. The signal at the output of the amplifier is then sent to the different dynamic sinks.

 

The modulation format is controlled by the ModType design parameter, which can be tuned in the tune window or using the corresponding ModType slider.

 

The non-linear amplifier has a fixed 1 dB compression point of 15 dBm. The Gain block right after the mapper has a tunable gain controlled by the GainDB design parameter. When this parameter is tunned (in the tune window or through the corresponding GainDB slider) the non-linear amplifier is pushed into and out of compression.

 

The third slider (DSamplingPhase) is used to adjust the down sampling phase and offset for the Constellation and EyeDiagram sinks. This ONLY affects the constellation and eye diagrams created by the Constellation and EyeDiagram sinks. It does not affect the constellation and eye diagrams created by the DigitalDemod sink.

 

The shorted model at the output of the amplifier can be used to introduce fractional sample delays, so we can observe the effects of such delays in the constellation and eye diagrams.

 

 

Exercises

 

Run the simulation with the AmpOut sink and the S2 SpectrumAnalyzer enabled (all other sinks disabled). Two dynamic graphs will be created. Arrange the SystemVue main window and the dynamic graphs window side by side so you can tune parameters in the SystemVue window and see the results in the dynamic graphs window. Tune the ModType parameter and observe the changes in the Raw Signal and Spectrum Power graphs. The spectrum graph should not change much since the design is set up to have a constant Symbol rate regardless of the modulation format. The Raw Signal graph should show greater variation with the higher modulation formats. Now tune the GainDB parameter. As GainDB increases, the spectrum graph shows spectral regrowth. The y axis values in both graphs increase so you will need to rescale the graphs to see the entire signal or spectrum. Keep increasing GainDB. Spectral regrowth increases and at some point, clipping (from amplifier saturation) should be visible in the Raw Signal graph.

 

Stop the simulation, disable the AmpOut sink and the S2 SpectrumAnalyzer, and enable the Constellation and EyeDiagram sinks. Reset GainDB to -5 and run the simulation. Tune the DSamplingPhase value and see the effect is thas on the constellation and the eye diagrams. Choose the DSamplingPhase value that results in a "clean" constellation and the eyes being centered. Now tune the ModType parameter and observe the changes in the constellation and eye diagrams. Next tune the GainDB parameter and again observe the effect it has on the dynamic graphs. They eyes should be more closed and the outter constellation points should be "pulled" in closer to the origin.

 

Stop the simulation, disable the Constellation and EyeDiagram sinks, and enable the DigitalDemod sink. Reset GainDB to -5 and run the simulation. Constellation, eye diagrams, Error Summary table (from EVM analysis), EVM, Magnitude Error, and Phase Error dynamic graphs are created. Again tune the ModType and GainDB parameters and observe how the graphs update. The EVM sink performs the same digital demodulation analysis as DigitalDemod but it does not create the constellation and eye diagram graphs.

 

Stop the simulation, leave the DigitalDemod sink active, enable the Constellation and one EyeDiagram sink as well as the FractionalDelay at the output of the Amplifier. The FractionalDelay is set to introduce a 1/2 sample delay. Reset GainDB to -5 and run the simulation. This simulation will demonstrate the difference between the constellation and eye diagrams created by the DigitalDemod sink and the ones created by the Constellation and EyeDiagram sinks. A lot of dynamic graphs are created in this simulation. You can close all but the constellation and eye diagram ones. Tune the DSamplingPhase parameter and try to get a "clean" constellation and centered eye diagram (look at the tab names to identify the constellation and eye diagram graphs created by the Constellation and EydDiagram models). You will find out that this is not possible, since the fractional sample delay introduced has removed (from the input signal) the sample that existed at the optimal sampling instant. The Constellation and EyeDiagram sinks do not do any demodulation or interpolation and so they cannot recover the sample at the optimal sampling instant. Unlike these sinks, the DigitalDemod sink performs demodulation including symbol timing recovery, which allows it to recover the sample at the optimal downsampling instant. You can play with other fractional sample delays. The smaller the delay the more clean the constellation from the Constellation sink, but it will never be as clean as the one from DigitalDemod. Similarly, if phase rotation is introduced, e.g. set the Modulator IQ_Rotation parameter to 30 degress, the Costellation and EyeDiagram sinks do not compensate for it, whereas the DigitalDemod does.

 

The eye diagram and constellation/trajectory dynamic graphs the DigitalDemod sinks creates can also be created from the data saved in the simulation dataset. See the graphs in the Graphs folder for an example. For more details refer to the DigitalDemod documentation.

Workspace.Name: MultiStandardRadio
Workspace.Description:
Multi-Standard Radio (MSR)

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates Multi-Standard Radio (MSR) signal generation using SignalCombiner. The resulting MSR signal combines 2 LTE, 2 WCDMA, 2 GSM, and 2 EDGE signals at different input sample rates and carrier frequencies.

 

For the SignalCombiner part, users specify the Sample Rate (SR), Carrier Frequency (Characterization Frequency, Fc), and Bandwidth (BW) of each individual input signal. Users also specify the desired output characterization frequency and can either specify the output sample rate or let SignalCombiner to compute the minimum output sample rate that can fully capture the entire spectrum and is a multiple of a base sample rate.

During simulation, SignalCombiner resamples and recharacterizes the input signals at the output sample rate and output characterization frequency, synchronizes the resampled signals (due to different input sample rates) and combines them into one signal at the "combined" output port. Users can also evaluate each resampled / recharacterized signal at the "output" multi-port. For further information, please refer to SignalCombiner model document.

 

In this example, eight wireless standard signals are combined at Fc = 1e9 Hz. Here is the list of the source signals and their respective Carrier Frequency (Characterization Frequency, Fc), Bandwidth (BW), and Sample Rate (SR):

  • LTE1: Fc 1e9+2.5e6, BW 5e6, SR 15.36e6, FDD
  • LTE2: Fc 1e9+7.5e6, BW 5e6, SR 15.36e6, FDD
  • WCDMA1: Fc 1e9-2.6e6, BW 5e6, SR 30.72e6
  • WCDMA2: Fc 1e9-7.6e6, BW 5e6, SR 30.72e6
  • GSM1: Fc 1e9-11.6e6, BW 0.6e6, SR 3.25e6
  • GSM2: Fc 1e9-12.2e6, BW 0.6e6, SR 3.25e6
  • EDGE1: Fc 1e9+11.6e6, BW 0.6e6, SR 3.25e6
  • EDGE2: Fc 1e9+12.2e6, BW 0.6e6, SR 3.25e6

 

The Equations tab of Design1 specifies the Fc, BW, and SR information of the above signals in the order of LTE1, LTE2, WCDMA1, WCDMA2, GSM1, GSM2, EDGE1, EDGE2. The order of input signals MSR(1:8) of the SignalCombiner need to match the order of SampleRate, Fc, and Bandwidth parameters.

 

In this example, the two LTE signals are generated from the "LTE" subnetwork using LTE_DL_Src @ LTE 8.9 library. The two WCDMA signals are generated from the "WCDMA" subnetwork using 3GPPFDD_DL_Source @ 3GPPFDD library. The carrier frequencies of these signals are exposes from the subnetwork models and can be set from the "Design1" schematic. The sample rate information of the LTE and WCDMA sources can be obtained from the "SamplingRate" variable defined inside the Equations tab of the "LTE" and "WCDMA" subnetwork respectively. The bandwidth information of the LTE and WCDMA sources can be obtained from the document.

 

The GSM and EDGE signals in this example are generated from the built-in SignalStudio files. If the SamplerRateOption the ReadSignalStudioFile sources ("GSM1", "GSM2, "EDGE1", "EDGE2" ) is set to "Timed from source data", the sample rate from these built-in files are 1.083333e6 Hz, which is the truncated version of infinite decimal 3.25e6 / 3. In data flow simulation, the ratio of the integer-valued data flow rates must match the ratio of the sample rates. To prevent extremely high multirate behavior introduced into the system due to infinite decimal or truncated version of infinite decimal sample rates, the ReadSignalStudioFile sources ("GSM1", "GSM2, "EDGE1", "EDGE2" ) use "Timed from sample rate" option and use the internal interpolator to resample the built-in SignalStudio GSM and EDGE files to 3.25 Mhz.

 

The spectrum graph "MSR_spec_Power" shows the combined spectrum. The spectrum graph "MSR_spec_Power with individual spectrums" shows the combined spectrum along with individual standard spectrum.

 

The graphs inside "Time Domain Graphs" folder compare input and output signals after resampling. For the purpose of comparison, the input signals are delayed in time and the output signals are recharecterized back to the input characterization frequencies.

 

In general, to use SignalCombiner for arbitrary signal sources, users can turn on "Display Data Flow Information" in the Data Flow Analysis Options tab to obtain the sample rate information from Data Flow Information Table and can use Sink to record characterization frequency in dataset and use SpectrumAnalyzer to measure bandwidth.

 

TRY THIS:

  1. Adjust the sliders to view amplitude changes to individual WCDMA and LTE signals.  Resimulate each time.  Also watch the CCDF change, since the peak-to-average ratio of the composite signal is a function of all the underlying signals being summed.
  2. Lower the P1DB power of the amplifier from +30dBm to +10dBm, and resimulate.  Do you see the notches filling in?
  3. Activate the 89600 VSA sink, and interactively tune the sliders, and watch the spectrum and CCDF change while you tune.  (you may need to retrigger some of the measurements inside the VSA software, in order to get that software to update a completed trace)

Workspace.Name: PN Seq
Workspace.Description:
PN Sequence Generator

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This is an example that demonstrates a simple Pseudo-noise sequence generator.  A subnetwork model called PN_Seq is used to generate the sequence.  A custom symbol was created to represent the part in a schematic.  Note that the model and symbol can be exported to model and symbol libraries for shared use by several workspaces.

  • The model defines several passed parameter values that are used to control its simulation behavior. 
  • The PN sequence model first generates random values from 0 to 1 at the symbol rate specified by the Rate parameter, using a uniform noise source.
  • The Quantizer bins the values according to the thresholds specified, creating discrete output values from -1 to 1.  The Amplitude parameter and Offset parameter are applied to scale the output and offset from zero.
  • The Repeat part generates an integral multiple of output samples for each symbol.

The expressions in the instance of Quantizer define arrays for the thresholds and output levels for the generator.

Workspace.Name: BPSK_BER
Workspace.Description:
BER vs. Eb/No waterfall curves for BPSK System

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This example shows the process for generating BER and Eb/No waterfall curves for a BPSK communications architecture that includes clock jitter and code spreading/despreading.  Code spreading/despreading is a spread spectrum technique often used to help make an RF communications channel more robust against RF interference and to reduce detection of the RF communications.

 

In general, good system BER performance requires that the receiver receive a signal without excessive intersymbol interference or excessive noise, and that the receiver provide automatic clock, data, amplitude, phase and frequency synchronization.

 

SystemVue provides capability for modeling and measuring communication systems BER performance.  Many of the wireless libraries included with SystemVue provide receiver models that work under dynamic RF fading conditions and provide automatic synchronization.

 

This example discussed here is for a simple BPSK system that uses some of the common system models included with SystemVue and relies on manual receiver synchronization setup. Automatic receiver synchronization requires design of custom algorithms in SystemVue for the specific communication system of interest.

 

BPSK System Design Examples

BER vs. Eb/No waterfall curves comparisons are made for BPSK systems 1) with no clock jitter or code spreading, 2) with code spreading, and 3) with code spreading and clock jitter.

 

In all cases, the BPSK systems contain a transmitter section, RF channel, receiver section, and BER measurement capability.  A pseudorandom bit source is formatted into BPSK, then filtered, upconverted, processed through AWGN, downconverted, and demodulated.  Then the input and output bits are compared to calculate BER using a Monte Carlo BER measurement process which is a sample by sample process.  Comparisons are made to the theoretical BER performance (included as an equation).

 

BPSK System BER Simulation Conclusions

The Graph BPSK_BER shows the simulated BER curves with the theoretical BER curve overlaid.  The theoretical BER curve is defined in the Equation2 page.  Excellent agreement is obtained between theory (Theory), the basic BPSK system (Simulated), and the BPSK system with code spreading/dispreading (With_Spread).  This shows that code spreading/dispreading is an excellent way to spread the spectral bandwidth of a BPSK signal to make it more robust against RF interference and multipath without compromising its data BER performance.  The BPSK system with code spreading/dispreading and transmit encoded chip data clock jitter (With_Spread_and_Jitter) is also shown to give close agreement with theory (Theory).  This shows that even when the encoded chip data has Gaussian distributed clock jitter with 0.125*chip time RMS jitter limited to range that is +/- 0.25*chip time, the code spreading/dispreading provides robust performance compared to theory.

 

Basic BPSK System Design

 

This system is defined and analyzed within the folder named BPSK_Basic_System.

 

This discussion is for Design:  BPSK_Design, with associated Analyses and Data:  BPSK_Analysis, BPSK_Data, and with associated Graphs:  BPSKSymbolOut, I_BPSKSymOut, and BitsOut.

 

The basic transmitter is setup with no clock jitter and no code spreading.  The BPSK symbol rate is 51.2 Mps (defined as SymbolRate in the Equation1 page).  The BPSK modulator is 300 MHz (defined as ModCarrier in the Equation1 page) and with +13 dBm power level (defined as ModPower_dBm in the Equation1 page).  The BPSK filtering is with a root raised cosine filter with 16X interpolation factor.

 

The RF channel is defined as a simple unity gain, zero delay, additive white Gaussian noise channel with noise density (NDensity) defined as a function of system Eb/No in the Equation1 page.

 

The basic receiver is setup with no code despreading. It provides matched filtering with its root raised cosine filter (including downsampling) and BPSK symbol demapping into bits. The receiver needs to be manually setup to synchronize its amplitude, phase and timing factors.  For the RF channel defined, the receiver gain G1 is set to unity.  The receiver timing is set with the delay DelayC to match the TX and RX filtering.  The setting of DelayC is critical for proper receiver data timing synchronization.

 

Besides the receiver DelayC used to set the receiver timing, the design schematic includes various other delay factors (DelayA, DelayB, DelayD) to synchronize various measurements to be made on the system.  See the design schematic for details. It is recommended that the delays A through D be setup in that order.

 

The Graph BPSKSymbolOut shows the BPSK input and output symbols for the oversampled (BPSKSymbolIn, BPSKSymbolOut) and for the single sample per symbol (BPSKSymIn, BPSKSymOut) signals.  Alignment of BPSKSymbolIn, BPSKSymbolOut is achieved with DelayA. Alignment of BPSKSymIn, BPSKSymOut is achieved with DelayB and DelayC. 

 

The Graph I_BPSKSymOut shows the BPSK input and output I channel symbols (I_BPSKSymIn, I_BPSK_SymOut).  Alignment of I_QPSKSymIn, I_QPSK_SymOut is achieved with DelayD.  This alignment process uses the ‘Cross Correlator’ model.  This model outputs the delay between the two signals at its ‘CorrDelay’ output.  With proper DelayD value, the resultant CorrDelay will be zero.  This also aligns signals BitsIn and BitsOut upon which BER measurement is made.  The Graph BitsOut shows the QPSK input and output bits (BitsIn, BitsOut).

 

Other than the DelayD value which is determined by the CrossCorr model, the other delay values can be more readily determined by observing their associate waveforms and tuning the delay values using the SystemVue Tuning Window.

 

This basic BPSK system is used in the other design used to make BER measurements with and without clock jitter and code spreading.

 

Basic BPSK System BER vs. Eb/N0 curves

 

This system is defined and analyzed within the folder named BPSK_Basic_System.

 

This discussion is for Design:  BPSK_BER_Design, with associated Analyses and Data:  BPSK_BER_Analysis, BPSK_BER_Data, BPSK_BER_Sweep, BPSK_BER_Sweep_Data, and with associated Graphs:  BPSK_BER.

 

The design is the same as the BPSK_Design.  Only the BER measurement is performed.  The DelayC value determined with the BPSK_Design is used to achieve the receiver data timing synchronization. The DelayD value determined with the BPSK_Design is used to synchronize the test and reference bit streams upon which the BER measurement is made.

 

The BPSK_BER_Sweep sweeps the system EbNo which sets the RF channel noise density (NDensity). 

 

The Graph BPSK_BER shows the simulated BER curve (Simulated) with the theoretical BER curve (Theory) overlaid.  The theoretical BER curve is defined in the Equation2 page.  Excellent agreement is obtained.

 

Model for Data with Clock Jitter and Filtering

 

This model is defined and analyzed within the folder named Jitter_Model_Test.

 

The subnetwork model NRZDataFilterWithJitter accepts an input NRZ data stream at one sample per symbol and outputs filtered data at Interpolation samples per symbol that includes clock jitter.  The settable parameters include various parameters for defining the raised cosine filtering (SymbolRate, RollOff, SquareRoot, FilterLength and Interpolation) and parameters for defining the data clock jitter (EnableJitter, JitterRMS, PosJitterLimit, NegJitterLimit and JitterOversampling).

 

When EnableJitter=No, then NRZDataFilterWithJitter performs just like a standard raised cosine filter.

 

When EnableJitter=No, then NRZDataFilterWithJitter oversamples the input NRZ data by factor Interpolation*JitterOversampling.  This enables data clock jitter that has time quanta of

1/( Interpolation*JitterOversampling)/SampleRate.

 

The effect of timing jitter not only affects the timing of the data zero crossings, but more importantly causes filtering intersymbol interference (ISI) that adversely affects the data BER performance.  The data zero crossing jitter is smoothed out due to the filtering effect.  However, the ISI introduced due to the jitter remains at the filter output.

 

The test design is Jitter_Design.  It contains two filtering paths for the NRZ data.  One with the standard SystemVue raised cosine filter.  The other is with the NRZDataFilterWithJitter model.

 

The output waveforms for both paths are shown in graph Jitter_S1.  When the NRZDataFilterWithJitter EnableJitter=NO, the two waveforms are identical.  When the NRZDataFilterWithJitter=YES, the ISI due to the timing jitter is readily visible.  The jitter test condition is setup with timing jitter limited to +/- 0.25 symbol time, with Gaussian RMS jitter set to 0.125 symbol time.

 

Model for Data Spreading and DeSpreading

 

This model is defined and analyzed within the folder named Spreading_Model_Test.

 

The subnetwork model Spread accepts an input NRZ data stream at one sample per symbol and spreads it with a PN code.  The settable parameter is ChipsPerSymbol.  One input symbol produces ChipsPerSymbol number of output chips.

 

The subnetwork model DeSpread accepts an input chip data stream at one sample per chip and outputs the despread symbol using a PN code matched to that used in the Spread model.  The output symbols are detected using an integrate and dump approach with suitable anti aliasing filtering applied before downsampling.  The settable parameters are ChipRate, ChipsPerSymbol and DisableSinks.  The DisableSinks parameter default is YES and when set to NO enables the internal model sinks.

 

The graph Spreader_Internal_Data shows the IntegratedData, SampledData, FilteredData, and DownsampledData (which is the output symbols).

 

The graph Spreader_Out shows the Spread input symbols and the identical recovered DeSpread output symbols.

 

BPSK System BER vs. Eb/N0 curves with Clock Jitter and Code Spreading

 

This system is defined and analyzed within the folder named BPSK_Spread_System.

 

The above discussed models NRZDataFilterWithJitter, Spread and DeSpread are applied to the basic BPSK system design to create the designs:  BPSK_Spread_Design and BPSK_Spread_BER_Design.

 

The BPSK_Spread_Design has associated Analyses and Data:  BPSK_Spread_Analysis, BPSK_Spread_Data, and with associated Graphs:  Spread_BPSKSymbolOut, Spread_I_BPSKSymOut, Spread_ChipOut and Spread_BitsOut.

 

BPSK_Spread_Design is set up with the NRZDataFilterWithJitter EnableJitter=NO and with the RF channel noise density (NDensity) disabled.

 

The approach used for the BPSK_Basic_Design is followed to set up the delays DelayA, B, C  and D. and should be set in the same way as discussed for the design BPSK_Basic_System. 

 

DelayE and DelayF are added to synchronize the Transmitter ChipsIn and the Receiver ChipsOut for wavefom and BER measurement. The DelayE, F should be set before DelayD. The DelayF was added to synchronize the chip frame received by the DeSpread model in the Receiver.

 

BPSK_Spread_BER_Design has associated Analyses and Data:  BPSK_Spread_BER_Analysis, BPSK_Spread_NoJitter_BER_Data, and BPSK_Spread_Withitter_BER_Data.

 

The BPSK design with the spreader and despreader was measured for its BER performance without and with the TX data clock jitter applied.

 

The Graph BPSK_BER shows the simulated BER curves with the theoretical BER curve overlaid.

 

Notes on BER Simulation Times

For the basic BPSK system (no code spreading/dispreading and no timing jitter), BER simulation for 1M bits will simulate a maximum 16M samples at some internal system points due to the set up for modeling 16 samples per BPSK symbol.

 

For the BPSK system with spreading/dispreading, BER simulation for 1M bits will simulate a maximum 496M samples (16*31*1M) at some internal system points due to the set up for modeling 16 samples per BPSK symbol and 31 chips per BPSK symbol.  This system will take about 30X more time to simulate than the basic BPKS system.

 

For the BPSK system with spreading/dispreading and with transmit chip clock timing jitter, BER simulation for 1M bits will simulate a maximum 7,936M samples (16*16*31*1M) at some internal system points due to the set up for modeling 16 samples per BPSK symbol, 31 chips per BPSK symbol, and 16 samples per chip sample for modeling timing jitter.  There is also longer simulation time due to the FIR filter with jitter that has 8*31*16=3968 taps.  The basic BPSK system FIR filters have only 8*16 taps. This system will take about 1000X more time to simulate than the basic BPKS system.  This 100X factor can probably be reduced to 60X if the NRZDataFilterWithJitter subnetwork model were converted to a C++ polyphase filter model.

 

Notes on BER vs. Eb/N0 curves

The ratio of Energy per Bit (Eb) to the Noise Energy (N0) is a calculated parameter that depends on the modulation format and other factors.  Once it is calculated, the appropriate noise spectral density is back-annotated onto the "NDensity" block to create the desired signal to noise ratio (SNR).  BER is then calculated for the system at this Eb/N0 setting.

 

In a sweep of Eb/N0 values, the NDensity amplitude is automatically adjusted, and the BER measurement performed at each value, creating a characteristic "waterfall" curve.  As the SNR improves, the BER falls dramatically.  To plot BER against the derived parameter EbN0, use the "Y vs X" post-processing option.

Workspace.Name: PAM-QAM_BER_Importance_Sampling
Workspace.Description:
Using "Improved Importance Sampling" for BER

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

 

This workspace shows simulated Bit Error Ratio (BER) performance vs. theory for several PAM and QAM modulation formats using the "BER_IS" measurement sink.  This measurement alogirthm uses the "Improved Importance Sampling" method to provide a highly-efficient analytical estimate of the true BER. 

 

For many systems, the uncorrected BER can be 1e-6 to 1e-12, or even lower.  "Monte Carlo" approaches to these low BER measurements may require hours or days of simulation BER estimates in seconds.

 

The folders of this workspace show BER vs. SNR plots (Eb/No or Es/No) for several modulation formats.  Within each format, the BER_IS is compared against the theoretical value of BER, in terms of ernergy per bit (Eb/No) and energy per symbol (Es/No).

 

In addition, the DelayDetection folder illustrates the the auto-synchronization feature of BER_IS.

Workspace.Name: QPSK_BER_Coded_Viterbi
Workspace.Description:
BER vs. Eb/No waterfall curves for Coded QPSK System 

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This example shows the process for generating BER and Eb/No waterfall curves for a QPSK communications architecture that includes convolutional coding and Viterbi decoding. 

 

In general, good system BER performance requires that the receiver receive a signal without excessive intersymbol interference or excessive noise, and that the receiver provide automatic clock, data, amplitude, phase and frequency synchronization.

 

SystemVue provides capability for modeling and measuring communication systems BER performance.  Many of the wireless libraries included with SystemVue provide receiver models that work under dynamic RF fading conditions and provide automatic synchronization.

 

The example discussed here is for a simple QPSK system that uses some of the common system models included with SystemVue and relies on manual receiver synchronization setup. Automatic receiver synchronization requires design of custom algorithms in SystemVue for the specific communication system of interest.

 

QPSK System Design Examples

BER vs. Eb/No waterfall curves comparisons are made for QPSK systems with no coding and with soft detection Viterbi decoding.

 

In both cases, the QPSK systems contain a transmitter section, RF channel, receiver section, and BER measurement capability.  A pseudorandom bit source is formatted into QPSK, then filtered, upconverted, processed through AWGN, downconverted, and demodulated.  Then the input and output symbols or bits are compared to calculate BER using a Monte Carlo BER measurement process which is a sample by sample process.  Comparisons are made to the theoretical BER performance (included as an equation).

 

Basic QPSK System Design

 

This discussion is for Design:  QPSK_Design, with associated Analyses and Data:  QPSK_Analysis, QPSK_Data, and with associated Graphs:  QPSKSymbolOut, I_QPSKSymOut, and BitsOut.

 

The basic transmitter is setup with no convolutional coding.  The QPSK symbol rate is 51.2e6 (defined as SymbolRate in the Equation1 page).  The QPSK modulator is 300 MHz (defined as ModCarrier in the Equation1 page) at with 13 dBm power level (defined as ModPower_dBm in the Equation1 page).  The QPSK filtering is with a root raised cosine filter with a X16 interpolation factor.  It is placed after the modulator in the design for convenience, but equivalent filtering could have been placed before the modulator.

 

The RF channel is defined as a simple unity gain, zero delay, additive white Gaussian noise channel with noise density (NDensity) defined as a function of system Eb/No in the Equation1 page.

 

The basic receiver is setup with no Viterbi decoding. It provides matched filtering with its root raised cosine filter (including downsampling) and QPSK symbol demapping into bits. The receiver needs to be manually setup to synchronize its amplitude, phase and timing factors.  For the RF channel defined, the receive gain G1 is set to unity and the complex signal rotation R1 is set to zero.  The receiver timing is set with the delay DelayC to match the TX and RX filtering.  The setting of DelayC is critical for proper receiver data timing synchronization.

 

Besides the receiver DelayC used to set the receiver timing, the design schematic includes various other delay factors (DelayA, DelayB, DelayD) to synchronize various measurements to be made on the system.  See the design schematic for details. It is recommended that the delays A through D be setup in that order.

 

The Graph QPSKSymbolOut shows the QPSK input and output I channel symbols for the oversampled (QPSKSymbolIn, QPSKSymbolOut) and for the single sample per symbol (QPSKSymIn, QPSKSymOut) signals.  Alignment of QPSKSymbolIn, QPSKSymbolOut is achieved with DelayA. Alignment of QPSKSymIn, QPSKSymOut is achieved with DelayB and DelayC. 

 

The Graph I_QPSKSymOut shows the QPSK input and output I channel symbols (I_QPSKSymIn, I_QPSK_SymOut) that may be used for BER measurements using the QPSK I channel symbols.  Alignment of I_QPSKSymIn, I_QPSK_SymOut is achieved with DelayD.  This alignment process uses the ‘Cross Correlator’ model.  This model outputs the delay between the two signals at its ‘CorrDelay’ output.  With proper DelayD value, the resultant CorrDelay will be zero.

 

Other than the DelayD value which is determined by the CrossCorr model, the other delay value can be readily determined by observing their associated waveforms and tuning the delay values using the SystemVue Tuning Window.

 

This basic QPSK system is used in the other designs to make BER measurements with and without convolutional coding.

 

Uncoded QPSK System BER vs. Eb/N0 curves

 

This discussion is for Design:  Uncoded_QPSK_Design, with associated Analyses and Data:  Uncoded_QPSK_Analysis, Uncoded_QPSK_Data, Uncoded_BER_Sweep, Uncoded_BER_Sweep_Data, and with associated Graphs:  Uncoded_BER.

 

The design is the same as the QPSK_Design.  Only the BER measurement is performed.  The DelayC value determined with the QPSK_Design is used to achieve the receiver data timing synchronization. In this design, we use the auto-alignment feature of the BER measurement.  To do this, we defined the SampleDelayBound to be large enough to account for the delays we expected in the system.  In addition, we used two pseudo random bit sequence (PRBS) sources, one for the transmitter, the other for the BER reference.  This matches what is typically done in a BER measurement system.  The PRBS sources have been configured with a LFSR length of 12.  This length defines the bit sequence to be 2^12 - 1 in length.  At the end of the sequence, the same bit sequence is repeated.

 

The Uncoded_BER_Sweep sweeps the system EbNo which then sets the RF channel noise density (NDensity). 

 

The Graph Uncoded_BER shows the simulated BER curve with the theoretical BER curve overlaid.  The theoretical BER curve is defined in the Equation2 page.  Excellent agreement is obtained.

 

Coded QPSK System BER vs. Eb/N0 curves

 

This discussion is for Design:  Coded_QPSK_Design, with associated Analyses and Data:  Coded_QPSK_Analysis, Coded_QPSK_Data, Coded_BER_Sweep, Coded_BER_Sweep_Data, and with associated Graphs:  Coded_BER.

 

The QPSK system is essentially the same as the QPSK_Design.  However, for the I and Q data channels a ConvolutionalCoder (transmitter side) and a ViterbiDecoder (receiver side) are inserted with adjustment made to the pseudorandom bit source to retain the desired QPSK symbol rate. Only the BER measurement is performed.  The DelayC value determined with the QPSK_Design is used to achieve the receiver data timing synchronization. The DelayE value is specific to this design and is set to a value somewhat larger than the ViterbiDecoder MaxSurvivorLength.  Its specific value can be established by tuning its value or by using the CrossCor model as was used in the QPSK_Design.

 

The SystemVue ViterbiDecoder model is usable for both hard decision detection and soft decision detection.  Soft decision detection gives much superior performance than hard decision detection.  To enable its use with soft decision detection the raw data, before quantization to zeros and ones, should be provided as its input.

 

The Coded_BER_Sweep sweeps the system EbNo which then sets the RF channel noise density (NDensity). 

 

The Graph Coded_BER shows the simulated BER curve with the theoretical BER curve overlaid.  The theoretical BER curve is defined in the Equation2 page.  This example demonstrates the substantial BER performance improvement when convolutional coding is used and soft decision detection is used.

 

Notes on BER vs. Eb/N0 curves

The ratio of Energy per Bit (Eb) to the Noise Energy (N0) is a calculated parameter that depends on the modulation format and other factors.  Once it is calculated, the appropriate noise spectral density is back-annotated onto the "NDensity" block to create the desired signal to noise ratio (SNR).  BER is then calculated for the system at this Eb/N0 setting.

 

In a sweep of Eb/N0 values, the NDensity amplitude is automatically adjusted, and the BER measurement performed at each value, creating a characteristic "waterfall" curve.  As the SNR improves, the BER falls dramatically.  To plot BER against the derived parameter EbN0, use the "Y vs X" post-processing option.

 

Automation

In this example we used sweep evaluations to sweep Eb/N0 and display the BER results in the graphs.  You can also use the SystemVue COM interface to implement the sweep as well.  We have provided three examples demonstrating sweeping the Eb/N0 for the uncoded design and displaying BER in the following environments:

  • LabVIEW
  • MATLAB
  • C#

See the Examples/Scripting directory for the various implementations.   The C# example is shipped precompiled - to run it simply double click on Examples/Scripting/C#/QPSK_BER.exe.

 

The three automation examples change the value of EbN0 in the EbN0 equation block.  This automatically fires the update in the Equation1 equation block, which in turn updates the parameters of the Uncoded_QPSK_Design schematic.

Workspace.Name: QPSK_BER_Importance_Sampling
Workspace.Description:
Generating BER vs Eb/No waterfall curves

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

 This example shows the process for generating BER and Eb/No waterfall curves for a simple communications architecture.  A pseudorandom bit source is formatted into QPSK, then filtered, upconverted, processed through AWGN, downconverted, and demodulated.  Then the Input & Output bits are compared to calculate BER.

 

Two methods for calculating BER are shown, with comparison to theoretical BER calculation (included as an equation).

 

First method is a pure Monte Carlo method which calculates BER on a sample by sample basis.   While accurate this method can take very long to simulate.

 

The second method uses importance sampling, which introduces noise artificially within it's algorithm to produce BER estimates very quickly.  This only works for certain modulation methods, including QPSK.  The technique is docuemented in the SystemVue manual underm "Parts Catalog / Algorithm Design Library / BER_IS".

How to Generate BER vs. Eb/N0 curves

The ratio of Energy per Bit (Eb) to the Noise Energy (N0) is a calculated parameter that depends on the modulation format and other factors.  Once it is calculated, the appropriate noise spectral density is back-annotated onto the "NDensity" block to create the desired signal to noise ratio(SNR).  BER is then calculated for the system at this Eb/N0 setting.

 

In a sweep of Eb/N0 values, the NDensity amplitude is automatically adjusted, and the BER measurement performed at each value, creating a characteristic "waterfall" curve.  As the SNR improves, the BER falls dramatically.  To plot BER against the derived parameter EbN0, use the"Y vs X" post-processing option.

Setting Delay for BER measurements

The delay between the Bits_In and Bits_Out sinks has already been set.  If you choose to enable the Communication Channel component to see additional channel effects, you will need to adjust the delay on the reference path, so that Input & Output bits are arriving at the same time.  You can determine this delay value by using the Cross Correlation function to compare the Input & Output sinks.  If you are using 8192 sample points, adjust the delay by N samples such that the cross correlation peak is maxmized at 8192.

Workspace.Name: Transceiver_BER_with_Scripting
Workspace.Description:
Generating BER vs Eb/No waterfall curves

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This example shows the process for generating BER and Eb/No waterfall curves for a simple communications architecture.  A pseudorandom bit source is formatted in one of several possible modulation formats, then filtered, upconverted, faded (to enable fading activate part C2; CommsChannel model), downconverted, and demodulated.  Then the Input & Output bits are compared to calculate BER and BLER.

 

How to Generate BER vs. Eb/N0 curves

The ratio of Energy per Bit (Eb) to the Noise Energy (N0) is a calculated parameter that depends on the modulation format and other factors.  Once it is calculated, the appropriate noise spectral density is back-annotated onto the "NDensity" block to create the desired signal to noise ratio(SNR).  BER is then calculated for the system at this Eb/N0 setting.

 

In a sweep of Eb/N0 values, the NDensity amplitude is automatically adjusted, and the BER measurement performed at each value, creating a characteristic "waterfall" curve.  As the SNR improves, the BER falls dramatically.  To plot BER against the derived parameter EbN0, use the"Y vs X" post-processing option.

Setting Delay for BER measurements

The delay between the Bits_In and Bits_Out sinks has already been set.  If you choose to enable the Communication Channel component to see additional channel effects, you will need to adjust the delay on the reference path and the SampleStart parameter of the BER sink, so that Input & Output bits are arriving at the same time.  You can determine this delay value by using the Cross Correlation function to compare the Input & Output sinks.  If you are using 8192 sample points, adjust the delay by N samples such that the cross correlation peak is maximized at 8192.

Try these: 

  1. Change Mod_Type variable in the Sim_Control equation object, and observe the effect of the modulation type on the BER curves
  2. Enable the channel model and see the effect on BER
  3. Hold the EbN0 constant and instead, sweep the Mod_Type

Note that with default the dataset does not exist in this workspace due to its huge size. To get the results, please run the simulation.

Workspace.Name: 256_APSK
Workspace.Description:
Selected Constellation Mappings for DVB-S2X

 

Mappings taken from pages 17-32 of "DVB Document A83-2 Part II: S2-Extensions (DVB-S2X)" - March 2014

 

Phase offsets

Note for all evenly spaced rings with "n" states per ring, the phase offset is an n/2 spacing so that there no states directly on either the I or Q axes.  For example, for a ring with 32 states, then offset by pi/32 = 180/32=5.625deg

 

Ring Ratios

Most of the ring ratios are optimized for nonlinearities and performance with AWGN noise.  In some cases there are several sets of ring-ratios defined for various LDPC coding states.  The list below is not exhaustive, but if you see an array in blue font, then you can cut & paste that into the Ring Ratio definition on the Custom APSK modulator.  If using the 89600 VSA software, be sure to define the ring ratios under "Custom APSK" tab under the "MeasSetup / DigitalDemod Properties..." command.

  • 64 APSK constellations
    • 16+16+16+16  (ring ratios of 1.000, 1.880, 2.720, 3.950)
    •                                             --> [0.253; 0.456; 0.689; 1.000]
    • 8+16+20+20    (ring ratios of 1.000, 2.200, 3.600(or3.500), 5.200(or5.000) )
    • 4+12+20+28    (ring ratios of 1.000, 2.400, 4.300, 7.000) 
    •                                             --> [0.143; 0.343; 0.614; 1.000]
  • 128-APSK constellations
    • 16+16+16+16+16+48 (but very irregular spacings, cannot be done with custom-APSK mode)
    • ring ratios of (1.000, 1.715, 2.118, 2.681, 2.750, 3.3819). 
    • Note rings 4&5 are essentially interleaved
  • 256-APSK constellations
    • 8 rings of 32 states each, each offset by 5.625deg
    • ring ratios for 4 different LDPC code identifiersare specified as follows:
    • LDPC code 116/180: (1.000, 1.791, 2.405, 2.980, 3.569, 4.235, 5.078, 6.536)
    •                                        [0.153; 0.274; 0.368; 0.456; 0.546; 0.648; 0.777; 1.000]
    • LDPC code 124/180: (1.000, 1.791, 2.405, 2.980, 3.569, 4.235, 5.078, 6.536)
    • LDPC code 128/180: (1.000, 1.794, 2.409, 2.986, 3.579, 4.045, 4.600, 5.400)
    • LDPC code 135/180: (1.000, 1.794, 2.409, 2.986, 3.579, 4.045, 4.500, 5.200)
    •                                        [0.192; 0.345; 0.463; 0.574; 0.688; 0.778; 0.865; 1.000]

Other notes

  1. Payload frames are typically 16200, 32400, or 64800 bits long.
  2. Filtering is comparable to DVB-S2 with the addition of these roll-off factors (alpha = 0.35, 0.25 and 0.20), the additional roll-offs alpha = 0.15; 0.10 and 0.05 shall be implemented.

 

Typical TWTA amplifier characteristics

  • Here are some GCOMP7 values  from the appendix of the DVB-S2X document that can be used to simulate a satellite transponder TWTA using the compressing Amplifier model in dataflow simulations.  The values have been interpreted off a graph and re-normalized to provide the deviation from the small-signal (linear) gain required by the model.  Just add commas and surround with square brackets.
  • Power level below is #dB effectively backed off from output Psat.
  • AM/AM - Gain Compression is in dB, delta gain compared to small signal dB(S21)
  • AM/PM - Delta Phase is not absolute phase, but deviation from phase(S21)

 256-APSK for DVB-S2X evaluation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

1. This workspace sets up a custom 256-APSK signal source according to specifications in the DVB-S2X physical layer document, dated March 2014.  The signal is then demodulated it using he 89600 VSA (with Option AYA, for vector demod). 

 

2. This is an uncoded signal, no framing, no DSSS applied.  The DigitalMod part is configured to generate the custom APSK format.   The ring ratios are nonlinear and provide a small amount of pre-distortion for AM/AM effects in the PA.  The 89600 VSA .setx file mirrors these ring ratios so that you can look directly at EVM.  The slider allows you to change the amplitude into the PA and see the EVM change.  Two different PA models are offered, one is a TWTA as referenced in the standard, the other is a regular compressing amplifier model.  EVM is also partly affected by the phase noise on the LO.   

 

3. This basic DigitalMod signal source is included free with the core SystemVue environment.  For more complete demodulation, reference receiver, and EVM/BER  directly in SystemVue, you can use the W1902 Digital Modem library.

Workspace.Name: C4FM
Workspace.Description:
APCO C4FM

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Template Workspace

 

 

This workspace illustrates how to generate APCO C4FM  in APCO system. The specification is ANSI/TIA-102.BAAA-A 2003.

 

The modulation sends 4800 symbols/sec with each symbol conveying 2 bits of information. The mapping between symbols and bits is given in Table 9-1.
                                                         Table 9-1 Dibit Symbol Mapping to Modulation Phase or Deviation
                                                                             Information                              C4FM
                                                                                    Bits             Symbol       Deviation
                                                                                     01                  +3            +1.80 kHz
                                                                                     00                  +1            +0.60 kHz
                                                                                     10                   -1             -0.60 kHz
                                                                                     11                   -3             -1.80 kHz

 

The modulation symbols are filtered with a Raised Cosine Filter which satisfies the Nyquist criterion minimizing intersymbol interference. The input to this filter consists of a series of impulses, scaled according to paragraph 9.2, and separated in time by 208.33 microseconds (1/4800 sec). The group delay of the filter is flat over the passband for |f| < 2880 Hz. The magnitude response of the filter is given approximately by the following formula.
                                                                     f = frequency in hertz
                                                               |H(f)| = magnitude response of the Nyquist Raised Cosine Filter
                                                               |H(f)| = 1 for |f| < 1920 Hz
                                                               |H(f)| = 0.5 + 0.5 cos(2 π f / 1920) for 1920 Hz < |f| < 2880 Hz
                                                               |H(f)| = 0 for |f| > 2880 Hz

 

The C4FM modulator consists of a Nyquist Raised Cosine Filter, cascaded with a Shaping Filter, cascaded with a frequency modulator. The Nyquist Raised Cosine Filter is described in paragraph 9.3. The Shaping Filter has a flat group delay over the passband for |f| < 2880 Hz. The magnitude response of the Shaping Filter is given approximately by the following formula. The response of the filter above 2880 Hz is not specified because the filter H(f) should cut off above 2880 Hz.
    

                                                              |P(f)| = magnitude response of the Shaping Filter
                                                              |P(f)| = (π f/4800) / sin(π f/4800) for |f| < 2880 Hz

 

In APCO_C4FM_Modulation, the second FIR (F2) was short. It was for Shaping Filter. If this shaping filter was turn ON, pls use P25_C4FM_SFilter.setx in VSA89600 software. Otherwise, use the default P25_C4FM.setx setup file for VSA89600.
