Workspace.Name: SignalStudioWFM_LTE_DL_5MHz_25RB
Workspace.Description:
Reading Keysight SignalStudio waveform files

 

This example requires a license for the W1910 LTE Baseband Verification Library.  An Keysight 89601 VSA configured with options 105 (dataflow link) and BHD (LTE FDD) is also helpful.

 

The encrypted LTE waveform provided with this workspace is a 5MHz wide LTE FDD signal with 25RB's, sampled at 7.68MHz (tstep=130.2083ns) for 76800 samples (10ms total).  It was generated with the N7624B Keysight SignalStudio LTE program.

 

ReadSignalStudioFile

This source is not currently in the part menus. Insert a ReadFile component, and then change the model to be the ReadSignalStudioFile model.  Then you can finish setting the parameters.  This step has already been completed for you.

 

Sample Rate

You have 2 ways to set the system "sample_rate":

  • Easy: Set the source to "Timed from source data". 
    This lets the internal sample rate of the data override the simulation "sample_rate". (The source drives the simulation) You get a good result, but it becomes awkward if you have other sources to control in your system.
  • Flexible: Set the source to "Timed from Sample_Rate". 
    (The simulation drives the source)  This submits to the master simulation clock, and leaves the user to configure the appropriate upsampling and filter/interpolation of the envelope data to achieve a clean initial waveform, without bandpass aliasing and folding effects. 

This workspace uses the latter, more manual method, but you are encouraged to try different values of parameters, and methods of upsampling to understand the tradeoffs.  For example, which interpolation method is most effective at reducing out of band aliasing?

 

Why Upsample at all?

The signal is ~5MHz wide and is timed at a specific signal processing clock rate.  This is necessary for baseband DSP algorithms.  However when the signal passes through RF/Analog components, you might want to see the effects of noise, interferers, channel models, and spectral regrowth (ACPR). In the part of the block diagram where you define the air interface, you may want to use a wider bandwidth to capture these effects, which implies some oversampling at those nodes, which you can filter away and decimate to return to normal, synchronous DSP.

 

How to upsample

As noted above, you have 2 places to increase this oversampling for the RFparts.

  1. Increase the simulation sample_rate on the controller, and use the interpolation parameters on the ReadSignalStudioFile source. This sample rate setting affects all the components in the entire system.
  2. Or, use the UpSampleEnv block to set the oversampling and filtering on just the handful of wireless air interface and channel blocks. (preferred).

    On the UpSampleEnv block, try different values of the "Mode" parameter.  Mode="Polyphase" with an ExcessBW="0.35" is a good setting. Observe the effects of your choices on the Waveform_Zoom (detail) and Spectrum plot windows.

Analog Effects

This workspace has two design files, one that is basic (Design1) and one that has some channel and frequency conversion (Design1_withMixer).  For the simple one, use 8192 sample points and investigate the relationships of all the filter and oversampling parameters.  Get familiar with the inter-relationships of the sample rates and aliasing using the tuning sliders and playing with filtering choices.

 

For the more complex design, change the controller to simulate Design2_withMixer, and increase your total number of points slightly to simulate more frames of data.  Then when you are confident, try the high-side/low-side LO exercise that is written on that page.

 

For more information about Keysight SignalStudio and the VSA software, or to obtain a free trial period of these applications, go to:

  • http://www.keysight.com/find/vsa
  • http://www.keysight.com/find/signalstudio

Workspace.Name: SignalStudio_WFM_BuiltIn
Workspace.Description:
Reading Keysight SignalStudio Files

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This example shows how to read unlicensed static waveforms stored from the Keysight SignalStudio software, for use as quick & easy communication sources and interferers in SystemVue simulations.  This demonstation example does not require a license for any SystemVue Baseband Verification Libraries, or for Keysight Signal Studio, but other Signal Studio waveforms you encounter may be encrypted and require additional licenses.  An Keysight 89601 VSA configured with options 105 (dataflow link) and the appropriate demoduation options would be helpful.

 

ReadSignalStudioFile

This source as shown, is not currently in the SystemVue part menus, but it is easy to create.  First, insert a ReadFile part from the Algorithmic Design library, and then change the model on the part to be the ReadSignalStudioFile model.  You see a new set of parameters.  Then you can finish setting the SignalStudio waveform file parameters.  This step has already been completed for you.

 

Built-in ".wfm" Waveforms and VSA ".set" files

A variety of Keysight unencrypted instrument waveforms have been provided for convenient signal sources for non-critical applications, such as interferers.  If you choose from the list of built-in SignalStudio WFM files, you may also find a corresponding ".set" file to preconfigure your Keysight 89600 VSA software to demodulate this waveform.  Both the WFM and SET files are located in the "Waveforms" subdirectory in your SystemVue installation.

 

Sample Rate

You have 2 ways to set the system "sample_rate" when using SignalStudio waveform files:

  • Easy: Set the source to "Timed from source data". 
    This lets the internal sample rate of the data override the simulation "sample_rate". (The source drives the simulation) You get a good result, but it becomes awkward if you have other sources to control in your system.
  • Flexible: Set the source to "Timed from Sample_Rate". 
    (The simulation drives the source)  This submits the source to the master simulation clock, and leaves the user to configure the appropriate resampling/upsampling and filter/interpolation of the envelope data to achieve a clean initial waveform, without bandpass aliasing and folding effects. You can cascade an UpSampleEnv block with filtering options, as described below.

This workspace uses the simple method, where the stored waveform sample rate drives the simulation.  If you choose the alternate method, to allow multiple sources, you are encouraged to try different values of parameters, and methods of upsampling to understand the tradeoffs.  For example, which interpolation method is most effective at reducing out of band aliasing?

 

Why do Upsampling?

Specific signals may be ~5MHz wide and timed at a specific signal processing clock rate.  This is necessary for baseband DSP filtering algorithms, to reduce intersymbol interference, for example.  However when the signal passes through RF/Analog components, you might want to see the effects of noise, interferers, channel models, and spectral regrowth (ACPR).  Therefore, in the part of the block diagram where you define the air interface, you may want to use a wider bandwidth to capture these effects, which implies some oversampling at the RF nodes.  When you go back to normal, synchronous DSP at baseband, you can filter away and decimate the extra bandwidth (ie - restore the original, intended, lower sample rate).

 

How to upsample

As noted above, you have 2 places to increase this oversampling for the RFparts.

  1. Increase the simulation sample_rate on the controller, and use the interpolation parameters on the ReadSignalStudioFile source. This sample rate setting affects all the components in the entire system.
  2. Or, use the UpSampleEnv block to set the oversampling and filtering on just the handful of wireless air interface and channel blocks. (preferred).

    On the UpSampleEnv block, try different values of the "Mode" parameter.  Mode="Polyphase" with an ExcessBW="0.35" is a good setting. Observe the effects of your choices on the Waveform_Zoom (detail) and Spectrum plot windows.

For more information about Keysight SignalStudio and the VSA software, or to obtain a free trial period of these applications, go to:

  • http://www.keysight.com/find/vsa
  • http://www.keysight.com/find/signalstudio

What additional software do you need for this example

What does this example do

How to execute this example

Theory of Operation

    The demodulation setup is embodied in the VSA setup files. Please refer to the Keysight 89600 VSA documentation on how to create such setup files.

  

Notes

Workspace.Name: VSA89600 Recall QAM512 Data
Workspace.Description:
VSA89600 Recall QAM512

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

What additional software do you need for this example

      Keysight 89600 VSA software.

 

What you need to know before executing this example

       How to create and execute a Data Flow simulation in SystemVue.

 

What does this example do

        Execution of this example will use 89600 VSA to recall the Qam512.sdf data for simulation, at the same time to bring up the 89600 VSA user interface to display the demodulated QAM512 data, including information such as Eye Diagram, EVM, ect.  The SpectrumAnalyzer part "Spectrum" is used to analyze the spectrum of the recalled time domain data and the resulted spectrum is plotted in the graph.  The original time domain data are captured by the Sink part "TimeDomain".

 

How to execute this example

     Before execute this example, make sure the "Qam512.set" file and the "Qam512.sdf" file are in the same folder as this example.

    Click on the schamatic and click the "Run Analysis" button on the tool bar. 

 

Theory of Operation

    This example demonstrate how to use the VSA 89600 Source to communicate with Keysight 89600 VSA software to bring pre-recorded data (stored in .sdf file format) into the simulation.  The time domain samples recalled are sent into a SpectrumAnalyzer (that uses complex envelope model SpectrumAnalyzerEnv ) to calculate the spectrum of the original data.  A Sink is also used simply for the purpose of capturing the original time domain data.

    The Qam512 data in this example has carrier frequency at 700MHz and span of 8MHz.  Since information such as sampling rate and carrier frequency are embedded in the original data, the parameters such as "TStep" or "CenterFrequency" (revealed by setting "SetCenterFreq" to YES) are left at their default value 0.

Workspace.Name: 3DChannelThroughput_LTE
Workspace.Description:
3DChannelThroughput_LTE

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates:

  • Swept Throughput vs. SNR measurements for LTE downlink in 3D MIMO channel environments. The configuration is tested: a 2x2 (MIMO Transmit Diversity).

MIMO_Environment

These examples measure the LTE MIMO throughput under 3D MIMO channel. The antenna patterns are configured to be omnidirectional. The 3D channel scenario is set to be UMi_3D (Urban micro-cell) with LOS (Line-of-Sight).

 

Notes: In this example, UE data are allocated to all subframes, while no data should be allocated to Subframe 5 according to the specs.

 

Closed-loop HARQ Simulation Instruction

To enable the closed-loop HARQ simulation for UE1, the following settings must be done in the RB allocation (PDSCH) tab in the properties of the LTE-A sources and receivers.

  1. Set the 'UE1_HARQ_Enable' parameter in LTE top-level sources and receivers to YES.
  2. Set the 'UE1_NumHARQ' parameter to specify the number of HARQ processes.
  3. Set the 'UE1_MaxHARQTrans' parameter to specify maximum number of HARQ transmission; The 'UE1_RV_Sequence' parameter specifies the redundancy version coding sequence whose array size should be equal to the 'UE1_MaxHARQTrans' parameter.
  4. Set the 'ReceiverDelay' parameter in LTE top-level receivers to 'one subframe delay (1ms)', which means one subframe is delayed in the receivers.
  5. Connect the 'UE1_HARQ_Bits' port in the receiver back to the 'UE1_HARQ_Bits' port in the source. Note that a Delay part (with the delay of (UE1_NumHARQ-1)) is placed between these two 'UE1_HARQ_Bits' ports in the receiver and the source.
  6. Use the 'LTE_Throughput' part to measure the simulated throughput. Note that the two input ports should come from the receiver corresponding output ports, and the measurement should at least begin with the second subframe (i.e. set SubframeStart >=1).

Simulation Control Instruction

 

1. To get stable BER performance, the "Data Flow Analysis -> Options -> Repeatable Random Sequences" option is selected to get the fixed noise. Set the parameter "Random Seed" in the System tab of the channel model properties to a non-zero value. With fixed noise, the waterfall BER curve can be obtained even when the simulation frame length is not long.
2. To enable random noise, uncheck the "Data Flow Analysis -> Options -> Repeatable Random Sequences" option.

3. The default setting is that the "Data Flow Analysis -> Options -> Repeatable Random Sequences" option is selected for all designs in this workspace.

Workspace.Name: Beamforming_Antenna_Analysis_Synthesis
Workspace.Description:
Antenna Analysis and Synthesis (Preliminary Release)

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

 

This is an example of a workspace that can be used as a starting point to simulate antenna analysis and synthesis, as well as LTE/LTE-A beamforming performance in SystemVue. The schematic designs provided in this example are described below.

  • Folder: Beamforming Antenna Analysis
    • Schematic: Antenna Analysis Design: with given antenna array, antenna pattern and excitation at each antenna element, simulate far-field radiation pattern.
  • Folder: Beamforming Antenna Synthesis
    • Schematic: Antenna Synthesis Design: with target far-field radiation pattern, calculate excitation at each antenna element.
  • Folder: Beamforming Performance Evaluation
    • Folder: LTE-A Beamforming Throughput Simulation
      • Schematic: LTE_A_DL_1x1_Throughput: simulate LTE-A downlink 1x1 throughput performance for transmission mode 8 with single layer in Rician channel. This simulation performance is the baseline for the benchmark with 8x1 beamforming performance.
      • Schematic: LTE_A_DL_8x1_Beamforming_Throughput: simulate LTE-A downlink 8x1 throughput performance for transmission mode 8 with single layer in Rician channel by applying beamforming weights calculated from Antenna Synthesis simulation. This simulation curve (throughput vs. angle with given SNR) matches the radiation pattern gotten in Antenna Synthesis simulation.
    • Folder: LTE-A Beamforming Verification with VSA 89600B
      • Schematic:  LTE_A_DL_8Ants_Beamforming_1Layer: Connect to VSA 89600B for LTE-A downlink 8 antennas for transmission mode 8 with single layer. The demodulation result matches the radiation pattern gotten in Antenna Synthesis simulation.
      • Schematic: LTE_A_DL_8Ants_Beamforming_2Layers: Connect to VSA 89600B for LTE-A downlink 8 antennas for transmission mode 8 with two layers. The demodulation result matches the radiation pattern gotten in Antenna Synthesis simulation.

 Note: VSA 89600B version 14 or above is required.

 

 

Antenna Analysis 

In this example, users can set the antenna array structure (the number of antenna elements, linear array distance), antenna pattern of each antenna element, and excitations, and simulate the far-field radiation pattern.

The file format for the input antenna pattern is described in Chapter “Antenna Pattern File Format” below.

Users can set the parameters in the “Equations” tab of “Antenna Analysis Design”.

 

Antenna Synthesis

In this example, users can set the antenna array structure (the number of antenna elements, linear array distance), antenna pattern of each antenna element, and the target far-field radiation pattern, and calculate excitations.

The file format for the input antenna pattern is described in Chapter “Antenna Pattern File Format” below.

The file format for the input target radiation patter is described in Chapter “Target Radiation File Format”.

Users can set the parameters in the “Equations” tab of “Antenna Synthesis Design”.

For more information on how to set parameters of Antenna Synthesis, refer to the documentation of the “AntennaSynthesis” model.

 

Beamforming Performance Evaluation

LTE-A Beamforming Throughput Simulation

In this example, users can simulate LTE-A downlink 8x1 throughput performance for transmission mode 8 with single layer in Rician channel by applying beamforming weights calculated from Antenna Synthesis simulation. This simulation curve (throughput vs. angle with given SNR) matches the radiation pattern gotten in Antenna Synthesis simulation.

In the “Parameters” tab, Theta is defined to set the angle of MS. SNR is also defined. We can sweep Theta to get the throughput performances versus angles with specified SNR. Also we can sweep SNR to get the throughput performances versus SNR with specified angle.

In the “Equations” tab, the weights (excitations) for transmitter antenna array are defined which can be calculated from the “Antenna Synthesis Design” schematic. This valuable is set to the “UE1_AntMappingMatrix” parameter in LTE-A source. To access this parameter, clicks LTE-A source UI, then go to System Tab, uncheck “Use Default” for Virtual Antenna Mapping, click “User Defined” button, then set “UE1_AntMappingMatrix” parameter.

In the meantime, a simulation of LTE-A downlink 1x1 throughput performance for transmission mode 8 with single layer in Rician channel is also provided as the baseline for benchmark.

LTE-A Beamforming Verification with VSA 89600B

In this example, users can connect to VSA 89600B for LTE-A downlink 8 antennas for transmission mode 8 with single layer and two layers. The demodulation result matches the radiation pattern gotten in Antenna Synthesis simulation.

In the “Equations” tab, the weights (excitations) for transmitter antenna array are defined which can be calculated from the “Antenna Synthesis Design” schematic. This valuable is set to the “UE1_AntMappingMatrix” parameter in LTE-A source. To access this parameter, clicks LTE-A source UI, then go to System Tab, uncheck “Use Default” for Virtual Antenna Mapping, click “User Defined” button, then set “UE1_AntMappingMatrix” parameter.

 

Antenna Pattern File Format

The format in each file is the arrays of radiation angle, radiation amplitude (in dB) and phase (in degree) across radiation angle from -90 to +90 degree with the resolution of one degree. Hence the file requires the data for 181 degrees and totally 543 data. Here is an example of the antenna pattern file format. 

-90 -3 10

-89 -3 12

-88 -2.8 15

.

0 0 0

.

88 -2.8 -15

89 -3 -12

90 -3 -10

 In this example workspace, all the antenna elements read the antenna pattern from the same file.

 

Target Radiation File Format

The format in this file is the arrays of radiation angle, radiation power (in dBi or dB), radiation pattern option and possible weighing factor across specified radiation angle between -90 and +90 degree. The resolution of radiation angles in this file is also one degree. The radiation pattern option is to specify the option for the desired radiation pattern with “0” for “lower bound” and “1” for “upper bound”.  

Depending on the "RadiationPatternWeighing" parameter, the required file format is different.

 

RadiationPatternWeighing = NO

No weighing factors are included in the file. Hence the format is the arrays of radiation angle, radiation power (in dBi or dB) and radiation pattern option. Here is an example of the file format. 

-70 -30 1

-69 -30 1

-68 -20 1

.

0 3 0

.

50 -15 1

51 -20 1

52 -20 1

RadiationPatternWeighing = YES

weighing factors are included in the file. Hence the format is the arrays of radiation angle, radiation power (in dBi or dB), radiation pattern option and weighing factor . Here is an example of the file format. 

-70 -30 1 1

-69 -30 1 0.5

-68 -20 1 0.8

.

0 3 0 1

.

50 -15 1 1.2

51 -20 1 1.1

52 -20 1 0.9

Workspace.Name: ChannelCapacity_Measurements
Workspace.Description:
Channel Capacity Measurements

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates the channel capacity for WinnerII channel and the correlation based channel. The channels are configured to be 2X2 MIMO mode. The correlation matrix used to calculate the channel capacity is the compositive correlation matrix of all paths. Two different antenna patterns are used in this example:

  • Antenna Pattern 1: TxPosition_Y and RxPosition_Y are set to 0.3,
  • Antenna Pattern 2: TxPosition_Y and RxPosition_Y are set to 0.5.

Channel Capacity Simulation Instruction

In the designs "CorrChannel_Capacity" and "WinnerIIChannel_Capacity", the channel correlation matrix is obtained by reading the following files:

 

CorrChannel_Capacity Analysis:

  • Antenna Pattern1: AntP1_CorrChMatrix_I.txt and AntP1_CorrChMatrix_Q.txt
  • Antenna Pattern2: AntP2_CorrChMatrix_I.txt and AntP2_CorrChMatrix_Q.txt

WinnerIIChannel_Capacity Analysis:

  • Antenna Pattern1: AntP1_WinnerIIChMatrix_I.txt and AntP1_WinnerIIChMatrix_Q.txt
  • Antenna Pattern2: AntP2_WinnerIIChMatrix_I.txt and AntP2_WinnerIIChMatrix_Q.txt

You can switch between different antenna patterns by editing the CorrMatrix_I_FileName, CorrMatrix_Q_FileName parameters in the properties of the related channel.

 

Run the SNR Sweep to get the curve channel capacity vs. SNR. And you can evaluate the channel capacities for different antenna patterns.

 

Simulation time:  about 10 seconds in the machine with Intel Xeon 2.0GHz, 4G RAM, Windows Vista system.

 

 

Files Generation Simulation Instruction

In the designs "Gen_CorrChannel_Files" and "Gen_WinnerII_Files", each channel model generates three files: The correlation matrix file, its real and imaginary parts files. 

 

For example, Correlation based MIMO channel model in the Gen_CorrChannel_Files schematic generates the following files when set for Antenna Pattern 1 configuration:

AntP1_CorrChMatrix.txt, AntP1_CorrChMatrix_I.txt and AntP1_CorrChMatrix_Q.txt

 

Simulation time: 3 minutes in the machine with Intel Xeon 2.0GHz, 4G RAM, Windows Vista system.

Workspace.Name: ChannelImR_Measurements
Workspace.Description:
Channel Measurements

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates the impulse response, power spectrum and the fading waveform for WinnerII channel or the correlation based channel. The channels are configured to be 2X2 MIMO mode.

 

Channel Response and Power Spectrum Simulation Instruction

In this design, the channel is driven by an impulse signal, to get the channel impulse response. You can clearly see the power an delay for each path in the "Channel CorrChannel ImR" and "Channel WinnerII ImR" graphs. The SpectrumAnalyzerEnv model can get the power spectrum of the impulse response, which is displayed in the "Channel CorrChannel PSD" and "Channel WinnerII PSD" graphs.

 

Simulation time: 40.054 seconds in the machine with Intel Xeon 2.0GHz, 4G RAM, Windows Vista system.

 

 

Received Signal Simulation Instruction

In this design, the channel is driven by a constant signal, and the channel output waveform is logged for the duration of the simulation (i.e., 10ms). You can find the time-selective fading in "Received CorrChannel Waveform" and "Received WinnerII Waveform" graphs. This effect depends on the Doppler Effect. You can modify the parameter "MSVelocity" i.e., the velocity of the mobile station, to get different results for different doppler frequency shifts.

 

Simulation time: 47.029 seconds in the machine with Intel Xeon 2.0GHz, 4G RAM, Windows Vista system.

Workspace.Name: ChannelThroughput_LTE
Workspace.Description:
ChannelThroughput_LTE

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates:

  • Swept Throughput vs. SNR measurements for LTE downlink in WinnerII channel and correlation-based channel environments. The configuration is tested: a 2x2 (MIMO Transmit Diversity).
  • Swept Throughput vs. RxPhiRotation measurements using User Defined 3D Antenna Pattens for LTE downlink in WinnerII channel and correlation-based channel environments. The configuration is tested for a 2x2 (MIMO Spatial Multiplexing). 

MIMO_Environment

These examples measure the LTE MIMO throughput under correlation-based channel and the WinnerII channel. The antenna patterns are configured to be omnidirectional or UserDefined 3D. The WinnerII channel scenario is set to be C1 (Urban macro-cell) with LOS (Line-of-Sight).

 

Notes: In this example, UE data are allocated to all subframes, while no data should be allocated to Subframe 5 according to the specs.

 

Closed-loop HARQ Simulation Instruction

To enable the closed-loop HARQ simulation for UE1, the following settings must be done in the RB allocation (PDSCH) tab in the properties of the LTE-A sources and receivers.

  1. Set the 'UE1_HARQ_Enable' parameter in LTE top-level sources and receivers to YES.
  2. Set the 'UE1_NumHARQ' parameter to specify the number of HARQ processes.
  3. Set the 'UE1_MaxHARQTrans' parameter to specify maximum number of HARQ transmission; The 'UE1_RV_Sequence' parameter specifies the redundancy version coding sequence whose array size should be equal to the 'UE1_MaxHARQTrans' parameter.
  4. Set the 'ReceiverDelay' parameter in LTE top-level receivers to 'one subframe delay (1ms)', which means one subframe is delayed in the receivers.
  5. Connect the 'UE1_HARQ_Bits' port in the receiver back to the 'UE1_HARQ_Bits' port in the source. Note that a Delay part (with the delay of (UE1_NumHARQ-1)) is placed between these two 'UE1_HARQ_Bits' ports in the receiver and the source.
  6. Use the 'LTE_Throughput' part to measure the simulated throughput. Note that the two input ports should come from the receiver corresponding output ports, and the measurement should at least begin with the second subframe (i.e. set SubframeStart >=1).

Simulation Control Instruction

 

1. To get stable BER performance, the "Data Flow Analysis -> Options -> Repeatable Random Sequences" option is selected to get the fixed noise. Set the parameter "Random Seed" in the System tab of the channel model properties to a non-zero value. With fixed noise, the waterfall BER curve can be obtained even when the simulation frame length is not long.
2. To enable random noise, uncheck the "Data Flow Analysis -> Options -> Repeatable Random Sequences" option.

3. The default setting is that the "Data Flow Analysis -> Options -> Repeatable Random Sequences" option is selected for all designs in this workspace.

 

Simulation time for Swept Throughput vs. SNR measurements for correlation-based channel: 820 seconds for each simulation point in a machine with Intel Core(TM)2 Due CPU 3.0GHz, 3G RAM, Windows Vista system.

Simulation time for Swept Throughput vs. SNR measurements for WinnerII channel: 820 seconds for each simulation point in a machine with Intel Core(TM)2 Due CPU 3.0GHz, 3G RAM, Windows Vista system.

Simulation time for Swept Throughput vs. RxPhiRotation measurements using User Defined 3D Anteen Pattens for correlation based channel: 2290 seconds for each simulation point in a machine with Intel Core(TM)2 Due CPU 3.0GHz, 3G RAM, Windows Vista system.

To enable the closed-loop HARQ simulation for UE1, the following settings must be done in the RB allocation (PDSCH) tab in the properties of the LTE-A sources and receivers.

  1. Set the 'UE1_HARQ_Enable' parameter in LTE-A top-level sources and receivers to YES.
  2. Set the 'UE1_NumHARQ' parameter to specify the number of HARQ processes.
  3. Set the 'UE1_MaxHARQTrans' parameter to specify maximum number of HARQ transmission; The 'UE1_RV_Sequence' parameter specifies the redundancy version coding sequence whose array size should be equal to the 'UE1_MaxHARQTrans' parameter.
  4. Set the 'ReceiverDelay' parameter in LTE-A top-level receivers to 'one subframe delay (1ms)', which means one subframe is delayed in the receivers.
  5. Connect the 'UE1_HARQ_Bits' port in the receiver back to the 'UE1_HARQ_Bits' port in the source. Note that a Delay part (with the delay of (UE1_NumHARQ-1)) is placed between these two 'UE1_HARQ_Bits' ports in the receiver and the source.
  6. Use the 'LTE_Throughput' part to measure the simulated throughput. Note that the two input ports should come from the corresponding receiver output ports, and the measurement should begin at the second subframe or after (i.e., set SubframeStart >=1).

Workspace.Name: IBIS AMI Modeling
Workspace.Description:
IBIS AMI Modeling

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how SystemVue can be used for IBIS AMI SerDes Modeling.  There are two top level designs in this workspace:

  • 10.3125 Gbps system (Molex 2006 Channel): SERDES_Tx_Rx_Schematic_10
  • 6.25 Gbps system (Tyco Channel): SERDES_Tx_Rx_Schematic_6

Before running these systems, please review the "Installation & Configuration Requirements" below.  Both of these designs use similar transmitters, the only difference is the settings for TimeResponseFIR filter which is used to model a transmitter driver (using HSPICE imported data - see equation block).  The BlindFFE part in the transmitter has 3 models available in the managed models list:

  • Native SystemVue Model
  • MATLAB Script Model
  • Matlab Coder Model

To run the Matlab Coder Model, follow the instructions in the "Loading the Matlab Coder Model" section below.

 

Both of these designs have multiple receiver implementations that can be selected using the manage model list (double click on the receiver part on the top level schematic).  Each of the designs has multiple C++ code generators which have been configured for the different implementations of the transmitter and receiver.

 

Running exported content in the ADS Channel Simulator

 

An ADS workspace has been provided installed in the same location as this example workspace:

    Examples\Model Building\IBIS-AMI Modeling\ADS_IBIS_AMI_wrk.7zap

 

To run, you should unarchive it into a location with no spaces in the directory path.  

 

Installation & Configuration Requirements

 

To run the examples in this workspace, you need to install the FlexDCA.  You can find more information on the FlexDCA at:

http://www.keysight.com/find/flexdca

 

If you don't have the FlexDCA installed, you will need to deactivate the FlexDCA_Sink part before running simulations or generating AMI models. 

 

Loading the Matlab Coder model

 

To run the Matlab Coder version of the BlindFFE you need to:

·         Compile the "SystemVue_Matlab_Coder_Models" modelbuilder example by following the directions in "<SystemVue Installation Directory>\ModelBuilder\SystemVue_Matlab_Coder_Models\ReadMe.txt

 

Now, you can load the "Matlab_Coder.dll" using the SystemVue Library Manager (Tools Menu).

 

Generating AMI Model for Matlab Coder and using it in ADS Channel Simulator

 

Follow the steps below to generate AMI model for Matlab Coder and use it in ADS

  • Make sure that you are using BlindFFE from Matlab Coder Model library in the sub-network AMI_Tx_6.
  • Generate AMI code using "AMI CPP 6.25 Gbps Tx Matlab Coder" code generator in the workspace tree.
  • Copy BlindFFE.h and BlindFFE.cpp from "<SystemVue Installation Directory>\ModelBuilder\SystemVue_Matlab_Coder_Models\source\SystemVue" to <Output Directory>\source\AMI-sv_tx_6_25_ghz_m_code, where <Output Directory> is the Output Directory set in the "AMI CPP 6.25 Gbps Tx Matlab Coder" code generator options dialog.
  • Open the file <Output Directory>\source\AMI-sv_tx_6_25_ghz_m_code\CMakeLists.txt and add the lines shown in red below

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 2.8.8)

# SystemVueInstallDirectory defined in ../CMakeLists.txt

include ( ${SystemVueInstallDirectory}/ModelBuilder/CMake/CodeGeneration.cmake )include_directories( ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/../Matlab_Coder_Model/codegen/lib/MyFFE )link_directories( ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/../Matlab_Coder_Model/codegen/lib/MyFFE )

# SystemVue code generation maintains this variable, do not add files to this variable

...

...

SVU_ADD_AMI_LIBRARY(

    AMI-sv_tx_6_25_ghz_m_code

    ${SVU_GENERATED_FILES}

    ${VERSION_FILE}

    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/sv_tx_6_25_ghz_m_code.ibs

    BlindFFE.cpp

)

 

target_link_libraries( AMI-sv_tx_6_25_ghz_m_code MyFFE.lib )

SVU_INSTALL_AMI_MODEL( AMI-sv_tx_6_25_ghz_m_code )

  • Copy the Matlab_Coder_Model folder (see section "Loading the Matlab Coder Model" earlier in this note) from the area where MATLAB generated the C code (not from "<SystemVue Installation Directory>\ModelBuilder\SystemVue_Matlab_Coder_Models") to <Output Directory>\source.
  • Select "Release" configuration and build the INSTALL project. This will generate the corresponding AMI dll.
  • To use this model in ADS, copy the generated dll to the data sub-directory of the ADS workspace ADS_IBIS_AMI_wrk, and simulate the corresponding design in that workspace.

To generate AMI code for model AMI_Rx_DFE, open schematic 'SERDES_Tx_Rx_Schematic_10' and change the model of part 'Data2' to AMI_Rx_DFE.

 

To create a TX AMI Model using the Matlab Coder, first follow the steps in the "Notes" note under the "Loading the Matlab Coder model" section to compile and load the Matlab Coder model. Then open the AMI_Tx_6 model, double click on the BlindFFE part (B2), and select "BlindFFE@Matlab_Coder Models" in the Model drop down list. Finally, right click the "AMI CPP 6.25 Gbps Tx Matlab Coder" Code Generator item on the workspace tree and select "Generate Now".

Workspace.Name: OpticalAMI
Workspace.Description:
Optical transceiver

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how SystemVue can be used to design a SerDes optical interconnection repeater.
(When using this example workspace, for file accessing reasons, please save it into another location and copy the measurement_data_device_1.txt into the same place.)

 

1. VCSEL_Extraction

In the optical link, the VCSEL device is a key part which takes the responsibility to convert electrical signal to optical signal.

And in SystemVue we use a model called VCSEL to simulate the real devices. However, the VCSEL is always working with a very high rate, so the dynamic behavior cannot be got directly.

The measurable data are the stationary L-I and V-I curves. As we know, the VCSEL is a laser device and it is working based on the rate equations.

So we can abstract a VCSEL device into a behavior model with the stationary data by the according curve fitting algorithms.

The VCSEL_Extractor is the model.

  • It takes measurement data file as the input, outputs the fitting results at the FittingOutput port and stores the device parameter values into the DeviceStorage location.
  • In this example, it reads the measurement_data_device_1.txt file and stores the extracted results into Device1.dat.
  • Graph LI Curve Fitting shows the fitting results.

2. Optical_Link

To simulate the process that voltage-current-light-current-voltage of  a optical link.

  • The subcircuit(OpticalLink) takes differential voltage signal as input.
  • The voltage signal is converted to single-ended current signal by a VCSEL driver to drive a VCSEL laser.
  • VCSEL converts the current signal into light pulse. 
  • Output light pulse is coupled to a multi-mode fiber suffering from pulse dispersion and energy attenuation.
  • The fiber output is then fed to an optical filter to remove light noise.
  • Light pulse is converted to single-ended current signal by the following P-i-N diode photo detector with noise added.
  • The current signal is filtered with a low-pass electric filter,
  • The current signal is ac coupled to a trans-impedance amplifier (TIA) and is converted to differential voltage signal.
  • The subcircuit takes the voltage signal as output and the signal is transferred by an optical link.
  • Graph Design1_S1_waveform shows the signal passing through the optical link.
  • Graph Design1_S1_eye shows the eye diagram.

3. CodeGen

  • The subcircuit is code generated as an IBIS-AMI receiver that can be used in ADS with channel simulator as a normal Rx AMI model.
  • If parameter DeviceParameters of the VCSEL model is set 'FromFile', the generated AMI model will depend on the device file specified. Alternatively, If parameter DeviceParameters is set 'ManuallyInput', the device file will not be needed.
  • To create a mid-channel Redriver model the OpticalLink and ThruTx models must be linked through a common *.ibs file. This file will need to be created manually after code generation is completed by combining the contents of the OpticalLink.ibs and ThruTx.ibs files which are created during the code generation. Examples of the combined file, OpticalLinkRedriver.ibs, and the two generated files are shown under the CodeGen folder. (Comparing the files will show that this a relatively straightforward process).

Workspace.Name: SerDes_with_CDR_PFLL
Workspace.Description:
SerDes System with CDR using PFLL

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how SystemVue can be used for IBIS AMI SerDes Modeling for 14.025 Gbps system. The top level design in this workspace is AMI_System_Schematic. In addition, an example of PAM4 SerDes system is also provided for reference.

 

Before running these systems, please review the "Installation & Configuration Requirements" below. The TimeResponseFIR filter is used to model a transmitter driver (using HSPICE imported data - see equation block).  Phase- and frequency-locked loop (PFLL) is used in clock recovery in the receiver.

 

Running exported content in the ADS Channel Simulator

 

An ADS workspace has been provided installed in the same location as this example workspace:

    Examples\Model Building\IBIS-AMI Modeling\SerDes_with_CDR_PFLL_wrk.7zads

 

To run, you should unarchive it into a location with no spaces in the directory path.  

 

Installation & Configuration Requirements

 

To run the examples in this workspace, you need to install the FlexDCA.  You can find more information on the FlexDCA at:

http://www.keysight.com/find/flexdca

 

If you don't have the FlexDCA installed, you will need to deactivate the FlexDCA_Sink part before running simulations or generating AMI models. 

 

Generating AMI Model and using it in ADS Channel Simulator

 

Follow the steps below to generate AMI model and use it in ADS

  • Generate AMI code using "AMI_System_CodeGen" code generator in the workspace tree.
  • This will generate corresponding ami dll.
  • To use this model in ADS, copy the generated dll to the data sub-directory of the ADS workspace SerDes_with_CDR_PFLL, and simulate the corresponding design in that workspace.

 Reference system for PAM4

 

The PAM4 signal in the example is represented by the sum of 2 binary signals with one of which twice the amplitude of the other. In a linear time invariant channel, the channel response for PAM4 is the same as that for binary signal, so FFEs in Tx and Rx are the same. The PAM4 signal has only 4 valid zero-crossing points out of 12 signal transition cases for clock edge detection, the clock recovery circuit in this example still work but with longer acquisition and lock time. The DFE model is replaced with the DFE_PAM model which has 3 decision levels, i.e. [-2, 0, +2].

There're 2 reference receiver models for PAM4, one is FFE+DFE_PAM and the other is CTLE+DFE_PAM. In the receivers, the DFE_PAM initial taps are calculated based on the FFE/CTLE impulse response and channel impulse responses.

Workspace.Name: USB31_Transceiver
Workspace.Description:
IBIS-AMI Modeling of USB3.1 SerDes System

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how SystemVue can be used for IBIS AMI SerDes Modeling of USB ver 3.1 system. The top level design in this workspace is Design1. This system is mainly composed of 3 parts: transmitter, channel and receiver.

 

1. Transmitter: The transmitter is composed of bit source, pulse shaping and TX equalization. Random jitter (RJ), periodic jitter (PJ), duty cycle distortion (DCD) and spread spectrum clock (SSC) can be added in the pulse shaping model. In USB 3.1 specification, the reference TX equalization shall implement a 2-tap FFE (Gen1) or 3-tap FFE (Gen2) to support de-emphasis and preshoot.

 

2. Channel: The example provides 2 calibration channels: short channel and long channel. The channels can be found in the Channels folder with the S21 curves shown in the graph. The short channel has 4dB and long channel has 13dB attenuation around 2.5GHz. The channel is implemented by using S2P touchstone file and the SData model.

 

3. Receiver: The behavioral receiver is composed of 4 parts: CTLE, CDR, DFE and DFEScaler. The CTLE and DFE can overcome the channel distortion to obtain an open eye. CDR is used to recover data clock. The DFEScaler part scales the signal so as for the DFE part to have a proper feedback.

 

  1) CTLE: CTLE is implemented by a S-domain IIR filter with poles and zeros as parameters to compensate the channel distortion.  In this example, a reference configuration is provided according to the spec (Gen2) with two poles at -1.5GHz and -5GHz.

 

  2) CDR: CDR is PLL based. The loop filter is configured as a 1st order IIR filter, which makes the CDR a 2nd order loop as shown in the spec.

 

  3) DFE: A blind DFE is provided to further remove inter-symbol interference (ISI). To make it work properly, a DFE scaler is used to automatically adjust the magnitude of DFE input.

 

Keysight FlexDCA Software (the download URL is documented in model help) can be used to display the eye diagram of Tx output, Rx input and Rx output.

Workspace.Name: VCSEL_Simulation
Workspace.Description:
VCSEL_Simulation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates how to use the VCSEL_Extractor and VCSEL to extract and simulate a real VCSEL device. The VCSEL_Extractor takes the measured LI, VI and frequency response curves as input, abstracts the measured data into a behavior model which is saved as a dat file. The VCSEL takes the generated dat file as a configuration, and simulates the behavior that transferring input current into light amplitude.

  1. VCSEL Extraction
    • This is an example of how to use VCSEL_Extractor model.
    • By running the Design1 Analysis, VCSEL_Extractor reads in the measured I-V-L data and extracts it into parameter values which stand for the current VCSEL device.
    • Graph LI Curve Fitting shows the LI curve fitting results.
    • Graph VI Curve Fitting shows the VI curve fitting results.
    • Graph TimeResponseTry gives a shot of how does the current VCSEL work.
  2. VCSEL Time Response
    • This is an example of the stationary analysis of VCSEL.
    • By running the Design2 Analysis, VCSEL will convert the input current into the light power.
    • Design2 SweepI takes the bias current as the variable and run the Design2 Analysis several times.
    • Design2 SweepTo takes the ambient as the variable and run Design2 SweepI several times.
    • Graph Time Response shows how the Po changes with a constant current input.
    • Graph Po Dynamiclly shows the stationary Po with different bias current.
    • Po_d with different To shows Po(I) under different To.
  3. VCSEL Frequency Response
    • This is an example of VCSEL working at small signal modulation mode.
    • By running Design3 Analysis, VCSEL will convert the input small modulation current signal into light power.
    • Design3 Sweep takes the frequency of input current as the variable and run the Design3 Analysis several times.
    • Design3 SweepIb takes the bias current as the variable and run the Design3 Sweep several times.
    • Graph Time Response2 shows the response for small modulation signal for once.
    • Graph Frequency Response - Single Ib shows the normalized frequency response (at 1GHz).
    • Graph Frequency Response - Multi Ib shows the normalized frequency response under different bias current.
  4. VCSEL Large Signal Response
    • This is an example of VCSEL working a large input signal mode.
    • By running Design4 Analysis, VCSEL will convert the large input signal into light power.
    • Graph TimeResponse_LargeSignal shows the Po changing with t when large signal as the input.

Workspace.Name: AdaptiveCTLE
Workspace.Description:
IBIS AMI Modeling

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how SystemVue can be used to model a 10Gbps IBIS AMI SerDes receiver with Adaptive Continuous Time Linear Equalizer (CTLE).

 

To use this workspace load the library .\AdaptiveCTLE_Models\output-<Visual Studio Version>\Release-SystemVue-Win64\AdaptiveCTLE.dll (.\ represents the current folder where this workspace is located) using Tools->Library Manager->Add From File... menu option and dialog. To reduce the workspace file size, no simulated data has been saved, so graphs will show the No Data annotation. Please re-run all Data Flow analyses in each folder to have the graphs display data.

 

This workspace is organized as follows:

 

Define a set of typical SerDes Channels (Folder "_0_Channels")

  • The typical SerDes system channel is a linear system that contains high frequency attenuation of the transmitted signal.  One specific SerDes system may need to work with many different system channels.
  • Graph Channel_s21 shows a set of 13 SerDes channel characteristics in the frequency domain that is typical for a SerDes system. The high frequency channel attenuation at 5 GHz varies from -16.4 dB to -32.7 dB, with about -1 to -2 dB change per step in Index value.

SerDes channel test (Folder "_1_SerDes_Channel_test")

  • To achieve low data bit error rates in a 10Gbps SerDes system, the high frequency attenuation needs to be restored to a flat response within the low frequency band (such as 0 - BitRate/2, i.e. 0 - 5 GHz for 10Gbps). A reference channel (RefChannel model in folder "Transceivers") is defined here to represent the expected overall system response including Tx pre-emphasis equalizer, channel attenuation and Rx CTLE.
  • Per the reference channel responses and transmitter equalizer response (for simplicity, Tx is defined as passthrough in this example), a set of Rx CTLEs are obtained in model VtCTLE_FIR (model RxAdaptiveCTLE in Folder "Transceivers"). The CTLE filters in the VtCTLE_FIR model are selected by the input pin CTLE_Control to work under different channels.
  • Graphs "Channel_Impulse" and "Channel_Spec" show the impulse response and the frequency response of the 10th channel, the Rx CTLE itself and the reference channel.

Adaptive channel status detection (Folder "_2_CTLE_Detection_test")

  • For a SerDes receiver with a set of CTLEs to work under different channels adaptively, a proper CTLE needs to be selected automatically per the total channel response (Tx, Channel, and Rx) on high frequency band. If the high frequency response is greater than that of the reference channel, a CTLE with lower high frequency compensation is selected. Otherwise, a CTLE with higher high frequency compensation is selected.
  • In this example, a Bandpass Filter (BPF) CTLE_BPF is used to filter out the signal components around 5GHz. The average signal amplitude of the BPF's output is measured (representing the signal power, for simplicity). Average signal amplitude of the filter's output under the reference channel is obtained by calculation or simulation beforehand.
  • The average signal amplitude is measured by model CTLE_Detect which update the average signal amplitude every SamplesPerBit*NumBitsToAvg samples. The average signal amplitude under the reference channel is about 0.15V when the peak-to-peak amplitude of NRZ input is 1.0V.

Fabricate a receiver with Adaptive CTLE (model RxAdaptiveCTLE in folder "Transceivers")

  • Model VtCTLE_FIR is a CTLE model with filter taps controlled by the CTLE_Control port. By increasing or decreasing the control word the CTLE filter taps will be switched to increase or decrease high frequency compensation. It works with the default filter taps of 7 when the receiver boots up.
  • The output of the VtCTLE_FIR model is measured by CTLE_BPF and CTLE_Detect. Based on the measurement results, the CTLE_Control model decides how to adjust the VtCTLE_FIR model. To avoid oscillation, the filter index of the VtCTLE_FIR is controlled to increase or decrease high frequency compensation with 1 step even if the gap is more than 1 step.
  • The ClockRecovery model and ClockTimes model recover the clock from equalized waveform and translate clock ticks to clock time for AMI code generation respectively.

SerDes System simulation with Adaptive CTLE (SerDes_System_Schematic in folder "_3_SerDes_System")

  • In the test SerDes system, the 10th channel is selected and the initial CTLE is for the 7th channel.
  • Graph SerDes_System_AdaptiveCTLE_IndexV_DetV displays the change of measured signal power at 5GHz and the control word of VtCTLE_FIR for each control period. The initial measurement results and control word is set unchanged in the first several control periods to bypass startup stage.
  • Graphs "SerDes_System_RxIn_Eye" and "SerDEs_System_RxOut_Eye" display the eye diagram of channel output and receiver CTLE output.
  • To view the receiver output without CTLE adaption, one can set parameter EnableAdaption of the receiver to 0 and re-run the analysis.

AMI Code generation (CodeGen_AMI_Model in folder "_3_SerDes_System")

  • For necessary information on model selection and parameter mapping in AMI code generation, please open Help and read section "Users Guide->Using SystemVue->Code Generation->C Plus Plus Code Generation->IBIS-AMI Model Generation".
  • Please make sure the workspace is placed in a writable directory.
  • Disable data sink model CTLE_IndexV and DetV (sink is not supported in AMI code generation).
  • Open "Tools->Options->Code Generation", check "Start Development Environment" and uncheck "Automatically build after code generation". The AdaptiveCTLE.dll is not a SystemVue built-in library so automatic compilation is NOT supported if models from this library are used in code generation.
  • Double click "CodeGen_AMI_Model" and click the "Generate Now" button in the left bottom corner. The generated code will be placed in a new directory called AdaptiveCTLE_AMI (located in the same directory where this workspace is located) and the Visual Studio IDE  will also be opened.
  • In the Visual Studio IDE, open project AMI-RxAdaptiveCTLE,
    • edit Header Files/RxAdaptiveCTLE.h by replacing lines
      #include "CTLE_Detection.h"
      #include "CTLE_BPF.h"
      #include "VtCTLE_FIR.h"
      #include "CTLE_Control.h"
      with
      #include "../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_Detection.h"
      #include "../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_BPF.h"
      #include "../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/VtCTLE_FIR.h"
      #include "../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_Control.h"
    • Edit CMakeList.txt by adding lines
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_BPF.cpp
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_BPF.h
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_Control.cpp
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_Control.h
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_Detection.cpp
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_Detection.h
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_FIR.cpp
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/CTLE_FIR.h
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/VtCTLE_FIR.cpp
      ../../../AdaptiveCTLE_Models/source/VtCTLE_FIR.h
      to
      set ( SVU_GENERATED_FILES
       RxAdaptiveCTLE_AMI.h
       RxAdaptiveCTLE_AMI.cpp
       RxAdaptiveCTLE.ami
       RxAdaptiveCTLE.h

       Add new lines here
      )
    • Build project AMI-RxAdaptiveCTLE. There may be a prompt that the project is regenerated, click YES, OK or Reload to go ahead. If the projects fails to reload, verify that the project modification is correct. A modified project AdaptiveCTLE_AMI_ref is attached for reference.
    • Build project INSTALL. The generated portable AMI models will be placed in directory AdaptiveCTLE_AMI\output-<Visual Studio Version>\Release-AMI.
      RxAdaptiveCTLE.ami
      RxAdaptiveCTLE.ibs
      RxAdaptiveCTLE_x64.dll

Running exported content in the ADS Channel Simulator

 

An ADS workspace has been provided AdaptiveCTLE_wrk. To use this model in ADS, copy the generated dll, ami and ibs files (RxAdaptiveCTLE.ibs, RxAdaptiveCTLE.ami, RxAdaptiveCTLE.dll and RxAdaptiveCTLE_x64.dll) to the data sub-directory of the ADS workspace, and simulate the corresponding design in that workspace.

To run, place the ADS workspace into a location with no spaces in the directory path.  

 

Installation & Configuration Requirements

 

To run the examples in this workspace, you need to install the FlexDCA.  You can find more information on the FlexDCA at:

http://www.keysight.com/find/flexdca

 

If you don't have the FlexDCA installed, you will need to deactivate the FlexDCA_Sink part before running simulations or generating AMI models. 

 

References

This example is a modified version of the adaptive CTLE example created by our consultant John Baprawski. You may find  the original version of this example at:

http://www.johnbaprawski.com/2012/06/29/creating_an_adaptive_ctle_ami_model/

Workspace.Name: PCIE30_Transceiver
Workspace.Description:
IBIS-AMI Modeling of PCIE3.0 SerDes System

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how SystemVue can be used for IBIS AMI SerDes Modeling of PCI express 3.0 8GHz system. The top level design in this workspace is Design1. This system is mainly composed of 3 parts: transmitter, channel and receiver.

 

1. Transmitter: The transmitter is composed of bit source, pulse shaping and TX equalization. Random jitter (RJ), periodic jitter (PJ), duty cycle distortion (DCD) and spread spectrum clock (SSC) can be added in the pulse shaping model. In PCIE 3.0 specification, the reference TX equalization shall implement a 3-tap FFE to support de-emphasis and preshoot. The spec has defined 10 groups of coefficients for transmitter FFE as shown in the following table:

With different coefficient sets, transmitter can achieve different preshoot/de-emphasis effects, for example, with coefficients [-0.125 0.75 -0.125], the de-emphasis is -3.5dB and preshoot is 3.5dB.

 

2. Channel: The example provides 2 calibration channels: short channel and long channel, which conform to PCIE 3.0 specification. The channels can be found in the Channels folder with the S21 curves shown in the graph. The short channel has -12dB and long channel has -20dB attenuation around 4GHz. The channel is implemented by using S2P touchstone file and the SData model.

 

3. Receiver: The behavioral receiver is composed of 4 parts: CTLE, CDR, DFE and DFEScaler. The CTLE and DFE can overcome the channel distortion to obtain an open eye. CDR is used to recover data clock. The DFEScaler part scales the signal so as for the DFE part to have a proper feedback.

 

  1) CTLE: CTLE is implemented by a S-domain IIR filter with poles and zeros as parameters to compensate the channel distortion.  In this example, a reference configuration is provided according to the spec, i.e. two poles: -2GHz and -8GHz. So it emphasizes signal in the frequency range of 2 to 8 GHz.

 

  2) CDR: CDR is PLL based. The loop filter is configured as a 1st order IIR filter, which makes the CDR a 2nd order loop as shown in the spec, i.e. -3dB point around 10MHz.

 

  3) DFE: A blind DFE is provided to further remove inter-symbol interference (ISI). To make it work properly, a DFE scaler is used to automatically adjust the magnitude of DFE input.

 

Keysight FlexDCA Software (the download URL is documented in model help) can be used to display the eye diagram of Tx output, Rx input and Rx output.

 

 

The example can be also used as the starting of receiver stressed jitter eye test. In stressed jitter eye test, a signal with specific impairments is applied to the Rx DUT, and the BER is monitored. To obtain the impaired signal (stressed signal), Rx DUT is replaced by a test equipment (including Rx package, behavioral CTLE/DFE and CDR), and the transmitter is adjusted until a target eye width is achieved at the output of the test equipment. Then the signal is used to test the Rx DUT. Per the PCI express 3.0 specification, the transmitter Rj amplitude with other parameters set are adjusted according to the table below:

Workspace.Name: PCIe4_Transceiver
Workspace.Description:
IBIS-AMI Modeling of PCIe Generation 4 SerDes System

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how SystemVue can be used for IBIS AMI SerDes Modeling of PCI express 4 16GHz system. The top level design in this workspace is Design1. This system is mainly composed of 3 parts: transmitter, channel and receiver.

 

1. Transmitter

The transmitter consists of a bit source, pulse shaper and TX equalizer. Random jitter (RJ), periodic jitter (PJ), duty cycle distortion (DCD) and spread spectrum clock (SSC) can be configured in the pulse shaping model. In PCIe Gen 4 specification, the reference TX equalization shall implement a 3-tap FFE to support de-emphasis and preshoot. The spec has defined 10 groups of coefficients for transmitter FFE as shown in the following table:

 

C-1

With different coefficient sets, transmitter can achieve different preshoot/de-emphasis, for example, with coefficients [-0.125 0.75 -0.125], the de-emphasis is -3.5dB and preshoot is 3.5dB. FFE (feed forward equalizer) taps can be converted to/from preshoot/de-emphasis pair with the Matlab script "prede2taps" and "taps2prede" attached with the workspace.

 

2. Channel

The example provides 2 calibration channels: short channel and long channel, which conforms to PCIe Gen 4 specification. The channels can be found in the Channels folder with the S21 curves shown in the graph. The short channel has -6.5dB and long channel has -22.5dB attenuation at 8GHz (Nyquist frequency). The channel is implemented using S2P touchstone file and the SData model.

 

3. Receiver

The behavioral receiver consists of 3 parts: CTLE, CDR and DFE. The CTLE is to overcome the channel attenuation to obtain an open eye. CDR is used to recover data clock. DFE is to cancel the echoes from return/reflection.

 

  1) CTLE: CTLE is implemented by a S-domain IIR filter with poles and zeros as parameters to compensate for the channel high frequency attenuation.  In this example, a reference configuration is provided according to the spec, i.e. two poles: -4GHz and -16GHz. It boost signals in the frequency range of 4 to 16 GHz.

 

  2) CDR: CDR is PLL based. The loop filter is configured as a 1st order IIR filter, which makes the CDR a 2nd order loop as shown in the spec with -3dB point around 10MHz.

 

  3) DFE: the DFE model calculates the bit level post-cursor taps of total channel response and removes the inter-symbol interference (ISI) by subtracting the response signal of previous symbols from current symbol.

 

Keysight FlexDCA Software (the download URL is documented in model help) can be used to display the eye diagram of Tx output, Rx input and Rx output.

Basic items to explore:

 

- When you first simulate this tutorial, you will notice that the simulation status window comes up and "pauses".  This is because a breakpoint has been set in the underlying MATLAB_Script Model.  Use the "Equation Debugger" window (this will pop up after clicking "Run Analyses") to see where the simulation has stopped and view the variable status.  You can temporarily remove the breakpoint in the editor window by clicking on the red dot, then pressing the "Go" button which is a green arrow in the debugger window.  Or, just close the debugger window to skip all breakpoints for the rest of the analysis.  The graph will update.

Workspace.Name: Dynamic Paths
Workspace.Description:
Dynamic RF signal paths

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example shows how MATLAB® ScriptTM blocks can be used in run-time tuning to select between signal processing paths for either baseband or for RF Envelope signals. A few S-parameter responses are used to simulate the bandlimited response of a channelized receiver front-end, chosen interactively with a slider.

 

1. Baseband Chooser

This shows a MATLAB® ScriptTM block that is essentially a dynamically-tunable single-pole triple-throw SP3T switch. As you move the slider, the simulation chooses between 3 possible signal processing paths.

  1. First, run the BB_Chooser_DF1 analysis.
  2. Next, position your windows so you can see both the slider and the Dynamic Graphs window showing the continuous plot. When you set a Sink to be "continuous" mode (see Enable Continuous run and Runtime tuning checkbox in the sink's UI), the simulation goes into a neverending data stream mode.
  3. Now move the slider and observe the changes on the continuous plot.

To set the y-axis limits in the continuous plot:

  1. Move you mouse over the y axis. You will see the lower and upper axis limits highlighted in yellow. Move your mouse inside the yellow box and press the left mouse button. This enters you into edit mode. You can now type a value and press enter.
  2. Set the y axis range to be:
    Minimum = -10
    Maximum = 10

2. RF Chooser

This shows how to use the MATLAB® ScriptTM block to control RF Envelopes instead of baseband signals. This example chooses between a few possible RF S-parameter files that represent channel rolloff in an older, channelized analog receiver front end. To start, run the RF_Chooser_DF2 analysis. Position your windows so you can see both the slider and the Dynamic Graphs window showing the two continuous plot: the raw time domain waveform and the associated spectrum. Move the slider to different switch positions to see the spectrum change in realtime, as different RF pre-select filters are engaged.

 

To set the y-axis limits in the continuous plot for the raw time domain data:

  1. See notes of Baseband Chooser on how to set the y axis limits.
  2. Set the y axis range to be:
    Minimum = 0.0
    Maximum = 0.02

To set the y-axis limits in the spectrum continuous plot:

  1. See notes of Baseband Chooser on how to set the y axis limits.
  2. Set the y axis range to be:
    Minimum = -40
    Maximum = -120

Workspace.Name: MATLAB Script and Analog Distortion
Workspace.Path: Model Building\MATLAB Script Modeling\MATLAB Script and Analog Distortion.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Discovering MATLABScript & Tuning

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Tutorial Workspace

 

This workspace explores an analog modeling task, with a couple ways to do real-time tuning. The MATLAB Script model itself is a simplistic amplifier model with asymmetric TANH(x) clipping and push-pull crossover distortion.

 

TUNING #1 - sliders

  • This method of tuning re-simulates the whole analysis interval <start,stop> with a new set of values of variables. 
  • Each simulation is independent of previous simulations, and therefore can have arbitrary complexity and include co-simulations.
  • Sliders are used for this example; they are found on the "Annotation" toolbar.  You can also use the "Tune Window" and change the values of tunable variables with up/down arrows, or realtime mousewheel movement.

TUNING #2 - realtime plots

  • By setting a checkbox in the sink to "Continuous Mode", the nature of the Dataflow analysis changes from a <start,stop> to an ongoing, neverending analysis.  A dynamic display window pops up with a black background.  The continuous mode of SystemVue allows you to make realtime adjustments to certain values while the simuation is running.
  • Try this:
    1. Start by manually running the DF2 simulation controller.  You can open the controller and press "Calculate Now", or right-click the DF2 object on the workspace tree
    2. Two realtime windows pop up, one for Time-domain, and one for Spectum.  For the Spectrum plot, you need to make 2 changes after the simulation is running in order to see a reasonable result.. 
      • First, right-click on the plot, and choose "Configure Axes".  Change the setting from "Real(I)" to "Log Mag (dB)", and press "OK"
      • Second, right-click again, and choose "Set Y-axis Limits".  Change the vertical scale to Top=50, Bottom=-150 , and press "OK".  You should at least see a double-sided spectrum.
    3. Stretch the corners of the realtime windows to make them smaller, then position the windows in a convenenient place to see both the schematic and the dynamic plots at the same time.  Move the sliders, and watch the real-time changes in the plots.
  • For full visualization capability when doing SystemVue realtime tuning, it is recommended that you install the Keysight 89600 VSA software (with options 105 and 200), which supports sophisticated markers, Time & Frequency phenomena, Spectrograms, and much more. To download this software and receive a 14-day trial license, go to http://www.keysight.com/find/vsa.

Workspace.Description:
MATLABScript Multirate Demo

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

 

This example demonstrates the use of the MATLAB Script model to perform multi-rate signal processing.

 

The two branches of the design are identical in functionality - what is achieved by using built-in system level parts in one branch is performed via equations in a single MATLAB Script part.

 

This design features the multi-rate programmability of the MATLAB Script model.

 

The FIR co-efficients and sampling rates are set in the Equations page associated with the MultiRateFilter (Schematic). These values are used both in the MATLAB Script and non-MATLAB Script paths.

 

A square waveform is modified by down-sampling 7:1, filtering and up-sampling 1:5 (sample & hold) in each case.

 

Note how the input and output sample rates of the MATLAB Script part are setup on the I/O tab to perform sampling and how the internal input side register is set up in the Equations tab to store and shift the incoming samples for fixed-length filtering. To modify the equations, simply double-click on the MATLAB Script part.

 

The input and output samples within the ;MATLAB® ScriptTM part are referred to by the named variables inputML and outputML.

 

As shown in the graph display MultiRateFilter_Graph, the results from both branches overlap proving that that the two branches are functionally identical.

Workspace.Name: SimulinkCosim
Workspace.Description:
MATLAB Simulink Cosimulation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This is a simple example of SystemVue cosimulating with a Simulink model.

 

The Simulink model is a single inport connected to a gain block to an outport. Such a simple model can be simulated using a discrete fixed-step solver, which allows single step cosimulation. A typical Simulink model will use an adaptive solver which is a bit more complicated, as it needs the initial state and an array input, but the general approach is similar. In the Data Import/Export dialog of the Simulink model's Configuration Parameters you can set the input, initial state, output and final state variables which are used to pass data to and from the Simulink model. You may also want to turn off the automatic solver parameter selection warning because the round-off differences between SystemVue and Simulink timestamps are inevitable.

 

Simulink model is simulated by calling the MATLAB function sim. Please consult the MATLAB documentation for details on using this function. In this particular case, the model is set to accept [t, u] array as input and place output in yout. The timestamp is not really used in this example, but when it is used setting the time step is very important, because otherwise sim will change the timestamp to match the default model parameters and produce wrong results.

 

Instead of open_system you may prefer to call load_system, because when the system is visible setting its parameters programmatically will mark it as modified and you will be asked whether you want to save changes.

 

Note that t and u variables are placed in the Simulink model workspace before sim is called.

Workspace.Name: IO_Customizations
Workspace.Description:
SystemC IO customizations

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace contains five designs that demonstrate the SystemVue - SystemC cosimulation flow, the range of datatypes supported as well as the support for two different SystemC predefined interfaces, sc_signal and sc_fifo.

One or more SystemC models, in the designs described below, contain Enumeration Custom Parameter(s). Before proceeding, user has to load the Enumeration Library that defines this(these) parameter(s) in SystemVue. To do so, user has to go to Tools --> Library Manager. The Library Manager dialog will open. Then, user should click "Add Library". Inside this workspace's directory, there is an xml file called SystemC Examples Enumeration Library. User must select and open this file. To finish, user should close the Library Manager window

 

The workspace has been split into five categories to cover different use cases. Every category contains a relevant design. A short description of each design is following: 

  • Adder design contains three template SystemC adders. Each adder works with different datatype (integer, double or fixed-point). It is a combinational logic example that demonstrates a portion of the diverse datatypes that SystemCCosim block supports. In Graph1, the difference in the precision of the results is presented.
  • FFT design contains a FFT SystemC model. In this model, both "sc_signal" and "sc_fifo" interfaces are being used. The SystemC model is being compared to a native FFT model for verification purposes. To acquire the same results, delay blocks have been used to synchronize the output timestamps. A verification of the correct functionality is demonstrated in Graph2.
  • FFT numeric design contains a pure numeric SystemC FFT model that operates exactly as the built-in SystemVue FFT model. This example demonstrates the use of complex types for ports as well as the multirate property (in this example port rate is defined to 256). A verification of the correct functionality is demonstrated in Graph3.
  • Downsampling Design demonstrates a possible use of the multirate property for "sc_signal" ports. The Downsampler SystemC model contains a "Phase" custom parameter that controls which of the input samples will be "sampled" and will be passed to the output. Initialy, Phase has been chosen such as to "sample" the first input value, at each firing. After running the example using different Phase values, the user will notice that, for Phase value greater than 0, the outputs produced by the "signal" model are one sample later than the input. This is happening because SystemCCosim block that uses "sc_signal" ports adds no latency to the time of the output samples in SystemVue. Thus, the value of a signal at time greater than the timestamp of the last output sample in one simulation cycle is postponed to the next cycle, if no other change happens to the value of the signal. Graph4 and Graph5 represent the input and the output signals, respectively.
  • DFF Design contains a synchronous D flip-flop (block DFF) and a "Pseudorandom Logic Vectors" generator. DFF is configured to have multirate ports. A subnetwork block "LogicVectorToInt" is converting the Logic Vector value to an integer value, for representation purposes. This example demonstrates the use of logic SystemC types. DFF needs a positive clock event (produced by W1) and a positive enable value ( produced by W2) in order to pass the input to the output. This example demonstrates how to obtain a greater detail of the DFF functionality by using a clock signal with higher Rate than the System Sample Rate. A visualization of the operation of the DFF is presented in Graph6.

 

The source code of all the examples is located inside the "source" directory. It resides at the same path as the current workspace.

Do not run this example from a Read-Only location. First, copy the current workspace (IO_Customizations.wsv) and the "source" folder in a location with write access and then open the workspace from that location.

 

For more information on "SystemC Cosimulation" consult SystemVue Documentation (under Simulation \ Cosimulation \ SystemC Cosimulation).

Workspace.Name: SystemC_Controller
Workspace.Description:
SystemC Controller

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace contains a SystemC design. Its purpose is to demonstrate the SystemC Model Library and SystemC Analysis feature of SystemVue. The demonstrated functionality is that of MCU that is wrapping messages into Frames (adding CRC and other control bits) and sends them serially through a noisy Bus Channel. Then a receiving MCU is trying to remove the control bits and read the message.  

 

This example is separated in two steps:

  1. Users must use the SystemC Model Library flow to generate the missing models of the design. The source code of the models is provided within the same directory as this workspace.
  2. Users can run the SystemC Analysis and observe the results. Users can also update the parameter values of the design through the Equations1 window to obtain different results.

Step 1:

  • Go to: Action > Create SystemC Models Library…
  • Fill the dialog:
    • For “Library Name” use “SystemC_Controller”.
    • Specify a “Location” where you have write-access
    • “Add” SystemC Files ( select all the files that exist in the “SystemC_Controller_models/include” and the "SystemC_Controller_models/source" directories, located in the directory of this workspace)
    • Click “Create”
  • When the SystemC Model Library process finishes, a library with the name “SystemC_Controller” should exist in the Part Selector A window on the right.

For more information on "SystemC Model Library" consult SystemVue Documentation (under Users Guide > Using SystemVue > User Defined Models > SystemC Models > SystemC Model Library).

 

Step 2:

  • Save the workspace in a location with write-access
  • Run the SystemC Analysis
  • Observe the results
    • The Bits Transmitted to the bus and the Bits Received from the bus are rendered in Graph 1.
    • The distortion of the transmitting signal through the bus is rendered in Graph 2.
    • The control signal from both MCUs are rendered in Graph 3.
    • The Results (transmitted messages - received correctly - received incorrectly) are displayed in table Results 

 

For more information on "SystemC Simulation" consult SystemVue Documentation (under Simulation \ SystemC ).

Workspace.Name: SystemC_FIR_Spectrum
Workspace.Description:
SystemC FIR Spectrum

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace contains a SystemC design. Its purpose is to demonstrate the SystemC Model Library and SystemC Analysis feature of SystemVue. The main models of the design are Sine Wave generators, a Clock models, a synchronous FIR model and a synchronous FFT model. Other models are also used to make the design functional (Constant Sources, Converters, Sinks). The demonstrated functionality is that of a sinusoidal signals that is passing through a low-pass FIR filter. Then the FFT module is used to obtain the frequency spectrum of the FIR output.

To create the sinusoidal signal, we use two Sine Wave generators (SystemC_SineGen built-in model) which are combined and amplified using arithmetic units (SystemC_ALU). Then, we add to the created sinusoidal signal random noise, using the SystemC_NoiseChannel model, before we pass it through the FIR filter (fir model). The output of the FIR is finally passed to the FFT model to produce the coefficients that will help us calculate the frequency spectrum.

 

This example is separated in two steps:

  1. Users must use the SystemC Model Library flow to generate the missing models of the design. The source code of the models is provided within the same directory as this workspace.
  2. Users can run the SystemC Analysis and observe the results. Users can also update the parameter values of the design through the Equations1 window to obtain different results.

Step 1:

  • Go to: Action > Create SystemC Models Library…
  • Fill the dialog:
    • For “Library Name” use “SystemC_Algorithmic”.
    • Specify a “Location” where you have write-access
    • “Add” SystemC Files ( select all the files exist in the “SystemC_FIR_Spectrum_models” folder at the same directory as this workspace)
    • Click “Create”
  • When the SystemC Model Library process finishes, a library with the name “SystemC_Algorithmic” should exist in the Part Selector A window on the right.

For more information on "SystemC Model Library" consult SystemVue Documentation (under Users Guide > Using SystemVue > User Defined Models > SystemC Models > SystemC Model Library).

 

Step 2:

  • Save the workspace in a location with write-access
  • Run the SystemC Analysis
  • Observe the results
    • The Sinusoidal Signal along with the additive noise is captured and rendered in Graph 1.
    • The output of the FIR model is rendered in Graph 2.
    • Using the post-processing mechanism provided by SystemVue, the output of the FFT is processed to produce the frequency spectrum of the resulting signal(Graph 4).

 

For more information on "SystemC Simulation" consult SystemVue Documentation (under Simulation \ SystemC ).
