Workspace.Name: SystemC_OFDM
Workspace.Description:
SystemC OFDM

Keysight Technologies SystemVue

 

 

This workspace is a simple implementation of the OFDM method with the use of SystemC blocks. To run this example, copy the workspace and the source folder to a location that you have write access.

 

The OFDM functionality is achieved through the serial connection of an "IFFT" module and a "Cyclic Prefix" one, both implemented in SystemC. The level of abstraction of this implementation is close to the RTL level as there are individual signals to implement a handshaking scheme between the modules.

 

More specifically:

  • A complex number generator is used to produce the inputs of the system ( relatively to the data created after a QAM modulation scheme ).
  • These inputs are stored inside the buffer* module and are only propagated to the IFFT module when the latter module is ready to read them ( "data_req" port of the IFFT module is '1' ).
  • The IFFT module calculates the Inverse Fast Fourier Transform of 16 complex samples. It only reads valid data (when "data_valid" is '1'). It writes the results at its output ports (realOut and imageOut). Every time that it outputs a valid sample, it waits for this to be acknowledged in order to proceed to the next one.
  • The Cyclic Prefix module reads 16 complex numbers from its inputs and copies the last 4 in the front as a prefix. Like the IFFT module, it only reads data when "valid" is '1' but also it acknowledges the correct reception of a sample by raising the "ack" value to high.
  • Finally, the unbuffer** modules are used to clean up the result values so that only the "valid" ones reach the sinks.  
  • Moreover, a built-in IFFT module is used for comparison purposes in the upper path of the system

The sizes of the SystemC IFFT and Cyclic Prefix modules cannot be changed from within the workspace. If someone wants to have different sizes, he should update the source code of the modules.

So for the IFFT module, open the [Workspace Directory]\source\fft\fft_ifft\FFT_DIF_rtl.h header file and change the value of the "c_uiFFTLength" constant (line 6) to another value (power of 2).

For the Cyclic Prefix one, open the [Workspace Directory]\source\Cyclic Prefix\CyclicPrefix_rtl.h header file and change the values of the "uiCPLength" constant (line 33) and the "uiInSamples" constant (line 34) for the prefix size and the symbol size, respectively.

  

*We use the buffer module/sub-system as a fifo module that only outputs a stored sample, when its control value goes to '1'. In order to achieve this, we use a Dynamic Pack and a MATLAB Script module. The Dynamic pack outputs one sample when the control value is '1', otherwise it outputs an empty matrix. Then the MATLAB Script module outputs zero and also sets the "valid" port to zero, when it reads an empty matrix, or the correct value and sets the "valid" port to high, in the other case.

**The unbuffer module/sub-system is used to "filter" the non-valid results. We use again a Dynamic Pack and a MATLAB Script module. Now, firstly the MATLAB Script module reads a sample and propagates it to its output port only if the value of the "data_valid" port is '1', otherwise it outputs an empty matrix. Then, the Dynamic Pack outputs a value only when its input is different from an empty matrix.

Workspace.Name: SystemC_Parameters_Passing
Workspace.Description:
SystemC Parameters Passing

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace contains three examples that use the SystemVue - SystemC cosimulation flow and demonstrate how to use custom parameters to pass values to SystemC models.

One or more SystemC models, in the designs described below, contain Enumeration Custom Parameter(s). Before proceeding, user has to load the Enumeration Library that defines this(these) parameter(s) in SystemVue. To do so, user has to go to Tools --> Library Manager. The Library Manager dialog will open. Then, user should click "Add Library". Inside this workspace's directory, there is an xml file called SystemC Examples Enumeration Library. User must select and open this file. To finish, user should close the Library Manager window

  • In the Adder design there are three SystemCCosim blocks that implement the SystemC model of a template Adder. The data type of the addition depends on the template parameter of the Adder. So for an addition between integers (see block Adder_Int), the "SystemC Module" name should be Template_Adder<int>, where Template_Adder is the name of the module. After you run the simulation, open the Adder_graph to realize the differences in the precision between the integer and the double(or float) curves. 
  • In the FFT_parameters_passing design there are two SystemC FFT blocks. Inside the "Custom Prameters" page of the User Interface of the blocks, two extra parameters have beed added - apart from the default "ModuleName" parameter - the FFTsize and the FFTtype, which define the size and the type (FFT or IFFT) of the FFT, respectively, as their names imply. The user can notice the use of text (ModuleName), number (FFTsize) and enumeration (FFTtype) parameters. After you run the simulation, open the graphs FFT_16 and FFT_32 to verify that the results are identical to the ones of the built-in FFT models of SystemVue.
  • Finally, in the FIR design there is the block of a SystemC FIR model. This design demonstrates the use of an array parameter, as the coefficients of the model are determined by an integer array custom parameter called "Coefficients".

You can find the source code of all the examples inside the "source" folder which is located at the directory as the current workspace.

Do not run this example from a Read-Only location. First, copy the current workspace (SystemC_Parameters_Passing.wsv) and the "source" folder in a location that you have write access and then open the workspace from that location.

 

All the examples are set up and ready to play. You just have to run the simulations in each case.

For more information on "SystemC Cosimulation" consult SystemVue Documentation (under Simulation \ Cosimulation \ SystemC Cosimulation).

Workspace.Name: PLL_Osc_Design
Workspace.Description:
Oscillator Phase Lock Loop Design and Performance

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This is a template that sets up a phase lock loop (PLL) for a noisy RF oscillator by phase locking it a low noise crystal oscillator and shows the PLL loop filter response, PLL step response, PLL closed loop swept frequency response, and reduction of the noisy oscillator noise that is close in to the carrier within the defined PLL closed loop bandwidth.

 

PLL Design Setup:

The design is set up by setting variables in the Equation1 sheet.  The design is for a 2nd order phase type 1 phase lock loop.

 

In the Equation1 page set these RF parameters:

RF_Freq = the RF oscillator frequency.

DivN = the frequency divider integer value.  The reference crystal oscillator will have the frequency RF_Freq/DivN.

 

In the Equation1 page set these control loop parameters:

BW = Closed loop bandwidth in Hz.
NZ = Normalized zero for the PLL.
DF = Damping factor for the PLL.
PDGC = Phase detector gain constant, volts/deg
KV = VCO tuning sensitivity, Hz/volt

Once these values are set the rest of the simulations are set up automatically.  This includes the simulation sample rate and stop time.  The number of simulation points is preset to 2^12.

 

The Equation1 sheet also shows derived 2nd order PLL responses based on PLL theory.  These theoretical PLL responses include:

  • BWn = Closed loop noise bandwidth, Hz
  • FP = closed loop frequency for maximum gain, Hz
  • AP_dB = maximum closed loop gain in dB at frequency FP
  • PO = Step response percent overshoot
  • Tmax = Step response time to maximum overshoot

The preset design is set with:

RF_Freq = 320 MHz

DivN = 8;  this implies that the crystal oscillator is at 40 MHz.

BW = 100 Hz.
NZ = 1.
DF = 1/sqrt(2).
PDGC = 0.1*pi/180
KV = BW

 

Loop Filter Response:

With the PLL Design Setup defined above, the resultant loop filter response is evaluated.  See the folder 'Loop Filter Response'.

 

The design is 'LoopFilter_test' with associated analysis and data 'LoopFilter_Analysis' and 'LoopFilter_Data'.

 

This PLL loop filter pole and zero frequencies are designed based on the PLL specifications for BW, DF, and NZ.  Additionally, the gain of the loop filter is defined based on the amount of gain external to this filter.  The loop filter is a subnetwork model named LoopFilter with parameters NormalizedZero, DampingFactor, BW and ExternalGain.

 

The preset design values for NormalizedZero, DampingFactor, and BW are shown above.  The present value for ExternalGain is derived in the Equation1 page as variable ExtG.

 

The loop filter gain versus frequency is shown in graph 'LoopFilter_Gain_vs_Freq'.

 

For the preset values, the loop filter has a low frequency gain of 41.8 dB, a pole at about 15 Hz, a zero at about 150 Hz and a high frequency gain of 34.2 dB.

 

Note that though the closed loop bandwidth, BW, is preset to 100 Hz, the required loop filter pole is about 15 Hz.

 

PLL Step Response:

With the PLL Design Setup defined above, the resultant loop step response is evaluated.  See the folder 'PLL Step Response'.

 

The design is 'PLL_StepResponse' with associated analysis and data 'StepResp_Analysis' and 'StepResp_Data'.

 

The PLL design is defined to control the oscillator/modulator combination with instance names RF_Osc and RF_Osc_Modulator.  The RF_Osc is operating at frequency RF_Freq defined in the Equation1 page  is an input to the RF_Osc_Modulator.  The output of the RF_Osc_Modulator is routed to a frequency divider, FreqMpyDiv, with frequency division ratio DivN defined in the Equation1 page.  The FreqMpyDiv output is an input to the PhaseComparator whose other input is from another Modulator that serves as the PLL reference signal at frequency RF_Freq/DivN.  This reference Modulator has a frequency step applied to its as a square wave at its frequency control input.

 

As the reference oscillator frequency has a step in frequency, the PLL will drive the RF_Osc_Modulator to have the same frequency step, but with dynamics controlled by the PLL Design Setup defined above.

 

The loop step response is shown in graph 'Step_Response'.

 

For the preset values, the Equation1 page shows that the theoretical step percent overshoot (PO) expected is 10.7% and the time at which the peak overshoot is expected is at 5.9e-3 sec.

 

From the graph 'Step_Response', the simulated percent overshoot is 11.4% and the time at which the peak overshoot occurs is at 6.0e-3 sec.

 

Thus, the simulated PLL step response performance agrees quite closely to the expected theoretical values.

 

PLL Swept Freq Response:

With the PLL Design Setup defined above, the resultant closed loop frequency response is evaluated.  See the folder 'PLL Swept Freq Response'.

 

The design is 'PLL_FreqResponse' with associated analysis and data 'FreqResp_Analysis' and 'FreqResp_Data' and associated sweep and data 'Sweep1' and 'Sweep1_Data'.

 

The PLL design is essentially the same as the one defined in the PLL_StepResponse design, but with a swept sinusoid modulating the frequency of the reference modulator instead of a frequency step.  The sinusoid frequency is defined by variable FNom in the Equation2 page.

 

The swept sinusoid is achieved by use of the Sweep1 evaluation which sweeps the sinusoid frequency logarithmically from FNomStart to FNomStop.

 

The Equation2 sheet is used to set FNom.  It typically is set to a value within the loop bandwidth.  BW/10 is the recommended value.  This value needs to be manually set by the user since SystemVue does not allow FNom to be set to an expression if it is to be tuned and used in the Sweep1.

 

The Equation3 sheet contains functions used in the Equation2 and Equation3 sheets.

 

The Equation4 sheet contains expressions that extract the closed loop frequency response from the Sweep1_Data.

 

The closed loop frequency response is shown in graph 'ClosedLoop_SweptFreqResponse'.

 

For the preset values, the Equation1 page shows that the theoretical closed loop frequency which has the maximum amplitude (FP) is expected to be 41.4 Hz and this occurs with maximum amplitude (AP_dB) expected as 0.8 dB.

 

From the graph 'ClosedLoop_SweptFreqResponse', the simulated maximum closed loop frequency is 41.7 Hz and this has the maximum amplitude of 0.9 dB.

 

Thus, the simulated PLL closed loop frequency response performance agrees quite closely to the expected theoretical values.

 

PLL Osc Noise Response:

With the PLL Design Setup defined above, and with the PLL design verified in the tests for 'Loop Filter Response', 'PLL Step Response' and 'PLL Swept Freq Response', a noise oscillator at frequency RF_Freq can be used in a PLL with a low noise reference oscillator at RF_Freq/8 to clean up the RF_Freq noise close in to the carrier within the PLL closed loop 3dB bandwidth (BW).  See the folder 'PLL Osc Noise Response'.

 

The design is 'PLL_Osc_Response' with associated analysis and data 'PLL_Osc_Analysis' and 'PLL_Osc_Data'.

 

The PLL design is essentially the same as the one defined in the PLL_StepResponse design, but with a constant low noise oscillator at RF_Freq/DivN used as the reference oscillator for the RF_Freq oscillator/modulator.

 

The RF_Freq oscillator is defined with phase noise.  The objective of the PLL is to clean up the close in phase noise within the closed loop bandwidth.

 

The oscillator RF spectrums are shown in graph 'PLL_Osc_SpecOutRF_Power'.

 

The blue curve is the RF spectrum for the original RF_Freq oscillator.  Note the phase noise about the RF carrier, especially close in to the carrier.

The red curve is the RF spectrum with the PLL applied and referenced to the low noise oscillator.  Note that the phase noise is reduced close to the RF carrier within the defined closed loop bandwidth.

 

The graph 'PLL_SpecOut_Power' shows the single sided spectrum with the carrier at DC.  This graph shows more clearly the noise reduction due to the use of the PLL and low noise oscillator.

Workspace.Name: EA_Deception_jamming
Workspace.Description:
Simulation Template for Generating EW Deception

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace as a template shows how to generate EW deception signals including RGPO and VGPO.  

A RADAR_EW_Jamming model is in the design1.

A radar, in order to maintain range track on a target, has an early gate and a late gate that are centered on the return pulse reflected from the target. The radar determines the range to the target by centering the division between these two gates on the return pulse, equalizing the energy in the two gates. If the target moves farther away, the round-trip time for the pulse will increase. The deceptive jammer transmits a stronger pulse synchronized with the pulse it receives from the radar. Then the jammer delays its pulse, gradually increasing the amount of delay. The radar sees more energy in its late gate and delays the early/late border out to compensate. Eventually the radar’s resolution cell moves completely away from the target. This causes the radar to lose lock on the target. If the user wants to generate RGPO deception, the Jamming Type is set to Jamming Deception and the DeceptionType is set to Range Pull. 

If the user wants to generate VGPO deception, the Jamming Type is set to Jamming Deception and the DeceptionType is set to Velocity Pull.  In this case it is better to make sure the VSA_Sink is activated to observe the VGPO jamming.

 

[1] David Adamy, Introduction to Electronic Warfare Modeling and Simulation (Artech House Radar Library) (2002)

Workspace.Name: EA_jamming
Workspace.Description:
EW Jamming

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example workspace include 4 designs to demonstrate how to generate cover jamming with EW_Jamming models in the radar library.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

The object of cover jamming is to reduce the quality of the signal output from the enemy receiver. Noise modulation is normally used for the jammer because it fills the entire bandwidth of the receiver and reduces the signal to noise ratio (SNR) in the output, causing the same effect as a reduction in the desired signal power. This may prevent an operator from determining that jamming is taking place. Cover jamming is almost always used for communication jamming and is typically used by standoff radar jammers. Although a skilled operator can often read through the noise to track a target return, it may become impossible for the radar processor to automatically track a target. This will have the desirable effect (from the jammer’s point of view) of reducing the number of targets that can be engaged by a weapon system. Thus, the defense network can be more easily saturated.

These 4 types jamming are:

  1. Barrage cover jamming generates the AWGN noise which mean and stdev values are determined by the parameters Mean and Stdev in the full band width. The simplest type of cover jamming is called barrage jamming. It fills a wide frequency spectrum with noise. It covers every frequency at which the communication radio or radar might be operating. The problem with this type of jamming is that most of its power is wasted. Only the noise that falls within the enemy receiver’s operating band actually contributes to the J/S. However, the advantage in barrage jamming is that you don’t need to know very much about the signal or signals you are jamming.
  2. Spot cover jamming generates the band-limited AWGN noise and the normalized bandwidth is determined by the parameter Bandwidth. If you know the enemy’s operating frequency, you can narrow the jamming noise around that frequency. In the case of a monostatic radar, this information is available if you receive the radar transmissions. One problem, of course, is that it is very hard to receive a communication or radar signal while you are jamming it, since you will be jamming your own (presumably much closer) receiver more effectively than you will be jamming the enemy receiver. Because the enemy may tune the communication radio or radar to avoid jamming (or improve signal quality even though the jamming is not detected), you need to have a look-through scheme. There are several clever schemes to optimize look-through, but sooner or later you will have to turn off the jammer for a short time while you receive the signal you are jamming. This means that the enemy will receive a few unjammed pulses or get a short period of unjammed communication. There needs to be a satisfactory compromise between jamming and looking to optimize jammer performance.
  3. Multi-spot cover jamming generates band-limited AWGN noise in the several sub-bands which are determined by the parameter MultiSpotBand which can be used to set up the normalized start and cut-off frequencies of several pass-band.
  4. Swept-spot cover jamming generates the band-limited AWGN noise which can sweep in the scope of full band. The sweep rate can be decided by the parameter SweepFreqStep. A compromise noise-jamming technique is to transmit noise over less than the full band that the enemy might be using but to sweep that narrow band across the whole range. This means that the enemy will definitely get some unjammed pulses, but it may prevent the automatic tracking of targets, causing the enemy to use manual tracking by expert operators. This will make the defense network subject to saturation.

[1] David Adamy, Introduction to Electronic Warfare Modeling and Simulation (Artech House Radar Library) (2002)

Workspace.Name: ES_Channelized
Workspace.Description:
Channelized

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example contains 3 designs. The ChannelizedRx design demonstrates a full band wideband digital receiver based on channelized technique which includes polyphase filter and FFT. The ChannelizedTx design demonstrates one multi-channels transmitter which is composed of channelized polyphase structure and FFT technique. The ChannelizedTxRx design demonstrates one multi-channels transmitter and one channelized receiver. The wideband channelized transmitter and wideband channelized receiver are widely used in the EW field.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

In the ChannelizedRx design, the receiver works at 1.024GSps, so it can receive the signals in the band from 0-500MHz simultaneously. The full band is divided into 8 sub-channels, each channel's filter characteristics are:

1. -1dB bandwidth: 64MHz

2. -40dB bandwidth: 128MHz

3. ripple in passband: <0.1dB

4. stopband attenuation: >40dB

5. Filter length is 255(coefficient number is 256)

The input signal is 10MHz real signal, so the spectrum of output includes two spectral lines at 1344 and 704 position.

The frequency of output signal computation is as follows:1.024e9/8/4096 * (1344-704)/2 = 10e6;(The sampling rate is 1.024Gsps, the observation length is 4096 samples)

 

In the ChannelizedTx design, there is one top level design in this workspace:

l  This structure is a standard multi-channels digital polyphase channelized transmitter structure.

l  To transmit 8 channel signals (the channels number can be up to thousands).

l  The channelized filter uses the polyphase structure to decrease the computing resource.

The output will show the 8 channels spectrum diagram.

 

In the ChannelizedTxRx design, there is one top level design which includes one channelized transmitter and one channelized receiver in this workspace. The spectrum of the output of transmitter and receiver can be observed with spectrum diagram and VSA 89600.

Workspace.Name: ES_DOA
Workspace.Description:
EW DOA Detection Workspace

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example workspace shows three typical designs in EW (Electronic Warfare) DOA (Direction Of Arrival) detections using different algorithms. The DOA design is used to estimate the number of interference signals and all possible arriving directions.

There are several classical algorithms for DOA detection. MUSIC and ESPRIT algorithms are used to find the 1-D DOA in the RADAR_DOA (built-in model). The angle will output at Elevation port. For 2-D DOA estimation, the MUSIC-2D algorithm is used.

The first folder, EW_DOA proposes DOA estimation using the built-in RADAR_DOA model and the 1D ESPRIT DOA algorithm.

The second folder, EW_ESPRIT design demonstrates an ESPRIT DOA detection algorithm in MathLang model. ESPRIT is the abbreviation of Estimation of Signal Parameters via Rotation Invariance Techniques.

The third folder, EW_MUSIC workspace demonstrates a DOA algorithm named MUSIC and it is widely used in the EW field. MUSIC is the abbreviation of MUltiple SIgnal Classification.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

All the three examples in this workspace use the coordinate setup as:

(1)  EW receiver antenna aperture on XOY plane (boresight pointing to +Z direction);

(2)  Phi values are all 0 deg (theta sweeping on XOZ plane);

(3)  Theta is regarded as azimuth angle (boresight theta = 0 deg).

The detailed example notes are proposed below:

(1) EW_DOA Example

In this design, three signals from three predefined DOA angles are generated as three isolated interferences, and after directional phase shifts, they are combined and fed into RADAR_DOA model. The 3 azimuth theta angles are -30, 0 and 20 degs (all the azimuth angles are distinguishable).

The RADAR_DOA model angle measurement type is selected as ESPRIT, which is 1D angle estimation. In other words, ONLY the azimuth angle output is valid. The 3 radar sources have different pulse width (20e-6, 20e-6, 10e-6), the sample rate is 50e6, So the first snapshot 1024, the model RADAR_DOA captures the combined 3 pulses, and the 1st data of RADAR_DOA Azimuth is 3*1 array (-30,20,0) deg. This time slot refers to the 1st pulse width samples (20e-6*50e6 = 1000) The detected DOA results are matched to the specified DOA angles. The next 4*1024 samples’ duration is approximately the pulse idle time, so the corresponding data of Azimuth is NOT useful (meaningless DOAs are reported). For the 6th time sample in Azimuth, the model RADAR_DOA captures the 3 pulse again, and the DOA output is 3*1 array (-30,20,0) deg as specified.

The final DOA results require further statistical processing and sorting.

(2) EW_ESPRIT Example

Three interference signals from distinguishable azimuth angles (DOAs of 3*1 array (-30, -10, 20) deg) are generated in the example using RADAR_PhaseShift model. The ESPRIT algorithm is realized with MathLang script model with input on a SnapShot-by-SnapShot basis.

The estimated DOA results are displayed using post processed DOA results.        

(3) EW_MUSIC Example

Three interference signals from distinguishable azimuth angles (DOAs of 3*1 array (-30, -10, 20) deg) are generated in the example using RADAR_PhaseShift model. The MUSIC algorithm is realized with MathLang script model with input on a SnapShot-by-SnapShot basis, by the theta “sweep and search” method. Theta search range is from -40 to +40 deg.

The estimated DOA results are displayed using post processed DOA results from the theta sweep-and-search results.

 

NOTE:  More about SnapShotLength

SnapShotLength is one core parameter in DOA detection algorithms. It is defined as the time-slot or sample number that the virtual EW receiver captures the hostile radar signal.

In this example, we define the SnapShotLength as the capture sample number (1024), which is near to the pulse width sample number (1000) but NOT identical. In real EW receiver systems, this parameter would be defined by the system designer.

Workspace.Name: ES_DRFM_SingleChannel
Workspace.Description:
DRFM Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example introduces a single channel DRFM concept and the target echo signal and interference signal will be seen in the result.

The concept of a DRFM is simple. DRFM implementation required a number of technological advances before it could become a very effective device. Its function is the coherent storage (for ideally an infinite amount of time) of the threat signal both for its coherent reproduction as well as for its manipulation (in time delay and frequency content) by means of digital techniques in order to provide deceptive returns to the threat.

DRFM has many applications in the EW domain, such as

• Radar/communication signal storage for subsequent ELINT/COMINT analyses;

• Deception of covert communications;

• Jamming operations;

• Anti-ARM decoys replicating radar signals;

• Radar signal generation for simulation and test equipment. 

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

DRFM (Digital Radio Frequency Memory) technology is widely used in the EW field. The interference signal based on DRFM is coherent with radar signal.

The DRFM receive path is very similar to a conventional superheterodyne receiver with regard to the rejection of spurious signals. At the device RF input, a bandpass filter (BPF) followed by an amplifier are used to pass and amplify only the signals of interest. The RF intercepted signal is downconverted to baseband by a LO. A lowpass filter (LPF) removes the aliasing frequency components above the Nyquist rate and the unwanted mixer intermodulation products. The digital samples are recorded into a high-speed dual-ported memory so that the stored signal can be replayed simultaneously through memory control. Recording in the dual-ported memory usually requires the use of a serial-to-parallel circuitry at input to reduce the conversion data rate in order to match the dual-ported memory’s input bandwidth. Replay of the stored signal vice versa requires a parallel-to-serial circuitry at output to match the dual-ported memory’s output bandwidth. The retrieved digital signal from memory is fed to a DAC followed by a LPF in order to reproduce the analog signal. The baseband signal is then mixed with the same LO used in the downconversion in order to reconstitute the RF signal. The RF output is then passed through a BPF to provide the transmitter section with only the desired signal spectrum.
[1] De Martino, Andrea, Introduction to modern EW systems-Artech House (2018)

Workspace.Name: Clutter_Statistical_Modeling
Workspace.Description:
Statistical Clutter Modeling Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example demonstrates how to apply statistical distribution based clutter modeling for SystemVue radar library.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Clutter refers to radio frequency (RF) echoes returned from targets which are of no-interest to the radar operators. Generally clutter is caused by environmental factors such as sea, terrain, vegetation cover, etc. By traditional radar clutter theories, clutter could be modeled by several types of statistical models and add into the received echo.

 

For this workspace, the clutter modeling methodology is proposed as:

1. A statistical model is set up to simulate the real world clutter.

2. The clutter has certain magnitude probability density functions and power spectrum densities.

 

This workspace contains two folders to demonstrate different aspects in statistical clutter modeling:

 

1, Clutter statistical distribution:

 

This example helps the user to understand how to generate statistical distribution based clutter using the ClutterGen part.

 

The generated envelop clutter signal is transformed to complex baseband then gathered to see their corresponding statistical distribution functions.

 

If the clutter amplitude follows K-distribution, Design2 Analysis proposes the PDF with K distribution clutter data generation. The Ref_Dist_MATLAB equation applies 3 methods to generate the K-distribution curves with identical results shown in "PDF_K-RefCompare" figure. The generated K-distributed clutter is shown in "PDF_K" figure.  

 

If the clutter amplitude follows other distribution types, Sweep1 invokes Design4 Analysis to demonstrate LogNormal, RayLeigh, Weibull for amplitude PDF data generation, and their PSD definitions are AllPole, Cauchy and Gauss based distributions, respectively.

 

By equation file vars_graph (Automatic calculation DISABLED), the clutter data generation results by Sweep1 are compared with standard PDF/PSD distribution curves for each PDF/PSD type.

 

2, Clutter generation with Targets 

 

This example demonstrates how to add clutter impacts into multi-target detection scenarios.

 

The traditional LFM source and transmitter with RF impariments are implemented, and three targets are designed in this example. Clutter modeling is performed with Radar_Clutter subnet, with Clutter_H and DelayEnv parts inside to simulate the clutter doppler frequency change and target echo delay effects (2*Range/C). The clutter power, clutter-to-signal power ratio modeling methods are shown in the equation of Design3 schematic.

 

The three-target echoes and clutter are added together then output to Sink and Spectrum Analyzer. If clutter is ENABLED (using s(1:4) for input port of AddEnv), then the target-2 echo amplitude is much higher than when clutter is DISABLED (using s(1:3) for input port of AddEnv).

 

Note:

For all the examples shown in this workspace, statistical clutter generation can only be applied with one specific set of range/doppler group. In other words, the generated clutter is ONLY applicable to ONE INTERESTED TARGET ONLY. For other targets or scatter groups, the clutter range/doppler must be redesigned and re-run simulation to see their impacts again.

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

  

************************************************

************************************************

This example workspace shows how to generate the Barker Code and its auto-correlation function.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

  • Biphase Barker codes exhibit a peak sidelobe to mainlobe voltage ratio of 1: N, where N is the code length. 
  • The peak sidelobe ratio is defined in terms of power and is expressed as 20 log10(1/N). The Barker codes achieve the lowest possible PSR for an aperiodic code.
  • The longest known Barker code is length 13 with a corresponding peak sidelobe ratio of -22.3 dB.
  • It has been shown that no odd length biphase Barker sequence exists longer than length 13. No even-length sequences have been found above length 4.
  • The example shows a Barker pulse train with parameters as, SubPulsewidth=1us, PRI=100us, CodeLength=13, BB_SamplingRate=10MHz.

Workspace.Name: Channelized_Rx
Workspace.Description:
Channelized Wideband Receiver

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

In this example, a technique is described for building a highly efficient full-band wideband digital receiver based on the polyphase filter and FFT structure.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

The receiver works at 1.024GSps, so it can receive the signals in the band from 0-500MHz simultaneously. The full band is divided into 8 sub-channels, each channel's filter characteristics are:

1. -1dB bandwidth : 64MHz

2. -40dB bandwidth: 128MHz

3. ripple in passband: <0.1dB

4. stopband attenuation: >40dB

5. Filter length is 255(coefficient number is 256)

The input signal is 10MHz real signal, so the spectrum of output includes two spectral lines at 1344 and 704 position.

The frequency of output signal computation is as follows:

1.024e9/8/4096 * (1344-704)/2 = 10e6;

(The sampling rate is 1.024Gsps, the observation length is 4096 samples)

This example workspace demonstrates one multi-channels transmitter which is composed of channelized polyphase structure and FFT technique. The wideband channelized transmitter and wideband channelized receiver are widely used in the EW field.

************************************************

Workspace Description

Workspace.Name: FrankCode
Workspace.Description:
Radar Frank and Polyphase Signal Generation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace shows how to generate Frank signal and polyphase signal with RADAR_Frank model and their ACF(auto-corrleation function).

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

In 1963, R. L. Frank devised a polyphase code that is closely related to the linear frequency modulation and Barker codes. The Frank code has recently been used successfully in LPI radars. The Frank code is derived from a step approximation to a linear frequency modulation waveform using M frequency steps and M samples per frequency. The Frank code has a length or processing gain of Nc = M*M. For FrankCode example, the PRI is 64us, the SubPulseWidth is 1us, M is 8(Nc = 64), the sampling rate is 4Msps.

 

The P1 code is also generated using a step approximation to a linear frequency modulation waveform. For example, the PRI is 64us, the SubPulseWidth is 1us, M is 8(Nc = 64), the sampling rates is 4Msps.

 

For the P2 code M even, the phase increment within each phase group is the same as the P1 code, except that the starting phases are different. For example, the PRI is 64us, the SubPulseWidth is 1us, M is 8(Nc = 64), the sampling rate is 4Msps.

 

The P3 code is conceptually derived by converting a linear frequency modulation waveform to baseband, by using a synchronous oscillator on one end of the frequency sweep (single sideband detection), and sampling the I and Q video at the Nyquist rate (first sample of I and Q taken at the leading edge of the waveform).  For example, the PRI is 64us, the SubPulseWidth is 1us, M is 64(Nc = 64), the sampling rate is 4Msps.

 

The P4 code is conceptually derived from the same linear frequency modulation waveform as the P3 code, except that the local oscillator frequency is offset in the I and Q detectors, resulting in coherent double sideband detection. For example, the PRI is 64us, the SubPulseWidth is 1us, M is 64(Nc = 64), the sampling rates is 4Msps.

Workspace.Name: PolyTimeCode
Workspace.Description:
PolyTimeCode

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace demonstrates how T1(n), T2(n), T3(n) and T4(n) code generate and the generated phase state and their autocorrelation result are given in this example.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

The Frank, P1, P2, P3, and P4 codes were developed by approximating a stepped frequency or linear frequency modulation waveform, where the phase steps vary as needed to approximate the underlying waveform, and the time spent at any given phase state is a constant.

 

Another approach to approximating a stepped frequency or linear frequency modulation waveform is to quantize the underlying waveform into a user-selected number of phase states. In this case, the time spent at each phase state changes throughout the duration of the waveform. The code sequences that use fixed phase states with varying time periods at each phase state are given the name polytime coding.

 

Two types of polytime coded waveforms can be generated from the stepped frequency model and are denoted as T1(n) and T2(n), where n is the number of phase states used to approximate the underlying waveform.

The T3(n) and T4(n) polytime sequences are approximations to a linear frequency modulation waveform.

 

Increasing the number of phase states increases the quality of the polytime approximation to the underlying waveform, but also reduces the time spent at any given phase state, complicating the generation of the waveform. The phase state (or bit) durations change as a function of time. The minimum bit duration sets the waveform bandwidth.

 In an FSK radar, the transmitted frequency fj is chosen from the FH sequence {f1, f2, . . . , fNF } of available frequencies for transmission at a set of consecutive time intervals {t1, t2, . . . , tNF }. The frequencies are placed in the various time slots corresponding to a binary time-frequency matrix. The Costas example shows how to generate the Costas signal with the frequency sequence fj = {2, 4, 8, 5, 10, 9, 7, 3, 6, 1} * 2e5 Hz.

The hybrid FSK/PSK example shows how to generate the hybrid FSK and PSK signal with frequency sequence = [2,4,8,5,10,9,7,3,6,1]*2e5 and the PSK code is Barker code with the length of 13 code.

Workspace.Name: ADBF
Workspace.Description:
Adaptive Beamforming Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example demos how to use RADAR_ADBF model to estimate the weights with received signal samples across all receiving channels (with "guessed" incoming signal directions), and the weights are fed into RADAR_DBF to implement digital beamforming, realizing adaptive beamforming for jamming suppression purposes.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

In this example, we designed two incoming signals from different directions: one interested signal from theta = 30 deg, while the other jammer signal is from theta = 60 deg. Both signal directions are designed by Phased Array Antenna Rx models (RADAR_PhasedArrayRx).

 

The combined signal is imported into RADAR_ADBF which is applied to generate the adaptive estimated weights for all receiver channels. The adaptive Rx weights are divided into two paths:

 

1) For the upper path, we designed a theta sweep mathlang block which displays the ADBF results in theta-pattern format;

 

2) For the lower path, we need to realign the weights for RADAR_DBF model.

Firstly, we use the commutator block to align the signal on a Rx channel group basis. That is, for instance, we have 16 channels, then the complex beam weights are aligned by the weights of the first 16-Rx group, and then a second 16-Rx group, and so on. In the corresponding sink data limit, we set to 10 such groups.

Then, we use the PRI data length (NumSamp_PRI) to upsample (repeating) the regrouped weights to fit the length of PRI. After that, we apply the distributor to rescale the output weights on a PRI-by-PRI basis, to fit the input data length requirement of RADAR_DBF block.

 

With the adaptive beamforming design described above, the desired steering direction can be set to near to the real interested direction. In this example we propose 35 deg, and both the ADBF theta-sweep pattern and the DBF output signal have shown imperfect suppression of jamming signal. (If the user tries setting the ADBF desired theta direction to = 30 deg, then the jammer would be perfectly suppressed.)

 

NOTE:

Desired Beamforming Direction Setting

The angle of interested direction can be set with parameter Theta (elevation angle in antenna frame) and Phi (azimuth angle in antenna frame) when input ports el and az are not connected. When they are connected, the angle values in the parameter are disabled and the angles are decided by the input angle values.

Workspace.Name: Radar_PhasedArray_DataFlow
Workspace.Description:
Radar DataFlow Phased Array Simulation Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example proposes radar system simulation with DataFlow phased array antenna designs. The traditional 3-layer architecure is applied with one target and one monostatic radar.

 

For phased array modeling, the pointing angle defined beam weights are calculated by the BeamformerWeights parts and transferred to DataFlow Tx and Rx beamforming channels. Then the Tx envelop signal is transported to the Air Interface parts. The PhasedArray Tx and Rx parts are applied to transform the signal from Tx channel number sizing to target number sizing, then back to Rx channel number (in this example is equal to Tx channel number). After the virtual PhasedArrayTx, EchoGenerator and PhasedArrayRx, the signal sizing is transformed back to Rx channel number and the Rx beamforming is performed.

 

The RF impairment modeling configurations are realized in the equation "SystemLevel_RFImpair_Params". The global RF impairment modeling "Switch" is shown at the top, while the following parts gives the parameter settings for "No RF Impairment" and "With RF Impairment". This is proposed to the user as a template to setup his/her own system-level RF impairment schematic.

 

The Tx waveformed is designed as simplified LFM, and signal processing chain is realized by pulse compression and PD. The range-doppler matrix and PD result are presented. The filtering incurred delay compensations (Const + ChopVarOffset after pulse compression part) are bypassed, since without filters in dataflow design no additional delays are involved.

 

The SystemLevel_Parameters equation provides all system level parameters, including phased array design parameters. After all simulations are done, the Equation_ResultPlots equation helps the user to plot the RD map and PD result figures.

 

Folders in this workspace:

  • 1. Coupling 8*8 Case 
    • Defines an optional Tx element-to-element coupling design
  • 2. Radar_PhasedArray_Link
    • Defines the system level radar design by "RadarSys_Main" schematic.
    • Contains intermediate signal plots in various connection points.

 

About Element-to-Element Coupling

 

In an NxN matrix of array elements, the "ArrayCoupling_M" matrix allows you to specify the coupling coefficients from every element to every other element.  For an 8x8 rectangular array, this is a 64x64 mathematical matrix.  In Dataflow, this coefficient has no physical basis, it is strictly a matrix operation.

 

However, the coefficients can be harvested from an S-parameter matrix of the driving point impedances of the antenna manifold in an EM simulator.  In this example, an 8x8 array of microstrip patches was solved in Keysight Momentum, and then exported to an .SNP file.  This file was imported into this workspace, and the off-diagonal elements converted to the coefficients needed for this Dataflow analysis. 


This allows the coupling to have a more physical basis.

Workspace.Name: Radar_PhasedArray_SpectraSysRFLink
Workspace.Description:
Radar Spectrasys RFLink Phased Array Simulation Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 


This example proposes radar system simulation with Spectrasys PhasedArray RFLink based designs. The traditional 3-layer architecure is applied with one target and one monostatic radar. From the perspective of RF phased array modeling method, one Basic design (using Spectrasys built-in RF phased array parts) and one advanced (using Spectrasys RF phased array parts + ADI ADAR1000 chipset parametric designs) are proposed. For this workspace, the 8*8 for both Tx and Rx phased array designs are presented.

 

For both design methods, phased array pointing angle defined beam weights are calculated by the BeamformerWeights parts and transferred to the Spectrasys RF_Link phased array channels. Then the Tx envelop signal is transported to the Air Interface parts (inside magenta blocks) to regroup the signal from Tx channel sizing to target number sizing. After the virtual PhasedArrayTx, EchoGenerator and PhasedArrayRx, the signal sizing is transformed back to Rx channel number and the Rx beamforming is performed.

 

The Tx waveformed is designed as simplified LFM, and signal processing chain is realized by pulse compression and PD. The range-doppler matrix and PD result are presented. The filtering incurred delay compensations (Const + ChopVarOffset after pulse compression part) are bypassed, since without filters in dataflow design no additional delays are involved.

 

The SystemLevel_Parameters equation provides all system level parameters, including phased array design parameters. After all simulations are done, the Equation_ResultPlots_Basic or _Advanced equation helps the user to plot the RD map and PD result figures.

 

Folders in this workspace:

  • 1. Result_Figures_Advanced
    • Contains RD Matrix and PD result for Advanced phased array design simulation using ADAR1000 beamforming chipset parameters.
    • These figures are obtained by enabling the "bigger" phased array RF_Link part in the RadarSys_Main schematic in SystemDesign_PhasedArray_RFLink folder.
  • 2. Result_Figures_Basic
    • Contains RD Matrix and PD result for basic phased array design simulation using built-in Spectrasys RF beamforming parts.
    • These figures are obtained by enabling the "smaller" phased array RF_Link part in the RadarSys_Main schematic in SystemDesign_PhasedArray_RFLink folder.
  • 3. Result_Figures_RFImpairmentCompare
    • Contains complex signal behavior comparisons between no impairment case and with impairment case for the Basic mode simulation (see above topic-2 for confiiguration).
    • User can check the signal distortions at various positions of the phased array design due to RF impairment effects.
    • For demonstration purposes, two major RF impairments are considered: phased array multi-channel amplitude error and phase error.
      • For amplitude error, Normal error distribution with 1dB stddev is applied for both Tx and Rx array attenuators;
      • For phase error, Normal error distribution with 5deg stddev is applied for both Tx and Rx array phase shifters;
      • For the RF phased array configurations in this workspace, the Tx RF impairment incurred RF distortions is more severe than the Rx side. 
      • The "NoImpair" dataset can be generated by selecting "None" for error type of amplitude and phase components in Main1/2 schematics, respectively.
  • 4. Spectrasys_PhasedArray_Advanced
    • This folder includes the detailed modeling by ADAR1000 both for Tx array and Rx array.
    • For Rx/Tx design, user is required to run the PhArrayDesign_Params first, then go to RunSim equation for array configuration and pattern plots.
    • The "Chipset_Modeling" folder contains parametric chipset design mapping to SystemVue models/subnets.
  • 5. Spectrasys_PhasedArray_Basic
    • This folder includes the detailed modeling by built-in Spectrasys phased array parts both for Tx array and Rx array.
    • For Rx/Tx design, user is required to run the PhasedArray1/2 analysis first, then go to PlotPattern_Tx/Rx for pattern plots.
  • 6. SystemDesign_PhasedArray_RFLink
    • The Coupling 8*8 case folder defines an optional Tx element-to-element coupling design.
    • The high level radar system simulation is realized in "RadarSys_Main" schematic. User can select "Basic" or "Advanced" phased array modeling method by enabling the "smaller" or "bigger" phased array RFLink parts, both for Tx and Rx. 

About Element-to-Element Coupling

 

In an NxN matrix of array elements, the "ArrayCoupling_M" matrix allows you to specify the coupling coefficients from every element to every other element.  For an 8x8 rectangular array, this is a 64x64 mathematical matrix.  In Dataflow, this coefficient has no physical basis, it is strictly a matrix operation.

 

However, the coefficients can be harvested from an S-parameter matrix of the driving point impedances of the antenna manifold in an EM simulator.  In this example, an 8x8 array of microstrip patches was solved in Keysight Momentum, and then exported to an .SNP file.  This file was imported into this workspace, and the off-diagonal elements converted to the coefficients needed for this Dataflow analysis. 


This allows the coupling to have a more physical basis.

Workspace.Name: FMCW_Radar
Workspace.Description:
RADAR System Simulation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace provides an example of a FMCW Radar system simulation.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************
  • Models
    Several new models using M code and subnetworks are created for modeling the FMCW Radar.
    • FMCW environment model is created for simulating the environment including return target including target velocity, range, and channel condition. Clutter, jamming, and interference can be also inserted. This model is built on top of the Radar target model of the Radar library, and it adds a subnetwork model to describe the linear relation between the time delay and the frequency.
    • Estimation of target velocity is created by using M code.
    • Estimation of Range is created by using M code.
  • Top level design
    A linear FM signal source in the Radar library is used for modeling the FMCW signal.  In this application case, we set the PRI=PulseWidth, then the continuous FM signal is archived. The FMCW environment model is used for the Radar channel. Then we use the target velocity estimator to estimate the velocity and the target delay estimator to estimate the range. Waveform and spectrum are also measured and plotted.

 

All the models in this example can be used as templates for custom models.   Users can open these models and modify them as needed to create custom models for their own system simulation.

Workspace.Name: PD_Radar
Workspace.Description:
Pulsed Doppler Radar System

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

 

This workspace provides a Pulse-Doppler (PD) radar system design with signal generator, RF transmitter, antenna, clutter, RF receiver, moving target detection (MTD), constant false alarm rate (CFAR) processor, and signal detector for simulation purpose. The simulation designs can be used as templates for different PD applications.

 

System Structure

 

A. Signal generation

The radar signal is a function of pulse repeat frequency (PRF), power, and pulse width.  These parameters can be modified for different cases. In the simulation the radar signal can also be replaced by any defined signal through data file reader in which recorded or other custom data can be easily used.

B. RF Transmitter

The RF transmitter includes oscillators, modulations, amplifiers, and filters. The gain, bandwidth, and carrier frequency can be specified based on the test case.

C. Antenna and Target Return Signal with Clutter

• Radar Antenna: Signal Incident Angle and antenna rotation angle can be specified to form the beam direction and propagation.

• Target return signal: Doppler frequency and channel delay are generated to describe the target return signal with different velocities and distances. The radar clutter model included and power spectrum can be shaped.

D. RF Receiver

The RF receiver includes oscillators, de-modulations, amplifiers, and filtering. The gain, bandwidth, and carrier frequency can be specified based on the test specification.

E. Moving Target Detection (MTD)

To detect moving target more effectively, the moving target detection (MTD) is used. The MTD is based on a high-performance signal processing algorithm for PD radar. A bank of Doppler filters or FFT operators cover all possible expected target Doppler shifts. The output of MTD is used for the constant false alarm rate (CFAR) processing. In this example, a MATLAB Script model for MTD is created. The algorithm code is open to users, who can implement their own MTD algorithm by modifying the code provided.

F. Constant False Alarm Rate (CFAR)

The CFAR is set in frequency domain. Input Data is passed from the output of MTD. The cell averaging (CA) algorithm is used. In this example, a MATLAB Script model for CFAR is created.  The algorithm code is open to users, who can implement their own CFAR algorithm by modifying the code we provided.

G. Measurements for Detection Rate and False Alarm Rate

To estimate the system detection rate, a measurement for the detection rate is provided.  Detection rate and false alarm rate can be measured.

 

System Setup

For the system performance we set main parameters as shown below:

Signal magnitude is set to 1 v, PRF = 10 KHz, Doppler Frequency Fd = 8125 Hz, corresponding to target speed = 243 m/s, Target distance = 12 km, corresponding to Delay=2*distance/3e8=800 μs, the clutter magnitude distribution is set to Rayleigh, and the clutter power spectrum is formed as Gaussian. FFT_size is set to 32 in the simulation.  Set the time step = 5 ns and for each pulse repeat period we collect N=2000 points data.  The MTD process is based on NxFFT_Size 2D process for both range and Doppler frequency.

 

Simulation Results

Under these settings, the simulation results are displayed below. The radar signal waveform is measured in time domain at the receiver input. As can be seen from Graph 2, the received target return is blocked by clutter, jam, and noise. So, there is no way to detect the target signal in the time domain and we have to use MTD.  In the MTD model, the collected data in the data bank is grouped for corresponding target range and Doppler frequency. The target appears in the 26 FFT group, which means detected target with Fd=PRF/FFT_Size*26 = (10000/32)*26=8125 Hz, corresponding to the speed 243 m/s.  Also the target distance can be estimated by using the target position shown in Graph3, delay 1608 (points) that is the delay time = DelayPoints/SamplingRate=80 μs corresponding to 12 km distance. In this design, CA CFAR has been used in the simulation. The output of the CFAR is displayed in Graph8.  As can be seen the CFAR process provides a stable detection for the target. The detection rate can be measured at the output of the CFAR and the results are in the PD Data table.   In the table S2=1 means the detection rate at this test is 100%. All these are automatically calculated/estimated and displayed in the table (Simulation_Results) below.

Workspace.Name: AntennaPolarTRx_BasicTest
Workspace.Description:
Antenna Polarization TRx Basic Test Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example shows how to generate the antenna pattern and scan data with AutomotiveRadar_AntennaPolarizationTx and AntennaPolarizationRx model. Under identical configurations, their output results are also identical. 

One pattern plot example and two antenna scan examples are demonstrated in this workspace. The different weighting window functions and scan mode can be selected from the parameter list.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

There are three folders for this workspace:

 

1, PatternPlot_TargetScan

 

For antenna radiation pattern plotting, the target scan mode is applied to both AntennaPolarizationTx & Rx models. By design, both AntennaPolarizationTx and Rx models could ONLY use externally imported antenna patterns (in this example is from HFSS pattern file), and both models work under radar coordinates for angle definitions, the PhasedArrayTx model is applied for pattern result comparison.

 

To generate the angle sweeps, we firstly use MathLang script models to realize target phi and theta sweeps under antenna coordinate definitions (Theta and Phi), then transform both angles into radar coordinates (elevation and azimuth). Then the angle sweeps are inserted into the target elevation and azimuth input ports of AntennaPolarizationTx and Rx models to generate the output pattern data in complex formats.

 

The desired output for Antenna Polarization Tx and Rx models are H and V polarized patterns, and one MathLang model is designed to recombine the H/V components. Mathlang combination is easier to understand, but with lower simulation efficiency, so the SystemVue Math blocks are applied in shipping example.The recombined pattern results are compared with PhasedArrayTx model, and the corresponding results are almost identical except for some rounding errors. For the Antenna Polarization Rx, the H/V pattern extraction and recombination can be realized in the same way. 

 

To view the patterns, we use two equations to plot antenna patterns under planar (UV) and spherical coordinates, respectively. For both coordinate display modes, Linear and dB formats are available.

 

2, Circular_Scan 

 

To demonstrate circular scanning capability, we set the AntennaPolarizationTx and Rx in circular scan mode and observe the output results. Multiple circular scan periods are shown.

 

3, UniBiRaster_Scan

 

To demonstrate UniRaster and BiRaster scanning capability, we set the AntennaPolarizationTx and Rx in Uni/BiRaster scan modes and observe the output results. In this design we select the UniRaster mode to demonstrate flyback time and retrace time effects on scan results.

Workspace.Name: AntennaTRx_Scan_Modes
Workspace.Description:
AntennaTRx Scan Modes

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace shows how to generate the transmitted signal with different antenna scan modes using the Antenna_Tx or Rx models. Five scan modes are demoed in the workspace: BiRaster, BiSector, Circular, UniRaster, UniSector.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

When work mode is set to search mode, the input pins of BeamElevation and BeamAzimuth are disabled. The values of elevation angle and azimuth angle are computed automatically with different scan modes. These scan modes are designed inside the model code bases. Customized scans can be designed by using the external Mathlang script models to drive the Antenna_Tx or Rx models. In this workspace, the common radar pulse without modulation is applied as the signal sources.

To speed up the scanning process, the scan speed can be configured to a  much larger value than the real value of mechanical scan radar.

Under Circular folder, the circular scan mode is used.

Under BiSector folder, bi-direction sector scan mode is used. (Azimuth scan only)

Under UniSector folder, uni-direction sector scan mode is used. (Aziumth scan only)

Under BiRaster folder, bi-direction azimuth scan and elevation scan mode is used. (Azimuth and Elevation scan)

Under UniRaster folder, uni-direction azimuth scan and elevation scan mode is used. (Azimuth and Elevaiton scan).

Workspace.Name: SAR_Echo_Point
Workspace.Description:
Synthetic Aperture Radar Echo Wave Genenration Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example illustrates how to generate the SAR echo wave with the new RADAR_SAR_Echo model. The output of RADAR_SAR_Echo model is the echo pulse train under different settings.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Synthetic aperture radar offers dramatically improved image resolution over radar without sophisticated post processing by utilizing the movement of the antenna with respect to the target.

 

The Range-Doppler (RD) algorithm is used to process the radar echo signal train to form an image.

 

Currently, single or multiple point targets input is adopted, the image input method will be ready soon.

 

The setting format for point target is [target0_range_position, target0_crossrange_position, target0_reflection, target1_range_position, target1_crossrange_position, target1_reflection,...].

 

To view the generated image with Matlab, please run Equation1.

 

Note that the dataset is not saved in this workspace due to its large size. Just run it locally, you will see the result.

 

Please run equation plot_figure to plot the result, and make sure Matlab R2014a or above installed.

Workspace.Name: FrameWork
Workspace.Description:
Simulation Template for Moving Platform Based on the Generalized Framework

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace as a template shows how to set up the arbitrary type radar simulation based on the generalized framework and how to generate the echoes from the scatters of targets.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

SystemVue has 88 models and 70 templates to cover all advanced radar system designs.

To design your own system, you don't have to start from scratch.  SystemVue provides uniform processes for designing and testing Radar systems using preconfigured simulation templates.  Users can begin by modifying a similar template to their system based on their system spec.  Additionally, your legacy IP in m co de or C/C++ code can be imported to SystemVue as SystemVue models, or save it in your own library and use it in conjunction with existing SystemVue models. 

 

This workspace as a template shows how to set up the arbitrary type radar simulation based on the generalized framework and how to generate the echoes from the scatters of targets.

The example includes three layers: trajectory layer, antenna layer and signal layer.

In the trajectory layer, the RADAR_Platform model and RADAR_TargetScatterLocation model are used to generate the trajectories of transmitter, receiver, and scatters of target. The output is at the ECI frame(x, y, z).

In antenna layer, the transmit antenna gains and the receive antenna gains to the scatters of targets can be computed according to the locations of transmit platforms and receive platforms and scatters of targets. The locations are at the ECI frame.

In the signal layer, the input signal will be changed to the echoes from different scatters of targets according to the locations at ECI frame at each sampling time and the antenna gains from antenna layer.

The RADAR_Platform model and RADAR_TargetScatterLocation model support two types of trajectory generation:

· User defined file import (Parameter Trajectory_Mode = 1: User Defined)

The file format is (x, y, z) in the ECI frame. Each line is the position value at each time step.

· Real time computation (Parameter Trajectory_Mode = 0: Cartesian )

The initial positions of platform and target are set with the parameter Position_Initial in the geodetic system (Longitude(degree), Latitude(degree), Height(meters)).

If the platform is not static, the Velocity_Initial and Accelerate_Initial parameters can be used to set the initial velocity (m/s) and accelerate (m/s2) in the body frame. The random value of jerk can be provided when IsRondomError = true.

The input roll, pitch and yaw angles are the Euler angles which are three angles introduced by Euler to describe the orientation of a rigid body. Although the relative orientation between any two Cartesian frames can be described by Euler angles, this model is focused merely on the transformation between the vehicle-carried (or the local) NED and the body frames, following a particular rotation sequence. More specifically, the adopted Euler angles move the reference frame to the referred frame, following a Z-Y-X (or the so-called 3–2–1) rotation sequence. These three Euler angles are also known as the yaw (or heading), pitch, and roll angles.

To run the template, please execute the following steps. 

1.      Open the workspace and observe the main design (design2).

General Setup for moving platform simulation is considered in three layers. 

a.      The Trajectory Layer with green color is to set Tx and Rx moving property.  Also the target moving properties with initial range, velocity, position are set here.

b.      The Antenna layer with green color is for setting the position of Tx and Rx array antennas. 

c.       The signal layer includes sub-Systems, Transmitter, Beamformer , Array Atenna, Environments, RF Receiver, Signal processor and measurements. 

b. Key parameters defined using slides for easy to use

2. Run the simulation by click on the 'Run Analysis' button in the first row of Manu bars.  Then you can observe the simulation results.  Look the bottom row.  In Figure 1, LFM transmission signal is shown.  In Figure 2, the received signal is hidden into the strong Clutter and noise.  In Figure 3, through MTI and MTD the pulse is recovered and detected.  In Figure 4, the signal at the CFAR output is cleaned up. 

Two 3D plots are shown in the design page to show the Detected signal in the Range-Doppler plane.  The first one shows the detected signal under the condition of without MTI.  The second one is for with MTI.  

4. Modify Key parameters by using slides to observe the results to know the system works Ok or not.

 

To create your own system you can modify the template by changing parameters or replace models that are either in the radar library or import your models in the design.

Workspace.Name: Framework_Basic
Workspace.Description:
Radar Echo Signal Generation Based on the Generalized Framework

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace shows how to set up the arbitrary type radar simulation based on the generalized framework and how to generate the echoes from the scatters of targets.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

The example includes threelayers: trajectory layer, antenna layer and signal layer.

In the trajectory layer, the RADAR_Platform model and RADAR_TargetScatterLocation model are used to generate the trajectories of transmitter, receiver, and scatters of target. The output is at the ECI frame(x, y, z).

In antenna layer, the transmit antenna gains and the receive antenna gains to the scatters of targets can be computed according to the locations of transmit platfoms and receive platforms and scatters of targets. The locations are at the ECI frame.

In the signal layer, the input signal will be changed to the echoes from different scatters of targets according to the locations at ECI frame at each sampling time and the antenna gaines from antenna layer.

The RADAR_Platform model and RADAR_TargetScatterLocation model support two types of trajectory generation:

· User defined file import (Parameter Trajectory_Mode = 1: User Defined)

The file format is (x, y, z) in the ECI frame. Each line is the position value at each time step.

· Real time computation (Parameter Trajectory_Mode = 0: Cartesian )

The initial positions of platform and target are set with the parameter Position_Initial in the geodetic system (Longitude(degree), Latitude(degree), Height(meters)).

If the platform is not static, the Velocity_Initial and Accelerate_Initial parameters can be used to set the initial velocity (m/s) and accelerate (m/s2) in the body frame. The random value of jerk can be provided when IsRondomError = true.

The input roll, pitch and yaw angles are the Euler angles which are three angles introduced by Euler to describe the orientation of a rigid body. Although the relative orientation between any two Cartesian frames can be described by Euler angles, this model is focused merely on the transformation between the vehicle-carried (or the local) NED and the body frames, following a particular rotation sequence. More specifically, the adopted Euler angles move the reference frame to the referred frame, following a Z-Y-X (or the so-called 3–2–1) rotation sequence. These three Euler angles are also known as the yaw (or heading), pitch, and roll angles.

**********************************************************************

Design: MonoStatic_SingleTarget

In this example, three layers are used.

Trajectory Layer: one mono-static radar is at the 0 degree(longitude), 0 degree(latitude), and 1500m (height). The velocity and acclerate is set to zero. All the Euler angles are not connected, which means three Euler angles are the default values(0s). The target is at 0.01 degree(longitude), 0 degree(latitude) and 1500m(height). For 1 latitude, the distance is about 111km.

Antenna Layer: RADAR_LocInAntenna model is used to compute the azimuth angles and elevation angles of target in the radar antenna frames for both Tx and Rx.

Signal Layer: The antenna work mode is set to circular scan and scan rate is set to 1500(round per minute). This value is much larger than real speed of mechnical scan in order to speed up the simulation. The antenna pattern is produced by various aperture distributions. In this example, the pattern is produced by uniform distributions.

**********************************************************************

Design: MonoStatic_SingleTarget_Moving

In this example, two layers are used.

Trajectory layer: one mono-static radar is at the 0 degree(longitude), 0 degree(latitude), and 1500m (height). The velocity and acclerate is set to zero. The target is at 0 degree(longitude), 0.1 degree(latitude) and 1500m(height). The velocity is 100m/s in the velocity frame. (When three Euler angles are set to 0, which means the direction of target moving is towards the north.

Antenna Layer: Not used. In some radar simulation cases, especially for some new algirthm simulation, the radar antenna gain can be ignored first.

Signal layer: When antenna layer is not used, the RADAR_AntennaTx/Rx may not be used. In this layer, the echo is generated by RADAR_EchoGenerator based on the positions of radar and target at each timestep. After MTI and MTD signal processing models, the range-doppler matrix is acquired and the velocity can be computed if there is no velocity ambiguity.

**********************************************************************

Workspace.Name: LocInAntennaFrame
Workspace.Description:
Azimuth and Elevaiton angle computation in Radar Antenna Frame

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace shows how to compute the antenna gains of Tx and Rx for targets in the antenna. The radar antenna frame is used.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

There are 6 folders in this workspace.

1. Antenna Scan_ECI and Antenna Scan_SimpleXYZ folders:

The Antenna Scan_ECI example demonstrates the basic theory of 3 layer simulation architecture.

The azimuth angle and elevation angle in the radar antenna frame for Tx chain is computed with RADAR_LocInAntennaFrame model. These two angles are input of RADAR_AntennaTx. When search mode is selected, different scan mode can be selected in the RADAR_AntennaTx/Rx model. In this example, the circular scan mode is used. The antenna gain of target in this scan antenna can be acquired.

The Antenna Scan_SimpleXYZ example proposes using SimpleXYZ frame for radar simulations.

If the user choose to use SimpleXYZ mode for simulation, the platform coordinate setup could be explained as:

(1) The roll, pitch, yaw angles are bound to X, Y, Z axes, respectively. The positive X axis points to the forward direction of the moving target platform; the positive Y axis refers to the transverse direction of the platform; the positive Z axis points toward the vertical direction of the platform, completing a right-handed XYZ coordinate system.

Therefore, the XZ plane mode refers to the antenna aperture positioned at target nose, with boresight pointing at positive X axis (forward direction of the target motion). The XY mode is generally not supported (and not demostrated) for A/D radar platform setting, since the antenna boresight would be pointing at the vertical direction. (One generic guideline for SimpleXYZ is that if the antenna is setup as a certain plane mode, then its boresight is by default the positive direction of the 3rd axis.)

(2) For the calculation of antenna pointing angle towards the target, under the radar coordinate, there are two methods. The 1st is platform rotation: to set the roll/pitch/yaw angles of the platform. The 2nd is to target initial position rotation, realized the matrix calculations as seen from Equation. The resultant LocInFrame output angles would then be identical.

3. Latitude and Latitude2 folders:

In these two folders, suppose radar Tx part is static, the target is moving from south to north. The different of them is the height of target. The elevation angle at different latitude can be computed by sweeping latitude. (Be careful, 1 latitude = 111km).

4. Longitude and Longitude2 folders

In these two folders, suppose radar Tx part is static, the target is moving from west to east. The different of them is the latitude of target. The elevation angle at different longitude can be computed by sweeping the longitude.

The example includes threelayers: trajectory layer, antenna layer and signal layer.

Azimuth and Elevation angle computation in Radar Antenna Frame

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace shows how to use Frame work infrastructure to scan and find the target.

In this example a target moves around a ground based radar. The Radar is  monostatic and searches for the target by performing a circular scan. It collects the return signal and paints the antenna pattern on a polar plot.

 

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Radar position and Target positions are read from Google maps as per a chosen trajectory.  The picture in the Design1 schematic shows this trajectory. To read the latitude and longitude from Google maps right click on the mouse at the desired position and choose "What is here?".  It displays the Latitude and longitude on the upper left hand side. Once the positions of target are read place them in a file as shown below.  A value of 1000 meters is arbitrarily chosen here for the altitude of the target. Please note that the Google maps gives the Latitude first and longitude next and same format [ Latitude Longitude Altitude ] is used in SystemVue.

40.111604   -75.282615  1000
40.296202   -75.139793  1000
40.507450   -74.865135  1000

The file containing the above data is named Trajectory_Positions.txt with the same format [ Latitude Longitude Altitude ] and is supplied with the workspace.

The simulation of this design is controlled from the script.  The target positions are read from the file and analysis is run in a For loop for each of the target positions.

**************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************

What to observe?

Run the script "1Tx1Tgt1Rx" by right mouse clicking and selecting Calculate Now.  Position the design schematic in view as well as the Matlab plot in view next to the trajectory map.  As the simulation runs you will be able to see that the antenna beam searches and finds the target as it moves in an anti clock wise direction.
