Workspace.Name: PhaseArrayRadar_MultiTargetSearch
Workspace.Description:
Simulation Template for Multi-Target Search Phase Array Radar Framework

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace as a template shows how to set up the multi-target search in phase array radar system based on the generalized framework and how to solve the multi-target positon by PD signal processing.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

This workspace as a template shows how to set up multi-target radar search mode simulation based on phase array radar system.

The example includes three layers: trajectory layer, antenna layer and signal layer.

In the trajectory layer, the RADAR_Platform model and RADAR_TargetScatterLocation model are used to generate the trajectories of transmitter, receiver, and scatters of target. The output is at the SimpleXYZ_frame(x, y, z).

In antenna layer, the transmit antenna gains and the receive antenna gains to the scatters of targets can be computed according to the locations of transmit platforms and receive platforms and scatters of targets. The locations are at the SimpleXYZ_frame.

In the signal layer, the input signal will be changed to the echoes from different scatters of targets according to the locations at SimpleXYZ_frame at each sampling time and the antenna gains from antenna layer.

The workspace build up phase array radar 2D search mode, 2D means the radar could get target azimuth and range information. Because of the radar signal processing adopt PD processing, target velocity is obtained, too.

In the signal layer, the matlab script is the beam control, the beam control generates the beam pointing angle based on the detection area and beam width. The beam weights model generates the array weighted coefficients then control the beam rotation. Very beam has some dwell time, the transmitting antenna transmits pulse train, the receiving antenna receives pulse train and do PD processing, the next dell time, the beam switch next position and do the same signal processing. If the detection area needs N beams to cover, the workspace will generate N Range -Doppler spectrum graph.

************************************************

Note

************************************************

The workspace is about the 2D radar, only scan in the azimuth, which is used for early warning. So the target position coordinate should specify as [x, 0, z]. Otherwise, the measurement result is not match the target parameter setting.

Workspace.Name: PhaseArrayRadar_TAS
Workspace.Description:
Simulation Template for PhaseArray Radar Track add Seach Framework

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace as a template shows how to set up the multi-target track add search processing in phase array radar system based on the generalized framework and how to solve the multi-target positon, angle usd sum-diff beam method.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

This workspace as a template shows how to set up multi-target radar track and search mode simulation based on phase array radar system.

The example includes three layers: trajectory layer, antenna layer and signal layer.

In the trajectory layer, the RADAR_Platform model and RADAR_TargetScatterLocation model are used to generate the trajectories of transmitter, receiver, and scatters of target. The output is at the SimpleXYZ_frame(x, y, z).

In antenna layer, the transmit antenna gains and the receive antenna gains to the scatters of targets can be computed according to the locations of transmit platforms and receive platforms and scatters of targets. The locations are at the SimpleXYZ_frame.

In the signal layer, the input signal will be changed to the echoes from different scatters of targets according to the locations at SimpleXYZ_frame at each sampling time and the antenna gains from antenna layer.

The workspace build up phase array radar track and search  mode, and shows the target detection, confirm and tracking task switch. In the start,  the radar is working in the seaching mode, when the radar detect target, the phase radar shoot the confirm beam, if the target exsit, the radar switch to tracking mode, the radar beam will revisit the target according the tracking data rate (0.1s=10Hz), So, the radar could get some plots of the targets, and then use the plots data to get the target traces.

In the signal layer, the matlab script is the beam control, the beam control generates the beam direction, based on target position prediction data. The beam weights model generates the array weighted coefficients then control the beam rotation. Every beam has some dwell time, the transmitting antenna transmits pulse train, the receiving antenna receives pulse train and do pulse compression processing, the next dell time, the beam switch next position and do the same signal processing. In the angle measuremet, the workspace adopts sum-diff method to get target accurate angle value, the sum-diff curve is in the Function AngleInterp.

************************************************

Note

There is one monostatic radar which means radar tx and rx use the same antenna and two targets in the example. The target echoes from targets are received by radar antenna and antenna received combined signal is generated. The antenna works at circular scan mode.

Workspace.Description:
Digital Array Radar Angle Error Measurement Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example measures the angle error with  digital phased array radar.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

1. The radar signal is a linear frequency modulation pulse.

 

2. The radar array is divided into two 16x1 sub-arrays. The sum signal of the two sub-array outputs is used for range and doppler tracking, and serves as the phase reference for the error signals. The difference signal's polarity of the two sub-array outputs indicates phase, with reference to the sum signal.

 

3. delta_theta is the result of target angle error compared to antenna direction.

 

4. delta_theta = (lambda /(pi * D * cos(theta0)) * arctan(E_difference / E_sum).

c. The CFAR (Constant False Alarm Rate) algorithm is Cell Average (CA)

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace provides an example of a FMCW Radar system simulation.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

·        Top level design

This workspace consists of Transmitter, Receiver, FFT processor, Range and Velocity measurement. Radar CW waveform is generated from RADAR_CW model and transmitted via model Noise Density and RADAR Target to reach Receiver part. After Mixer, FFT process takes effects and FFT result is ready for Range and Velocity Measurement, which consists of RADAR MTD, Range and Velocity Estimation. As we can see, Estimation of target velocity and Range is created by using M code.

·        Highlights

The user could change input parameters like Radial Velocity and Distance and estimated results will be displayed after simulation.  Besides, a picture named MTD Matrix will show MTD result.

·        Note

If PRF is set to 50KHz in this example, the maximum un-ambiguity velocity is PRF/2 * wavelength / 2 = 50e3/2 * 3e8/77e9 / 2 = 48.7013m/s . (For triangle LFM CW signal applied in this example, the effective PRF should be halved.)


So when the velocity is between -48.7013 and 48.7013, the velocity measured result should be correct (please refer to the measured range/velocity table).

·        Additional Notes

With default, the dataset does not exist in this workspace due to its huge size. To get the results, please run the simulation.

Workspace.Name: Freq_Step
Workspace.Description:
Stepped Frequency Signal Generation and Synthetic High Range Resolution Processing Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace is aimed to demonstrate how to generate stepped frequency signal

 

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

In this example, a technique is described for obtaining target range-profile signatures synthetically by processing echoes resulting from narrowband transmitted pulses stepped in frequency.

 

The process for generating a synthetic range profile of one or more illuminated targets in the radar beam in this example can be described as follows:

1. Transmit a series of monotone narrowband pulse, where each pulse is a sequence consisting of n pulses stepped in frequency from pulse to pulse by a   fixed frequency step size.

2. Collect and digitize I and Q samples of the target's baseband response for each transmitted pulse.

3. Store the digitized quadrature components of each of the n received signals from each transmitted pulse. Each stored burst of target signal data approaches the equivalent of the instantaneous discrete spectral signature of the target seen at the same bandwidth and center wavelength if the following conditions are met:

    a. burst times are short relative to time associated with significant target aspect change;

    b. the duration of the baseband response exceeds the target range-delay extent;

    c. the frequency stepsize is less than the reciprocal of the target range-delay extent.

4. Apply frequency weighting to each burst of data and corrections for target velocity, system phase and amplitude ripple, and quadrature sampling bias and imbalance errors.(In this example, this step is omitted)

5. Take an IFFT of the resulting set of n complex frequency components of each burst to obtain an n-elementary synthetic range-profile signature of the target from each burst.

 

For this example, the instantaneously bandwidth of transmitted pulse is 4MHz, so the range resolution is 3e8/(2*4e6) = 37.5m.

In this example, two targets 10 meters away cannot be distinguished with this monotone pulse train.

With stepped frequency, the synthetic bandwidth is 64*4 = 256MHz, so the range resolution is 3e8/(2*256e6) = 0.59m. So these two targets can be distinguished.

Workspace.Name: Freq_Step_Test
Workspace.Description:
Step Frequency Radar Test Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue 

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace is aimed to demonstrate how step frequency radar system works.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Stepped Frequency Radar (SFR) is well known for non-destructive testing and ground searching applications. With SFR, the echoes of stepped frequency pulses are synthesized in the frequency domain to obtain shorter pulses in the time domain. Using frequency hopping, both high resolution and a high signal-to-clutter ratio can be achieved. As a high range resolution radar technique, SFR offers a number of key advantages over other techniques like regular pulse radar. Such advantages include target classification, resolution of multiple targets, accurate range profile, detection of low radar cross section (RCS) targets in clutter, and low cost.  Because of these advantages, SFR is today widely used in both the commercial and aerospace/defense (A/D) industries.

 

This application note introduces a simulation platform based on Keysight SystemVue electronic system level (ESL) design software that easily links to measurement tools to enable the design, validation and test of SFR systems under different environments. The simulation platform with test environment includes return signal RCS and background clutter. A template SFR design is also provided. SFR design is performed in SystemVue. Then, simulation results are evaluated with Tx and Rx measurements. Users can customize the template SFR design to their own systems and run simulations in the platform to evaluate the performance. The simulation platform also can be used as a test platform for SFR component test. As an example, an SFR system with target returns and ground clutter will be presented that uses the platform for both simulation and test. The proposed platform works very well for design, as well as for verification and testing of SFR systems.

 

Four Designs are included:

Design SFR_Sim provides a SFR simulation. Design Pulse_Sim provides a regular Pulse Radar simulation to be compared to SFR performance. Design SFR_Gen is for generating SFR signal to do component test.  Design SFR_Rec is for capturing HW signal and performs a receiver test.

Workspace.Name: PDRADAR_Design_Template
Workspace.Description:
Radar System Design Template

Keysight Technologies SystemVue 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace is aimed to demonstrate how a Pulse Doppler Radar system works. This PD Radar system works in L band with 1GHz of Center Frequency. 

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

SystemVue has 88 models and 70 templates to cover all advanced radar system designs.

To design your own system, you don't have to start from scratch.  SystemVue provides uniform processes for designing and testing Radar systems using preconfigured simulation templates.  Users can begin by modifying a similar template to their system based on their system spec.  Additionally, your legacy IP in m code or C/C++ code can be imported to SystemVue as SystemVue models, or save it in your own library and use it in conjunction with existing SystemVue models. 

 

In the example, a design for Simulation of a Pulse Doppler Radar system is introduced as a template.  A PD system in L band with 1  GHz of Center Frequency is shown in the example. 

With a LFM source, a Transmitter designing in DSP and RF cross domain (Non-Linear Amp and ADC, DAC), environment scenarios such as RCS for moving target plus clutter as well as noise, Receiver with mixed RF-DSP structure, Signal processing, (pulse compression, MTI and MTD), detector, CFAR and Detection Rate measurement.  Performance measurements include radar transmission signal, target return plus clutter, recovered target through MTI and MTD, signal at the CFAR output.  A 3D plot is provided to observe the detected target in the radar environments.  Also a performance curve, Detection Rate vs ranges in nautical miles for targets under FFT sizes of 2, 8 and 16 .

 

To run the template, please execute the following steps. 

1. Open the workspace and observe the main design (design2). 

a. Sub-Systems: you can see Transmitter, Environments, RF Receiver, Signal processor and measurements.  By the way, the design supports Cross-Domain architectures in Mod and Demod models.  If you push into the models you will see it in details. 

b. Key parameters defined using slides: Target Rages using Nautical Miles, Target Velocity using Radial Velocity, GC Type parameter for Non-Linear Amp in Mod using GC_Type,  DAC_NBits parameter  for DAC in Mod using NBits and System Signal to Clutter Ration using SCR

2. Run the simulation by click on the 'Run Analysis' button in the first row of Manu bars.  Then you can observe the simulation results. 

a. Tx and Rx Measurements: Look the first column In Figure 1, LFM transmission signal is shown.  In Figure 2, the received signal is hidden into the strong Clutter and noise.  In Figure 3, through MTI and MTD the pulse is recovered and detected.  In Figure 4, the signal at the CFAR output is cleaned up. 

b. Read Parameter Estimation Results. Fidn the Estimated Velocity as well as Estimated Range in the Text Box with light blue color near the slides to specify Key parameters.  As can be seen it very closes to its original values specified in the green Text box.

3. Run Sweep Analysis1 – SweepAnalysis3 to get three curves shown the probability of Detection rate VS the ranges in Nautical Miles under different FFT size of signal processor.

4. Modify Key parameters by using slides to observe the results to know the system works Ok or not.

 

To create your own system you can modify the template by changing parameters or replace models that are either in the radar library or import your models in the design.

Workspace.Name: CW_Signal
Workspace.Description:
Radar CW Signal Generation Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace shows how to generate sawtooth, triangle, flexible & FMCW pulse train signal with RADAR_CW and RADAR_LFM models.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

The frequency variation patterns and the generated waveforms can be observed by the graphs. Three example folders are designed for different kinds of CW signal generations.

1) CW_Basic

Design1 proposes a basic CW design using the RADAR_CW model to generate triangle, sawtooth and fixed frequency waveforms, will full CW signal generation demonstrations (duty cycle = 100%). When the parameter DeltaFreq is set to zero (the lowest example in Design1 Schematic), the FMCW signal will be single frequency Sine/Cosine waveform.

2) CW_Flexible

Design2 proposes an advanced design using the RADAR_CW model and chop model to generate periodic fixed frequency CW + triangle periodic FMCW waveform patterns. Chop and ChopVar models from the Algorithm library are applied to realize distinctive signal truncations.

In this example, the combined signal realizes the 20 kHz fixed frequency CW and DC-50 kHz triangle FMCW signal generations alternately.

3) CW_Sawtooth Pulse Train

Design3 proposes a pulse-train design using RADAR_LFM model to generate a sawtooth FMCW pulse train with different bandwidth, pulse-width, and the pulses can be arbitrarily concatenated.

The first pulse in the PRI_Total is realized with 10e-6 sec PulseWidth and 30e-6 sec PRI, and the second two-pulse group uses  5e-6 sec PulseWidth and 15e-6 sec PRI. The total PRI is therefore 30e-6*1 + 15e-6*2 = 60e-6. Please refer to the design equation tab and RADAR_LFM model help for more technical descriptions.

References:

[1] B.M.Mahafza, <Radar Systems Analysis and Design Using MATLAB (3rd Edition)>, 2013, CRC Press.

[2] Nadav Levanon and Eli Mozeson, <Radar Signals>, 2004, John Wiley & Sons Inc.

Workspace.Name: DDS_Model
Workspace.Description:
Radar Signal Generation with DDS Model

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace shows how to generate LFM signal and Sine signal with RADAR_DDS model and some related processing, such as DAC and pulse compression.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Direct digital synthesizers (DDS), or numerically controlled oscillators (NCO), are important components in many digital communication and radar systems.

In this example, one complex signal having frequency of 1MHz with this model is generated, the corresponding parameters can be set as following: waveform_type = CW, Freq_output = 1e6(or freq = 1e6), SampleRate = 20e6(or clk_in = 20e6), Accumulator_bitlength = 32, Freq_modulate_bitlength = 32, and Magnitude_bitlength = 10.

The sampling rate of this model is determined by the parameter SampleRate or the input port clk_in. When the clk_in is dis-connected, the sampling rate is the value of SampleRate, or else it will be the value of clk_in. The input port phase_dither is used to decrease the spur components which are caused by the quantization. The magnitude and phase input can be used to control the magnitude and phase of the output. The input port freq is used to control the frequency of output. When it is disconnected, the frequency of output is determined by the parameter Freq_output. The input port startfreq is used to determine the start frequency of LFM and stepped LFM. When it is disconnected, the start frequency of LFM and stepped LFM is determined by the parameter Bandwidth.

Workspace.Name: Frequency_Modulation_Signal
Workspace.Description:
Radar Frequency Modulation Signal Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace shows how to generate several forms of frequency modulated signals, including FSK signal, Costas Frequency Hopping signal, Hybrid FSK/PSK signal, and nonlinear FM signal.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

The Linear Frequency Modulation (LFM) is NOT the only frequency modulation law used in radar. For LFM the volume of the ambiguity function was concentrated in a slowly decaying diagonal ridge, and the LFM suffered from high autocorrelation sidelobes, therefore some form of amplitude weighting was necessary in order to reshape the spectrum and thus reduce those sidelobes.

This example introduces the various other kinds of frequency modulation, including Costas frequency coding, FSK, Hybrid FSK/PSK and Nonlinear FM as complementary demonstrations. The 1st three types belong to the FSK category, and the 2nd is shown in a separate folder.

1, FSK Examples

1) Costas Code Example

The Costas Code is actually a discrete frequency coding that is practically the opposite of the LFM linear law. The hoppling order strongly affects the ambiguity function of the signal. The uniqueness for a Costas signal is that the number of coinciding dots cannot be larger than one for all but the zero-shift case, and this implies a narrow peak of the ACF at the origin and low sidelobes elsewhere.

This Costas frequency coding example shows how to generate the Costas signal with the frequency sequence fj = {4, 7, 1, 6, 5, 2, 3} * 1e5 Hz. The ACF, time-domain complex waveform and power spectrum are shown.

2) FSK Example

In an FSK waveform, the transmitted frequency fj is chosen from the Frequency Hopping (FH) sequence {f1, f2, . . . , fNF } of available frequencies for transmission at a set of consecutive time intervals {t1, t2, . . . , tNF }. The frequencies are placed in the various time slots corresponding to a binary time-frequency matrix. Each frequency is used once within the code period, with one frequency per time slot and one time slot per frequency.

This FSK example shows how to generate FSK signal with FHSequence = [1e6, 2e6, 3e6] Hz and TimeIntervals = [10e-6, 10e-6, 10e-6]s, for which each time interval is 1/10 of PRI. The time-domain complex waveform and power spectrum are shown.

3) Hybrid FSK/PSK Example

The hybrid FSK/PSK example demonstrates how to generate the hybrid FSK and PSK signal with one of the typical Costas frequency sequence = [2,4,8,5,10,9,7,3,6,1]*2e5 (Delta_Frequency) and the PSK code is Barker code with the length of 13. The time-domain complex waveform and power spectrum are shown.

 2, Nonlinear FM Example

As mentioned earlier, the linear frequency modulation waveform suffers from high sidelobes in the ACF curves, and some form of amplitude weighting is a must. However, this variable amplitude transmission requires linear power amplifiers, which are less efficient than saturated power amplifiers. This drawback naturally leads to the design of nonlinear FM, to deviate from the constant rate of frequency change and spend more time at frequencies that need to be enhanced.

This workspace shows how to generate Non-Linear Frequency Modulation Waveform signal with  Radar NLFM model, and the corresponding results from the LFM model are provided for comparison.

As it is difficult to distinguish NLFM and LFM signal in the time domain, the Power Spectrum, Frequency-Time Graph and Chirp Rate (with simple post simulation processing scripts) comparisons between NLFM and LFM signal are proposed. The blue curve represents NLFM signal and the red one is LFM signal.

Compared with LFM waveform, NLFM frequency ramp is non-linear, with steeper slope at the beginning and at the end of the pulse. Thus, chirp rate pattern of NLFM is like "U" shape.

References:

[1] Nadav Levanon and Eli Mozeson, <Radar Signals>, 2004, John Wiley & Sons Inc.

[2] Phillip E. Pace, <Detecting and Classifying Low Probability of Intercept Radar>, 2009, ARTECH HOUSE, MA.

[3] Mark Richards, <Fundamentals of Radar Signal Processing>, 2005, MCGraw-Hill, New York.

[4] Merrill I. Skolnik, <Introduction to Radar Systems, Third Edition>, 2001, MCGraw-Hill, New York.

Workspace.Name: Phase_Coding_Signal
Workspace.Description:
Phase Coded Signal Generation Example

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

  

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This example workspace shows how to generate the phase coded signal generation examples, including Barker code, PRN code, ChirpLike code (Frank Code, P1 to P4 and Px Code) and PolyTime (T1(n), T2(n), T3(n), T4(n)) example folders.

 

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

Phase coded waveforms are generated by changing initial phases for pulses/subpulses to improve radar detection performances. In general, two sub-category of phase coded waveforms are realized in SystemVue Radar Library: Binary Phase Codes, Polyphase Codes and PolyTime Codes.

 

For binary phase codes, Barker Code and PRN Codes waveform generations are realized.

 

For Polyphase Codes, ChirpLike PolyPhase Code such as Frank Code and P1-P4, Px Code examples are proposed.

 

For PolyTime Codes, the T1-T4 PolyTime phase coded examples to approximate stepped frequency or linear frequency modutation are proposed.

 

1, Binary Code:

 

1) Barker Code

 

This example shows how to generate the Barker code and calculates its auto-correlation function. The main features of Barker Code are: 

  • Biphase Barker codes exhibit a peak sidelobe to mainlobe voltage ratio of 1: N, where N is the code length.
  • The peak sidelobe ratio is defined in terms of power and is expressed as 20 log10(1/N). The Barker codes achieve the lowest possible PSR for an aperiodic code.
  • The longest known Barker code is length 13 with a corresponding peak sidelobe ratio of -22.3 dB.
  • It has been shown that no odd length biphase Barker sequence exists longer than length 13. No even-length sequences have been found above length 4.
  • The example shows a Barker pulse train with parameters as, SubPulsewidth=1us, PRI=100us, CodeLength=13, BB_SamplingRate=10MHz.

2) PRN Codes

 

This folder includes two examples, GoldCode and Radar_PRNSeq.

 

-> GoldCode

 

Gold code is also known as Gold sequence, which is a type of binary sequence used in telecommunications (CDMA) and satellite navigation (GPS). Gold code sequences have the property of minimal circular auto-correlation values for non-zero lag.

 

A Gold code sequence is generated by taking the exclusive or (XOR) of the outputs of two LFSRs (Linear Feedback Registers) of the same length. This two LFSRs are called G1 and G2. Also, the model provides the code output port.

 

-> Radar_PRNSeq

 

Radar Pseudo-Random Number (PRN) codes are also known as Maximal Length Sequences (MLS) codes. These codes are called pseudo-random because the statistics associated with their occurrence are similar to those associated with the coin-toss sequences. Maximum length sequences are periodic.

The initial state, feedback generator and phase shifter of output can be set in the parameters of RADAR_PRN model. The sampling rate and chip rate can be configured arbitrarily.

2, Chirp-Like Code:

 

1) Frank Code

 

This example shows how to generate the Frank code and calculates its auto-correlation function.

In 1963, R. L. Frank devised a polyphase code that is closely related to the linear frequency modulation and Barker codes. The Frank code has recently been used successfully in LPI radars. The Frank code is derived from a step approximation to a linear frequency modulation waveform using M frequency steps and M samples per frequency. The Frank code has a length or processing gain of Nc = M*M. For its example, the PRI is 64 us, the SubPulseWidth is 1 us, M is 8 (Nc = 64), the sampling rate is 4 MSPS.

 

2) P1, P2, Px Code

 

These three examples demonstrates how to generate the modified versions of Frank Code: P1, P2 and Px, all with DC frequency term in the middle of the pulse instead of at the beginning. Frank, P1, P2 and Px codes are ONLY applicable for perfect square lengths.

 

The P1 code is generated using a step approximation to a linear frequency modulation waveform. For P1 code, M can be even or odd. For its example, the PRI is 16 us, the SubPulseWidth is 1 us, M is 4 (Nc = 16), the sampling rates is 4 MSPS.

 

For the P2 code, M must be even, and the phase increment within each phase group is the same as the P1 code, except that the starting phases are different. For its example, the PRI is 36 us, the SubPulseWidth is 1 us, M is 6 (Nc = 36), the sampling rate is 4 MSPS.

 

The Px code is a more generic code designed to yield the same aperiodic peak sidelobe as the Frank code but having lower integrated sidelobe level. For Px code, M can be even or odd, and for this example, the PRI is 16 us, the SubPulseWidth is 25 us, M is 5 (Nc = 25), the sampling rates is 4 MSPS.

 

3) P3, P4 Code

 

The P3, P4 polyphase codes are specific cyclically shifted and decimated versions of the Zadoff-Chu code. Unlike the P1 and P2 codes applicable only for square length (such as the Frank code), the P3 and P4 codes are, like the Zadoff-Chu code, applicable for any length M.

 

The P3 code is derived by converting a linear frequency modulation waveform to baseband, by using a synchronous oscillator on one end of the frequency sweep (single sideband detection), and sampling the I and Q video at the Nyquist rate (first sample of I and Q taken at the leading edge of the waveform).  For its example, the PRI is 32 us, the SubPulseWidth is 1 us, M is 32 (Nc = 32), the sampling rate is 4Msps.

 

The P4 code is also derived from the same linear frequency modulation waveform as the P3 code, except that the local oscillator frequency is offset in the I and Q detectors, resulting in coherent double sideband detection. For its example, the PRI is 32 us, the SubPulseWidth is 1 us, M is 32 (Nc = 32), the sampling rates is 4Msps.

 

3, PolyTime Codes:

 

As shown above, the Frank, P1, P2, P3, and P4 codes were developed by approximating a stepped frequency or linear frequency modulation waveform, where the phase steps vary as needed to approximate the underlying waveform, and the time spent at any given phase state is constant.

 

Another approach to approximating a stepped frequency or linear frequency modulation waveform is to quantize the underlying waveform into a user-selected number of phase states. In this case, the time spent at each phase state changes throughout the duration of the waveform. The code sequences that use fixed phase states with varying time periods at each phase state are given the name polytime coding.

 

Two types of polytime coded waveforms can be generated from the stepped frequency model and are denoted as T1(n) and T2(n), where n is the number of phase states used to approximate the underlying waveform.

The T3(n) and T4(n) polytime sequences are approximations to a linear frequency modulation waveform.

 

Increasing the number of phase states increases the quality of the polytime approximation to the underlying waveform, while at the same time reduces the time spent at any given phase state, making the generation of the waveform more complicated. The phase state (or bit) durations change as a function of time. The minimum bit duration determines the waveform bandwidth.

 

This example group demonstrates how T1(n), T2(n), T3(n) and T4(n) code generate and the generated phase state and their ACF results are given in this example. For detailed technical descriptions please refer to Ref[3].

 

References:

[1] B.M.Mahafza, <Radar Systems Analysis and Design Using MATLAB (3rd Edition)>, 2013, CRC Press.

[2] Nadav Levanon and Eli Mozeson, <Radar Signals>, 2004, John Wiley & Sons Inc.

[3] Phillip E. Pace, <Detecting and Classifying Low Probability of Intercept Radar>, 2009, ARTECH HOUSE, MA

This workspace provides two examples for basic UWB Radar system simulation.

  • Example1 - Pulse UWB Signal
    This example shows the Pulse UWB Radar signal generation capability in SystemVue.  The Baseband Pulse UWB signal is generated by Pulse_Cx subnetwork model, in which the pulse is formed and windowed by a Gaussian or a Rectangular window. Then, through RF Transmitter the RF UWB signal is generated and measured.  In this design, a radar channel delay is included for modeling the range information. An RF Receiver is provided to demod the received data.   • Example2 - Pseudo Random UWB Signal

All the models in this example can be used as templates for custom models. Users can open these models and modify them as needed to create custom models for their own system simulation.

 

Due to the large amount of data generated by the simulations in this workspace, the workspace is shipped without any saved simulation data. This is why the graphs display "No Data". To enable saving of the simulation data when the workspace is saved open each Data Flow analysis and in the Options tab check the check box labeled "Data Persistence".

Workspace.Name: Radar_RF_Modeling_SingleTRx
Workspace.Description:
Single Channel RF Impairment Modeling for 

Radar System Simulation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

************************************************

Simulation Task

************************************************

This workspace demonstrates the 3-layer architecture based radar simulation with single channel Tx & Rx RF impairment modeling, using both the dataflow behavior RF models and Spectrasys RF models.

************************************************

Workspace Description

************************************************

This workspace is designed as a template to show the way to set up the arbitrary type radar simulation based on the generalized 3-layer framework and how to generate the echoes from the scatters of targets, together with RF impairment modeling capabilities. The example includes three layers: trajectory layer, antenna layer and signal layer. For waveform and signal processing design, we just give LFM and traditional pulse-compression and pulse-doppler results.

 

This RF modeling capability is demonstrated by two ways, one is the behavioral models (mixers, amplifiers, filters) from the algorithm library (Design0 schematic), and the other is using the frequency domain models in the Spectrasys RF Design library and the channel is represented by RF_Link in the high-level simulation (Design1 schematic). 

 

1) Behavioral RF Modeling (No additional license)

 

This is the basic way to model the RF impairments for any radar system. This method is very straight-forward with very fast simulation speed, and only requires several basic parts to model a single RF channel (mixer -> amplifier -> BP filter, etc.), for instance. Also some fundamental RF modeling parameters are provided in each part for user input.

 

2) Spectrasys RF_Link Modeling (Requires Spectrasys license)

 

This is a more advanced way to model the RF impairments for any radar system. This method requires separate channel building for Tx & RF channels (see RF_Designs folder for more details), and user would need to establish RF Spectrasys analysis to analyze the RF impairments for both channels.

 

Although it seems complicated, the Spectrasys provides more accurate frequency domain analysis to the RF channels (frequency domain RFuW modeling methodology with Keysight IP), then transforms the freq-domain results back to dataflow.

 

To create your own system, you can modify the template by changing parameters or replace models that are either in the radar/beamforming library or import your customized RF models in the design.

 

NOTE: Spectrasys Filtering Delay Compensation Realized in the Design1 Schematic

 

One important point in Spectrasys RF_link modeling is the additional delayed sample issue caused by Spectrasys filters. User can read the Spectrasys filtering either from the additional automatic folders (in this case they are the Design1/2_Data_Folder) or the simulation log from the 1st time simulation.

 

Then, for the 2nd time simulation, the compensation can be done using the Const + ChopVarOffset models after the pulse compression part. Related sample point calculation is simple and is presented in the Equation tab of Design1 schematic.

 

The “NoDelay” dataset is generated by shorting (bypassing) all filters in Tx & RF spectrasys RF designs, and the “TxRxFltrDelay” dataset is generated by enabling all the filters (except the 1st BPF in Tx channel) in both designs. It can be observed that by compensating these delays, the pulse compression Range-Doppler spectrum maps and PD results are identical.

Workspace.Name: 3GPP_LTE_DL_BER_RF_Link
Workspace.Description:
3GPP_LTE_DL_SISO_BER_RF_Link

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates swept BER and BLER for an LTE downlink SISO system using a realistic LTE RF downconverter sub-system.  To run this example you will need a license for both the RF Design Kit AND the 3GPP LTE Baseband Verification Library.

 

The RF subsystem is modeled using SystemVue's RF System analysis with the resulting sub-system model embedded into a time domain simulation for LTE DL BER.

 

 

Simulation Control Instruction

 

1. To get stable BER performance, the "Data Flow Analysis -> Options tab -> Repeatable Random Sequences" option is selected to get the fixed noise. With fixed noise, the waterfall BER curve could be gotten even when the simulation frame length is not long.

2. To enable more realistic random noise sequences, uncheck the "Data Flow Analysis -> Options -> Repeatable Random Sequences" box.

 

With the SNR set to -1 dB expect a BER near 6e-03. SNRs higher than this will result in far lower BER.

 

 

RF Subsystem Analysis

 

The RF subsystem is modeled in design "RFcircuit" using the RF System analysis "System". This analysis shows the spectral performance of the RF subsystem from RF input to IF output. Also calculated are Cascaded Noise Figure (CNF) and individual stage gain (GAIN) for the system. These are plotted in graphs "RF_System_CNF" and "RF_System_GAIN", respectively. Other measurements can be plotted by adding a graph to the workspace and selecting the appropriate variable from the "System_Data_Path1" dataset.

 

Note that the channel bandwidth is set to the default of 1 MHz so all of the noise powers, including the LO phase noise, will scale by this bandwidth. Set this to the desired value and/or be sure to set the LO phase noise to the desired level.

 

 

LTE BER Simulation

 

The design titled "LTE_FDD_DL_AWGN_BER" is setup to perform a BER/BLER simulation for a 5MHz BW LTE DL signal.  Other LTE DL configurations can be established by using the LTE DL Source GUI and LTE DL Receiver GUI parameters respectively.   The basic LTE system simulation is enhanced by inserting the RF/IF subsystem into the time domain simulation flow using SystemVue's "RF_Link" capability. The full impairments of this subsystem are modeled showing proper degradation of system performance with "REAL" RF.

 

The simulation is set up for a RX power level of -100 dbm/sub-carrier with an SNR = -1 dB.  These parameters can be changed by using the Parameters tab of the "LTE_FDD_DL_AWGN_BER" design and in the LTE source GUI on the "Power" tab.

 

 

Non-HARQ Simulation Instruction

 

To enable the non-HARQ simulation for UE1, the following settings must be met.

  1. Set the 'UE1_HARQ_Enable' parameter in LTE top-level sources and receivers to NO. Ignore the  'UE1_NumHARQ'  and 'UE1_MaxHARQTrans' parameters
  2. The first value in the 'UE1_RV_Sequence' parameter (i.e. UE1_RV_Sequence(1)) is read as the redundancy version coding index.
  3. Set the 'ReceiverDelay' parameter in LTE top-level receivers to 'one frame delay (10ms)', which means one frame is delayed in the receivers.
  4. Leave the 'HARQ_Bits' port in sources unconnected.

Use the 'LTE_BER_FER'' part to measure the simulated BER/FER. Note that the input port to the 'Ref' part should not come from the source that is sent to the LTE source because of platform limit, and the measurement should at least begin with the second frame (i.e. set FrameStart >=1).

Workspace.Name: AmplifierGComp_AM-AM_AM-PM
Workspace.Description:
Amplifier Gain Compression, AM2AM, AM2PM

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how to use the Data Flow amplifier model in the two GCType modes:

  • Gain compression vs input power
  • AM/AM and AM/PM vs input power

Please read the documentation for more details on how the amplifier nonlinearity is modeled in these two cases.

 

These two modes are meant to be used with measured data. One common amplifier measurement is PwrOut vs PwrIn and PhaseOut vs PwrIn. Data from such a measurement cannot be used directly in the amplifier model in the above two modes. However, this workspace provides functions that can convert this data to the appropriate form (see Functions folder).

 

The three datasets Amplifier1, Amplifier2, Amplifier3 have data representing PwrOut vs PwrIn and PhaseOut vs PwrIn for three different amplifiers. PwrOut and PwrIn are in dBm and PhaseOut is in deg. These datasets were actually created by simulating the amplifier in some of its other modes (TOI, dBc1, TOI+dBc1, PSat+GCSat+TOI, RappNonlinearity, etc.) with some additional signal processing to introduce some phase distortion. The input signal for these measurements was a single tone with phase of 0. If the phase of the input is not 0, then the output phase has to be adjusted to represent NOT the actual phase at the output but how much phase shift the amplifier has introduced.

 

First explore the graphs showing different amplifier measurements in the AmplifierData folder.

 

In the Amplifier Measurements equation, select the amplifier you want to see graphs for (set Data variable to one of Amplifier1, Amplifier2, Amplifier3). In addition, select the appropriate linear gain by commenting/uncommenting the proper lines defining G. The Amplifier Measurements equation calls the functions GetGCompData and GetAM2AM_AM2PM (defined in the Functions folder) to extract the Gain and Phase Change data (to be used in the Gain Compression vs input power mode) and the AM/AM AM/PM data (to be used in the AM/AM and AM/PM vs input power mode). Then run the equation and look at the three graphs

  • PwrOut and PhaseOut vs PwrIn: shows output power and phase vs input power
  • Gain Change and Phase Change vs PwrIn: shows gain and phase change (from small signal gain and phase) vs input power
  • AM2AM and AM2PM vs PwrIn: shows AM/AM and AM/PM  vs input power

Next open Desing1. This design uses two amplifiers, one with GCType set to Gain compression vs input power and one with GCType set to AM/AM and AM/PM vs input power. The data used in these amplifiers (GComp parameter) is the data extracted in Amplifier Measurements equation.

 

Next run Sweep1 and observe the results in the graphs PwrOut vs PwrIn Compare and PhaseOut vs PwrIn Compare. These graphs compare the output power and phase vs input power from the "reference" AmplifierN dataset (red Reference curves) with the simulation results from the two amplifier models in Design1 (blue curves from the Gain compression vs input power mode and greem curves from the AM/AM and AM/PM vs input power mode). Try this with each of the three AmplifierN datasets.

Workspace.Name: Low_IF_Receiver_test
Workspace.Description:
LOW_IF_Receiver_test

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demostrates the performance of a low-IF receiver with the IQ mismatch estimation and compensation algorithm.

 

The workspace has been saved without simulation data to reduce its size, so the graphs/tables will show no data and the equation EVM_Equations will trigger an error until you run the analysis DF2.

 

The low-IF receiver has an advantage over other architectures because it does not require image filtering. It can completely reject the image band when two conditions are satisfied. First, the LO must produce signals with a phase difference of exactly 90 degrees. Second, the gains and phase responses of the I and Q branches must be matched. Unfortunately, the requirements are impossible to meet in practice. Mismatches in analog components cause an imbalance in the gain and phase responses of the branches. Therefore, the image band can no longer be rejected completely.

 

In this example, a low IF architecture is proposed which enables the estimation and compensation of the IQ mismatch, therefore, minimize the impact of IQ mismatch.

 

Reference:

1. A Low-complexity Feed-forward I/Q Imbalance Compensation Algorithm

2. I/Q IMBALANCE COMPENSATION ALGORITHM BASED ON NEUTRAL NETWORKS

Monte Carlo And Yield

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates how to create scattergrams for Monte Carlo analyses and yield sensitivity plots for Yield analyses.

 

Design1 generates a QPSK signal with a symbol rate of 0.5 MHz sampled at 4 MHz. The RollOff factor of the raised cosine filters is defined in the Equations tab and is set to be tunable.

 

The PeakToAverage Equations page post processes the data saved in the ModOut sink to compute the peak to average ratio of the QPSK singal. The peak to average ratio is a function of the raised cosine filter RollOff factor.

 

In the Monte Carlo analysis MonteCarlo1 we statistically vary the RollOff factor uniformly in the range [0, 1] and record the peak to average ratio. The Equations page MC_Scattergram extracts data from the MonteCarlo1_Data dateset to create a scattergram of the peak to average ratio values versus the RollOff factor. This scattergram is shown in Graph MC Scattergram Graph.

 

In the Yield analysis Yield1 we statistically vary the RollOff factor uniformly in the range [0, 1] and track the pass/fail status of a peak to average ratio target of less than 3.75 dB. The Graph Yield Sensitivity Graph shows the histogram of the Rolloff factor values. In addition, this graph shows the percent of runs with a pass status in each histogram bin (plotted on the right y-axis). These values are calculated in the YieldSensitivity Equations page, which  post processes the data in the Yield1_Data dataset.

Workspace.Name: Oscillator_Phase_Noise
Workspace.Description:
Oscillator Phase Noise

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

Phase noise modeling and impact on system BER performance is demnstrated in these examples.

 

1. "Random PN"

This design demonstrates an oscillator with random phase noise..  An Oscillator source is used to generate a 1 GHz tone at a power level of 10 dBm into 50 Ohms. The tone is colored with phase noise, whose frequency specification is defined in the PhaseNoiseData parameter. For this example, f offsetMin is 1 kHz and f offsetMax is 400 kHz.

The simulation time step is set to (1 / 2 13 ) msec, which is small enough to resolve the maximum phase noise frequency offset data point at 400 kHz. The simulation stop time is set to 1 msec, which is large enough to resolve the lowest phase noise frequency offset data point at 1 kHz.

 

The spectrum of the signal is measured using a SpectrumAnalyzer block. The spectrum is shown in graph DF1_S1_Power. The resolution bandwidth of the spectrum measurement is 1 / ( Stop - Start ) = 1 / ( 1 msec ) = 1 kHz. This means that each spectral tone displayed will be at multiples of 1 kHz from the carrier frequency of 1 GHz.  For noise power integrated over a 1 kHz bandwidth, the power would be 30 dB (=10 × log10(1000)) more than that in a 1 Hz bandwidth.

 

2. "Fixed Frequency Offsets & Amplitudes"

This design shows the signal spectrum when PN_Type= Fixed freq offset and amplitude and TStop=2 msec. This PN_Type is available only for better observation of the phase noise specification.  One would typically use PN_Type=Random PN for system analysis. The resolution bandwidth of the spectrum measurement is 1 / ( Stop - Start ) = 0.5 kHz.  All phase noise signal power will be located at frequencies that are integer multiples of f offsetMin = 1 kHz and the spectrum values at frequencies (M+0.5) kHz (where M is an integer) will be practically 0.

3. "Random PN with Freq Multiplication"

This design demonstrates how an oscillator with random phase noise changes when sent through a frequency multiplier.  The frequency multiplier causes the phase noise to increase as 20*log10(N) where N is the multiplication factor (MultFactor).  An interactive slider is usable in the schematic to tune MultFactor from 1 to 9. 

4. "QPSK BER with Phase Noise"

Many systems use a lower frequency Reference LO that is multiplied to a higher  frequency, at the expense of poor phase noise.  This design demonstrates how the BER of a QPSK system degrades with increasing frequency mulitplication factor MultFactoForBER.   The variable MultFactoForBER is swept from 1 to 6 in steps of 1, representing a fundamental LO freq = 800MHz at the start, to a 6th harmonic of a 133MHz source at the end. The phase noise sidebands are declared as an array of amplitude/offset pairs in the variable PhaseNoiseForBER.  The resultant swept BER plot is in Sweep4_BERvsMult.

5. "QPSK BER"

This design demonstrates a QPSK system that will serve as the reference against which the 'QPSK BER with Phase Noise' is compared.  This design is used to set up alignment of the Bits input and BitsOut signals with appropriate setting of the delay instances D1 and D2 parameter N.  This QPSK ssytem is set up with ideal root raised cosine filters.  The BER is ideal at zero.

Workspace.Name: QPSK_RF_Link_Demo
Workspace.Description:
RF Link Demo Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This workspace illustrates a tops-down DSP/RF design flow that combines Data Flow (signal processing simulation, included with the SystemVue environment) with Spectrasys (RF system tool, found in the W1719 RF Design Kit add-on product).  RF sections for the Transmit (TX) and Receive (RX) functions are characterized and then pass realistic communications Layer 1 signals.  This provides greater RF accuracy to baseband simulations, and greater signal complexity to Spectrasys.  It also allows the Baseband and RF teams to use each other's engineering data/designs directly and concurrently.

 

You might want to print this page for easy reference as you explore this example.

Combined RF/DSP Electronic System-Level (ESL) Design Flow

 

Demo 1: DATAFLOW: Design DSP algorithm for comms PHY signal (QPSK)

  • Design the QPSK signal.
  • Define RF TX IF frequency.
  • Run analysis "DF_QPSK_Source".
  • The graph 'DS_QPSK_Source_SpecMod_Power' show the generated QPSK RF spectrum.

Demo 2: SPECTRASYS: Design the RF Transmit system, and evaluate its broadband frequency response.

  • The RF TX system is a single mixer upconverter design that takes an IF input frequency at 220 MHz and outputs an RF frequency at 1960 MHz.
  • First task is to create an RF TX design that does not contain undesirable levels of intermods, harmonics, or other spurious in the RF TX output information bandwidth.
  • Characterize the bandpass response for this design; Gain vs Frequency In, Power In; Output noise vs Freq.
  • Run analysis "TX_Section_Analysis".
  • The graph 'TX_Section_PTX_RF_output' shows the broadband frequency response with the fundamental and all generated intermodulation (IM) products and harmonics.  Expand the spectrum about the fundamental output 1960 MHz frequency and observe the level of IM products produced.  The odd order IM products due to the nonlinearities are clearly visible (displayed with wider spectral widths since the fundamental was defined to have a spectral width of 1 MHz).
  • The graph 'TX_Section_Data_EntirePath_CP' shows the main signal path gain profile with an overall gain of 45 dB with display of the progressive gain along the signal path.
  • The graph 'TX_Section_Data_EntirePath_COMP' shows the amount of gain compression for each component along the main signal path.  RFAmp_3 has the greates gain compression at 0.5 dB.

Demo 3: DATAFLOW: Evaluate the combined DSP/RF Transmit design for its bandpass time domain (complex envelope) response with the comms PHY signal.

  • Use RF_Link to embed the RF TX system designed in Demo 2 within a Data Flow bandpass analysis and combined with the QPSK signal designed in Demo 1.
  • Ensure acceptable degradation of the comms PHY signal quality.
  • Run analysis "QPSK_RF_TX_test".
  • Signal quality can be observed by measuring the RF TX output spectrum (looking at spectral regrowth due to nonlinearities) and EVM performance. 
  • Notice the use of the AddNDensity at the output of the Modulator to set the noise density for the signal into the RF TX system at -174 dBm/Hz.
  • Optionally, the user can use a floating point to fixed point converter at the input of the Modulator with possible choices including AtoD, AtoD_ADI, FltToFxp models.
  • The graph 'QPSK_RF_TX_SpecIn_Power' shows the QPSK RF spectrum at the input of the RF TX system.
  • The graph 'QPSK_RF_TX_SpecOut_Power' shows the QPSK RF spectrum at the output of the RF TX system and shows the spectral sideband growth due to the nonlinearities in the RF TX system and includes the noise from the RF TX system.
  • The table 'QPSK_RF_TX_EVM' shows the EVM measurement at the input (REF_EVM_RMS) and output (RFLINK_EVM_RMS) of the RF TX system (EVM values are in %).  As expected, the output EVM is degraded, but within an acceptable level to validate the design of the RF TX system as acceptable for use in an overall QPSK comms system.

Demo 4: SPECTRASYS:  Transmit path is done, now design the RF Receiver system and evaluate its broadband frequency response .

  • The RF RX system is a single mixer downconverter design that takes a primary RF input frequency at 1960 MHz and outputs an IF frequency at 150 MHz.
  • Tones are used to represent three RF RX input adjacent channel PHY signals; it also includes an input tone for an input image signal.
  • Create an RF Receiver design that does not contain undesirable intermods, harmonics, or other spurious in the RF RX output information bandwidth.
  • Characterize the bandpass response for this design;  Gain vs Frequency In, Power In; Output noise vs Freq
  • Run the analysis "RX_Section_Analysis".
  • The graph 'RX_Section_PRxOut' shows the broadband frequency response with the fundamental and all generated intermodulation (IM) products and harmonics.  Expand the spectrum about the fundamental output 150 MHz frequency and observe the level of IM products produced.  The IM products and harmonics due to the nonlinearities and mixer are clearly visible.
  • The graph 'RX_Section_Data_EntirePath_CP' shows the main signal path gain profile with an overall gain of approximately 104 dB with display of the progressive gain along the signal path.
  • The graph 'RX_Section_Data_EntirePath_COMP' shows the amount of gain compression for each component along the main signal path.  RFAmp_3 has the greatest gain compression at 0.16 dB.

Demo 5: DATAFLOW: Evaluate the combined DSP/RF Receiver design for its bandpass time domain (complex envelope) response with the comms PHY signals.

  • Use RF_Link to embed the RF RX system designed in Demo 4 within a Data Flow bandpass analysis.
  • Include the three input adjacent channel PHY signals and an image signal.
    Ensure acceptable degradation of the comms PHY signal quality.
  • Run the analysis "QPSK_RF_RX_test".
  • Signal quality can be observed by measuring the RF RX output spectrum (looking at spectral regrowth due to nonlinearities) and BER performance. 
  • BER is not measured in this design.
  • The graph 'QPSK_RF_RX_SpecIn_Power' shows the QPSK RF spectrum at the input of the RF RX system including adjacent channel QPSK signals.
  • The graph 'QPSK_RF_RX_SpecOut_Power' shows the QPSK RF spectrum at the output of the RF RX system (red trace) as well as the noise from just the RF RX system (blue trace). Observe the spectral sideband growth due to the nonlinearities in the RF RX system and the filtering of the adjacent channel QPSK signals.

Workspace.Name: QPSK_with_Interferer_VSA
Workspace.Description:
QPSK Transmitter with RF Blocks

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Tutorial Workspace

 

Building simple to complex RF architectures is easy with SystemVue!   This example workspace illustrates basic capability in SystemVue for creating custom RF architectures and modulation structures that can be quickly and easily analyzed, including incorporation of RF impairments and channel interferrence.

 

We have setup the simulation to be controlled directly from the schematic.  Simply move the sliders to control:

 

- Amplifier TOI

- Interferer Frequency

 

You can also enable Keysight's VSA sink to look at the signal dynamically.   This VSA interface virtualizes actual instrumentation directly in SystemVue

 

For more information on Keysight's VSA signal analsis SW and to request an eval please visit.:

     http://www.keysight.com/find/VSA

 

Unlike other simualtion platorms that utilize strict time domain simualtion technologies, SystemVue incorporates a unique envelope simulation engine that simplies modeling of modulated systems and speeds simulation by orders of magnitude.

 

In this simualtion QPSK modulation is created using simple baseband signal processing blocks.  The complex signals are converted to "envelope" timed signals in the Modulator block.   The output of modulator is further processed with standard "RF" building blocks to add noise and interference as well as non-linear characteristics.

Workspace.Name: SData Demo
Workspace.Description:
Using a frequency response
from an S-parameter file
in a Dataflow simulation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Tutorial Workspace

 

This example shows how the SData model can be used to incorporate an arbitrary frequency response into a time-domain data flow simulation.  S-parameter data is common in RF systems, especially for antennas and amplifiers.

 

The S-parameter data is imported from an external file "SDataDemo.s2p" in the "Touchstone" S2P format.  Although S21 has been chosen out of all possible S-parameters in the file, you can choose whichever term you need from the data.  At runtime, it is turned into an FIR filter within the modulation bandwidth of the system sample rate, around the RF carrier frequency at that node, within tolerances specified under the "Advanced Parameters" tab.  This particular data file has a gain tilt from -8dB at 950 MHz to +10dB at 1050 MHz.  The group delay varies between 5-6ns across most of the band.

 

         The QPSK constellations are plotted before the S-parameter block, and after.  The EVM degradation is shown, and some equalization would be necessary in a real system.

 

How to execute this example

  1. Before running this example, make certain the "SDataTest.s2p" file is in the same folder as this example. (if you import the data into your SystemVue workspace, you no longer need to be concerned about the external file)
  2. Run the DF1 dataflow analysis, either from the toolbar, or from the controller itself.

For Finer Control...

 

This feature does not require an extra license.  However, for greater control over the quality of the transformation of the data, more control is possible with the RFLink capability that is included with the W1719 RF System Design Kit option to SystemVue.  This provides an additional RF block-level simulator called Spectrasys that accounts for much more than just frequency response.

 

Further Exploration

    The SDtata part can also use S-parameter information embedded in an SData dataset. 

 

    To bring the data inside a Touchstone file into an SData dataset on the workspace tree, use File -> Import -> S-Data File ...

   To use the S-parameter data from the SData dataset, set up the SData part to use the SData dataset.

Workspace.Name: SPDT
Workspace.Description:
SPDT

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates the use of a Single Pole Double Throw (SPDT) switch. The switch transfers the signal at port 1 to port 3 (when the signal at port 2 is below the threshold specified) or port 4 (when the signal at port 2 is above the threshold specified).

 

This example uses the switch in two configurations: an ideal one and a non-ideal one.

 

In the ideal one, the input signal gets transfered to the proper output with no loss, the isolation between the input and the other output is perfect, and the switch turns on and off instantaneously.

 

In the non-ideal one, the input signal gets transfered to the proper output with 1 dB loss, the isolation between the input and the other output is not perfect (30 dB), and the switch takes some finite time to turn on and off (0.1 ms).

 

Look at the graphs Port 3 and Port 4 and observe the differences between the signals in the ideal and non-ideal configuration.
