Workspace.Name: VarAmpAGC_RF_Link
Workspace.Description:
VarAmpAGC_RF_Link

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates a simple AGC system using the Spectrasys VarAmp model in an RF_Link simulation

 

The design RF_Design in the RF folder is the basic building block of an AGC system; an amplifier with a variable gain controlled through the signal applied to a special "control" port. The variable gain amplifier (VarAmp model) in RF_Design is set up to provide a gain in the range -10 dB to 10 dB with a sensitivity on the signal applied to its control port of 1 dB per Volt (Slope parameter). The gain of -10 dB is achieved when the voltage applied to the control port is -10 V (Vmin parameter). Following the linear line of 1 dB/V we can compute that the maximum gain of 10 dB is achieved when the the voltage applied to the control port is 10 V (there is no parameter for this since it can be uniquely determined by GVmin, GVmax, Slope, Vmin parameters). For control voltages below -10 V, the gain stays constant at -10 dB. For control voltages above 10 V, the gain stays constant at 10 dB.

 

The VarAmp model also provides parameters to define its non-linear behavior as well as noise performance. The model is implemented as a hierarchical design (right click on it and select Open > Model/Subcircuit) to see its implementation. It is a variable attenuation linear attenuator followed by a non-linear amplifier. An alternative topology would be to have the non-linear amplifier first followed by the variable attenuation linear attenuator. The choice of topology you choose depends on the trade-offs you want to make between non-linear distortion and noise perfromance. In this example, we will use the first topology (attenuator followed by amplifier).

 

As a first exercise, we are going to run some "static" simulations, where the control voltage is swept but stays constant through each simulation, to verify the performance of the VarAmp model in the frequency domain as well as in the time domain. Then we will set up an AGC system and run some dynamic time domain simulation, where the control voltage changes during the simulation.

 

Compression Curve Simulation

 

The System analysis System1 is set up with a Compression Curve Quick Sweep path on the RF_Design. Sweep RF_Sweep1 is set up to sweep the DC control voltage applied to the VarAmp control port. In the graph DCP_vs_Pin_Sweep you can see how the compression curve varies with the control voltage. The curves moves parallel to iteself (left to righ). If the alternate topology was used (amplifier followed by attenuator) the compression curve would move parallel to itself up and down.

 

Design Design1 in the folder DF > 1. Compression Curve is set up to do a compression curve simulation in the time domain using the RF_Design through RF_Link. The input signal to the RF design is a power ramp from -40 dBm to 40 dBm with a step of 1 dB (see equations of Design1). The voltages at the input and output of RF_Link are recorded and the corresponding powers are computed in the dataset DF1_Data using the user defined variables InPwr and OutPwr. Sweep DF_Sweep1 is set up to sweep the control voltage so we can get the compression curves vs control voltage. Graph Graph1 shows the compression curves from DF_Sweep1 (blue) on the same graph with the compression curves from the Spectrasys sweep RF_Sweep1 (red). There is very good agreement between the results of the time domain simulation (DF) and the frequency domain one (RF).

 

 

Noise Figure Simulation

 

The System analysis System2 is set up with a Normal path, which provides noise performance data. Sweep RF_Sweep2 is set up to sweep the DC control voltage applied to the VarAmp control port. Table NoiseTable_Sweep shows the Carrier to Noise Ratio at the input (CNR 1), the Carrier to Noise Ratio at the output (CNR 2), and the Noise Figure (CNF) of the RF design versus the control voltage. As we can see as the control voltage increases, the variable attenuation linear attenuator provides less and less attenuation and so the noise figure improves.

 

Design Design2 in the folder DF > 2. Noise Figure is set up to do a noise figure simulation in the time domain using the RF_Design through RF_Link. The input signal to the RF design is a CW tone at 100 MHz with -20 dBm power (same as in the RF design). The Oscillator model used to generate this tone is also establishing a noise floor at -173.975 dBm/Hz (this is important for being able to measure Noise Figure). The spectrum at the input and output of the RF_Link is measured and the corresponding SNRs are computed in the dataset DF2_Data using the user defined variables In_TonePwr, In_NoisePwr, In_SNR_dB,  Out_TonePwr, Out_NoisePwr, Out_SNR_dB. Then NF is computed by simply subtracting the output SNR from the input one (see variable NF_dB). Sweep DF_Sweep2 is set up to sweep the control voltage so we can get the SNRs and NF vs control voltage. Table DF_NoiseTable_Sweep shows the results from DF_Sweep2. If you compare these values with the ones in the table NoiseTable_Sweep you will see very good agreement (within 0.2 dB).

 

Note that the CNR/SNR results in the tables above depend on the bandwidth over which we measure the noise power. It just happens that the default channel measurement BW in the System analysis is 1 MHz and the default simulation Sample_Rate in the Data Flow analysis, which sets the simulation bandwidth for a complex envelope simulation, is also 1 MHz. Therefore, we are measuring noise power over the same bandwidth in both simulation and this is why the CNR/SNR values match. If for example you change the Data Flow simulation Sample_Rate to 10 MHz, the SNR values will drop by 10 dB compared to the ones with 1 MHz simulation sampling rate (since now the noise power will be 10 times bigger assuming we have a flat noise density). However, the NF results will still match since they are the difference between the two SNR values and both SNR values increased by the same amount. If you change the sampling rate in the DF simulation, you should delete RF_Link dataset (by manually deleting it from the workspace or by double clicking on the RF_Link part and pressing the Clear Behavioral Data button) and let it be regenerated when the DF2 analysis or the DF_Sweep2 sweep is run.

 

In addition, note that the noise figure results in the DF time domain simulation depend on the random seed used (see Repeatable Random Sequences setting in the Options tab of the Data Flow analysis dialog) and could vary from simulation to simulation depending on the settings.

 

AGC with CW Signal

 

Design Design3 in the folder DF > 3. AGC with CW shows an example of how to maintain the level of a received CW signal constant regardless of some variable gain/attenuation that can occur between the transmitter and the receiver. It uses the RF design we have used in the previous two designs along with some control system that detects the level of the received signal and generates the appropriate control voltage to be sent to the control port of the Rf design (VarAmp model).

 

The CW tone is generated by the Oscillator O1 at 100 MHz and -20 dBm. A variable gain is applied to this signal using the Amplifier model A1 and the dynamically tunable (through the variable Gain_dB) constant C2 connected to the amplifier control port. Then we establish the noise floor at the input of our AGC system at -173.975 dBm/Hz so we can perform NF measurements. The AGC system includes the RF system (VarAmp) brought into the Data Flow design using RF_Link and blocks to compute a control voltage such that at the output of the AGC we compensate for the variable gain introduced by the Amplifier A1 and the dynamically tunable constant C2. Spectrum measurements are set up at the output of the CW tone generator (Tx), at the input of the AGC system (RxAGC_In), and at the output of the AGC system (RxAGC_Out).

 

To generate the control signal we first have to detect the received signal level. A good measure of that is the RMS value of the received signal voltage. So after getting the magnitude of the received signal we square it, average it over a window of 1000 samples, and take the square root of the average. The next step is to compare the RMS voltage with a reference level and decide the value of the control signal we need to generate. As we saw earlier, the RF design can provide a variable gain in the range [-10, 10] dB with a sensitivity on the control signal of 1 dB/V and Vmin of -10 V. Therefore, a gain of 0 dB is achieved with a control voltage of 0 V, and this should correspond to our reference level. If the RMS voltage is equal to our reference (desired) level, then the AGC should not provide any adjustment (0 dB gain), which means we need to generate a control signal of 0 V. Since our goal is to compensate any dynamically introduced gain and recover the original signal level (at -20 dBm of power), our reference RMS level is sqrt(1.0e-3) V (for an envelope signal P = Venv_rms^2/(2*50), so Venv_rms = sqrt( P * 100 ), and for P = -20 dBm = 10e-6 W, Venv_rms = sqrt( 10e-6 * 100 ) = sqrt(1.0e-3)). So we take the ratio of the measured RMS voltage to the reference RMS voltage (Gain G1), and then compute -20*log10( ) of the result (since the sensitivity is defined as dB/V). Let's try a few test cases

  • if the measured RMS voltage is equal to the reference one, then the ratio of the measured RMS to the reference is 1, and log10 of that will be 0, so the generated control signal is 0
  • if the dynamic gain introduced is 1 dB, the measured RMS voltage will be sqrt(1.0e-3) (generated by the Oscillator) times sqrt( 10^(0.1) ), so the ratio of the measured to the reference is sqrt( 10^(0.1) ). In this case, we want the AGC to provide a gain of -1 dB, so the control voltage should be -1. Indeed -20*log10( sqrt( 10^(0.1) ) = -20 * 0.5 *log10( 10^(0.1) ) = -10 * 0.1 = -1
  • if the dynamic gain introduced is -2 dB, the measured RMS voltage will be sqrt(1.0e-3) (generated by the Oscillator) times sqrt( 10^(-0.2) ), so the ratio of the measured to the reference is sqrt( 10^(-0.2) ). In this case, we want the AGC to provide a gain of 2 dB, so the control voltage should be 2. Indeed -20*log10( sqrt( 10^(-0.2) ) = -20 * 0.5 *log10( 10^(-0.2) ) = -10 * (-0.2) = 2

Now let's run the simulation and look at some results. The spectrum analyzers are set up to bring up dynamic graphs so when we dynamically change the gain introduced we can see the effects in the spectra in real time. The dynamic graphs are also set up to measure noise power so we can quickly perform some NF calculations and see NF change due to the control voltage changes (as a result of dynamically introducing a gain between the generated signal and the input of the AGC). The generated control signal is also recorded in a sink with dynamic display enabled so we can monitor it too.
 
Make sure the Tune Window is visible. Let's start with the Gain_dB tunable variable set to 0. Run the analysis DF3. A Dynamic Graphs window will pop up. You should see three spectrum graphs at the top (in separate tabs): Spectrum Power (Tx), Spectrum Power (RxAGC_In), and Spectrum Power (RxAGC_Out). You should also see a time domain graph showing the control voltage at the bottom. The control voltage is at 0 V, the Tx spectrum shows a pure tone at -20 dBm and noise floor less than -300 dBm, the RxAGC_In spectrum shows a tone at -20 dBm and noise power (in half of the bandwidth) at -117 dBm, and the RxAGC_Out spectrum shows a tone at -20 dBm and noise power (in half of the bandwidth) at -104 dBm. If we were to compute the SNR at the AGC input and output (assuming the noise power in the other half of the BW is the same):
AGC_In_SNR = -20 - ( -117 + 3 ) = 94 dB
AGC_Out_SNR = -20 - ( -104 + 3 ) = 81 dB
The degradation in the SNR is 13 dB and agrees with the NF value shown in the table DF_NoiseTable_Sweep for a control voltage of 0 V.
 
No let's change the Gain_dB variable in the tune window to -2 dB. You will notice that the control voltage jumps to 2 V, the RxAGC_In spectrum now shows the tone at -22 dBm and the noise power at -117 dBm, and the RxAGC_Out spectrum stays the same as before. So the AGC was able to compensate for the 2 dB loss introduced. Let's compute the NF again.
AGC_In_SNR = -22 - ( -117 + 3 ) = 92 dB
AGC_Out_SNR = -20 - ( -104 + 3 ) = 81 dB
The degradation in the SNR is 11 dB and again agrees with the NF value shown in the table DF_NoiseTable_Sweep for a control voltage of 2 V.
 
Try different values for the Gain_dB variable, observe the changes in the dynamic graphs, and verify that the AGC NF agrees with the results we got from the static Noise Figure simulations.
 
Note that if you change the Gain_dB variable outside the range [-10, 10], then the AGC will no longer be able to compensate for the dynamically introduced gain, since its range of operation is [-10, 10] dB of gain.
 
 

AGC with QAM 16 Signal

 

Design Design4 in the folder DF > 4. AGC with QAM 16 shows an example of an AGC system used with a modulated signal. The goal again is to maintain a constant signal level at the output of the AGC regardless of variations in the signal level at the input of the AGC. The AGC control system setup is similar to the one in the previous example but with some diffrences as will be explained below.

 

The QAM 16 signal is using an RRC filter with a roll-off factor (Alpha) of 0.5 as the pulse shaping filter. It has a symbol rate of 1 MHz and is sampled at 8 samples per symbol (see Design4 equations for the defintions of these variables). It is then used to modulate a 100 MHz carrier. The power at the output of the modulator is 10 dBm as can be measured with the SpectrumAnalyzer Tx. The modulated signal then goes through a channel that is modeled by a fixed loss (Amplifier A3) a variable loss (Amplifier A1 and Const C2) and an AWGN generator (AddNdensity A2). The channel is set up so that the noise floor at the input of the receiver is -173.975 dBm/Hz and the SNR at the nominal (fixed) channel loss is 30 dB (see Design4 equations for more details).

 

The AGC control system first filters the input signal with a matched RRC filter to remove any ISI (InterSymbol Interference) and also maximize the receiver SNR. Then the signal is demodualted and downsampled to recover the QAM 16 symbol values. The optimal downsampling phase of 6 was determined by using the decativated ConstellationEnv C3 sink, shorting the AddNDensity A2 part, and tuning the downsampling phase of C3 until we get a clean constellation. Note that if you make changes to the design you may have to adjust the downsampling phase. After the symbol values are recovered we get their magnitude and perform an RMS average over 1000 symbols. Then we need to compare the RMS value with a desired reference and (as in Design3) take -20*log10() of the ratio of the measured to the reference RMS value. Since we downsampled by a factor of 8 to get the symbol value we have to upsample by a factor of 8 (Repeat part R1) to keep the rate at the input and output of the control system the same. The way we compute the reference RMS voltage is explained next.

 

Since the goal of our AGC system is to compensate for the variable gain/loss on top of the nominal channel loss, our reference RMS should be the RMS value of the recovered symbols at the nominal (fixed) channel loss. The RMS value of the QAM 16 symbols generated by the Mapper model is 1. The RRC filters in Tx and Rx are set up to preserve this RMS value. So if there was no channel loss, the RMS value measured would be 1. When the nominal loss is ChannelLoss, the RMS value would be 1 * sqrt( 10^( -ChannelLoss/10 ). So this is the reference RMS value we need to use for our AGC control system (see Gain G1).

 

Now let's run the simulation and look at some results. We have set up spectrum analyzers and DigitalDemod sinks at the input and output of the AGC system to measure the spectrum, constellation, EVM, SNR, etc. Make sure the Tune Window is visible. Let's start with the Gain_dB tunable variable set to 0. Run the analysis DF4. A Dynamic Graphs window will pop up. The top left corner of the window has three tabs for the three spectra (Tx, RxAGC_In, RxAGC_Out). The top right corner has two tabs showing the constellation at the AGC input and output. The bottom right corner has two tabs showing the EVM Errors Summary at the AGC input and output. Finally, the bottom left corner shows the control voltage.

 

With Gain_dB set to 0, we get our nominal (fixed) channel loss, so the control voltage should be 0. The EVM Errors Summary at the AGC input shows an SNR of approximately 36 dB (if the numbers fluctuate too fast you can press the pause button in the Dynamic Graphs window to get a few readings). This is actually about 6 dB higher than the target SNR we set in the Design4 equations. The reason is that the SNR used in Design4 equations measured the noise power across the entire 8 MHz simulation BW. However, the DigitalDemod sink uses an RRC measurement filter to limit the noise to the actual BW of the QAM 16 signal. The BW of a bandpass RRC filter with roll-off factor (Alpha) is SymbolRate * (1+Alpha) = 1 * 1.5 = 1.5 MHz in our case. So the noise power is reduced by a factor of 8 /1.5 = 5.333 = 7.3 dB. This matches approximately the 6 dB improvement we see in SNR reported by the DigitalDemod sink connected to the AGC input. The EVM Errors Summary at the AGC output shows an SNR of approximately 23 dB. The SNR degradation between the AGC input and output is 13 and matches the NF of the AGC system for a control voltage of 0 V (see table DF_NoiseTable_Sweep). Observe some of the other graphs in the Dynamic Window before we change the Gain_dB variable.

 

Now change Gain_dB variable in the Tune Window to 4 dB. Notice how the control voltage drops to -4 V. The level of the spectrum RxAGC_In increased as did the level of the constellation RxAGC_In_Demod. However, the level of the spectrum RxAGC_Out and of the constellation RxAGC_Out_Demod remained the same. The reported SNR at the AGC input is approximately 40 dB and at the SNR output is approximately 23 dB. The degradation of 17 dB again matches the NF of the AGC system for a control voltage of -4 V (see table DF_NoiseTable_Sweep). Try a few more values for Gain_dB and observe how the dynamic graphs react. Stop the simulation.

 

The last exercise would be to replace the dynamically tunable Const source that controls the variable gain/loss to the channel model with a slow time varying function like a sinusoid of 5 Hz. This is more like what would happen in a real world fading scenario where the channel loss would vary slowly rather than change abruptly in steps of a a couple of dBs. So disable (open) the Const source C2, enable the SineGen source S1, and run the simulation. In the Dynamic Graphs window make the RxAGC_In spectrum and RxAGC_In_Demod constellation plots visible. Observe how their levels "oscillate" between a max and min value as the control voltage also "oscillates" between -10 V and 10 V. Now make the RxAGC_Out spectrum and RxAGC_Out_Demod constellation plots visible. Observe that their levels stay constant.

Workspace.Name: ZIF_3GPP_test
Workspace.Description:
Zero-IF (ZIF) DownConverter - 3GPP Stimulus

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace demonstrates SystemVue's capability for simulating RF Subsystems, showing 

  • RF-aware dataflow models that account for a useful range of RF effects, such as higher-order nonlinearities, mixer images, noise, and jitter
  • RF-aware dataflow engine that accounts for frequency conversion, GHz carriers and low IF in the same simulation (envelope).  Instead of lowpass-sampling at a 6 GHz rate, the system is sampled closer to the symbol rate (~60MHz), yielding 10kHz of ResBW in only 6k simulation points, instead of requiring 600k points.  The simulation is therefore 100x faster than other engines when running RF-caliber models

The ZIF model in this workspace includes 2nd order and 3rd order nonlinear modeling to simulate the effects of DC at baseband.   ZIF model parameters are set in the "Design Variables" equation block located on workspace tree and the most influential ones have been made "tunable".

 

Explore these changes (make each change, then restore the value and try the next change)

  • Tune the Lo_to_Rf_Isolation to -10 and observe the output DC offset term
  • Tune the Rf_to_Lo_isolation to -10 and observe the 1 MHz term
  • Power: Tune the Second Order Intercept parameter (SOI) of the mixer down to +10dBm
  • Power: Tune the incident RX_power to -50 dBm and then -10 dBm input power.  Change the LNA_TOI and Mixer_SOI to +20 and try changing the input power again.
  • Noise: Give the LNA a noise figure of 5dB.  (simulate) Enable the RF source with phase noise, and disable the RF source without phase noise. (simulate).

Workspace.Name: ADI_PMF_SNR_test
Workspace.Description:
A to D Converter
Performance Measurements

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This workspace measures the output performance of an A-to-D device using a single sinusoid excitation.

 

AtoD model selection:

Within the schematic Design1

  • open the dialog for the AtoD_ADI_Model and select the desired ADI AtoD model.
  • Then set NBits and Range in the Equation1 page

Single frequency performance:

Simulation setup: within the Design1 analysis,

    • set the desired 'System Sample Rate' and 'Number of Samples'.
  • At the top of the Equation1 page,
    • set the nominal test frequency, Fnom.  When this value is above the Nyquist rate ( 'System Sample Rate' /2 ), the AtoD is operated in an undersampled mode
    • set the dB level from full scale, dBFS
    • set EnableNCO=1. This AtoD model is a PMF model has a mode enabled that displays the NCO_Freq parameter.
    • set NCO_FreqNom if EnableNCO=1.

NOTE: If EnableNCO=1, then the harmonics are not evaluated.  Instead, the levels for S2_dBc, S3_dBc, S4_dBc, S5_dBc and THD are set to -400 dBc.  Also, SNR = SINAD.

  • Run the 'Design1 Analysis' and observe the AtoD output spectrum in graph 'Design1_SpecOut' and the AtoD performance measures in Table1.

The output performance measures shown in Table1 includes:

  • SNR (Signal to Noise Ratio) in dB.  SNR is the ratio of the fundamental power to the noise power.
  • THD (Total Harmonic Distortion) in dB.  THD is the ratio of the fundamental power to the sum of the harmonic powers.
  • SINAD (Signal to Noise and Distortion) in dB.  SINAD is the ratio of the fundamental power to the sum of the harmonic and noise powers.
    • Generally, only the first 5 harmonics are significant. THD+N is the same as SINAD.
  • SFDR (Spurious Free Dynamic Range Ratio) in dB.  SFDR is the ratio of the fundamental power to the largest non-fundamental signal power.
  • ENOB (Equivalent Number of Bits).  ENOB is (SINAD_dB - 1.76 dB)/6.02; used when the input is a full scale sinusoid.
  • F1 through F5.  These are the AtoD output frequencies for the fundamental and upto the 5th harmonic with wrap around the Nyquist rate as needed.

Workspace.Name: DtoA_Jitter
Workspace.Description:
D to A Converter Jitter Performance Measurements

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This is a template that measures the output jitter performance of a D-to-A converter using a single sinusoid excitation.  DAC impairments are specified here in more familiar "output" terms, such as jitter, harmonic distortion levels, and intermodulation products between the sample clock harmonics & the signal.  INL and DNL are still possible but are not covered here. 

 

Additional Notes

Also, the "RepeatOutput" parameter effectively "upsamples" the incoming signal to a smaller timestep and repeats the output value, creating a staircase type output that adds a SIN(X)/X coloration to the spectral response to the higher order images in the reconstructured waveform.  (In the response plots you can easily see this SINC envelope).

 

The impairments can either be relative to the absolute full scale amplitude (dBFS) of Vref, or to the signal amplitude itself.  dBFS is the default. 

 

TRY THIS
There are several equations and variables that can be tuned interactively.  A few have been set up with sliders on the schematic. Others are available as constants in the EQUATION objects.

 

Some of the parameters in the CommonEquations page:

    • Common AtoD and DtoA_Model parameters:  NBits, VRef
    • AtoD specific parameters:  SNR
    • DtoA specific parameters:  dBFS, DtoA_Repeat
    • Signal source parameters:  FNom
    • Analysis parameters:  SampleR, NPts

SystemVue-GoldenGate Dual TX/RX Co-Simulation - LTE Uplink

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

In this workspace, SystemVue co-simulates with two GoldenGate instances:  one for transmitter RF circuit, and the other for the receiver.

  • GG_mixer is the SystemVue co-simulation block that communicates with the first GoldenGate instance, for transmitter RF circuit (mixer).
  • GG_LNA is the SystemVue co-simulation block that communicates with the second GoldenGate instance, for receiver RF circuit (LNA).

Instructions

  1. Copy "GG_example_mixer" directory to the Linux machine where GoldenGate is installed.
  2. Set the Path parameter of the GG_mixer part to the path on the Linux machine from home directory to GG_example_mixer directory.

  4. Copy GG_example_LNA to the same or another Linux machine where GoldenGate is installed.
  5. Set the Path parameter of the GG_LNA part to the path on the Linux machine from home directory to GG_example_LNA directory.
  6. In GG_example_LNA\runGoldenGate.sh, set XPEDION to your GoldenGate installation on that machine.
  7. Make sure GoldenGate license is set properly on the Linux Machine.
  8. Follow the instructions in SystemVue Document -- Simulation -- Distributed Simulations to setup user name, host name, and other relevant settings for remote connection.

Workspace.Name: 3GPP_LTE_UL_TX_PA
Workspace.Description:
LTE Uplink TX Verification

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates a fast verification (about 3 seconds) of a CMOS power amplifier with a realistic 2505MHz LTE Uplink Transmit signal as a stimulus.  The device-under-test is a Fast Circuit Envelope (FCE) model extracted from GoldenGate.  (alternatively, a full co-simulation with GoldenGate could also be used).  You will need licenses for the W1719 RF System and W1910 LTE library for the hands-on exercises.

 

First, a tour of the measurements.  Several simple measurements are presented here, using native SystemVue post-processing capabilities.  As an optional further step, the Keysight 89600 VSA software and its LTE personality can be used to de-modulate the output of the simulated PA.  The 89600 VSA allows more detailed measurements of signal degradation, but does require access to the separate VSA application.

 

Model Validation - Measurements

  • The spectrum analyzer plot is captured using the SpectrumAnalyzer sink. This is used to quickly assess ACLR and spectral re-growth, for spec pre-compliance.
  • The CCDF measurement shows the percentage of time (y-axis) that the instantaneous LTE signal envelope spends above the average power level (x-axis).  The "crest factor" of the signal is essentially the dB value of the x-axis intercept, and shows the amplitude of the highest signal peaks normalized to the RMS signal power.  A second CCDF trace is a reference trace of white gaussian noise, for comparison. A CCDF curve that abruptly falls to a low value shows lower power handling, or clipping.
  • The AM-AM and AM-PM plots show the normalized power gain and output phase of the LTE signal (vs. power level) on a point-by-point basis for the complex-valued modulated carrier envelope. 
    • When the these traces are flat lines, the DUT is operating in a very linear region.  (no change from nominal, regardless of time or amplitude)
    • When these traces curve upward or downward vs. power, then DUT is showing some nonlinearity.   This level of simulation modeling is common, and is a considered "Level 1" model.
    • When the traces spread into a statistical distribution, then the DUT is  demonstrating that some output values depend on the previous signal history in addition to the absolute power levels.  These are so-called "baseband memory effects", which are possible with Level 3 Models.  This modeling capability is somewhat unique to the GoldenGate FCE modeling process, and also of Keysight's Circuit Envelope simulation technology. 

EXERCISES:

You might want to print this page, or cut & paste it into a word processor document, for easier reading.

  1. Adjust the LTE source power level using the tuning slider.  Change the value from the minimum to the maximum power levels, and note the changes to the output traces.  Note the observed power levels and Crest Factors right on the schematic. (You may need to touch these areas with your mouse to get them to re-read the dataset/EQ's)
  2. Change the FCE model file.  Three FCE models for this 2.505 GHz amplifier are provided in the same example directory as this workspace.  Double-click on the FastCircuitEnvelope part, and browse to the model file called "SIM_PA_2p505GHz_m7dBm_level3_ampaccuracy5_freqaccuracy2.fce".  Now re-simulate at the minimum and maximum power levels.  What changes do you see in the AM2AM traces?
  3. (optional ) Use the 89600 VSA software for deeper post-processing.

    If you have access to the Keysight 89600 VSA software (release 11 or later with its LTE options), activate the VSA measurement sink, and re-simulate.  (It takes about 40 seconds the first time it runs).  The VSA gives you further measurement ability on the LTE signals, such as EVM for each of the LTE data and control sub-signals; integrated bandwidth power measurements to measure ACLR, and many more capabilities.

    User Tip:  After you have simulated into the VSA and observe the results, you can "STOP" the SystemVue simulation, but leave the VSA running; this saves time when you next re-simulate.  Slide the slider to a new power level, and this time the VSA continues within about 3 seconds.  Explore different FCE models and signal settings.  The convenience of this method reduces the amount of time you spend doing verification.

SUMMARY

 

In this example, the simulations only take a few seconds (about 3sec), yet are fairly realistic modulated PA results.  This level of verification would be nearly impossible for an analog IC with thousands of transistors using transient Spice and primitive signal sources.  A few key capabilities make this easy:

  • The circuit envelope simulation and model extraction in GoldenGate
  • A fast dataflow simulation backplane in SystemVue, with a full LTE reference library and native FCE model integration;
  • The SystemVue environment to bridge the design flow gap between Architecture, Implementation, Verification, and Test & Measurement. 

The exact same tools and signals used here can also be used to generate signals after tape-out to measure the real hardware transceiver with Keysight signal sources and analyzers.  This allows you to compare the results directly ("apples to apples"), and to feed back measurements into the architecture process to close your modeling loop.  Bring your hardware measurements back into SystemVue, and be using real waveforms for your next design start!

Workspace.Name: LNA_ParameterizedFCE
Workspace.Description:
Parameterized Fast Circuit Envelope (FCE)
simulation of an LNA

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates use of a parameterized FCE file. Parameterized FCE files store FCE models for the same circuit extracted under different conditions (e.g. bias voltages, load resistances, temperatures).

 

The parameterized FCE file used in this example (L1_2var.fce) is for an LNA. Models have been extracted for varying drain supply voltages (VDD) and load resistances (ROUT). The ranges over which these were varied can be seen in the custom GUI of the FastCircuitEnvelope model:

  • VDD range is 3 - 5
  • ROUT range is 30 - 100

The LNA FCE model has one input (QPSKPS1) and three outputs:

  • CDC: current consumption (freq of interest is 0, i.e. DC)
  • Pin: voltage at the real input of the LNA (freq of interest is 1.96GHz)
  • Pout: output voltage of the LNA (freq of interest is 1.96GHz)

In Design1 the FastCircuitEnvelope model has been configured to only use the CDC and Pout outputs. A QPSK signal with symbol rate of 1 MHz modulating a 1.96 GHz carrier is applied to the input of the FastCircuitEnvelope model. The signal at the CDC output is recorded in the Sink CDC and plotted in the Graph DC Current Consumption. The spectrum and EVM of the signal at the Pout output is measured and the results are shown in the Graph Output Spectrum and EVM.

 

Run the simulation for different values of VDD and ROUT and observe how the DC current consumption, output spectrum and EVM change.

Workspace.Name: ExplorePolarization
Workspace.Description:
Explore Polarization

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

 

This workspace illustrates how polarization is modeled in phased array simulations in SystemVue.

 

Since the workspace was saved without simulation data you may see errors from equations or text boxes trying to access datasets from simulations that have not run yet. These errors will go away once you run all simulations in this workspace.

 

BACKGROUND

 

The polarization of an electromagnetic wave describes the changes in magnitude and direction with time. It is characterized by two orthogonal components Etheta and Ephi. The polarization of an antenna is defined as the polarization of the electric field it radiates.

 

Depending on the values of Etheta and Ephi, there are three types of Antenna polarization:

1. Linear: Etheta and Ephi are in phase or 180 degrees out of phase.

2. Circular: Etheta and Ephi have the same magnitude and 90 degrees difference in phase.

3. Elliptical. Etheta and Ephi do not satisfy either of the above two conditions.

 

In SystemVue, antenna polarization can be set using the Etheta and Ephi parameters of the ArrayAnt model (Phased Array Analysis simulations) or the BeamPattern model (Data Flow Analysis simulations). These parameters can be:

1. scalar complex values; in this case, every element in the array will have the same polarization.

2. arrays of complex values; in this case, elements can have different polarization setting based on the mapping characterized by this array.

 

Review the documentation of Etheta and Ephi antenna parameters to understand how the values of these parameters define the polarization of the different phased array elements for different phased array configurations.

 

In addition, polarization mismatch can be modeled for antennas in "receiver" mode by setting the IncidentEtheta and IncidentEphi parameters of the ArrayAnt model (Phased Array Analysis simulations).


SETUP

 

In all the exercises below, observe the PolarizationEllipseGraph and the corresponding BeamPattern 3D graphs. NOTE that both PlotRxPatterns and PlotTxPatterns equations (plotting results from the corresponding simulations) plot on the same graphs (BeamPattern, BeamPolarization1Pattern, BeamPolarization2Pattern). For the PolarizationEllipseGraph to display properly you need to make sure the graph window is (approximately) square on your monitor. Otherwise a circle might look like an ellipse and vice versa.

 

TxDesign (under TxPolarization folder) and RxDesign (under RxPolarization folder) represent simple 8x8 element phased array transmitter/receiver with a single stage splitting/combining. TxDesignDF is the equaivalent Data Flow Tx design.

 

The following variables are defined in Constants equation and are tunable:

* beamPhi and beamTheta used to set the direction of the beam

* EthetaMag, EthetaPhase, EphiMag, EphiPhase used set the Etheta and Ephi antenna parameters

* polarizationOption used to select one of the following polarization decompositions:

0: Etheta/Ephi, 1: Eleft/Eright, 2: Eco/Ecross, 3: Ludwig 2 (Elevation/Azimuth), 4: Ludwig 2 (Alpha/Epsilon), 5: Ludwig 3 (Horizontal/Vertical)

* IEthetaMag, IEthetaPhase, IEphiMag, IEphiPhase all represent the incident wave properties.

 

ANALYSIS

 

The sliders in the schematic will tune the polarization peroperties and the corresponding analysis (PhasedArrayRx, PhasedArrayTx, DF1) is run when set to AutoRecalc.

 

EXERCISES

 

Tx Polarization

 

Tune the sliders in the schematic

 

1. Tune the variables EthetaMag, EthetaPhase, EphiMag, EphiPhase and observe the results. For example, try the following cases:

  • Linear polarization
    • EthetaMag =1, EphiMag= 0, EthetaPhase= EphiPhase= any value  gives Horizontal polarization
    • EphiMag=1, EthetaMag=0,  EthetaPhase= EphiPhase= any value  gives  vertical polarization
    • EthetaMag=any value, EphiMag=any value, EthetaPhase=EphiPhase, gives slant polarization. Vary magnitude of one while fixing the other. The angle of slant polarization changes.
  • Circular polarization
    • EthetaMag=EphiMag,  EhetaPhase-EPhiPhase=+/- 90, gives circular polarization. One is right hand circular (RHC) and the otherone is left hand circular (LHC).
  • Elliptical polarization
    • EthetaMag=any value, EphiMag=any value, EthetaPhase<>EphiPhase, gives elliptical polarization. As you change (EthetaPhase-EphiPhase) the ellipse rotates. It will go through right handed to left handed. 

2. For the same polarization, tune the polarizationOption to see a different polarization decomposition. For example, for linear polarization you should see two equal strength Eleft/Eright components, or a very strong Eco and a very weak (almost non-existent) Ecross component. For LHC/RHC you should see two equal strength Etheta/Ephi components and two equal strength Eco/Ecross components. For elliptical polarization, you should see two unequal strength Etheta/Ephi, or Eleft/Eright, or Eco/Ecross components.

 

3. Tune beamPhi and beamTheta and notice changes in the graphs (beam main lobe direction).

 

4. Evaluate the results again by playing with the sliders in the corresponding schematic of RxPolarization.

 

Rx Polarization

 

Select the PhasedArrayRx analysis in the Tune window (Analyses to Run area).

 

Try the same type of experiments above for linear, circular and elliptical polarization. In addition you have to choose the incident wave polarization using the corresponding sliders for IEthetaMag, IEphiMag, IEthetaPhase and IEphiPhase. If the incident polarization does not match the antenna polarization you will see a mismatch loss in the Output signal power (see values inside yellow text box). The far field antenna patterns are NOT dependnent on the incident wave polarization; ONLY the receiver output power is.

 

Tx Polarization DF

 

Select the PhasedArrayTx and DF1 analyses in the Tune window (Analyses to Run area).

 

Follow the same exercises as in Tx Polarization.

Workspace.Name: Phased Array Active Loading
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\Phased Array Analysis\Phased Array Active Loading.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phased Array with Active Loading

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This workspace shows the effect of antenna array coupling and active loading on the final beam pattern.  For the ideal case, the resulting far field is just a linear sum of all the individual elements and their weighting factors.  But in realistic arrays, the array itself has internal coupling, and this is often used in phased array design.  Loading can be specified a few different ways using the "ActiveLoading" parameter on the "ArrayAnt" component.  By switching different options, you can compare the beam measurement results in the tables.

  1. Most Ideal case:  You can set the "ActiveLoading" option to "Ideal Coupling Matrix". The coupling matrix is computed in the equation Equation1. It computes an idealized, non-physical coupling based on the distance between the elements (dB_per_m and deg_per_m = 10; play with these values to see the effect they have on beam measurements).  For example, if a signal appears on element 41, then a small amount of that signal will also be added to element 42, based on how far apart they are.
  2. A more accurate option is to set ActiveLoading = "S-Parameter Dataset". The model uses "8x8_array_touchstone.s64p" dataset in the workspace tree.  An 8x8 patch antenna array was solved in the ADS Momentum field solver, and the S-parameters stored to file, and then imported into this workspace.  Each of the 64 patches can "talk" to the other 63 patches, resulting in a 64x64 S-matrix at one frequency, at one scan angle (4096 values!).  This is much more accurate, and provides a physical basis for the coupling.  But these matrixes can get large.
  3. You can also set ActiveLoading ="Active Reflection Coefficients". The model uses "activeRefCoefs" from Equation3 in the workspace tree.

Results with No Loading:

  • The PhasedArrayTxData dataset was stored as a reference with no active loading. Beam pattern is displayed in the BeamPatternTx 3D graph.

Results with Loading:

  • The schematic and simulation can be modified, and will output to the PhasedArrayTxActiveLoading dataset.  A default one has been stored with this workslace. It was created with active loading applied. Its beam pattern is displayed in BeamPatternTxActiveLoading.
  • SampleMeasurements and SideLobeLevels tables show sample measurements and sidelobe levels from both simulations for comparison purposes.  Note that with coupling, the deep notches fill in a little bit, among other changes.
  • Another effect of the coupling is to modify the impedance seen "looking" into each antenna array element. We are referring to this as the Active Impedance. Active Impedance is saved in the dataset in the variable PartInfo_AntennaZinActive_<ArrayAntPartInstanceName> (this variable is ONLY available in Phased Array simulations in Tx mode and when Active Loading is set to S-Parameter File or S-Parameter Dataset). Active Impedance depends on the excitation of each element and so it changes with scan angle (as the excitations change to make the beam point to a different direction). The graph Active Impedance shows the Active Impedances of each antenna array element. Tune ArrayPhase2.Phi and ArrayPhase2.Theta in the Tune Window and observe how the active impedances change. Make sure PhasedArrayTx analysis is checked in the Analyses To Run area inside the Tune Window.

Workspace.Name: Phased Array Filter Tx
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\Phased Array Analysis\Phased Array Filter Tx.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phased Array TX with Frequency Variation 

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace adds a bandpass filter to the phased array TX chain, in order to demonstrate how RFLINK renders Spectrasys array designs with frequency response.

 

Please note that due to the large amount of data produced by the simulations the workspace has been saved without some of the simulation datasets so som graphs may show no results.

 

About this workspace:

 

In Folder #1, the RF TX array is designed using the Phased Array analysis.  (You may need to right-click on the "PlotPattern" to update the 3D plot)

 

In Folder #2 and 3, the RF array is brought to the dataflow level using RFLINK, and evaluated two different ways in the dataflow simulator.

  • FOLDER #2 - A CW tone is swept in Dataflow, and the frequency response is plotted from one of the 64 array outputs.  Simple, but plotting swept data can involve more post-processing.
  • FOLDER #3 - An "Envelope Impulse" pings the RFLINK network, and the spectrum analyzer at the output displays the magnitude of the Impulse Response.  Single analysis (not swept).  Arguably easier to plot.

Additional Notes

  1. Frequency response method #2 assumes that original input spectrum is flat (perfect impulse) across the bandwidth.  In a real measurement you would need to ratio the input and output spectrums to infer the frequency response.  Or, use a network analyzer.  Flatness calibrations are common for wideband AWG and up/downconverters.
  2. Since there are no statistical variations between the array elements, all 64 array paths are going to be similar, except for the windowing and phase shift between elements.  (The active beamforming components, such as the windowing and gain/phase states, are not frequency-dependent.  If you want to reflect additional sources of ripple/response, you need to explicitly add .s2p data files or other components to the TX path to see these imperfections.)

Workspace.Name: Phased Array Sky Temperature
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\Phased Array Analysis\Phased Array Sky Temperature.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phased Array Sky Temperature Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

 

This workspace demonstrates how to include the effects of noise due to sky temperature in a phased array Rx simulation.

 

BACKGROUND

 

Antennas receive signal and noise from the objects they point at. Noise received from objects in sky can have widely varying noise temperatures. In the phased array antenna model the user can choose between a fixed sky temperature value (independent of direction of arrival) or they can configure a sky temperature that varies based on the direction ot arrival.


SETUP

 

Design Design1 is a simple 64 element phased array receiver with an LNA and single stage combining. Sweep Sweep1 sweeps the Theta angle the array beam is pointing to from 0 degrees to 90 degrees with a step of 10 degrees. Equation InEqns defines a sky temperature distribution. Graph ArraySkyTemperature shows the  ArrayMeas_ArraySkyTemperature measurement vs the swept theta angle.

 

EXERCISES

 

The ArrayAnt model is set up to use a constant sky temperature (Rx Parameters tab, Sky Temperature Mode = '0:Constant') of 290 degrees Kelvin. Run the sweep and observe the ArrayMeas_ArraySkyTemperature measurement in the graph ArraySkyTemperature. The result should be a flat line at 290 degrees Kelvin.

 

Set the ArrayAnt model to a non-constant sky temperature. Double click on it, go to Rx Parameters tab and set Sky Temperature Mode = '1:ThetaPhiGrid'. The Sky Temperature Grid, Theta Grid, and Phi Grid are already set up to the variables defined in InEqns. Run the equation PlotSkyTemp to see the sky temperature variation for different theta/phi angles. As you can see, the sky temperature is hot at theta = 80 degree and phi = 180 degree direction (e.g., assuming it is the direction of the sun) and it is cool at 290K everywhere else. Run the sweep and observe the ArrayMeas_ArraySkyTemperature measurement in the graph ArraySkyTemperature. When you keep phi at 0 degree and scan theta from 0 degree down to 90 degree, the grating lobe comes up from horizon at phi = 180 degree as you increase scan theta angle. The grating lobe receives higher sky temperature from hot source, and as a result, ArrayMeas_ArraySkyTemperature has the highest value when scan theta is close to 90 degrees.

Workspace.Name: PhasedArray DC Power Calculation
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\Phased Array Analysis\PhasedArray DC Power Calculation.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phased Array DC Calculation Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example shows how to use two methods of determining the DC power draw for the entire array. One method is using imported PAE data and the other is multiplication of the linear DC power calculated from user specified supply voltages and currents.

 

BACKGROUND

PAE DC Calculation Method

Sys-parameter files can be imported as datasets. The data from these files can then be used in equations and designs. In this case, PAE data for the RF Amp ADL-5545 was imported into the workspace. PAE data along with input and output power can be used to calculate DC power using the equation DC Power = 100*(RF Output Power - RF Input Power) / PAE.

 

Direct DC Power Calculation Method

Active devices can have their DC power consumption calculated based on user supplied supply current and voltage. Since users only draw a schematic for a single array element the DC power consumption will be multiplied by the number of element to get the total DC power consumption for an array.


SETUP

This workspace consists of a simple 4x4 phased array in Tx mode. The Dataset 'PAE_Raw_Data_ADL_5545' was created by importing a Sys-Parameter file called 'PAE Raw Data ADL 4445.xlsx'. It contains the amplifier ADL-5545 data for Input Power, Output Power, and PAE at 1000 MHz and 2000 MHz.

 

SIMULATION STEPS

1. Import the PAE data file using File > Import > Sys-Parameter Files > Excel File ...

2. Set the Main Independent variable to 'Pin'

3. Set the desired input power level and frequency

4. Run 'SetupTx' equations

5. Run 'Phased ArrayTx' analysis

6. Run 'ProcessTxGainAndPower' equations

7. Run 'CalculateDCPower' equations

 

 

NOTE

The PAE data for this example has been fabricated for illustration purposes only.

 

EQUATIONS

1. The Equation block 'SetupTx' sets up the tunable Tx parameters and extracts PAE data for the given temperature and frequency. The input power PowerIn is initially set to -20 dBm and the frequency is set to 2000 MHz.

2. The Equation block 'ProcessTxGainAndPower' takes in data from the Phased Array Analysis and calculates the gain and output power for the phased array. This data is organized in table 'Phased Array Gain Power'.

3. The Equation block 'CalculateDCPower' calculates DC Power using the PAE method. The variable AmpPin is the RFAmp input power and AmpPout is the RFAmp output power that drives each antenna element. The PAE value for each amplifier is extracted using the amplifier input power AmpPin. Using the input power the amplifier PAE can be determined. Using amplifier input and output power along with PAE the DC power can be determined for each amplifier. The DC power for each amplifier is summed to give the total DC power draw.

 

ANALYSIS

Array Gain and Power for Element - This table contains shows the Gain and Output Power at each stage for the Phased Array Analysis for a selected antenna element.

 

Array DC Power Data - This table shows the DC power for each amplifier in the array along with the PAE for the given input power.

 

Direct DC Power - This tables shows the power calculation for the amplifier based on the direct multiplication of supply current and voltage.

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Run the Phased Array Analysis, then run the Equation 'CalculateDCPower'. Notice the PAE values in the vector AmpPAE, the DC Powers for each amplifier AmpDCPower and the sum of the DC powers for each antenna TotalDCPower. Tune PowerIn to a saturation input power and repeat this process to see a lower DC power consumption.

Workspace.Name: PhasedArrayAnalysis_Nonlinearity
Workspace.Description:
Phased Array Analysis, Nonlinearity

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace shows the effect of amplifier nonlinearity on amplitude tapering, compared to the baseline result in Folder 01.  In each case you will observe the integrity of the final beam shape, expressed as a directivity. 

 

In most cases you will be either running the PhasedArray analysis controller directly, or right-clicking on the "PlotPattern" script in that folder, and running the MATLAB Script ("Run Equations"), which runs both the analysis, then executes some automated post-processing.

 

Description of experiments in each folder:

  • 01 BaseLine_Taylor_Theta30Phi270_Pin0 :  contains the RF beamforming Tx design with 8x8 URA, Taylor window, -20 dBm isotropically received power, and the phase shifters pointing the beam to theta = 30 degree and phi = 270 degree. You can run "PlotPattern" to run the phased array analysis and plot the directivity pattern. You can also access the phased array measurement variables in the dataset.
  • 02 Compression_Pin20: Increase the input power to 20 dBm and observe the amplifier compression effect to the Taylor side lobes.
  • 03 Saturation_Pin30: Increase the input power to 30 dBm and observe the amplifier saturation to the Taylor side lobes.
  • 04 AMPM_Pin20: Observe the impact of amplifier AM to PM to the directivity pattern with 20 dBm input power.

TIP: for a 3D pattern plot, you can measure the beamwidth and direction using a marker function.  Select the 3D trace itself, right-click and add "Marker/Maximum" to put a marker on the tip of the pattern (usually called "m1").  Now select the new marker, and right-click again.  Choose "Beamwidth/50% of Max".  You will see the marker measurements in the lower left corner of your 3D plot.

 

NOTE: The lineup in the schematics are for demonstration purpose. They are not meant to be a starting point for realistic phased array design.

Workspace.Name: PhasedArrayAnalysis_Rx_OneStage
Workspace.Description:
Phased Array Analysis, 1-stage Receiver

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace a variety of experiments that show the effect of individual phased-array/beamforming features, compared to the baseline result in Folder 01.  In each case you will observe the integrity of the final beam shape, usually expressed as a directivity. 

 

In most cases you will be either running the PhasedArray analysis controller directly, or right-clicking on the "PlotPattern" script in that folder, and running the MATLAB Script ("Run Equations"), which runs both the analysis, then executes some automated post-processing.

 

Description of experiments in each folder:

  • 01 BaseLine_Taylor_Theta30Phi270_Pin-20 :  contains the RF beamforming Rx design with 8x8 URA, Taylor window, -20 dBm isotropically received power, and the phase shifters pointing the beam to theta = 30 degree and phi = 270 degree. You can run "PlotPattern" to run the phased array analysis and plot the directivity pattern. You can also access the phased array measurement variables in the dataset.
  • 02 Compression_Pin0: Increase the isotropically received power to 0 dBm and observe the amplifier compression effect to the Taylor side lobes.
  • 03 Saturation_Pin20: Increase the isotropically received power to 20 dBm and observe the amplifier saturation to the Taylor side lobes.
  • 04 AMPM_Pin0: Observe the impact of amplifier AM to PM to the directivity pattern with 0 dBm isotropically received power.
  • 05 PhaseErrorUniform: Apply phase shift errors with uniform distribution and observe the impact to the directivity pattern.
  • 06 PhaseErrorNormal: Apply phase shift errors with normal distribution and observe the impact to the directivity pattern.
  • 07 AttenuationErrorUniform: Apply attenuator errors with uniform distribution and observe the impact to the directivity pattern.
  • 08 AttenuationErrorNormal: Apply attenuator errors with normal distribution and observe the impact to the directivity pattern.
  • 09 PhaseQuantization_Theta33Phi255_3bits: Apply 3-bit phase shifter quantization to the phase shifters pointing the beam to theta = 33 degree and phi = 255 degree.
  • 10 GainQuantization_3bits: Apply 3-bit attenuator quantization.
  • 13 CosineAntenna: Use CosineAntenna element pattern instead of Isotropic in the antenna array.
  • 14 CosineAntenna_ElementRotation: Use CosineAntenna element pattern and rotate each element 45 degree around Y axis.
  • 15 HFSS: Use HFSS pattern file for each element. Note that the maximum directivity of the HFSS element pattern does not point to theta = 0.

TIP: for a 3D pattern plot, you can measure the beamwidth and direction using a marker function.  Select the 3D trace itself, right-click and add "Marker/Maximum" to put a marker on the tip of the pattern (usually called "m1").  Now select the new marker, and right-click again.  Choose "Beamwidth/50% of Max".  You will see the marker measurements in the lower left corner of your 3D plot.

 

NOTE: The lineup in the schematics are for demonstration purpose. They are not meant to be a starting point for realistic phased array design.

Workspace.Name: PhasedArrayMonteCarlo
Workspace.Description:
Beamforming with Element Variations & Failures

Keysight SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace shows how to use the Monte Carlo feature to measure the changes in a phased array beam caused by variations in the array elements:

  • gain (attenuatorn state) errors
  • phase shift errors
  • element failures

The key concept is the relationship of the external MonteCarlo analysis controller to the local Phased Array analysis in Spectrasys, and also to the randomized component values.  Syntax for post-processing is another key lesson.

 

This example uses an 8x8 uniform rectangular array, or 64 individual elements.  The variances are set up as separate variables from the nominal values.  For example, if one phase shifter value is 45 degrees, then the statistical parameter "Phase Errors" can vary from -5 to +5 degrees on top of this 45deg nominal, for a net variation of +40 to +50.  By separating the variation from the nominal value, and only varying the perturbation, the nominal value can be assigned programmatically by a window taper or a beamforming angle.  The variation doesn't care what the nominal was, it is only a perturbed value relative to it. 

 

In these folders, Monte Carlo is used to do two things:

  • randomize parameter values across the 64 elements, within a single array simulation
  • randomize variations across many simulation runs, or Monte Carlo "rounds"

One some of the phased array function parts (splitters, phase shifters, etc), you may see a 1x64 vector of values already on the "Phase Errors" parameter, such as "zeroes(1,64)", yet the variable is marked "tunable.".  The stated value becomes the mean for the variation, and the actual distribution is declared on the Monte Carlo controller.  By marking that parameter "tunable", the Monte Carlo controller is able to pre-load a dashboard of all the changing values in the whole design, and lets you conveniently adjust those variations right on the controller tab itself, instead of moving from component-to-component throughout a larger design.

 

The folders in this workspace set up variations such as 

  • amplitude vairations of +/- 1 dB
  • phase variations of +/- 5 degrees
  • and up to 10% element failures.

While the monte carlo is simulating, you can watch the traces update.

Workspace.Name: PhasedArrayPathMeasurements
Workspace.Description:
Phased Array Path Measurements 

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example

 

 

The objective of this example is to demonstrate Phased Array Analysis path measurements (DCP, DCV, CNP, CGAIN, CNF, etc.) and compare them with Spectrasys path measurements (DCP, DCV, CNP, CGAIN, CNF, etc.) on an equivalent Spectrasys design. The level diagrams show that the path measurements from phased array analysis and Spectrasys are the same.

 

The graphs also show the Rx array version of CGAIN_Array and CNF_Array that are computed by the Phased Array Analysis for the Rx design. The definition of "array receive path measurements" are described in the table below.

 

Phased Array Path Measurements can be turned on by checking "Save path measurements for Level Diagrams" checkbox in the Measurements tab of the Phased Array Analysis. After simulation, you can right click on the "PathMeas_" variables in the dataset, "Add to Graph" then "New Graph" to plot the level diagrams. By default, all channels are included in the level diagrams. You can also right click on the "PathMeas_" variables and "Plot Selected Channels on New Graph" to choose or specify the selected channels on level diagrams.

 

Note:

1. Measure Phased Array Path measurement variables have "PathMeas_" prepended to the Spectrasys equivalent measurement name in the dataset.

2. For array receive path measurement variables, "_Array" is appended to the variable name in the dataset. Comparing to the original path measurements that are based on single channel, the "array receive path measurement" correctly account for combiner stages for the full array.

 

Array Receive Path Measurements available are:

Variable Unit Description
PathMeas_CGAIN_Array Relative Power Cascaded gain of the signal. CGAIN_Array[n] = DCP[n] - DCP[0] (dB) up to a combiner. After the combiner, the sum of the total input power for the channels that have been combined are used instead of DCP[0].
PathMeas_CNF_Array Relative Power Cascaded noise figure. CNF[n] = CNP[n] - CNP[0] - CGAIN_Array[n] (dB)
PathMeas_IIP2_Array Power Input 2nd order intercept point.  IIP2[n] = OIP2[n] - CGAIN_Array[n] (dBm)
PathMeas_IIP3_Array Power Input 3rd order intercept point.  IIP3[n] = OIP3[n] - CGAIN_Array[n] (dBm)
PathMeas_IP1DB_Array Power Input 1dB compression point. IP1DB[n] = OP1DB[n] - ( CGAIN_Array[n] - 1 dB )
PathMeas_IPSAT_Array Power Input saturation point. IPSAT[n] = OPSAT[n] - CGAIN_Array[n]

Where n = stage number

Workspace.Name: PhasedArrayWithSParameter
Workspace.Description:
Phased Array with S-Parameters

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example

The objective of this example is to demonstrate the use of the ArraySParam model. The ArraySParam is used to model a generic N-input to M-output (total N+M ports) device characterized using S-parameters in a phased array design. A Rx Combiner and a Tx Phase Shifter test cases are included.

 

 

Rx Folder

 

In the SParam16to1Combiner design in this folder, the ArraySParam model is used to model a 16-to-1 combiner with SParameter data. For comparison purposes, the design SParam16to1CombinerRef implements the same system but using the "ideal" ArraySplit model to implement the 16-to-1 combiner.

 

The graph Splitter_SParams shows the S-Parameters for the 17-port, 16-to-1 combiner. Open the graph and tune the PortIdx variable with the slider provided on the graph to see S(N,PortIdx) responses, where N=1, 2, ..., 17.

 

Run the analyses SParam16to1CombinerAnalysis and SParam16to1CombinerRefAnalysis and then run the equation PlotRxPatterns. Observe the differences between Rx Beam (from the design using SParameters) and Rx Beam Ref (from the design using the "ideal" ArraySplit). You can also see the difference in the receiver output power in the table RxOut.

 

In the Tune window Analyses To Run area, select SParam16to1CombinerAnalysis and SParam16to1CombinerRefAnalysis and then tune the variable Finc_GHz. Observe the differences in the beam patterns and the receiver output power levels.

 

 

Tx Folder

 

In the SparamPhaseShifter design in this folder, the ArraySParam model is used to model an RFIC implementing 16 parallel phase shifters that can be controlled to steer the beam to 5 different preconfigured directions. For comparison purposes, the design SparamPhaseShifterRef implements the same system but using the "ideal" ArrayPhase model.

 

The equation TxConfigure defines 5 sets of 16 phase shift values that will steer the beam at 5 different directions (see thetas and phis variables in same equation). These 5 sets have been calculated for the frequency of 10 GHz. The tunable variable pick is used to select one of these sets. The selected set of phase shift values is stored in the variable PhaseShifts, which is used in the SparamPhaseShifterRef design.

 

In the design SparamPhaseShifter, the ArraySParam model is set to have 5 states (NumStates parameter) and the State parameter is set to the tunable variable pick, to select one of the 5 states of operation. Each state of operation is modeled by a different 32-port SParameter file. You ONLY have to specify one SParameter file in the FileName parameter of the ArraySParam component, as long as you follow a convention for naming the set of SParameter files that will be used. The convention is:

<BaseName><StateNumber>.<OptionalArbitraryDescriptiveText>.sNp.

 

Using SParameters to model the operation of this set of 16 phase shifters allows us to include coupling effects between the 16 outputs (the specific SParameter files used in this example do not include any coupling effects) as well as model frequency dependent behavior. The 5 SParameter files used in this example have data from 9 GHz to 20 GHz with 1 GHz step and at the frequency of 10 GHz the phase shifts introduced are exactly the same as the ones used in the SparamPhaseShifterRef design.

 

Run the analyses SparamPhaseShifterAnalysis and SparamPhaseShifterRefAnalysis and then run the equation PlotTxPatterns. Observe the differences between Tx Beam (from the design using SParameters) and Tx Beam Ref (from the design using the "ideal" ArrayPhase).

 

In Tune window Analyses To Run area, select SparamPhaseShifterAnalysis and SparamPhaseShifterRefAnalysis (unselect Param16to1CombinerAnalysis and SParam16to1CombinerRefAnalysis), make sure Fc_GHz is set to 10, and then tune the variable pick. You can use the slider provided on either Tx schematic since they are identical sliders. Also you can use the tune window to do this but make sure you stay with the pick range (1≤ pick ≤ 5).

 

Notice that the beam patterns are identical. You can place maximum markers to track the beam peak. It should match the corresponding value in the thetas and phis variables in the equation TxConfigure.

 

Now fix the value of the pick variable and tune Fc_GHz. In addition to squinting effects (due to the fact that the phase shifts for the reference design were computed for 10 GHz), you can see the additional effects due to the frequency dependent behavior in the beam pattern of the SparamPhaseShifter design.

Workspace.Name: RF Phased Array 8x8 Squinting
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\Phased Array Analysis\RF Phased Array 8x8 Squinting.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Time Delays vs. Phase Shifts to Reduce Squinting

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This example demonstrates how to setup and simulate a TR module and observe squinting effect using frequency sweep. Folders 1-3 show the RF Phased Array analysis using just Phase Shift, just Time Delay, and then a 2-stage approach.  Folders 4-6 apply these to the Dataflow level using RFLINK, so you see how the control pins roll up to the next level. 

 

Please note that due to the large amount of data produced by the simulations the workspace has been saved without some of the simulation datasets so some graphs may show no results.

 

The Array configuration

 

The variable ArrayState (defined in Settings Equation) is used to control whether the system will simulate as a receiver (ArrayState=1) or a transmitter (ArrayState=2). This variable controls

  • the Phased Array analysis (PhasedArray1) "Rx / Tx" setting
  • the RxTx parameter of the ArrayAnt and ArrayPort
  • the State parameter of the two switches

The phased array antenna is configured as an 8 x 8 Uniform Rectangular Array with 15mm absolute distance between elements (corresponds to half wavelength for a frequency of 10 GHz).

 

The phased array analysis is set up to save the entire antenna directivity pattern in the dataset. The PlotPattern equation is reading the directivity data from the dataset and plots it in a 3D graph. In the DirectivityPatternCut graph, we use some post processing equations to take a cut of the Directivity pattern across a certain phi angle (see tunable variable PhiCutAngle).

 

Contents of the Workspace

 

The phase shifter in Design1 is set to manual mode with pre-computed phase shift values that point the array to 10 deg theta and 20 deg phi at 10 GHz. By sweeping frequencies, you can observe the squinting effect.

 

The time delay in Design2 is set to manual mode with pre-computed time delay values that point the array to 10 deg theta and 20 deg phi at 10 GHz. By sweeping frequencies, you can observe no squinting effect using time delay.

 

Sweep1 is configured to sweep the input frequency from 5 GHz to 15 GHz in steps of 1 GHz for Design1 using phase shifter. This sweep is going to be used to measure directivity, main lobe direction, direction difference to spec, 3dB beamwidth, and pattern phi cut over frequency.

 

We can see that as the frequency increases, the directivity increase, beamwidth decreases, and the beam direction varies in Theta. In the directivity pattern cut graph, we can see that as the frequency increases (mouse over the individual traces to see the frequency value they are associated with; freqSweepIndep value) the beam becomes narrower and the direction varies.

 

Sweep2 is configured to sweep the input frequency from 5 GHz to 15 GHz in steps of 1 GHz for Design2 using time delay. This sweep is going to be used to measure directivity, main lobe direction, direction difference to spec, 3dB beamwidth, and pattern phi cut over frequency.

 

We can see that as the frequency increases, the directivity increase, beamwidth decreases, and the beam direction remains the same. In the directivity pattern cut graph, we can see that as the frequency increases (mouse over the individual traces to see the frequency value they are associated with; freqSweepIndep value) the beam becomes narrower and the direction remains the same.

 

Sweep3 is configured to sweep the input frequency from 5 GHz to 15 GHz in steps of 1 GHz for Design3 using time delay in the first 2x2 stage and using phase shifter in the second 8x8 stage. This sweep is going to be used to measure directivity, main lobe direction, direction difference to spec, 3dB beamwidth, and pattern phi cut over frequency.

 

We can see that as the frequency increases, the directivity increase, beamwidth decreases, and the beam direction varies in Theta, but the squinting is much less then sweep1 using two-stage time-delay and phase shift approach. In the directivity pattern cut graph, we can see that as the frequency increases (mouse over the individual traces to see the frequency value they are associated with; freqSweepIndep value) the beam becomes narrower and the direction varies.

 

Sweep4 is configured to sweep the input frequency from 5 GHz to 15 GHz in steps of 1 GHz for RFLink in Design4. The RFLink uses the phase shift based RF beamforming in Design1. You can observe the same squinting effect in DF simulation by using the pre-computed phase shift values inside RFLink.

 

Sweep5 is configured to sweep the input frequency from 5 GHz to 15 GHz in steps of 1 GHz for RFLink in Design5. The RFLink uses the time delay based RF beamforming in Design2. You can observe no squinting effect in DF simulation by using the pre-computed time delay values inside RFLink.

 

Sweep6 is configured to sweep the input frequency from 5 GHz to 15 GHz in steps of 1 GHz for RFLink in Design6. The RFLink uses the time delay based RF beamforming in Design3. You can observe slight squinting effect in DF simulation by using the pre-computed two stage time delay and phase shift values inside RFLink.

 

Open the Tune Window and tune the variables ArrayState (ONLY between 1 and 2), FRxTx, PhiCutAngle (between 0 and 180) to see how the Beam Pattern, the Directivity Pattern Cut, and the measurement results are affected.

 

Note: You do not need to run the simulation again when tuning PhiCutAngle, so you can uncheck the checkboxes next to the PhasedArray1 and System1 in the Analyses To Run area of the Tune WIndow. The PhiCutAngle only affects the Directivity Pattern Cut graph.

Workspace.Name: RF Phased Array 8x8 TR Module
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\Phased Array Analysis\RF Phased Array 8x8 TR Module.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phased Array 8x8 T/R Module

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

(NOTE: Sweep1 must be run before the graphs in Graphs Sweep folder will have data to display)

 

This example demonstrates how to setup and simulate a T/R module.

 

The variable ArrayState (defined in Settings Equation) is used to control whether the system will simulate as a receiver (ArrayState=1) or a transmitter (ArrayState=2). This variable controls

  • the Phased Array analysis (PhasedArray1) "Rx / Tx" setting
  • the RxTx parameter of the ArrayAnt and ArrayPort
  • the State parameter of the two switches

The phased array antenna is configured as an 8 x 8 Uniform Rectangular Array with a distance between elements equal to 0.015 m (corresponds to half wavelength for a frequency of 10 GHz).

 

The phased array analysis is set up to save the entire antenna directivity pattern in the dataset. The PlotPattern equation is reading the directivity data from the dataset and plots it in a 3D graph. In the DirectivityPatternCut graph, we use some post processing equations to take a cut of the Directivity pattern across a certain phi angle (see tunable variable PhiCutAngle). The RxArrayMeasurementsAtThetaPhi and RxArrayMeasurementsAtThetaPhi tables show some other measurement results. Depending on whether a receiver or transmitter is simulated, some of these results will not be available in the dataset and you may see errors if you open the table.

 

Open the Tune Window and tune the variables ArrayState (ONLY between 1 and 2), FRxTx, PhiCutAngle (between 0 and 180), beamPhi (between 0 and 360), beamTheta (between 0 and 90) to see how the Beam Pattern, the Directivity Pattern Cut, and the measurement results in the RxArrayMeasurementsAtThetaPhi and RxArrayMeasurementsAtThetaPhi tables are affected.

 

NOTE: if you simulate in Rx mode (ArrayState = 1), then the TxArrayMeasurementsAtThetaPhi table will be missing some variables, since it contains Tx specific measurements not present in the dataset when simulating Rx mode. Similarly, if you simulate in Tx mode (ArrayState = 2), then the RxArrayMeasurementsAtThetaPhi table will be missing some variables, since it contains Rx specific measurements not present in the dataset when simulating Tx mode.

 

Note: You do not need to run the simulation again when tuning PhiCutAngle, so you can uncheck the checkboxes next to the PhasedArray1 and System1 in the Analyses To Run area of the Tune WIndow. The PhiCutAngle only affects the Directivity Pattern Cut graph.

 

Sweep1 is configured to sweep the input frequency from 5 GHz to 15 GHz in steps of 1 GHz. This sweep is going to be used to measure Directivity, G/T, and TotalGain over frequency. Make sure the system is in the Rx mode (ArrayState = 1), since G/T is not defined for transmitters. Open the four graphs under the Graphs Sweep folder (to reduce the size of the workspace, the workspace was saved without the swept data, so when you open these graphs they will be empty).and run the sweep.

 

We can see that as the frequency increases, the Directivity, G/T, and TotalGain all increase as well. In the Directivity Pattern Phi Angle Cut graph, we can see that as the frequency increases (mouse over the individual traces to see the frequency value they are associated with; freqSweepIndep value) the beam becomes narrower.

 

You can change the beamPhi and beamTheta variables to change the direction the main beam is pointing to and run the sweep again to get the results for the new beam direction.

 

You can also add some frequency dependent models in your system and see the performance vs frequency. For example, double click on the LNA amplifier (amplifier in the top Rx path) and uncheck the Use Default checkbox for the parameters G and ParamFreqList to introduce a frequency dependent gain. Run the sweep again and compare the results to the ones when the amplifier had a constant gain across frequency.
