Workspace.Name: RF Phased Array Intermods and Harmonics
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\Phased Array Analysis\RF Phased Array Intermods and Harmonics.wsv
Workspace.Description:
RF Phased Array Intermods and Harmonics

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This workspace demonstrates simulation of intermods and harmonics in a Phased Array Tx system. It also illustrates how to plot intermod and harmonic spectrum, EIRP spectrum, and EIRP patterns.

 

 

Overview

 

TxDesign represents a simple 4x4 element phased array transmitter with a single splitting stage. The source (ArrayPort2) is set up to generate two tones at Fsignal (10) and Fsignal+1 (11) GHz (Fsignal is a tunable variable defined in Constants equation page). When these two tones go through the two non-linear amplifiers (DriverAmp and FinalAmp) intermods and harmonics will be generated. Due to the Taylor window used (ArrayAttn2) before the first amplifier the levels of intermods and harmonics will vary for the different paths (16) in this system.

 

 

How to setup Intermod and Harmonic simulation in Phased Array Analysis

 

Generation of Intermods and Harmonics is controlled by several settings in the Options tab of the PhasedArray1 analysis.

  • Check Calculate Intermod and Harmonic Spectrum to enable intermod and harmonic computation for Tx phaed array designs.
  • Check Calculate maximum Tx EIRP at each intermod frequency to compute the maximum (across all direction) of the EIRP (equivalent isotropically radiated power) at each intermod frequency.
  • Check Report Tx EIRP pattern at frequencies to save EIRP patterns at the specified frequencies in the dataset.

 

How to Plot Intermod and Harmonic Spectrum

 

Run the simulation and open the dataset PhasedArray1_TxDesign_Data. When Calculate Intermod and Harmonic Spectrum is enabled in the Options tab of the Phased Array analysis, new variables are created in the dataset. For example:

  • Spectrum_Power_06_FinalAmp_RFAmpHO_Output : this dataset variable represents the power spectrum at the output of FinalAmp_RFAmpHO, which is the 6th part along the chain. The naming convention for power spectrum variable is Spectrum_Power_<N>_<Part Instance Name>_Output.
  • Spectrum_Voltage_06_FinalAmp_RFAmpHO_Output : this dataset variable represents the voltage spectrum at the output of FinalAmp_RFAmpHO. The naming convention for voltage spectrum variable is Spectrum_Voltage_<N>_<Part Instance Name>_Output.

These variables provide Spectrasys-Spectrum-like plots for the phased array system. You can plot them by:

  • Right click on the variable > Add to Graph > New Graph.

For example, when you plot Spectrum_Power_06_FinalAmp_RFAmpHO_Output, you will see an overlap of spectrums for all 64 channels at the output of FinalAmp_RFAmpHO.

 

You can easily plot a single channel or a subset of channels by:

  • Right click on the variable > Add to Graph > New Graph of Selected Channel(s), then select the desired channel number.
  • If the desired channel number is not shown in the dropdown, you can select the More... option and enter the channel number. In this case you can also enter a list of numbers (e.g. 1 5 18 40) or a MATLAB Script expression evaluating to an array of integers (e.g. 1:2:20 to plot all odd-numbered channels up to 20).

In dataset, you will also see variables like Spectrum_CH_06_FinalAmp_RFAmpHO_Output, Spectrum_F_06_FinalAmp_RFAmpHO_Output, Spectrum_ID_06_FinalAmp_RFAmpHO_Output. They are only used as independent variables for Spectrum_Power_06_FinalAmp_RFAmpHO_Output and Spectrum_Voltage_06_FinalAmp_RFAmpHO_Output.

 

 

How to Show Maximum EIRP in Spectrum Graph

 

If Calculate maximum Tx EIRP at each intermod frequency is checked in the Options tab of the Phased Array analysis, then the following variable is created in the dataset.

  • Spectrum_Power_EIRP

Right click on Spectrum_Power_EIRP > Add to Graph > New Graph. This generates a spectrum-like plot showing the maximum (across all direction) of the EIRP for each intermod frequency. If you mouse over the points in this graph you will see the direction (theta/phi) at which the maximum occured.

 

 

How to Plot EIRP Patterns

 

To see the entire EIRP pattern for select frequencies, check the Report Tx EIRP pattern at frequencies checkbox and list the desired frequencies in available field. The frequencies must be valid intermod and harmonic frequencies, otherwise they will be ignored. You can obtain the valid intermod and harmonic frequencies from the tones in Spectrum_P_EIRP. After the simulation runs, the following variables are created in the dataset:

  • Spectrum_EIRP_Pattern_<FreqValue>Hz

To plot these EIRP patterns run the equation PlotPatterns. You can follow the equations in PlotPatterns to plot EIRP patterns for other designs. For example:

using('PhasedArray1_TxDesign_Data');

graph1=graph_figure('EIRP_Pattern_1e10Hz');
graph2.add_spherical_data( Spectrum_EIRP_PhiGrid , Spectrum_EIRP_ThetaGrid, max(10*log10(Spectrum_EIRP_Pattern_1e10Hz)+30,0) );

 

Observation

 

For all the parts before the first amplifier (DriveAmp), this spectrum will only include the two input tones. At the output of the ArrayAttn1 you can see the variation of the level of these two tones due to the Taylor window applied. You can mouse over the points in this graph to see channel identification information (channel number the point corresponds to) as well as Intermod identification (what source frequencies intermodulated to create this spectral component). Since there are many points close to each other (many overlap since the Taylor window will provide the same attenuation level to several groups of channels) you may want to zoom in so that the points are separated and the mouse over will give you information only about the point you mouse over. At the output of the two amplifiers you can see the harmonics and intermods.

Workspace.Name: RF PhasedArray Dual Polarization
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\Phased Array Analysis\RF PhasedArray Dual Polarization.wsv
Workspace.Description:
RF PhasedArray Dual Polarization

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

 

This workspace explores different ways of modeling dual polarization phased array systems.

 

Since the workspace was saved without simulation data you may see errors from equations trying to access dataset variables from simulations that have not run yet. These errors will go away once you run all simulations in this workspace. In addition, the table RxOutPwr displays data that are ONLY available in Rx simulations, so if you simulate in Tx mode, you will get errors from the table of the form "Undefined function or variable ...".

 

BACKGROUND

 

The polarization of an electromagnetic wave describes the changes in magnitude and direction with time. It is characterized by two orthogonal components Etheta and Ephi. The polarization of an antenna is defined as the polarization of the electric field it radiates.

 

Depending on the values of Etheta and Ephi, there are three types of Antenna polarization:

1. Linear: Etheta and Ephi are in phase or 180 degrees out of phase.

2. Circular: Etheta and Ephi have the same magnitude and 90 degrees difference in phase.

3. Elliptical. Etheta and Ephi do not satisfy either of the above two conditions.

 

In SystemVue, antenna polarization can be set using the Etheta and Ephi parameters of the ArrayAnt model. These parameters can be:

1. scalar complex values; in this case, every element in the array will have the same polarization.

2. arrays of complex values; in this case, elements can have different polarization setting based on the mapping characterized by this array.

 

Review the documentation of Etheta and Ephi antenna parameters to understand how the values of these parameters define the polarization of the different phased array elements for different phased array configurations.

 

In addition, polarization mismatch can be modeled for antennas in "receiver" mode by setting the IncidentEtheta and IncidentEphi parameters of the ArrayAnt model (Phased Array Analysis simulations).


SETUP

 

The Constants equations define four tunable variables EthetaEphiMagRatio, EthetaEphiPhaseDiffDeg, IncidentEthetaEphiMagRatio, IncidentEthetaEphiPhaseDiffDeg, which can be used to set the polarization of the antenna and the incoming wave. They also define the RxTx tunable variable that can be used to simulate the phased array systems in Rx (1) or Tx (2) mode and the PolOption tunable variable that can be used to select what polarization components (0: Etheta/Ephi, 1: Eleft/Eright, 2: Eco/Ecross, 3: Ludwig 2 (Elevation/Azimuth), 4: Ludwig 2 (Alpha/Epsilon), 5: Ludwig 3 (Horizontal/Vertical)) the polarization patterns will be computed for.

 

Design1 (under Configuration 1 folder) defines the dual polarization system with NumAntennasPerLocation = 2 (so there are twice as many signals generated at the output of the antenna). The antenna polarization is specified as two in-phase equal strength components by setting Etheta = [1;0] and Ephi = [0;1]. This means that of the two antennas at the same location the first one has Etheta = 1 and Ephi = 0 (first elements of the Etheta and Ephi arrays) and the second one has Etheta = 0 and Ephi = 1 (second elements of the Etheta and Ephi arrays). The circuitry after the antenna implements the desired polarization by introducing the appropriate phase shift and scaling to the signals sent to the two antennas located at the same position. Read the notes in this design for more details.

 

Design2 (under Configuration 2 folder) is similar to Design1 but order of polarization control and beam steering is switched. Read the notes in this design for more details.

 

Design3 and Design4 are equivalent and should produce the same results.

 

EXERCISES

 

Tune the EthetaEphiMagRatio, EthetaEphiPhaseDiffDeg, IncidentEthetaEphiMagRatio, IncidentEthetaEphiPhaseDiffDeg variables to set up differnt polarizations for the antenna and the incoming wave. Run the simulations for the different configurations and observe the results in the graphs. NOTE that both PlotPatterns1 and PlotPatterns2 equations (plotting results from the corresponding simulations) plot on the same graphs (BeamPattern, BeamPatternPol1, BeamPatternPol2). If you simulate in Rx mode (RxTx = 1), then you can also observe the receiver output power (after the last combiner stage) in the RxOutPwr table. There you can observe the effect of polarization mismatch between the antenna and the incoming wave.

 

To achieve different polarizations use the following values for the MagRatio and PhaseDiffDeg variables:

  • Linear: MagRatio any value; PhaseDiffDeg 0 or 180.
  • Circular: MagRatio 1; PhaseDiffDeg 90 or -90.
  • Elliptical: any values not satisfying above conditions.

Workspace.Description:
RF PhasedArray With Mixer

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates the use of mixers in a Phased Array TR design.

 

1. Make the Tune Window visible and set Settings.ArrayState to 1 to configure the switches so that the system operates as a receiver. Run the Phased Array analysis PhasedArray. The graphs PathMeas_CF, PathMeas_CGAIN, and PathMeas_CNF show the Channel Frequency, Cascaded Gain, and Cascaded Noise Figure for all 64 paths of this 8 x 8 phased array system. As you can see in the PathMeas_CF graph, the mixer downconverts from 5 GHz to 1.5 GHz. In addition, you can see that after the ArrayAttn2 part, which implements a Taylor window, the traces in the PathMeas_CGAIN graph separate into groups (due to the different attenuation applied) and then the traces converge back to a common trace after the combiner (ArraySplit1 part).

 

2. Now set Settings.ArrayState to 2 to configure the switches so that the system operates as a transmitter. Run the Phased Array analysis PhasedArray and again observe the graphs PathMeas_CF, PathMeas_CGAIN, and PathMeas_CNF.

 

To see the impact of the mixer in the non-linear behavior of the system you can plot the various non-linear path measurements available in the dataset, such as IIP2, IIP3, IP1DB, IPSAT, OIP2, OIP3, OP1DB, OPSAT.

Workspace.Name: RFAMP_BPF_Intermods
Workspace.Description:
RFAMP_BPF_Intermods

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This workspace demonstrates use of a filter to limit the harmonics and intermods generated in a Phased Array Tx system.

 

The frequency response of the filter is shown in the graph DCP_vs_Freq (obtained by a Spectrasys Quick Sweep).

 

In the Phased Array design TxDesign, first short the filter and run the simulation. Observe the spectrum at the output of the Driver Amp in DriverAmp_Output graph. This graphs plots the sepctrum at the output of the amplifier for the 6-th channel. This is a 4 x 4 array system so channel 6 is one of the channels corresponding to the center of the array and due to the Taylor window it will have the highest power level and so the highest levels of intermods and harmonics. The table ChannelMap shows the channel number associated with each array element.

 

Checkpoint the graph (to remember the values of this simulation), activate the filter, and run the simulation again.

 

Now observer the spectrum at the output of the filter (Filter_Output graph) for the 6-th channel. The filter's frequency response is overlaid on this graph.

 

Compare the orginal levels (checkpointed values) of tones at different frequencies in the DriverAmp_Output graph with the ones at the output of the filter (Filter_Ouptut graph) and confirm that they have attenuated based on the filter's response.

 

With the filter present the tones at the output of the DriverAmp are also attenuated compared to its orignal levels due to the mismatch the filter provides at the different frequencies. This is why the graph needs to be checkpointed after the original simulation so we can compare the orignal levels to the ones at the output of the filter.

Rx Phased Array 4x4 System

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example shows simulated system level measurements on a 4x4 receive array. The design is a simple receiver modelled with some front end losses, a limiter, LNA, time delay, attenuators, combiner, more losses and a final Rx amplifier.

 

When the 'Save Path Measurements for Level Diagrams' option is enabled on the 'Measurements' tab of the phased array analysis data for each element path is shown in the dataset. The originial variables shown above are values referred to a single path and do not reflect the results of the entire array. These same variable with a '_Array' name have been adjusted to account for the all elements in the array.

Workspace.Name: SParamDatasetPhaseShifterAtten
Workspace.Description:
SParamDatasetPhaseShifterAtten

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This workspace demonstrates use of S-parameter data in the Phased Array Attenuator (ArrayAttn) and Phase Shifter (ArrayPhase) models.

 

Since the workspace was saved without simulation data, you may see errors from equations or graphs trying to access datasets from simulations that have not run yet. These errors will go away once you run all simulations in this workspace.

 

 

SETUP

 

S-parameter data for the Analog Devices parts HMC1019ALP4E (5-bit Digital Attenuator) and HMC543ALC4B (4-bit Digital Phase Shifter) have been imported in the folders with the corresponding names (imported S-parameter data is for each state of these devices; 32 states for Attenuator and 16 states for Phase Shifter). The graphs under these folders show the S(2,1) magnitude and phase.

 

The Designs folder has four designs representing (at different levels of accuracy/detail) an 8 x 8 URA system with element spacing set to half a wavelength for a 10 GHz wave (see Equation1) using a Taylor window and pointing the beam at Theta = 25 degrees and Phi = 250 degrees.

  • DesignIdeal is using an ideal attenuator and phase shifter
  • DesignQuant is using a 5-bit attenuator and a 4-bit phase shifter, whose response is frequency independent
  • DesignQuantSParams is using a 5-bit attenuator and a 4-bit phase shifter, which also use the S-parameter data for the Analog Devices parts described above.
  • DesignQuantSParamsNL is the same as DesignQuantSParams described above with the addition of nonlinear parameters specified in the the ArrayAttn model. The nonlinear parameters were adjusted to be around the 1 dB compression point of the array.

The following graphs under the Graphs folder compare the attenuations and phase shifts introduced by the ArrayAttn and ArrayPhase in the first three designs

  • Attenuation_ArrayAttn1 compares the attenuation introduced by the ArrayAttn model in the first three designs.
  • Attenuation_ArrayPhase1 shows the attenuation introduced by the ArrayPhase model in DesignQuantSParams. This attenuation should not vary too much, otherwise the taper introduced by ArrayAttn could be distorted and the desired sidelobe level may not be achieved. ArrayPhase DOES NOT introduce any attenuation in designs DesignIdeal and DesignQuant. Even if the InsertionLoss parameter is set to 1, the insertion loss would be the same for all paths and would not distort the taper
  • PhaseShift_ArrayPhase1 compares the phase shift introduced by the ArrayPhase model in the first three designs.
  • PhaseShift_ArrayAttn1 shows the phase shift introduced by the ArrayAttn model in DesignQuantSParams. This phase shift should not vary too much, otherwise the phase shifts introduced by ArrayPhase could be distorted and the beam may not end up pointing to the desired direction. ArrayAttn DOES NOT introduce any phase shift in designs DesignIdeal and DesignQuant.

These graphs do not show the attenuations and phase shifts introduced by the ArrayAttn and ArrayPhase for the fourth design DesignQuantSParamsNL because they are identical to the ones introduced in the design DesignQuantSParams.
 
The graph PhaseShifterOutputSpec shows the spectrum at the output of the ArrayPhase model. The harmonics seen were generated by the ArrayAttn model.
 

Equation PlotPatterns creates 3-D beam patterns for the four designs so that we can compare the effects of quantization, S-parameters, and non-linearity.

 

 

EXERCISES

 

Run all four Phased Array anlyses.

Observe the attenuations and phase shifts introduced by ArrayAttn and ArrayPhase in the three designs (graphs in Graphs folder).

Run Equation PlotPatterns to see the four beam patterns.

Observe the effects of quantization, S-paramters, and non-linearities in the beam patterns.

Tune the Freq variable to see how the attenuations, phases shifts, and beam patterns change.

Add another frequency in the ArrayPort1 part in design DesignQuantSParamsNL (set Freq, TxPwrIn, and Phase parameters to arrays with two elements) and observe the intermods in the graph PhaseShifterOutputSpec.

Workspace.Name: Spectrasys4x4_vs_PhasedArray
Workspace.Description:
Comparing Phased Array Analysis
vs. Spectrasys (brute force)

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Workspace

 

This workspace contrasts a full Spectrasys analysis of a 4x4 TX array vs. a more streamlined Phased Array analysis.  By comparing the two results side-by-side, you can gain confidence in the accuracy and convenience of the Phased Array analysis results, vs. the difficulty of drawing and solving large networks in Spectrasys. 

  • In Folder #1, you draw and manually implement a 16-element array, complete with manual gain/phase states in Spectrasys.  Because Spectrasys has no native post-processing functions for beam measurements and array functions, many of these calculations are shown manually. (This requires a W1719 license)
  • In Folder #2, you use the Phased Array controller, and the special phased array parts.  The design problem, the simulaiton setup, and the post-processing are all much simpler. (This requires both W1719 and W1720 licenses)

For you to try:

  • Run the simulations, and and run the scripts called "PlotPattern1" and "PlotPattern2" to refresh the 3D plots.
  • Explore the numeric results, such as Channel Power (DCP), Gain, Cumulative Noise Figure (CNF), and EOIP3
    • do you see any differences?  can you explain them?
    • do you have confidence for a larger problem?
  • Now, consider making some basic changes such as the parameters suggested below
    • change from 4x4 to 8x8 array (64 elements)
    • change the beamforming angle (PHI & THETA)
    • change the gain parameter on the TX PA.
  • QUESTIONS to consider:
    • To make these changes, how many places you need to touch? 
    • How much time does it take to make the changes?  Did you do it right?
    • How much simulation time and RAM does it take? 
    • Would the topology change break your existing RFLINK, to Dataflow?

To consider RFLINK and Dataflow beamforming, please look at additional examples in the \Examples\Beamforming\ directory, including "Discovering_Beamforming.wsv".

Workspace.Name: XParameterIntermods
Workspace.Description:
X-Parameter Intermods

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example demonstrates use of X-parameters in Phased Array analysis performing Intermod and Harmonic Calculation.

 

The X-parameter data represent an amplifier. The data has been exracted up to 3rd order.

 

The number of input tones, their frequencies, powers, and phases are configured in the equation Config. The default setup is of 5 tones spaced at 5 MHz apart and centered at 1 GHz. All the tones are at 0 dBm power and 0 degrees phase.

 

Run the simulation and observe the spectrum at the output of the X-parameter amplifier in the graph XParamAmp_Output. For simplicity ONLY the output of Channel 10 is plotted (this is an 8 x 8 array so there are a total of 64 channels). Since there is no taper (window) used in this system, all channels will have the same output.

 

Increase/Decrease the tone power level and observe how the level of intermods and harmonics goes up/down. Use a Taylor window (in the ArrayAttn1 part) and observe the different levels of intermods and harmonics for the channels corresponding to the corners of the array (channels 1, 8, 57, 64) and the channels corresponding to the center of the array (channels 28, 29, 36, 37). To plot the spectrum for a specific channel, right click on the Spectrum_Power_05_XParamAmp_Output variable in the dataset MultiTones_data and select  Add to Graph > New Graph of Selected Channel(s) and select the channel you want. The ChannelMap table shows the channel number associated with each array element.

 

Since the X-parameter data was extracted up to 3rd order, increasing the Maximum order setting in the Options tab of the Phased Array analysis MultiTones, will NOT produce more harmonics/intermods in the graph.

Workspace.Name: Dual Band Frequency Plan
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Dual Band Frequency Plan.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Dual Band Frequency Band Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates the IF performance of a dual band CDMA receiver.

 

BACKGROUND

Frequency planning is one the first steps performed during the RF architecture design phase. During this phase several frequency schemes are considered to ensure performance reliability internally as well as externally. External performance is typically controlled by a regulatory agency (i.e. Federal Communications Commission FCC or European Telecommunications Standards Institute ETSI) and the designer must comply with requirements before products are shipped and revenue collected. Spurious integrity for RF design is an age-old problem. Spurious responses, which occur naturally in the frequency conversion process, can render a particular design completely useless and non-compliant.

 

SETUP

This example shows a frequency plan of dual band receiver at Cellular and PCS frequencies. The goal of this example is to show the performance tradeoffs in intermediate frequency selection for two receive bands being down converted to common IF frequency. The parameters for each of the bands and the drive levels associated with each mixer is configured on the 'Inputs' tab of the WhatIF dialog box. It is assumed that the amplitude performance of each mixer can be represented by double balanced mixer equations. The amplitude performance of the mixer can be changed on the 'Type' tab of the WhatIF dialog box. Furthermore, it assumed that the maximum intermod order of 10 is all that is important and only spurious products within 100 dB of the desired IF output is all that is important.

 

ANALYSIS

CDMAPlan Graph - The performance of every valid IF frequency that meets the requirements for both RF bands appears on the graph (this is NOT the type of plot that you would see on a spectrum analyzer). Mouse fly-over text is used to identify each spur and spur free region. The spurs due to the 800 MHz band is shown in one color and the 1900 MHz band in the other. Spurious free regions are highlighted in another color.

 

CDMAPlan Graph_Compare - This graph compares two different 800 MHz mixer input drive levels. See the following exercises for more information.

 

EXERCISES

  1. Use the mouse to find the tiny spur free region located between 772.804 and 772.931 MHz.
  2. Select an IF frequency in the spur free range identified in the previous step and enter that frequency on the 'Settings' tab for the 'Single Intermediate Frequency'. After the 'Apply' button is clicked a spectrum analyzer type of plot will be displayed. The IF frequency is highlighted in the center of the graph. The rest of the traces on the graph is similar to having the spectrum analyzer placed on max hold and sweeping the input frequency and LO frequencies across their entire range.
  3. Go back and examine the performance of 'All Intermediate Frequencies'. Click the 'Apply' button.
  4. Change the 'Amplitude Range' from 100 to 50 dB. Click the 'Apply' button. Notice how the the spurious free regions are wider since the dynamic range only needs to be 50 dBc instead of 100 dBc.
  5. Change the spurious 'Maximum Order' to 15 and click the 'Apply' button. Notice how the spurious free regions have decreased.
  6. Lets suppose the we wanted to examine the effect of increasing the drive level on the 881.5 MHz mixer by 10 dB. Change the name of the dataset from 'CDMAPlan_Data' to 'CDMAPlan_Data_Hi' and the 'Input Drive Level' from -10 dBm to 0 dBm on the 881.5 MHz mixer. Click the 'Apply' button.
  7. Plot the trace from the new dataset on the graph. Change the graph 'Default Dataset or Equations' back to the original dataset. Add a new series then add the following measurements a) 'CDMAPlan_Data_Hi.Spur1' and b) CDMAPlan_Data_Hi.Spur2. Change the colors and names as desired.

Workspace.Name: RF Link with Noise
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\RF Link with Noise.wsv
Workspace.Description:
RF Link with Noise Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This workspace illustrates how to properly model thermal noise in a Data Flow / RF cosimulation.

 

BACKGROUND

Remember, all source ports in RF simulations generate port noise automatically. However, in Data Flow the ports do not generate noise. This noise must be explicitly added. These two methods are at odds with each other and it is very easy for users to be confused and end up with too much or too little noise. In Data Flow simulations it is difficult to quickly recognize whether the noise is wrong since noise is random and the peak to minimum noise power range can be on the order of 20 dB. This makes it hard to determine what the average noise power is. Furthermore, the resolution bandwidth needed to determine the integrated noise power may not be obvious or intuitive.

 

During a Data Flow / RF cosimulation the Input port in the RF schematic is disabled so the RF input is simulated as noiseless. Consequently, it is assumed that the input signal to the RF Link has the proper thermal noise if noise is being simulated. There is an option on the RF Link to Add source thermal noise to input if the Data Flow input signal does not contain thermal noise. An internal Data Flow thermal noise source will be created whose noise power is based on the temperature specified in the RF Link. This noise source will be added to the Data Flow input signal driving the RF Link.

 


SETUP

The RF design contains a single amplifier whose gain and noise figure are tunable. The system temperature is also tunable. The Data Flow design comtains an oscillator, RF Link, and a spectrum analyzer. The resolution bandwidth is 1000 Hz and the spectrum analyzer is set to average 100 segments.

 

ANALYSIS

DF Spec Out - This graph shows the Data Flow spectrum analyzer output along with the calculated thermal noise. The calculated thermal noise should always be at the same value as what the average measured noise would be.

 

RF Spec Out - This graphs shows the output spectrum from the RF simulation.

 

Noise Table - This table shows the calculated average noise power.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune Gain, Noise Figure, and Temperature and notice that the average value of the 'Measured' noise is the same as the 'Calculated' noise on the DF Spec Out graph.

2. Disable the 'Add source thermal noise to input'  on the RF Link and notice the differences in measured and calculated noise.

3. Add  an 'AddNDensity' block between the Oscillator and RF Link on the Data Flow schematic. Set the noise power to the value of the 'NoiseFloor' in the 'InEquations' block. The measured and calculated noise should now be consistent.

Workspace.Name: Transceiver_RFLink
Workspace.Description:
Using RF LINK

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example workspace explores the mechanics of using a Spectrasys "RF Architecture" block diagram in a Dataflow simulation.

 

WHAT IS IT?

 

A modulated source is upconverted and propagated through an RFLINK block.  The RFLINK is a behavioral model derived at run-time from the RF path performance, as predicted using the Spectrasys frequency-domain RF simulator (a W1719 RF Design Kit license is required).  This behavioral model is profiled for frequency response across the modulated bandwidth, as well as basic power dependence for compression effects.  A noise floor can be included.

 

HOW DO YOU USE IT?

 

To use the RFLINK, you simply drag the Spectrasys circuit from the workspace tree - here it is called "RFcircuit" - and you drop it on the Dataflow schematic.  SystemVue sets up the default parameters automatically.

 

WHO IS THIS MEANT FOR?

 

The feature allows Spectrasys users to surround their RF chains with real modulation, coding, and VHDL to see coded EVM, BER, and other parameters not possible with Spectrasys alone.  The feature also allows Baseband DSP engineers to have easy access to RF tools, in a format that is fast and easy to use, without dragging around an entire RF design flow.  Thus, teams can callobrate, and cross-domain partitioning penetrates deeper into both RF & BB, eliminating waste design margin.

 

NOTE: The phase parameter is used to select the timing sample (0-7) at the maximum eye opening. It is possible that changes in RF delay through filters could affect the optimum timing phase.

 

TRY THIS

  1. Enable the "Tune" docking window using the "View/Tune" menu.
  2. Change the "TX_PowerAmp.G" (gain) parameter from 10 to 30dB.
    What did the extra signal power do to the constellation?  To the Spectrum?
  3. Change the "Sim_Control.FilterBW" from 5 down to 2 (MHz)  What did this narrower RF filter do to the constellation? Could you determine the EVM degradation by looking only at the Spectrum?

Want to set up BER and other parameters?  Continue on to the Transceiver_BER workspace in the "Comms" example directory.

Workspace.Name: VTB_64QAM
Workspace.Description:
VTB_64QAM

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This workspace is similar to the VTB_Example tutorial workspace elsewhere in SystemVue, except that this also includes two additional RF PAs to measure locally before exporting to ADS as a Verification Test Bench.  It can be used to see the flow back & forth between SystemVue and ADS.

One of the PA models is an X-parameter device, exported from a 850MHz celluar amplifier example often used in ADS as for demonstrations.  The other is its behavioral equivalent, a compressing dataflow amplifier with a nominal gain of 12.95dB and a input 1dB compression power of about +16dBm (ie - P1DB=28dBm).  In addition, this workspace can be used as a VTB in ADS to test the original transistor-level amplifier using Circuit Envelope, and compare the results.

The 3 simulation results should be fairly comparable, as long as you match the power levels and impedance loading conditions here.  Based on load-pull simulations, the X-parameter device was loaded here in the Spectrasys subcircuit with ZL=32ohms to give optimal PowerOut; the dataflow simulation really doesn't know about voltages and currents and just assumes ZL=50ohms.  In ADS, you will want to play with both input power and load impedance to see their effects.

THINGS TO TRY HERE

1. 3 parameters have been marked for mousewheel up/down "tuning":

  • Modulation Type
    (4=16QAM, 6=64QAM, 8=256QAM)
  • RF input power level
    (Pin=16dBm --> P1DB point)
  • X-parameter load impedance
    (32=best Pout, 50=0.5dB lower)

2. If you want to use this as a VTB, deactivate the RFLINK and AMPLIFIER device models in this workspace, and then activate the SVE_LINK model that's in the middle.  Then save the workspace your local working directory.  Close SystemVue, run ADS, and import the .WSV file into ADS using the instructions for "Custom VTB"s in that product.  It becomes a VTB library that is local within your open ADS workspace.

LICENSES REQUIRED

In SystemVue, this simulation just uses a basic license.  If you simulate the X-parameter device, you will need the W1719 RF Sys license. 

In ADS, this VTB just requires either a "VTB Engine" or "Ptolemy" license; along with Harmonic Balance and Circuit Envelope for the circuit co-sim.

 

FURTHER INSTRUCTIONS/TUTORIALS

For more information on how to create VTB designs please refer to the following sections of the SystemVue documentation:

  • Simulation > Verification Test Bench (VTB)
  • Tutorials > Verification Test Bench Tutorial

 

The VTB designs included in this workspace are:

 

EVM_Measurement

 

This VTB design performs an EVM measurement on a modulated signal. The symbol rate of the signal is fixed at 0.2 MHz. Several modulation formats can be selected and modulation impairments can be added to the signal.

 

When adding impairments (IQ Offset, Gain and Phase Imbalance) the constellation plot (EVM_Meas_Tx_Constellation) may seem inconsistent with the trajectory one (EVM_Meas_Tx_Trajectory). For example, applying an offset only along the x-axis might show (in the constellation plot) as offset along the other axis, both axes, or the expected axis but in the opposite direction. The reason is that the constellation plot uses data generated by the EVM sink, whereas the trajectory plot uses data created by just filtering the signal with a Root Raised Cosine filter. The EVM sink performs demodulation on the input signal and may arbitrarily rotate it by any angle that is an integer multiple of the angle to which the constellation is phase invariant (rectangular QAM constellations are 90-degree phase invariant and Star-QAM constellations are 45-degree phase invariant).

 

ACPR_Measurement

 

This VTB design demonstrates how to post-process simulation data in a VTB design.  It measures ACPR for a modulated signal. The symbol rate and the modulation format of the signal can be set using VTB parameters. The modulated signal goes through a non-linear amplifier whose output 1 dB compression point is also controlled by a VTB parameter.

 

ACPR is measured by computing the spectrum power in different bands using a custom ACPR function defined inside the SystemVue workspace. This ACPR function is for demonstration purposes only. It does NOT comply with any standard. Four user defined variables have been created in the dataset (MyACPRMinus1, MyACPRMinus2, MyACPRPlus1, MyACPRPlus2) that are calculated by calling the ACPR function. This function takes as arguments data created by the simulation (S2_Power, and S2_Power_Freq) as well as values computed based on the top level design parameters (FCarrier, SymbolRate). To get these parameters in the dataset you need to check the Save Design Parameters to Dataset check box in the Options tab of the Data Flow analysis.

Workspace.Name: WhatIF Block UpConverter Comparison
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\WhatIF Block UpConverter Comparison.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Block Up Converter Spur Analysis Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates a swept spectrum graph on a 2 to 10 GHz block up converter. The results are displayed similar to WhatIF instead of the spectrum comb that is traditionally seen.

 

BACKGROUND

WhatIF is a frequency planning tool used to help locate spurious free regions or analyze spurious performance for a single agile conversion stage. The graphical output is unique since each spurious product is represented as a horizontal bar whose length tracks the spur across the entire frequency range of the system. The height of these bars on the graph represents the amplitudes of the spurs.

 

The upside is that WhatIF is extremely fast, has small workspaces, can analyze the performance of every IF both in up and down conversion cases. The downside is that it only handles a single agile mixer stage. To overcome this limitation and help users visualize spur performance of arbitrary topologies a 'sweepplot()' function has been created.

 

This 'sweepplot()' function points to sweep spectrum data. The swept data is resorted and organized in a fashion where traces are created from each piece of spectrum. These pieces of spectrums are tracked across the sweep range and then plotted as a frequency response bar. The height of the bar corresponds to the amplitude of the spur at that particular sweep frequency.

 

SETUP

There are three sections in this workspace. Each is stored in its own folder. Spurious analysis will take place up to 5th order. It is assumed there are 6 RF blocks each having a 250 MHz bandwidth for a total of 1500 MHz.

 

1) A WhatIF analysis of a 2 to 10 GHz block up-converter. The default configuration is using the summing process between the IF input and mixer LO.

 

2) A Spectrasys sweep that contains a single mixer was created to compare the 'sweepplot()' to the plots in WhatIF. 

 

3) A complete block up converter with front end IF filter and variable gain control. Also included are some post mixer filtering along with amplification and coupling.

 

A variable called 'LOInjection' was created to compare a 'IF + LO = RF' and a 'LO - IF = RF' response. A '0' corresponds to the sum configuration and a '1' the high side LO configuration.

 

ANALYSIS

FreqPlan1 Graph - This graph is an analysis of the block up-converter created by WhatIF. To toggle between the sum and difference configurations change the 'Desired Output Frequency' on the 'Inputs' tab from 'Sum' to 'Difference Show Hi Side LO, LO > RF'. Notice an in-band '3 x 2' response exists in the 'Sum' configuration.

 

Sweep Plot - This graph is similar to the 'FreqPlan1 Graph' created by WhatIF except that this uses the 'sweepplot()' function.

 

NOTE: When comparing graphs between WhatIF and the 'sweepplot()' the spurious bandwidths are slightly different because the 'sweepplot()' function only tracks the center of the spectrum and doesn't take into consideration the bandwidth of the carrier. Also, WhatIF graphs are displayed in 'dBc'. The '0 dBc' reference point in this example = - 20 dBm.

 

Full Tx Sweep Plot - This graph shows the true spurious response due to the entire block up-converter. This graph can be compared with the 'FreqPlan1 Graph' and 'Sweep Plot' graphs to see the effects the additional stages have on the spurious responses.

 

EXERCISES

1. Which mixer configuration (sum or difference, high side LO) has the best in-band spurious performance?

 

2. For the 'Full Tx Sweep Plot' who creates the positive sloped spurs located between 14 and 20 GHz?

 

3. Tune the variable gain amplifier bias and notice the affects of the intermod spectrum.

 

ANSWERS TO EXERCISES

1. The high side LO in a difference configuration gives better in-band spurious performance.

 

2. These positive sloped spurs are created by the 'TxAmp'.

Workspace.Name: WhatIF Dual Analysis Output
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\WhatIF Dual Analysis Output.wsv
Workspace.Description:
WhatIF Dual Analysis Output Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This illustration shows how to see both the sum and difference outputs on the same graph. 

 

BACKGROUND

WhatIF is a powerful tool used to illustrate the performance of every IF. Once the IF has been selected it is useful to see the entire spurious spectrum at the mixer output. WhatIF lets you see and analyze the sum or difference spectrums independently. To see both responses at the same time the solution is simple and requires plotting the results from a sum and difference dataset.


SETUP

In this particular example we have an RF input spectrum from 275 to 325 MHz. The desired IF is a difference IF at 800 MHz derived from a high side LO. Since we have chosen the IF frequency to be 800 MHz and the IF bandwidth is 1 MHz then the LO will range from 1075.5 to 1124.5 MHz. In this given example we are looking at the 'Single Intermediate Frequency' behavior only. We know from experience that this same LO range plus the RF input spectrum will yield another IF centered at 1400 MHz. This too can also be displayed. However, by default these can only be seen one at a time.

 

This is an easy problem to solve since a dataset can easily be generated for the 800 MHz IF difference case and another dataset generated for the 1400 MHz IF sum case. The results from both datasets can be displayed on the same graph.

 

ANALYSIS

Dual Output - This graph shows how the spurs and the valid IF regions are plotted from both datasets. From this graph it becomes very clear to see the various spurious and the filtering that would be required to meet a given level of performance.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the mixer input drive level one of the configurations (sum or difference) and notice the change in results.

Workspace.Name: Zero IF Rx Impairments
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Zero IF Rx Impairments.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Zero IF Rx Impairments Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates the RF impairments found in an analog Zero IF receiver. The Keysight VSA software can be used to examine streaming data results in real time.


SETUP

A QPSK modulator and demodulator have been created in their own schematics. The RF downconverter has also been created in its own schematic. All three of these pieces have been brought together in a co-simulation schematic called 'DF Receiver'.

 

The RF downconverter consists of an front end filter followed by a low noise amplifier (LNA) and a zero IF receiver block. Several parameters in the downconverter have been made tunable. There are equations associated with the downconverter schematic that tie the entire phase noise response relative to the phase noise at the 10 kHz offset.

 

The baseband receive trajectory is plotted. Tunable parameters can be changed and the impact on the trajectory can be determined.

 

ANALYSIS & GRAPHS

  • Bits In Out - This graph shows the bits before modulation and after demodulation.
  • RFin Trajectory - This graph shows the modulator trajectory after upsampling.
  • RFout Trajectory - This graph shows the demodulated trajectory after decimation, at only the true sample points.
  • Modulator Out Spec - This graph shows the modulator output spectrum.

 

EXERCISES

  1. Change the gain imbalance. What changes were made to the output trajectory and why?
  2. Change the phase imbalance. What changes were made to the output trajectory and why?
  3. Reduce the LO to RF isolation to something like 20 dB. What changes were made to the output trajectory and why?  How would you go about filtering this effect away?
  4. Enable phase noise calculations in the RF_Link part. What changes were made to the output trajectory and why?
  5. Increase the phase noise at the 10 kHz offset. What changes were made to the output trajectory and why?
  6. Enable the filter ahead of the LNA. What changes were made to the output trajectory and why?
  7. Enable the ADC's in front of the baseband receiver.  Try changing the "RXbits" to 6, 8, and 16-bit resolutions.  How does the DC offset affect the EVM of the signal?  the Dynamic Range? 

NOTE: The RF Link is only characterized once during the startup of the dataflow simulation. Therefore real time tuning will not work for the RF schematic and the dataflow simulation needs to be stopped and re-started in order for RF changes can take place.

 

 

 

ANSWERS TO EXERCISES

  1. Gain imbalance causes the trajectory to become rectangular and not square
  2. Phase imbalance causes the trajectory to become a parallelogram and not a square.
  3. As the LO to RF isolation decreases the DC offset value at the output of the zero IF receiver will increase. This increasing DC offset will cause to the origin of the trajectory to shift up and to the right.
  4. Enabling phase noise will cause the symbol sample points to become obscure and not so crisply confined to single points in the trajectory plane.
  5. Increasing the phase noise will increase the sample point obscurity.
  6. Because the filter changes the trajectory from a square to a parallelogram there is phase imbalanced caused by the filter.

AGC Using Power Dependent Atten

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example shows how the power dependent attenuator works in an IF AGC scenario.

 

BACKGROUND

The power dependent attenuator model will change its attenuation in the forward direction once the input power crosses the specified input threshold. The name of this parameter is ThresholdPwrIn. When the power level is below the input threshold the power dependent attenuator has only an insertion loss (according to the IL parameter) and adds no additional loss. A Resolution parameter is used to control the attenuation step size. When set to 0 dB the attenuation will hold the output power of the attenuator perfectly constant and equal to the threshold input power. This simulates an analog voltage controlled attenuator.

 

A digital attenuator can be simulated by changing the Resolution to the step size of the digital attenuator. The Range parameter is used to control the dynamic range of the attenuator. For example, if the Range is set to 31 dB with a Resolution of 1 dB, a 5-bit digital attenuator is simulated. The maximum value of attenuation is equal to its range. The Isolation parameter sets the attenuation of the signal in the reverse direction.

 

NOTE: The first attenuation step does not occur until the total node input power is greater than the ThresholdPwrIn + Resolution. The input power is the total integrated power right at the input pin of the attenuator.


SETUP

There are two analyses in this workspace: 1) Analog Attn and 2) Digital Attn. Both attenuators are set up with the same input threshold power of -50 dBm and a Range of 31 dB. "Analog Attn" has a Resolution of 0 dB and "Digital Attn" a value of 1 dB. The input power is swept over a 50 dB range from -60 dBm to -10 dBm in 0.5 dB steps using the amplitude Quick Sweep inside each system analysis (see 'Path2').

 

 

ANALYSIS

Analog Attn vs Pwr - This graph shows the narrowed output power range versus the input power for the analog attenuator.

 

Analog Attn Out Spec - This is the output spectrum of the analog attenuator.

 

Digital Attn vs Pwr - This graph shows the narrowed output power range versus the input power for the digital attenuator. Note that the output follows the input linearly until the RF input reaches -53 dBm (which is equivalent to -50 dBm at the input pin of the attenuator). At that point the attenuator begins to level the output power over a range of 31 dB, up to the point where the RF input reaches -22 dBm or so. As the input continues to increase beyond this level the attenuator output also increases since the attenuator is already at its maximum attenuation level. The 1 dB resolution creates the +/- 0.5 dB 'sawtooth' pattern in the AGC range. Note also the mixer compression beginning at an input of -13 dBm. [HINT: Plot the compression of each stage (COMP) to see that most of the compression is occurring at node 9, the mixer output.]

 

Digital Attn Out Spec - This is the output spectrum of the digital attenuator.

 

Atten Signal Levels - [Table] Shows the input & output power levels of the digital attenuator with nominal RF input of -50 dBm. If the RFPwr variable is changed (or tuned) and re-simulated, the attenuator will attempt to keep its output level constant within the limits of ThresholdPwrIn and Resolution.

Digital Attenuator w Basic AGC Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: The Sweep needs to be calculated before the data can be display)

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple example that illustrates the implementation of a simple AGC circuit using a digital attenuator. A function was created in the equation block that will change the attenuation of the digital attenuator based on the input power level.

 

BACKGROUND

A digital attenuator is a discrete step attenuator whose lease significant bit comes in different resolutions. The maximum attenuation is given by the formula:

 

Max Attn = ( 2^Bits - 1  )  * LSB_dB


SETUP

A simple attenuator and signal source are placed in the schematic. The attenuator has a minmum insertion loss of 0.1 dB. A 4 bit attenuator is shown with a 1 dB LSB. When the input threshold exceeds -2 dBm the AGC will begin. A power sweep has been created to sweep the input power from -5 to +20 dBm in 0.5 dB steps. The 4 bit attenuator will have a maximum range of 15 dB so maximum attenuation will be reached before the maximum input power is achieved.

 

ANALYSIS

Gain vs Input Power - This graphs shows the gain and channel power versus the swept input power at the output port.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the number of bits and LSB of the attenuator and observe the effects. Note: you may need to set the graph to autoscale to see the results.

Open Loop AGC Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: The sweep must be calculated before the data can be displayed)

 

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates how to setup an open loop AGC based on input power and and IF attenuation table.
 
BACKGROUND
Automatic Gain Control (AGC) loops are important in transceiver design. Closed loops are more difficult to work with since loop response issues must be addressed. However, open loops are easy to setup and maintain since stage gain parameters can be determined from input power levels.
 
SETUP
This example shows a simple receiver that has a variable IF attenuator. The equation block is used to define a matrix that contains an IF attenuation value based on an RF input power. When the RF input power is changed the IF attenuation in the table is linearly interpolated. This interpolated value is used as the IF attenuation. The IF attenuator in this example has a 40 dB range which covers the input power from -90 to -50 dBm.
 
An sweep has been created to sweep the RF input power from -100 dBm to -30 which is outside the complete AGC range.
 
ANALYSIS
Chan Pwr Levels - This level diagram shows the channel power for each input power level.
 
Out Chan Pwr vs In Pwr - This graphs shows the channel power at the IF output versus the RF input power level. It is clear where the AGC range begins and ends.
 
Out CNF vs In Pwr - This graph shows the cascaded noise figure at the output versus the RF input power level.
 
EXERCISES

1. Remove the '-60,30; -70,20; -80,10;' entries from the 'IFAttnTable' in the equation block and rerun the simulation. Notice that the response is still the same since the remove entries where just linear interpolated values between the table end points.

2. Change the entries in the 'IFAttnTable' and observe the affects on cascaded noise figure and channel output power.

Conversion Report

  • Information: VersionConverter: Converter has run successfuly.
  • Information: MultiSourceConverterConverter: Converter has run successfuly.

AM to PM Basics Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to model AM to PM. 

 

BACKGROUND

In a nonlinear device the phase of the desired output signal can rotate as a function of the input power. This is known as AM to PM distortion. A typical compression curve is an example to AM to AM distortion.


AM to PM SETUP

 

1. Point Deivative approach

The amplifier at Sch1 has been configured for a -5 deg/dB phase change (AMtoPM) for every 1 dB increase in input power. This slope or derivative is specified at a power level of +10 dBm (PwrAMtoPM). The AMtoPM parameter can have either a negative or positive value.

 

2. Data Points approach

The amplifier at Sch2 has been configured for AM to PM using a list of measured AMtoPM data points.For comparison with 1st (Point Derivative) approach the input data PwrAMtoPMpoints and PwrPwrAMtoPMpoints  is used from simulation data (copy of System1_Data_Path2 dataset) calculated with Point Derivative AMtoPM amplifier parameters settings.

As we expected - both methods of AMtoPM parameters settings are based on the same data and therefore give identical results.

 

ANALYSIS

AM/AM and AM/PM - This graph shows the compression curve (AM/AM) as well as the swept power phase response (AM/PM).

 

Spec Out - This plot shows the output spectrum. 

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the AMtoPM amount and notice the effects in the simulation.

2. Change the sign of AMtoPM. What happened to the phase response?

3. Change the power level of the AMtoPM (PwrAMtoPM). What effects does this have on the simulation results?

Workspace.Name: AM_to_PM_RF_model_LTE
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\AM to PM\AM_to_PM_RF_model_LTE.wsv
Workspace.Description:
AM_to_PM_RF_model_LTE

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates AM-to-PM parameters in the nonlinear RFAMP model.

 

The workspace uses a 2505 MHz LTE Uplink signal as a stimulus. Because of this, you will need licenses for the W1719 RF System and W1910 LTE Library to run the simulation as shown. Otherwise, you can replace the source signal with another desired signal.

 

The device-under-test is a RFAMP model in the "RF_PA_with_AM_PM" schematic with the following parameters:

 

Gain = 17 dB

OP1dB = +25 dBm

OPSAT = +28 dBm

AMtoPM = +2.1 degrees/dB

PwrAMtoPM = (the output power level at which the slope is specified) = +24.5 dBm

 

Several simple measurements are presented here, using native SystemVue post-processing capabilities. Enabling the Keysight 89600B VSA sink on the schematic allows demodulation of the signal using its LTE personality, including spectrum, constellation, EVM, AM/AM and AM/PM measurements. There is excellent agreement between the SystemVue calculations and the displayed measurements on the 89600B VSA.

 

 

Model Validation - Measurements

  • Spectrum Measurements is captured using the SpectrumAnalyzer sink. This is used to quickly assess ACLR and spectral re-growth, for spec pre-compliance.
  • CCDF_Measurements shows the percentage of time (y-axis) that the instantaneous LTE signal envelope spends above the average power level (x-axis). The "crest factor" of the signal is essentially the dB value of the x-axis intercept, and shows the amplitude of the highest signal peaks normalized to the RMS signal power. A second CCDF trace is a reference trace of white gaussian noise, for comparison. A CCDF curve that abruptly falls to a low value shows lower power handling, or clipping.
  • The AMtoAM_and_AMtoPM graph shows the normalized power gain and output phase of the LTE signal (vs. input power level) on a point-by-point basis for the complex-valued modulated carrier envelope. 
    • When these traces are flat lines, the DUT is operating in a very linear region.  (no change from nominal, regardless of time or amplitude)
    • When these traces curve upward or downward vs. power, then DUT is showing some nonlinearity. This level of simulation modeling is common, and is considered a "Level 1" model.
    • When the traces spread into a statistical distribution, then the DUT is demonstrating that some output values depend on the previous signal history in addition to the absolute power levels. These are so-called "baseband memory effects", which are possible with Level 3 Models.

Incidentally, note that there is no explicit sweep taking place; we use the fact that the time domain simulation captures the output signal at many levels of the input signal ranging from zero to maximum level, and these data are used to generate the statistical scatter plots vs. input power level. This is a cool trick!

 

 

EXERCISES

 

  1. Adjust the LTE source power level using the tuning slider. Change the value from the minimum to the maximum power levels, and note the changes to the output traces.  Note the observed power levels and Crest Factors right on the schematic.
  2. (optional ) Use the 89600 VSA software for deeper post-processing.

    If you have access to the Keysight 89600B VSA software (release 11 or later with its LTE options), activate the VSA measurement sink and re-simulate. (It takes several seconds the first time it runs).  The VSA gives you further measurement ability on the LTE signals, such as EVM for each of the LTE data and control sub-signals; integrated bandwidth power measurements to measure ACLR, and many more capabilities.

    User Tip:  After you have simulated into the VSA and observe the results, you can "STOP" the SystemVue simulation, but don't close the VSA; this saves time when you next re-simulate. Slide the slider to a new power level while the simulation is running and see the effect on the signals. The convenience of this method reduces the amount of time you spend doing verification.

SUMMARY

 

In this example, the simulations only take a few seconds, yet are fairly realistic modulated PA results.  This level of verification would be nearly impossible for an analog IC with thousands of transistors using transient Spice and primitive signal sources. A few key capabilities make this easy:

  • The envelope simulation mode
  • A fast dataflow simulation backplane in SystemVue, with a full LTE reference library and native AM-to-PM model integration
  • The SystemVue environment to bridge the design flow gap between Architecture, Implementation, Verification, and Test & Measurement.

Finally, for a more realistic model, consider either generating an X-parameter model, a Fast Circuit Envelope model from GoldenGate, or co-simulating with the DUT schematic in ADS or GoldenGate.

 

The exact same tools and signals used here can also be used to generate signals after tape-out to measure the real hardware transceiver with Keysight signal sources and analyzers.  This allows you to compare the results directly ("apples to apples"), and to feed back measurements into the architecture process to close your modeling loop.  Bring your hardware measurements back into SystemVue, and be using real waveforms for your next design start!

10th Order Amplifier w 4 Tones

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This simple example illustrates the powerful capability of the higher order amplifier.  This amplifier is represented by a 10th order polynomial.  4 input signals drive the amplfier input and the resulting output spectrum is shown in the graph.

 

SETUP

Four wideband signals have been created and applied with the same power level to the input of the high order amplifier.  These four input signals will create all combinations of intermods and harmonics up to the order of the polynomial that represents this amplifier.  In this particular case we have 10 polynomial coefficients so all intermod orders up to 10 will be created.

 

A function has been written in the equation block relating output intercept point to the output intermod level for a specific intermod combination.  All 10 intermod levels are specified using typical intercept relationships between odd and even orders. The amplifier model will then determine the 10 coefficients of the non-linear transfer function needed to generate intermod levels. Measured intercepts follow these general guidelines:

 

Even Products

IP2 ~= P1dB + 20 dB

IP4 ~= P1dB + 13 dB

IP6 ~= P1dB + 11 dB

IP8 ~= P1dB + 9 dB

IP10 ~= P1dB + 8 dB

 

Odd Products

IP3 ~= P1dB + 10 dB

IP5 ~= IP3 - (4 to 6) dB

IP7 ~= IP5 - (2 to 3) dB

IP9 ~= IP7 - (0 to 1) dB

 

Each of the 4 input signals have a different phase value.  Consequently, their output phase will vary as a function of the particular intermod combination.

 

NOTE: Intercept points are not independent of each other nor are they independent of the 1 dB or saturation points. Therefore, extreme caution should be used when specifying intercepts points greater than 3rd order as the simulation results can be non-physical and the results will have poor correlation to measured results.

 

ANALYSIS

The mouse cursor and mouse wheel (zooming) can be used to quickly identify the intermod combination of each and every spectrum.  A plot of both amplitude and phase is available.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the phase of the signal sources in the in the input port and notice the changes in the phase plot.

Amplifier Compression Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how do perform a simple RF power sweep to determine the 1 dB compression point of an RF amplifier.

 

BACKGROUND

As RF amplifiers are driven with more input power they eventually reach a point where their output power is limited which is called the saturation region. Before this occurs a point will be reached where the gain of the amplifier is 1 dB less than the small signal gain. This is referred to as the 1 dB compression point.

 

SETUP

This workspace consists of a CW signal source defined by a multisource and an RF amplifier. The input power is swept from -10 to +14 dBm. The specified 1 dB output compression point of the amplifier is +20 dBm and the output saturation level is +23 dBm. A variable representing input power (RFPwrIn) is created in the equation block associated with the design. This variable is used in the CW source as well as the sweep.

 

The 'Output Equations' block contains the necessary equations to form the swept data in a format that can be used for graphs or tables.

 

ANALYSIS

Power Sweep - This graph contains the swept input power versus the channel output power. A 1 dB compression marker has been placed at 0 dBm input power which yields a linear gain of 20 dB but an actual gain of about 19 dB. Another marker has been placed at +10 dBm input power highlighting the output saturation power level of the amplifier.

 

Sweep Table - This table shows the numerical results of swept input power, the output power, linear gain, and difference in dB between the linear power and actual power.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the compression and saturation points and rerun the sweep to see the effects.

Workspace.Name: Dual Hybrid Matrix Amp
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Amplifiers\Dual Hybrid Matrix Amp.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Dual Hybrid Matrix Amplifier Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: System1 must be calculated before the data can be displayed)

 

ABSTRACT

The hybrid matrix amplifer is a popular power amplifier configuration that encorporates redundancy. With the traditional design of using a single power amplifier for every transmitter the power amplifier becomes a single point of failure. If the amplifier dies then so does the carrier and all of the transmitted information. The hybrid matrix amplier will still provide output power (albeit a lower output power ... due to the loss of the amplifier) for all input signals. Furthermore, the reliability of power amplifiers is typically lower than the transmitter so the likelyhood of lossing a carrier can be very high.

 

BACKGROUND

90 Degree hybrid couplers are used at the input to split each input signal (IN and ISO) by 90 degrees (ISO to 0 is a 90 degree shift and ISO to -90 it a 0 degree shift). These hybrid couplers are also used on the output to combine the amplified signals back together. Because of the phasing carriers will either add or cancel at the output leaving a dedicated output for each carrier. To illustrate this point let's look at a simple dual hybrid matrix amplifer (Hybrid1, RFAmp1, RFAmp2, and Hybrid2). Signals at the IN port of Hybrid1 we will have a 90 degree phase shift into RFAmp2 and a 0 degree phase shift into RFAmp1. The output of RFAmp2 will have a 0 degree phase shift at the -90 output port of the Hybrid2. This same signal that has a 0 degree output through RFAmp1 will go through a 90 degree shift through Hybrid2 and will add constructively at the -90 output port to produce the desired, amplified output. However, RFAmp1 will produce a total 0 degree phase shift at 0 port of Hybrid2 and RFAmp2 will produce a total 180 degree phase shift at this same port and the signal will cancel. Consequently, the output port for the dual hybrid matrix amplifier is the -90 port of Hybrid2 for and the IN port of Hybrid1. The user can use the same logic to examine and verify that signals on the ISO port of Hybrid1 will appear at the 0 port of Hybrid2.

 

OBSERVATIONS

1. Output spectrums are available for each output. The user can easily verify by looking at the spectrum analyzer plot that these outputs have the correct carrier and all other carriers have been cancelled.

 

2. Level diagrams have also been added for each input. Notice that the loss through the hybrid couplers is equal to the 3 dB splitting loss plus the insertion loss. However, because the output coupler is combining the power the effects of the input splitting loss and the combining gain cancel out.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the isolation of the hybrid couplers and observe the levels of the cancelled carriers. Notice that a large change in isolation doesn't affect the cancelled carriers levels much. However, as the isolation is lowered spectrums will propagate for a longer period of time and the simulation will take longer to run.

 

2. Set the gain of one of the amplifiers and examine the power at each output. Notice every carrier is still present even though the power for each carrier is lower.

 

3. Change the 'Phase Balance' of Hybrid1 to 5 degrees and notice the A (1800 MHz) and B (1810 MHz) carriers are not cancelled as much as the other carriers.

 

4. If we want to improve the performance of the carrier cancellation the user must understand the origin of the spectrum at those carrier frequencies. Since the carriers are evenly spaced intermods will also appear at those carrier frequencies. To determine the origin of this spectrum enable the 'Signal', 'Intermods and Harmonics', and 'Show Individual Components ...' and place a marker at 1800, 1810, 1820, or 1830 MHz and notice that both carrier intermods and other components are present.

Feed Forward Amplifier Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is an example of a dual loop feed forward amplifier.

 

BACKGROUND

The power that can be achieved from a power amplifier will be largely determined by the non-linearities in the high power amplifiers stages. A dual loop feed forward amplifier can be used to reduce the level of of the intermods at the power amplifier output. The first loop of the feed forward amplifier will combine the non-linear output spectrum from the main amplifier with a phase and amplitude shifted input spectrum. These two spectrums will be combined coherently and the input carriers will be cancelled if the carriers are 180 degrees out of phase and the same amplitude. We then end up with only intermods in the spectrum. The second loop will amplify and phase shift the intermod only (error) spectrum and will be added back into the main amplifier path to cancel out the intermods from the output of the power amplifier if these two intermod spectrums are 180 degrees out of the phase and the same amplifier. In order to achieve cancellation the two spectrum need to be 180 degrees out of phase. Since amplifiers and other circuits have delay a delay line needs to be added to shortest delay path so that the spectrums can arrive at the same time. Phase shifters and gain adjustments are typically added so that the power amplifiers can be adjusted during manufacturing.

 

SETUP

RFAmp1 is the main amplifier. Input signals from the source port will be amplified by this amplifier and intermods will also be created. A sample of this distorted spectrum will be taken at Coupler2 this will be passed to the Splitter where it will be combined with the delayed input spectrum. A sample of the undistorted input spectrum is taken from Coupler1 and then delayed by about 190 degree by the delay line TL1. This delay line must be added because there will be delay through RFAmp1. Enough delay is added to place our phase adjustment Phase1 for this first loop at a good center point in its adjustment range. Out the ouput of Splitter the input carriers will be calcelled if they have the same amplitude and are 180 degrees out of phase. AttnVar1 is used to adjust the amplitude balance of the carriers. The user can examine the 'Error Amp Spec' graph to see the amplitude error and the 'Error Phase' graph to see the phase error of the carriers at the splitter output. The intermod only spectrum at the splitter output will be amplified by RFAmp2 (error amplifier) and will be combined back into the main path through Coupler3. A delay line TL2 is about 370 degrees long so that the phase shifter Phase2 of the second loop will be set at a good nominal center point. The intermods at the output (port 2) must be the same amplitude and 180 degrees out of phase. AttnVar2 is used to adjust the amplitude of the intermods.

 

OBSERVATIONS

1. The user can examine the output spectrum on the 'Out Spec' graph. With the 'Analyzer Mode' enabled the user is able to see the output of the power amplifier. Furtermore, having composite spectrum show the individual spectral components we can quickly see the cancellation level between the indivdual pieces of the intermods and the actual output.

 

2. SPECTRASYS know the direction of travel of all spectral components at every node in the system. The total power is represented by a trace for every travel direction at a node. By examining the 'Input Spectrum' the user can see the two input signals traveling from the input port into the power amplifier. Furthermore, the user can also see intermods and other spectrum traveling from inside the power amplifer to the output.

 

3. With spectrum identification it is very easy to identify the orgin and path the spectrum takes to arrive at the examination point. By placing a marker on the intermod at 1958 MHz on the 'Output Spec' plot the user can identify all of the pieces of spectrum that make up that intermod and the path that it took to get to the input node. We see that the largest offender is -54.1 dBm and its frequency is 1958 MHz which is the result of the frequency of source 1 minus the 2nd harmonic of source 2 [-Source#1+2xSource2]. This intermod was created at node 6, the output of RFAmp1. It then propagated to nodes Coupler2,Splitter,Phase2,VarAttn2,RFAmp2,Coupler3,C1. We can see that the week link in the chain is the reverse isolation of RFAmp2.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune Phase1 and examine the phase of the carriers traveling through both paths on the 'Error Phase' graph. 

 

2. Tune Phase2 and examine the phase of the intermods traveling through both paths on the 'Out Phase' graph.

 

3. Tune AttnVar1 and AttnVar2 and watch the respective amplitude balance for the carriers and intermods with the 'Error Spec' and 'Out Spec' graphs.

 

4. Tune the reverse isolation of RFAmp2 and observe the intermod spectrum on the input ('Input Spectrum' graph) and notice that the improvement will change linearly with this isolation until the next dominant component is reached.

Harmonic Suppressed Amplifier Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: System1 must be calculated before the data can be displayed)

 

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates a parallel amplifier configuration that cancels both 2nd and 3rd order intermod and harmonic products.  The complete amplifier consists of 4 individual amplifiers paralleled in such a way to suppress both 2nd and 3rd order products.  Two identical amplifier banks are paralleled and fed 90 degrees apart giving cancellation of 3rd order products.  Each amplifier bank consists of 2 amplifiers that are fed 180 degrees apart giving cancellation of 2nd order products.


 

SETUP

Two input signals have been created and applied to the input of the amplifier using the multicarrier signal source.  Noise calculations have been disabled as well as the identification of individual spectrums.  The spectrum analyzer mode has been enabled. Graphs have been created showing the input and output spectrum of the amplifier. Several variables have been created for the splitters.  The user can make these variables tunable and examine the performance impact based on parameter variation.


 

ANALYSIS

Examining the output spectrum (Out Spec) graph we see that the 2nd order intermod and harmonic products are non-existent.  The 3rd order products are about -150 dBc. The third order products are a function of the splitter isolation as well as the 3rd order intercept point of the amplifiers.


 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the isolation and notice the impact on the 3rd order products.

2. Make some of the splitter gain and phase parameters tunable (place a '?' infront of the variable name in the equation block) and observe the overall amplifier performance as these values are changed.

Workspace.Name: Hybrid Linear Nonlinear Amp
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Amplifiers\Hybrid Linear Nonlinear Amp.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Hybrid Linear Nonlinear Amp Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of the hybrid S parameter nonlinear amplifier model. The S parameters are used to determine the forward gain, noise figure, impedance matching, and reverse isolation. The nonlinear parameters are used to create intermods and harmonics. 

 

BACKGROUND

This model can be thought of a device that translates the nonlinear output parameters to input parameters then generates all the intermods and harmonics before being applied to the S parameter block. The S parameters are used to determine the forward gain, noise figure, impedance matching, and reverse isolation.

Key Assumptions

 

In real world nonlinear circuits a transfer function exists between the circuit input and the location where the nonlinearities are created.  Furthermore, there will be another transfer function located between the nonlinearity creation point and the circuit output.  Given only linear parameters (i.e. S-parameter data file) there is no way of knowing where the nonlinear creation point is located.  Consequently, the assumption is made that all nonlinearities will be created first before being applied to the linear parameters.

 

Compression and saturation is another problem that has to be dealt with for linear parameters.  By definition linear parameters contain no information about compression and saturation.  Since harmonics and intermods are generated behaviorally they can follow a smooth Power In vs. Power Out transfer curve.  1 dB compression and saturation will appear as a smooth function with varying input power level.  However, since the linear parameters are constant and do not model these nonlinear effects then a hard saturation algorithm was used to limit the maximum output power of the hybrid model.

 

Consequently, the following assumptions were made:

  • All nonlineartities will be created at the device input before being applied to the linear parameters.
  • The nominal gain will be used to refer all output nonlinear parameters to the input.
  • Compression, saturation, and intermod levels will be based on the behavioral parameters before being applied to the linear parameters.
  • Harmonics and intermods will follow a smooth Power In vs. Power Out curve since they do not use the linear parameters.
  • All other signals excluding intermods and harmonics created by this device will have their maximum output power limited to the saturation power.  Compression cannot be accurately modeled for this group of signals.  However, a warning will be given when the device is in compression.


SETUP

This example contains a two tone source followed by a single amplifier. S Parameters have been selected. The nominal gain used to translate output nonlinear parameters to input parameters is 20 dB.

 

ANALYSIS

Input Spec - Shows the amplifier input spectrum.

 

Output Spec - Shows the amplfier output spectrum.

 

Amp S Parameters - Shows the S parameters of the block diagram using linear analysis. Notice the correlation with the 'Output Spec' graph.
