Quad Hybrid Matrix Amplifier Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: System1 must be calculated before the data can be displayed)

 

ABSTRACT

The hybrid matrix amplifer is a popular power amplifier configuration that encorporates redundancy. With the traditional design of using a single power amplifier for every transmitter the power amplifier becomes a single point of failure. If the amplifier dies then so does the carrier and all of the transmitted information. The hybrid matrix amplier will still provide output power (albeit a lower output power ... due to the loss of the amplifier) for all input signals. Furthermore, the reliability of power amplifiers is typically lower than the transmitter so the likelyhood of lossing a carrier can be very high.

 

BACKGROUND

90 Degree hybrid couplers are used at the input to split each input signal (IN and ISO) by 90 degrees (ISO to 0 is a 90 degree shift and ISO to -90 it a 0 degree shift). These hybrid couplers are also used on the output to combine the amplified signals back together. Because of the phasing carriers will either add or cancel at the output leaving a dedicated output for each carrier. To illustrate this point let's look at a simple dual hybrid matrix amplifer (Hybrid2, RFAmp1, RFAmp2, and Hybrid3). Signals at the IN port of Hybrid1 we will have a 90 degree phase shift into RFAmp2 and a 0 degree phase shift into RFAmp1. The output of RFAmp2 will have a 0 degree phase shift at the -90 output port of the Hybrid3. This same signal that has a 0 degree output through RFAmp1 will go through a 90 degree shift through Hybrid3 and will add constructively at the -90 output port to produce the desired, amplified output. However, RFAmp1 will produce a total 0 degree phase shift at 0 port of Hybrid2 and RFAmp2 will produce a total 180 degree phase shift at this same port and the signal will cancel. Consequently, the output port for the dual hybrid matrix amplifier is the -90 port of Hybrid3 for and the IN port of Hybrid2. The user can use the same logic to examine and verify that signals on the ISO port of Hybrid1 will appear at the 0 port of Hybrid3.

 

OBSERVATIONS

1. Output spectrums are available for each output. The user can easily verify by looking at the spectrum analyzer plot that these outputs have the correct carrier and all other carriers have been cancelled.

 

2. Level diagrams have also been added for each input. Notice that the loss through the hybrid couplers is equal to the 3 dB splitting loss plus the insertion loss. However, because the output coupler is combining the power the effects of the input splitting loss and the combining gain cancel out.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the isolation of the hybrid couplers and observe the levels of the cancelled carriers. Notice that a large change in isolation doesn't affect the cancelled carriers levels much. However, as the isolation is lowered spectrums will propagate for a longer period of time and the simulation will take longer to run.

 

2. Set the gain of one of the amplifiers and examine the power at each output. Notice every carrier is still present even though the power for each carrier is lower.

 

3. Change the 'Phase Balance' of Hybrid1 to 5 degrees and notice the A (1800 MHz) and B (1810 MHz) carriers are not cancelled as much as the other carriers.

 

4. If we want to improve the performance of the carrier cancellation the user must understand the origin of the spectrum at those carrier frequencies. Since the carriers are evenly spaced intermods will also appear at those carrier frequencies. To determine the origin of this spectrum enable the 'Signal', 'Intermods and Harmonics', and 'Show Individual Components ...' and place a marker at 1800, 1810, 1820, or 1830 MHz and notice that both carrier intermods and other components are present.

Workspace.Name: ADC Noise
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Analog Digital\ADC Noise.wsv
Workspace.Description:
ADC Noise Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of the noise in an ADC and the aliasing of the ADC input noise into the first Nyquist zone.

 

BACKGROUND

Noise at the output of an ADC comes from two places:

1. Noise at the input

2. Noise generated by the ADC (ADC Noise Figure)

 

Noise at the Input - Noise across the entire bandwidth will be aliased into the 1st Nyquist zone. Therefore, input filtering to the ADC is very important to reduce the effects of this noise on the system performance.

 

Noise generated by the ADC - The user has the ability to set the signal to noise (SNR) ratio of the ADC. The full-scale value, sampling frequency and SNR are used to determine the noise figure of the ADC. This noise figure is independent of the noise at the ADC input.

 

The noise figure of the ADC is calculated as follows:

 

NF (dB) = Full Scale Pin (dBm) - SNR (dB) - 10 Log (Sampling Frequency (Hz) / 2) - Thermal Noise Power (dBm/Hz)

where:
   Pin (dBm)  = 10 Log ( Vin_rms^2 / Zin ) + 30
   Full Scale Pin (dBm)  = 10 Log ( Vrange^2 / ( 8 * Zin ) ) + 30
   Thermal Noise Power (dBm/Hz) = 10 Log ( kT ) + 30 = -173.975 dBm at 290 K (16.85 C)
   k is Boltzmann's constant (1.3806503e-23 J/K)
   T is temperature in Kelvin

Rewriting the noise figure equation in terms of ADC parameters:
NF (dB) = 10 Log( Vrange^2 / ( 8 * Zin ) )  + 30 - SNR (dB) - 10 Log ( FS / 2 ) - ( 10 Log( kT ) + 30 )
    or
NF (dB) = 10 Log( Vrange^2 / ( 8 * Zin ) )  + 30 - SNR (dB) - 10 Log ( FS / 2 ) + 173.975 dBm at 290 K


SETUP

This is a simple system of a IF amplifier followed by an IF bandpass filter and an ADC. A low-level input signal of -80 dBm at 224 MHz is put into the IF amplifier with 25 dB of gain and then filtered by a 100 to 300 MHz IF bandpass filter before entering the ADC.

 

The equation block contains the noise figure calculation equations. The SNR of the ADC can be tuned.

 

Showing individual noise spectrums have been enabled on the Composite Spectrum tab of the system analysis.

 

ANALYSIS

ADC Input Spec - This graph shows the individual noise generate in the Source, IFAmp, and IF_BPF. Also, the noise generated by the ADC that is traveling backwards through the system is also shown.

 

ADC Output Spec - This graph shows the individual noise appearing at the ADC input that has been aliased into the 1st Nyquist zone. All these noise pieces add along with the ADC self-noise (noise figure) to give the total noise at the ADC output. Notice that the with a SNR of 50 dB that the ADC Self noise is dominant, and the input noise has little effect on the total noise at the ADC output.

 

EXERCISES

1. Set the ADC SNR to 75 dB and rerun the simulation. What sources of noise are now dominant at the ADC output? Are they dominant across the entire 1st Nyquist zone?

Workspace.Name: ADC Spurious Output
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Analog Digital\ADC Spurious Output.wsv
Workspace.Description:
ADC Spurious Output Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This examples illustrates the ADC spurious output depending on spurious mode (dBc or dBFS). 

 

BACKGROUND

The ADC supports two modes of spurious output: dBc or dBFS. dBc means that all spurious responses created in the ADC will be relative to the peak input signal whereas dBFS means that these same spurious responses will be below the full scale of the ADC. Therefore in the dBc case spurious output levels will be dependent on the input power of the peak input signal. On the other hand dBFS will maintain the absolute spurious output levels regardless of the input power level since the full scale value of the ADC is fixed.

 

SETUP

The setup consists of a nonlinear block followed by an ADC for both dBc and dBFS configurations. Both designs are identical expect for the SFDR mode setting which in one case is dBc and the other dBFS. ADC input and output spectrum has been plotted.

 

NOTE: Spurious responses appearing at the input of the ADC that are aliased into the first nyquist zone will have the same value at the ADC output as the input (assuming no frequency rolloff due to input capacitance and resistance of the ADC). This is the case of the 2nd harmonic created by the nonlinear block that is aliased into the first nyquist zone and appears at 1.2 GHz.

 

ANALYSIS

dBc Spec Out - Shows the ADC output spectrum for the dBc design.

 

dBFS Spec Out - Shows the ADC output spectrum for the dBFS design.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the input capacitance on the ADC from 0 pF to the default value of 5 pF and note the change in the output response. Why did the spectrum response change?

2. Change the input power and note the spurious output responses in both cases. Did the spectrum change as expected?

 


 

 

 

ANSWERS TO EXERCISES

1. The input frequency to the ADC is extremely high, 15 GHz. The input capacitance of 5 pF is enough to create a low pass filter response where the 15 GHz signal is significantly attenuated.

2. The dBc response changed will the input power to preserve a 70 dB Signal to Interference ration. Whereas the dBFS spectrum remained constant.

Workspace.Name: Simple System w ADC
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Analog Digital\Simple System w ADC.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Simple System w ADC Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple system followed by an impedance matched analog-to-digital converter (ADC).

 

BACKGROUND

In general, a receiver is defined from the antenna port to the analog-to-digital converter (ADC). Selecting the right ADC and determining the appropriate receiver architecture plays an important role in the performance of the receiver. The ADC model in Spectrasys is unique since its output is analog and not digital. The converter can be thought of as an non-ideal ADC followed by an ideal digital-to-analog converter.


SETUP

A simple system has been created consisting of an IF amplifier followed by a filter. After the filter a transformer is used to transform the 50 ohm output impedance of the IF amplifier to the ADC input impedance of 200 ohms. The power level of the 70 MHz CW source is set to provide a full scale value of 1 Vpeak at the ADC output. A 12 bit ADC is used at a sampling rate of 65 MHz. Since the input signal of 70 MHz appears in the 3rd Nyquist zone no spectrum inversion takes place. The System Analysis has the channel bandwidth set to 30 kHz to represent post ADC filtering.

 

ANALYSIS

ADC Vin Peak - This graph shows the ADC peak input spectrum including the 70 MHz input signal as well as the broadband noise.

 

ADC Vout Peak - This graph shows the peak output spectrum of the ADC. The 70 MHz input signal has been aliased down to 5 MHz in the first Nyquist zone. Second and third harmonics generated by the ADC are also shown. The IF filter currently removes broadband noise in other Nyquist zones and the 2nd and 3rd harmonics generated by the IF amplifier.

 

ADC Pout - This graph shows the power output spectrum of the ADC. This plot can be used to see that harmonics created by the ADC are at the specified SNR value of 68 dBFS.

 

Table Data - This table shows some common receiver measurements.

 

EXERCISES

1. Disable the IF Filter by going to the 'Simulation' tab of the filter part properties and select 'Disable Part for All Simulations' and rerun the simulation. Notice that harmonics of the IF Amp appear at the ADC output, along with ADC generated harmonics, and also the rise in cascaded noise figure due to noise in other Nyquist zones now being aliased into the baseband.

2. Tune the input power up and down and observe performance changes. Note: An overdrive message will appear if peak input signals exceed the full scale value.

Workspace.Name: AppCAD 1.9 GHz CDMA Handset Receiver
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\AppCAD\AppCAD 1.9 GHz CDMA Handset Receiver.wsv
Workspace.Description:
AppCAD 1.9 GHz Handset Receiver Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how a dumbed down Spectrasys simulation will give the same answers as the AppCAD NoiseCalc example '1.9 GHz Handset Receiver'. Furthermore, a more realistic design is created showing the value of Spectrasys above spreadsheets.

 

BACKGROUND

AppCAD is great free engineering design tool that has been around for several years. One of its tools is called 'NoiseCalc' used to calculate simple noise and intermod performance of two port cascaded line ups. Many RF design engineers use spreadsheets containing the same underlying calculations. The 'NoiseCalc' tool is only used here to illustrate weaknesses associated with cascaded equations.

 

Cascaded equations have serious limitations and if not understood can lead to crippled RF architectures with poor performance.

 

The traditional cascade noise equation is as follows:

 

Fcascade = F1 + (F2 - 1) / G1 + (F3 - 1)/(G1*G2) + ... + (Fn - 1)/(G1* G2...Gn-1)

 

where Fn is the noise factor and Gn is the linear gain of stage n

 

Note: This equation contains no information about:

  • frequency
  • impedances or VSWR
  • bandwidth
  • image frequencies
  • or multiple paths

The traditional cascade third order intercept equation is as follows:

 

1 / OTOI = 1 / ((G2*G3*G4...Gn-1)(OTOI1) + 1 / ((G3*G4...Gn-1)(OTOI2) + ... + 1 / OTOIn

 

where OTOIn is the output third order intercept and Gn is the linear gain of stage n

 

Note: This equation contains no information about:

  • filtering or frequency response of interfering tones
  • cannot determine out-of-band intercept point
  • impedances or VSWR
  • interferers are equal amplitude
  • reverse traveling intermods were reverse isolation is not infinite
  • multiple paths
  • or don't help identify weak links in cascaded chains

The Spectral Propagation and Root Cause Analysis (SPARCA) engine in Spectrasys eliminated these restrictive assumptions associated with simple cascade analysis tools including spreadsheets.

 

AppCAD can be download free of charge at http://www.hp.woodshot.com/

 

This example illustrates how traditional cascaded equations can lead to simple design mistakes.


SETUP

This workspace contains two designs that reflect the startup example of 'NoiseCalc' in AppCAD (version 3.0.2). The example is the '1.9 GHz CDMA Handset Receiver'. The first design is called 'Dumbed Down Design' using only attenuators and amplifiers to accurately represent traditional cascaded equation assumptions. The second design called 'Realistic Design' shows a more realistic cascade analysis removing the underlying restrictions.

 

Dumbed Down Sch - The only way to compare Spectrasys to a spreadsheet is to reduce all passive stages to attenuators and any active stages to amplifiers. This must be so to present constant impedances across all simulation frequencies. Furthermore, amplifier reverse isolation must be set to infinity. The input signal drive level must also be low enough to keep all amplifiers way out of compression. This is generally 20 dB or more below the regular compression point.

 

Realistic Sch - This schematic uses standard behavioral models in Spectrasys . The duplexer is represented by a real 3 port duplexer. Liberties have been taken to define filter orders, corner frequencies, and insertion loss for all filters used in the design. An amplifier representing the transmit chain has been added to drive the transmit side of the duplexer. By default this device is shorted out so transmit noise is not added to the receive chain. The 2nd LNA uses S parameters for the linear parts of the simulation and the intermod parameters for the non-linear aspects like intermods. Three sets of S parameters are included representing bias currents of 10, 20, and 40 mA. An active mixer is used with an LO to give a 71 MHz IF. The LO includes phase noise. Realistic compression and saturation points have been added to all active devices. These parameters have been gleaned from datasheets where datasheets are available. A source has been selected to produce 2 out-of-band interfering signals at 2000 and 2100 MHz that create an in-channel intermod at 1900 MHz which is the same frequency as our desired signal. Spectrasys has the ability to separate the desired signal from the intermod signal even though they exist at the same frequency and the desired signal may be below the intermod power level.

 

ANALYSIS

AppCAD Notes - There are a few things to remember when looking at this example in AppCAD.

  1. The 'Noise Source (Ref)' parameter is fixed at 290 K which is 17 C. The is not the same at the 'Ref Temperature' of 25 C. Noise calculations in AppCAD are referenced to the 17 C or 290 K not the 'Analysis Temperature' or the 'Ref Temperature'. Consequently, SPECTRASYS must be set at 17 C not 25 C.
  2. The output power of stage 7 is +32.5 dBm which is almost 2 Watts. However, the output IP3 of this same stage is only +12 dBm. In a real system this device would surely be in saturation. Because of this large output power the input drive level in SPECTRASYS has been lowered from the AppCAD input level of -50 dBm to -100 dBm to keep all stages operating in the linear region.

AppCAD RX Data - This table contains the simulation results of the 'Dumbed Down Sch' schematic which is a direct correlation to AppCAD results other than some absolute powers levels because the input drive level difference of -100 dBm versus AppCAD's -50 dBm as described above. The table measurements are:

  • DCP ( Desired Channel Power ) - Same as AppCAD's 'Output Power' output
  • GAIN ( Device Gain ) - Same as AppCAD's 'Gain (Temp corr)' output
  • CGAIN ( Cascaded Gain ) - Bottom column entry same as AppCAD's 'Gain' output
  • CNR ( Carrier to Noise Ratio ) - Bottom column entry + 50 dB (to account for -100 dBm to -50 input drive difference) same as AppCAD's 'SNR' output
  • CNF ( Cascaded Noise Figure ) - Bottom column entry same as AppCAD's 'Noise Figure' output
  • MDS ( Minimum Detectable Signal ) - Bottom column entry same as AppCAD's 'MDS' output
  • SFDR ( Spurious Free Dynamic Range ) - Bottom column entry same as AppCAD's 'SFDR' output
  • OIP3 ( Output Third Order Intercept Point ) - Bottom column entry same as AppCAD's 'Output IP3' output
  • IIP3 ( Input Third Order Intercept Point ) - Bottom column entry same as AppCAD's 'Input IP3' output
  • DCR ( Desired Channel Resistance ) - This is the average resistance the carrier sees in the channel

AppCAD Equation Data - This table contains the equation based measurements that strictly use the gain, noise, and other non-linear parameters entered by the user. These measurements are identical to those used in spreadsheets. They have all the issues as outlined above. The table measurements are:

  • CF ( Channel Frequency ) - Frequency along the path
  • SGAIN ( Device Gain ) - User entered stage gain
  • SNF ( Stage Noise Figure ) - User entered noise figure
  • ECGAIN ( Equation Based Cascaded Gain ) - Derived from cascaded SGAIN
  • ECNF ( Equation Based Cascaded Noise Figure ) - Derived from SGAIN and SNF
  • EMDS ( Equation Based Minimum Detectable Signal ) - Derived from ECNF and thermal input noise power
  • ESFDR ( Equation Based Spurious Free Dynamic Range ) - Derived from EMDS and equation based IIP3
  • EOIP3 ( Equation Based Output Third Order Intercept Point ) - Derived from SGAIN and user entered stage OIP3
  • EIIP3 ( Equation Based Input Third Order Intercept Point ) - Derived from SGAIN and user entered stage OIP3

Realistic RX Data - The realistic data is obviously different than from the 'AppCAD RX Data'. Because of impedance and VSWR effects the DCP, GAIN, CGAIN, CNR, CNF, MDS, and RX_SFDR numbers are different. The intercept measurements are drastically different since the interfering tones of 2000 and 2100 MHz are attenuated by the IF filter. This is called an out-of-band intercept measurement which cascaded intermod equations are unable deal with. The following additional measurement is:

  • CNP ( Channel Noise Power ) - This is the noise output power level in the channel
  • SFDR, OIP3, and IIP3 are changed to RX_SFDR, RX_OIP3, and RX_IIP3 to gather the correct out-of-band intercept point information. Either of these measurement will give the same answers in the in-band intercept cases like 'AppCAD RX Data'

Notice that the DCR is not 50 ohms through out the system as in the dumbed down case. With this measurement it is easy to identify VSWR issues.

 

IF Out Spec - Shows the broadband IF output spectrum along with the IF noise pedestal.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the S parameters on the 'MGA-72543' part and notice the performance changes.

2. Increase the 1900 MHz input power level in the 'Realistic Sch' from -100 dBm to -50 dBm and notice that the last stage is seriously in saturation.

3. Enable the amplifier representing the TX Chain and notice the change in cascaded noise figure.

Workspace.Name: Reference Clock
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Coherency\Reference Clock.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Reference Clock Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how the source reference clock works in Spectrasys. 

 

BACKGROUND

By defnition there are 4 basic rules used by Spectrasys to determine coherency. They are:

 

1. Each source is only coherent with itself OR if the sources have the same reference clock.

 

2. Signals must be of the same type (i.e. signals, intermods, harmonics, noise, etc.)

 

3. Signals must have the same center frequency and bandwidth.

 

4. Must have the same LO source (mixers only).

 

Please refer to the Coherency section of the help file for an explanation of these rules.

 

Non-linear devices must work with coherent signals at their inputs to properly determine the operating point. Before a non-linear device can propagate its input spectrum all of the input signals must be combined into their respective coherency groups before being propagated to the output. If this wasn't the case two signal equal in amplitude and out of phase would drive a amplifier to a different operating point that the combined signal.

 

The reference clock used in Spectrasys is a name. All sources that have the same name will have the same phase reference plane. An empty 'Reference Clock' name means that there is no reference clock. This reference clock affects coherency rule number 1 as cited above.


SETUP

Two schematics have been created that are identical except one uses do different reference clocks and the other has the same reference clock for both sources. Each schematic is a simple system with a two carrier signal generator followed by an amplifier. To emphasize the reference clock aspect two CW signals have been created with the same power level and frequency. They both have the same phase. They have each been given a unique source name. Two system analysis have also been created, one for each schematic.

 

ANALYSIS

Two graphs have been created both at the amplifiers outputs. Each graph has a specific balloon callout to emphasize the aspects of the particular graph. Please refer to the specific graph depending on how the reference clocks have been set on the source.

 

Out Spec w Diff Clocks - When both sources have different reference clock names ( A and B ) this graph shows the two individual signals at the output along with the non-coherently combined signals. Notice that each signal source has a different coherency ID ( the value in braces {} ). Since each of these signals has a different name and reference clock by definition they are not coherent even though they have the same frequency. The combined total output power is 3 dB higher than each individual signal.

 

Output w Same Clocks - When both sources have the same reference clock names this graph will show how only 1 coherent signal appears at the output of the amplifier.  Both sources have the same reference clock and thus the same coherency as the input. These signals are combined at the input coherently then propagated through the amplifier. Note that output power is 3 dB higher than the non-coherent case.
Workspace.Models: *OUT@RF Design:MultiSource@RF Design:RFAMP@RF Design

Workspace.Name: Amp S Z Param Analysis
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Equations\Amp S Z Param Analysis.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Amp S Z Param Analysis Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a illustration that demonstrates how linear analysis, Spectrasys, and S and Z parameters equations are used to verify simulation results between these cases. 

 

BACKGROUND

Internally in the simulator an S parameter model is created from each behavioral model. The linear simulator is heavily used in Spectrasys to determine voltages, impedances and currents at each given frequency of the simulation. Remember, that S parameters are determined for each individual stage when the ports are terminated in the reference impedance of the system. What this really means is that if S11 is not 0, or not matched to the reference impedance, which most devices are rarely ideally matched, then the value of S21 means that this is the gain for the given S11 and S22 values.

 

Cascading S parameter matrices will not work to determine cascaded simulation results. It is more complicated than that. In the linear simlulator Jacobian matrices are created for each model and linear algebra techiniques are used to solve the voltages, currents and impedances in the circuit. However, S parameters can be converted to ABCD parameters which when multiplied represent the cascaded circuit. These ABCD parameters can then be converted back to S parameters to determine the cascaded linear analysis.


SETUP

The equation block shows the formulation of the S parameters for the two amplifier models in this example. Equation variables for some of the amplifier parameters have been created which are used in the models as well as the equation block. Parameters have also been created and used for the sources and ports. There are 3 designs in this workspace.

1) RFAmp1

2) RFAmp2

3) RFAmp1 followed by RFAmp2

 

A Linear and System Analysis has been created for each design. Only a single simulation frequency of 100 MHz is used with the same signal generator power for each design.

 

The equation block will calculate the output voltage and power for each of the designs by converting S parameters to Z parameters then calculating the Thevinin equivalent voltage and impedance for that circuit. This Thevinin equivalent circuit is then used with the load impedance to create a voltage divider circuit where the output voltage and power can be calculated. In the case of the cascaded design the S parameters of each amplifier must first be converted to ABCD parameters where they can be multiplied then converted back to the resultant S and Z parameters for the combined circuit. The Thevinin equivalent is once again created to determine the output voltage and power.

 

The resultant Zin and Zout impedances are also calculated as Zin of RFAmp2 will affect the input impedance seen by RFAmp1.

 

ANALYSIS

Pout1 Spec - Simulated output power for RFAmp1. Compare with equation Pout_1_dBm variable.

 

Pout2 Spec - Simulated output power for RFAmp2. Compare with equation Pout_2_dBm variable.

calculations verifying the simulation results.

Envelope Source Extraction Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to take an average spectrum envelope, reduce or smooth the number of points needed to represent the spectrum, then write this envelope to storage as a text file. This text file that represents an envelope source that can be imported into the MultiSource and simulated in the RF system simulator.

 

BACKGROUND

Spectrum envelopes can be simulated inside of the RF system simulator called Spectrasys. Often users would like to extract a digitally simulated spectrum and import this into the RF domain. The process of doing this is as follows:

 

  1. Import an average spectrum envelope.
  2. Reduce the number of data points that represent the spectrum envelope.
  3. Write the frequency, power, and phase vectors to a text file that can be imported into the source.
  4. Import the envelope source data stored in the text file into the RF source (MultiSource).
  5. Run the RF simulation


SETUP

Data from a simple QAM 16 modulator and demodulator is given in the Digital Sim Data dataset.

 

Several equation blocks have been created and are located in the Extraction folder. The equation blocks are as follows:

 

  • 2D Curve Smoothing - This script will extract envelope data points for user specified frequency and power steps. The smoothed or extracted results are shown in the graph called Smoothed Out Spec.
  • File Write Script - This script will write the PowerAve variable to a text file specified in the script. The default location is: C:\Temp\Source.txt. This can be changed by the user.

ANALYSIS

Envelope Source Text- This is a copy of the data in the text file that is written to C:\Temp\Source.txt.

 

Orig and Ave Out Spec - This graph shows the current QAM16 spectrum from the original digital analysis along with the averaged power spectrum.

 

 Smoothed Out Spec - This graph shows the averaged power spectrum along with that extracted from the 2D Curve Smoothing script.

 

RF Spec Out - This graph shows the results of an RF simulation using the imported envelope source.

 

EXERCISES

1. Delete the QAM16 dataset in the workspace tree and re-import the Source.txt file. The data is Double Sided and the Center Frequency of the envelope is 5 kHz. The envelope bandwidth is about 2 Hz.

2. Change the power and frequency resolution of the smoothing script and then write the envelope to a text file and re-import into the MultiSource. What is the effect on the envelope?

3. The Envelope Type to single sided and re-run the RF simulation. What happened to the simulated output spectrum?

 

 

ANSWERS TO EXERCISES

2. The resolution of the envelope should have changed.

3. The RF output spectrum will look like 2 QAM spectrum butted together.

Workspace.Name: Node Data to Text File
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Equations\Node Data to Text File.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Node Data to Text File Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example shows how the spectrum frequency, power level, and spectrum identification node data simulated by Spectrasys can be saved to a text file and imported into a spreadsheet.

 

BACKGROUND

In the System Analysis dataset each spectrum variable like 'P3' has two independent variables: 1) Frequency and 2) and identification mapping number (the values in the column 'ID3').

 

The variable name 'IDName' contains the actual text identification information and has an independent variable called 'IDNo' that contains the identification mapping number.

 

Since each spectrum has spectral density then it must be represented with at least two data points (except for spectrum at DC which will be represented by one data point).

 

To find the correct identification string follow this process:

 

1) Locate the frequency in the spectrum of interest (i.e. 'P3', frequency 500 MHz at Index = 341)

2) Find the identification mapping number (i.e. 'ID3' at Index = 341 is 430)

3) Find 430 in the 'IDNo' column of the 'IDName' variable ( i.e. {6}D[Source-Osc],Source,RFFilter,LNA,Iso,Mixer,IFFilter,IFAmp)

 

SETUP

This example contains a simple receiver.

 

To save the spectrum node data to a text file do the following:

 

1. Open the 'Node_Data_Extraction_Script' equation block

2. Enter the User Data (i.e. Node Name, Name of System Analysis and Dataset, File Name and Path)

3. Run the equation block (Gtrl+G OR right click menu "Run Equations" option OR Run Equations toolbar button).

4. Find the text file and drag and drop or import it into the spreadsheet

Workspace.Name: Spectrum Mask
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Equations\Spectrum Mask.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Spectrum Mask Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to create limit lines from an array of numbers used for a spectrum mask. Furthermore, cascaded gain measurements are used to scale the mask appropriately to other nodes along the path. Mask scaling due to channel bandwidth changes is also shown.

 

BACKGROUND

The equation capability of this product is very powerful. Arrays of values can be plotted on graphs just like a spectrum trace.


SETUP

The 'Equation Input' block contains all input variables use in this example. Variables for channel frequency, power level, and bandwidth have been created.

 

For channel bandwidths less than 200 kHz the mask is shifted down in power level by the ratio of 200 kHz to the current channel bandwidth. In the 'Equations Output' block a mask is created from a center frequency and a list of frequency offset values. When combined together an array of absolute frequency values for the mask results. This becomes the independent variable for the amplitude that is created in a similar manner. Units are then set on both the frequency and amplitude variables (FreqMask and GSMMask). The independent variable of the amplitude variable, GSMMask is set to create the mask variable.

 

The output mask is really just a scaled version of the input mask so the cascaded gain at output node is used to create a new variable.

 

ANALYSIS

Mask Graph - Shows the GSM mask by itself. (NOTE: This is very helpful during the development process to plot a single variable in its own graph so you can look at the auto scaled axis values to determine if the units, signs, and magnitudes of the variable is correct.)

 

Input Spec - Shows the GSM spectrum driving the cascade and the GSM mask scaled to the power level at that point.

 

Output Spec - Shows the output spectrum of the circuit along with the GSM mask that has be scaled to account for the cascaded gain of the channel was well as the channel measurement bandwidth (NOTE: Bandwidth scaling only occurs when the channel measurement bandwidth is less than the GSM modulation bandwidth of 200 kHz)

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the 'GSMFreq' and notice how the mask at both the input and output change with the source frequency.

 

2. Tune the 'GSMPwr_dBm' and notice how the mask changes with power level.

 

3. Tune the 'ChanBW' and note how the mask will scale appropriately for all bandwidths both greater and less than 200 kHz.

Workspace.Name: Two Tone Correlation
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Equations\Two Tone Correlation.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Two Tone Correlation Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates how two tone intermod amplitudes are correlated between the RF and theory.

 

SETUP

A 20 dB gain amplifier is examined in an RF analysis. Input parameters have been defined in the 'InEquations' equation block. Two tones have been defined and created at 95 and 105 MHz. 3rd order intermods will appear at 85 and 115 MHz. A purely mathmatical approach has also been created in the 'Equation Design' folder.

 

For the equation based calculations the compressin curve polynomial coefficients has been extracted ONLY for the following condtions: Gain = 20 dB, OP1dB = +20 dBm, OPSAT = +23 dBm, OIP3 = +40 dBm, and OIP2 = +50 dBm.

 

The 'MaxOrder' parameter is used by the equation method and Spectasys. This determines the order of the polynomial that represents the compression curve.

 

ANALYSIS

RF Amp Spec - This graph shows a close up of the RF amplifier output spectrum near the two carriers.

 

Equ Out Spec - This graph shows the output of the theoretical amplitude of the equation based two tone spectrum.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the RF input power 'RFPin' and compare 3rd order results.

 

NOTE

In Spectrasys when the power is 25 dB below the compression point the compression curve is only represented with a 3rd order polynomial. This provides better correlation with traditional 3rd order intercept calculations and avoids polynominal stability issue and low input powers. Hence the correlation between Spectrasys and the other methods will diverge. However, Spectrasys will have a more accurate prediction of the 3rd order intercept point.

 

Also the larger the difference between the third order intercept point and the 1 dB compression point (greater than 10 dB) the accuracy of the prediction of the third order intercept point might deminish.

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to use equations to create a user defined warning and error messages created from an equation block.

 

BACKGROUND

A warning and error message can be created in the equation block. These warnings and error are based on equation variable values. In a system simulation that are two special variables in the main system analysis dataset called RFElemList and RFPwrIn that contains the names of the parts and their respective RF input power. This data can be used to post a warning or error.


SETUP

A simple RF architecture has been create with a standard system analysis. A path has been added so the 'Total Node Power (TNP)' can be determined. A local vector of the 'Total Node Power' is created. These values are in MKS so they will be changed to dBm. The total amplifier input power is the first entry in the array or vector. This value is saved as the 'AmpIn' variable.

 

The 'AmpIn_dBm' variable is tested by the 'if' loop to determine if the power is greater than +10 dBm. If so a warning and error message will be thrown.

 

Also further down in the equation block it shows how a warning message is shown for power into the Isolator part. A warning message is given with the isolator input power is greater than +15 dBm.

 

ANALYSIS

Path Table - This table contains some generic measurements along a path. The 'TNP' measurement shows the total node power at the output of each stage. Obviously, the amplifier input power is equivalent to the output power of the source.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the source power and note the power level changes in the 'AmpIn' variable in the equation block. When the 'AmpIn' power is greater or equal to +10 dBm a warning and error message will be thrown.

Workspace.Name: Simple CATV Amplifier
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Freq Comb\Simple CATV Amplifier.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Simple CATV Amplifier Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration that demonstrates the capability and power of the frequency comb simulation technique.  82 channels for the US cable TV market is quickly simulated in a single non-linear amplifier.

 

BACKGROUND

The Frequency Comb  simulation technique is a special technique to simulate the intermods due to a large number of carriers. Instead of calculating and managing every single intermod, groups of intermods are calculated, displayed, and managed. Each intermod group is displayed and identified in a different color.

 

The coherency of the carriers is determined by the reference clock used in the Multisource. If the Reference Clock parameter is empty then the carriers for that block are NonCoherent. However, if any clock name has been specified then the carriers in that frequency comb block are Coherent.


SETUP

A Multisource is used to create CATV carriers. They are implemented as 4 blocks of carriers since the frequencies are not continuous. If the carrier block contains 3 or more carriers an frequency comb carrier can be used. In this particular case 3 frequency comb carriers will be used for blocks: CATV1, CATV3, and CATV4. CATV2 will consist of 2 CW carriers spaced 6 MHz appart.

 

ANALYSIS

CATV Output Spec - This graph shows the broadband spurious response due to the 82 input carriers.

 

CATV Input Spec - This graphs shows the input intermods due to amplifier reverse isolation.

 

EXERCISES

1. Make carriers coherent by specifying a reference clock for the carrier block and observe the effects.

2. Change the amplitude of the carrier blocks and note the changes.

Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Freq Dependence\Basic Mixer Frequency Response.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Basic Mixer Frequency Response Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of the frequency response of the basic mixer. 

 

BACKGROUND

The frequencies entered in the mixer are associated with non-IF frequencies. There is only one frequency vector for all frequency dependent parameters in the mixer. This frequency will have a different meaning dependent on the parameter it is being applied to. For all isolation and impedance parameters input and output frequencies are the same. However, for the other parameters like conversion gain, noise figure, and the non linear parameters are associated with the RF port. So the behavior will be different depending on whether the mixer is being driven from the RF port versus the IF port. At frequencies above or below the defined values in the table constant extrapolation is used.


SETUP

This example is a single mixer with a source at the input and one at the LO. The IF has been fixed at 100 MHz and the LO frequency is derived from the tunable RF input frequency. A sweep has been created and the RF is tuned from 800 to 1600 MHz. Conversion gain and the isolation parameters are frequency dependent over a narrow range from 1000 to 1500 MHz.

 

ANALYSIS

Path Data Table - This table contains some of the basic gain and noise measurements. Note that the cascaded noise figure is 3 dB higher than the conversion loss for the given frequency. This is due to image noise.

 

RF Spec - Shows the swept on the RF terminal of the mixer.

 

LO Spec - Shows the swept on the LO terminal of the mixer.

 

IF Spec - Shows the swept on the IF terminal of the mixer.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change frequency dependent parameters an observe simulation results.

ABSTRACT

This example shows how a frequency dependent attenuator can be used to create a filter mask. 

 

BACKGROUND

The frequency dependent attenuator model takes a list of frequencies and corresponding attenuation values as input parameters. Linear interpolation is used in between data points. The beginning attenuation value applies to all frequencies below the first frequency in the list and the last attenuation value applies to all frequencies above the last frequency in the list.


SETUP

There are two analysis in this workspace 1) System and 2) Linear.

 

System

A simple transmitter has been created. The transmit frequency range is from 1910 to 1990 MHz. A multiplier is used in the LO chain. The frequency dependent attenuator has been placed at the last stage in the chain to represent an ideal filter mask. The model for the filter in the system schematic points to the 'Filter Sch' schematic that is used by the linear simulator. The IF filter is centered at 220 MHz and has a 2 MHz bandwidth.

 

Equations and variables have been created to tie the carrier and LO frequencies together.

 

The frequency and attenuation lists for the frequency dependent attenuator have also been created in the equation block. Some of these list values can be tuned if the user needs to examine system performance while adjusting the filter mask.

 

Linear

A simple schematic has been created with only the frequency dependent attenuator and a linear analysis.

 

ANALYSIS

 

System

Out Spec - This the output spectrum of the transmitter. Part of the filter shape above the noise floor can be seen in the shape of the noise pedistal located around the TX carrier.

 

LO Spec - This is the mixer local oscillator spectrum.

 

Linear

Final Filter Resp - This is the linear frequency response of the filter.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the variable 'F1' and notice the frequency response change in the 'Final Filter Resp' plot.

2. Tune the variable 'Attn1' and notice the amplitude changes in the 'Final Filter Resp' plot.

Freq Dependent Params Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how do perform a create a table to change a parameter like noise figure or gain versus frequency.

 

BACKGROUND

Practical components have variation of frequency, temperature, bias, and other parameters. Most model parameters are constant versus the above listed parameters. A lookup table can be created consisting on a table of data. For example, gain vs frequency. The data in the table can then be interpolated to determine the operating condition.

 

SETUP

This workspace consists of a CW signal source and an RF amplifier. The input frequency is swept from 2100 to 2200 MHz.

 

The 'Equation' block contains two tables, one of frequency and noise figure and the other of frequency versus gain. Each entry in the table represents either the noise figure or gain at the specified frequency. A linear interpolation function (lininterp) is used to determine the interpolated value of the gain or noise figure based on the frequency. The gain and noise figure variables are substituted into the amplifier model.

 

A sweep is created to sweep the frequency from 2100 to 2200 MHz.

 

ANALYSIS

NF Level Diagram - This level diagram shows the noise figure along the path for each of the swept frequencies.

 

Gain NF vs Freq - This plot show the gain and noise figure versus frequency at the output of the amplifier.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the table values and notice the change in the noise figure and gain responses.

Workspace.Name: Freq Dependent Stats Basics
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Freq Dependence\Freq Dependent Stats Basics.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Freq Dependent Stats Basics Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This workspace shows the basics of how statistics work for frequency dependent parameters for both manual entry and file based.

 

BACKGROUND

Statistical distributions are applied to model parameters such as Gain. As the frequency is varied the nominal gain will also change with frequency. The selected distribution will be applied to the entire parameter vector. For example, if a uniform gain distribution is selected with a 10% up and 10% down variation then each value of the parameter vector will vary by the same percentage.


SETUP

In this example we look at statistics applied for manual entered data on the frequency tab of the part and the other is when using a data file like a spreadsheet.

 

Manual Frequency Entry

A simple amplifier is being evaluated. The gain is made tunable with a gain vector of [ 20, 10, 5 ] dB for frequencies of [ 100, 200, 300 ] MHz. A uniform distribution is selected for the gain with a 10% up and 10% down variation. A Monte Carlo analysis has been created to vary the gain and collected data on the simulated path which is just the gain of the amplifier. The Monte Carlo has been configured for 50 rounds.

 

File Frequency Entry

This configuration is similar to that of the manual entry mode however because the data is dynamically extracted from a file we have no direct way of applying statistics to a particular parameter. However, the circuit can be modified slightly so that statistics can be applied to the stage directly following the file based stage. In this case a gain block was added with a nominal gain of 2 dB. The noise figure was set to 0 for this block. A 2 dB attenuator was inserted to make the total added insertion loss 0 dB. Applying statistics to a 0 dB gain value will not work as anything times 0 is still 0. A distribution was added to the gain of the linear block. The distribution was selected to be uniform with a 50% up and 50% down. With a 2 dB nominal gain this should give a +/- 1 dB Monte Carlo gain variation.

 

ANALYSIS

Output Spectrum (Manual) - This shows the broadband output spectrum of the amplifier that uses a single tone at the input for the manual frequency entry mode.

 

Monte Gain (Manual) - This shows the simulated path gain versus each round of the Monte Carlo for the manual frequency entry mode.

 

Output Spectrum (File) - This shows the broadband output spectrum of the amplifier that uses a single tone at the input for the file frequency entry mode.

 

Monte Gain (File) - This shows the simulated path gain versus each round of the Monte Carlo for the file frequency entry mode.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the source frequency to one of the frequencies used in conjunction with the gain vector and re-run the Monte Carlo analysis. Notice the simulated gain is +10% / -10% of the gain value for the given frequency.

2. Instead of using manual entered values use the defined Gain vector variable in the amplifier and repeat the Monte Carlo runs.

Workspace.Name: Intermod Distortion vs Freq
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Freq Dependence\Intermod Distortion vs Freq.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Intermod Distortion vs Freq Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This workspace shows the spurious performance of intermods generated at different stages in an RF amplification chain.  Furthermore, a frequency dependent compression curve is extracted and plotted on a 3D graph.

 

BACKGROUND

Each amplifier has frequency dependent parameters specified in a spreadsheet. These amplifiers are cascaded together in an RF chain. Each of these nonlinear devices will generate intermods. The intercepts of these devices vary with frequency. As such each will have different levels of intermod contribution to the total spurious output. A spectrum sweep can be used to view the overall spurious response to a single swept tone.


SETUP

A cascade of three amplifiers was created with three frequency dependent behavioral models. High pass and low pass filters along with an attenuator are dispersed along the line up. This single design is used with two different System Analyzes, one for the spectrum sweep and the other for a compression sweep.

 

ANALYSIS

Output Swept Spectrum - We can see the bread crumb trail of intermod and harmonic spectrum at the output due to a single swept input tone.

 

Compression_vs_Freq - This graph is created using the 3DGraphCompression equation block. This is a result of the sweep that was run on the System2 analysis that contains the quick sweep of a compression curve. 

 

DC Supply Table - This is a simple table of DC power supply requirements needed for the cascaded lineup.

 

EXERCISES

1. Disable the filters and attenuator in the design and observe changes in the swept spectrum.

2. Can the spurious response on the entire system be improved by reordering the same components in the cascaded lineup?

ABSTRACT

This simple workspace shows how to extract data from an imported System Spreadsheet File.

 

BACKGROUND

The 'getinterpdata' function returns the interpolated data over a range of values for specified independent variables.


SETUP

In this example have imported a MiniCircuits System Spreadsheet File (LHA-1+ and PGA-105+) using the File > Import > System Spreadsheet Files > Excel File ... option. The imported dataset appear on the workspace tree. The 'Output Equations' block uses the 'getinterpdata' function to extract frequency dependent Gain, NF, OP1dB, RLin, and RLout for a specified value for Voltage, Current, and Temperature. 

 

ANALYSIS

Gain_List - Interpolated frequency dependent gain.

 

NF_List - Interpolated frequency dependent noise figure.

 

OP1dB_List - Interpolated frequency dependent output 1 dB compression.

 

RLin_List - Interpolated frequency dependent input return loss.

 

RLout_List - Interpolated frequency dependent output return loss.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune input parameters and note extraction changes.

Workspace.Name: L Band Transmitter
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Freq Dependence\L Band Transmitter.wsv
Workspace.Description:
L Band Transmitter Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE:All simulation data must be calculated before it can be displayed) 

 

ABSTRACT

This example shows a design make up of mostly frequency dependent MiniCircuits components.

 

BACKGROUND

MiniCircuit spreadsheet models are generally frequency, temperature, and bias dependent. This includes nonlinear parameters suchs as OP1dB and OIP3. Each model has an ambient temperature parameter. By default this parameter is blank which means that it will take on the temperature of the analysis unless it is set to a particular value.


SETUP

This simple transmitter uses a 400 MHz IF signal that is amplified and mixed  with a 1350 MHz agile LO to produce a 1750 MHz TX signal. The transmitter covers the frequency range from 1675 to 1825 MHz. The transmitter output power is +15 dBm. All MiniCircuit amplifiers are temperature, frequency, and bias dependent. The variable attenuator in the IF chain can be used to change the output power. Equations have been created to auto tune the LO frequency based on the RF carrier frequency (FRF). A sweep was created to sweep the transmitter across the transmit frequency range (a wider TX frequency range was used for this sweep). A temperature variable called SysTemp was created and is used in the System Analysis. All models will use this temperature.

 

EVM estimation has also been enabled in this workspace. Estimated EVM contributions can be examined as a function of IF power level and RF output frequency.

 

Note: some of the S parameter devices have temperature dependent S parameters. In this example this dependency has not been accounted for.

 

ANALYSIS

EVM Estimates - This graph shows the estimated EVM contributions along the RF chain.

 

EVME Table - This table contains the estimated EVM along the RF chain in table form instead a graph.

 

EVME_3D_Graph - This 3D graph shows the estimated EVM results along the RF chain versus frequency (the sweep must be ran first).

 

DCP_vs_Pin - Transmitter compression curve.

 

TX Spec Out - Output spectrum of the transmitter.

 

TX Spec Sweep - This plot shows the spectrum performance of the transmitter as it is tuned over the 1650 to 1850 MHz frequency range.

 

TX System Data - Table of common transmit parameters.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune temperature and notice the differences in the analysis output.

Workspace.Name: MDIF Import from ADS
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Freq Dependence\MDIF Import from ADS.wsv
Workspace.Description:
MDIF File Import

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This workspace shows you how to import an MDIF file from ADS.

 

The steps are as follows:

 

1. In ADS, perform a simulation with an SPOutput component that writes the results to an S2PMDIF file. (See PE64102_wrk.7zads in the same directory as this example.)

 

In this example, we created a file in ADS called "DTC.mdf" containing 32 sets of S-data.

 

2. To import the file, click on:

 

File  -->  Import  -->  ADS Files  -->  System MDIF File...

 

and browse to the file. A new dataset will be created in the workspace. In this example, the dataset is "DTC" in the MDIF data folder.

 

3. The dataset contains all 32 sets of S-parameters, but they have to be separated out. The page "Equation1" does this using the MATLAB Script function getinterpdata(). The user tunes "DTC_tune" to the desired state between 0 and 31, and the correct set of S-data is read from the MDIF dataset and into the part on the schematic, ready for simulation. The part is nothing more than an RFAMP that consumes the 4 S-parameters into its Gain, RISO, Zin and Zout parameters.

Workspace.Name: MiniCircuits Amp vs Temperature
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Freq Dependence\MiniCircuits Amp vs Temperature.wsv
Workspace.Description:
MiniCircuits Amp vs Temperature Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to set device temperature directly for a particular device or from a running analysis.

 

BACKGROUND

All Genesys models have a Device Ambient Temperature parameter - "Ta" the default value is "Empty" which means that the model will use the Temperature from the parent analysis simulating the design.

 

SETUP

This workspace consists of a CW signal source Pin = -30dBm @ 2 GHz, and the MiniCircuits RF amplifier LHA-1+. The 'Equation' block contains the tunable variable Ta. A frequency sweep is created as a "Quick Sweep" in System1 analysis Path1 from 20 to 6020 MHz, step size of 100 MHz. A temperature sweep is created for the System1 analysis to sweep Ta for the list values {-85 0 25 45}.

 

ANALYSIS

Gain CNF vs Freq - This plot show the gain and noise figure versus frequency at the output of the amplifier for a temperature of 25 C.

 

Gain CNF vs Freq and Temp - This plot show the gain and noise figure versus frequency at the output of the amplifier for all swept temperatures of -85, 0, 25, and 45 C.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the Ta values and notice the change in the noise figure and gain responses on the "Gain CNF vs. Freq" graph.

ABSTRACT

This workspace shows how to generate 3D graphs from multidimensional data extracted from a model that supports a spreadsheet.

 

BACKGROUND

Data for a behavioral model may be saved in a spreadsheet where each tab of the spreadsheet may consist of a different condition like temperature or voltage. The tab data contains model parameters versus frequency.


SETUP

This is a simple block diagram containing a single amplifier with a signal source and output port. When the system simulation runs the spreadsheet data is automatically extracted and placed on the workspace tree.

 

A equation block, 3DGraphEquations will generate 3D graphs using the imported multidimensional dataset.

 

 

ANALYSIS

3D Graphs - There are various graphs for different parameters over frequency and temperature.

 

EXERCISES

1. Place a different device down in the schematic and recreate the graphs. (NOTE: delete existing graphs before generating new ones. Remember to change the name of the new dataset in the equation block.)

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how an imported Power Amplifier 's2d' file can be imported and used in the simulator.

 

BACKGROUND

An power amplifier was created in ADS and an 's2d' file was exported. The S-Parameters in this file is dependent on two bias conditions BiasL (1.9 to 2.1) and BiasU (5.3 to 6.3) across a frequency range of 500 to 1000 MHz.  


SETUP

The PA_DUT.s2d file was imported and variables were created for the bias. The 'getinterpdata' function was used to extract the S-Parameters for the given bias conditions. The S parameters were used in the RF amplifier model.

 

Note: Since Gain and Reverse isolation parameters are based in power and the S-Parameter (S21 and S12) are in voltage the power values need to be calculated.

 

ANALYSIS

S11 and S22 at Bias - A graph of S11 and S22 for the given bias conditions.

 

S21 at Bias - A graph of S21 for the given bias conditions.

 

PA_DUT.s2d - Imported .s2d file.

 

Table Data - A table of basic data for the amplifier.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the bias values and notice changes in the parameters and simulation results.

Workspace.Name: Digital Divider Basic
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Freq Mult Div\Digital Divider Basic.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Digital Divider Basic Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of a digital frequency divider output including an input spur. 

 

BACKGROUND

This digital frequency divider model is different than the frequency divider model in the way that harmonics are specified and generated by the divider. The Fourier series for a specified square wave duty cycle is used to determine the harmonic level of the divided signal. Furthermore, rather than have a conversion gain parameter a generated output level (OutLvl) is specified for the given divided signal. The desired division (DIV) can be specified. The harmonic and division parameters are used to correctly mark the desired output of the frequency divider. The input power must exceed the input drive level minimum (InDrvMin) in order to turn on the divider but must be lower than the input drive level maximum (InDrvMax). The Maximum Order on the Calculate tab of the system analysis is used to determine the number of harmonics that are generated. All spurious products generated by the digital frequency divider will also appear at the input through the reverse isolation parameter (RISO). When the EnableSSB parameter has been enabled any spurious sideband signals at the input will be processed by the multiplier. These spurious products shrink or grow at the rate of 20Log(N) where N is net harmonic / division ratio.

 


SETUP

This is a simple digital frequency divide by 2 schematic that generates 4 harmonics. A main signal at 1 GHz called Main is created in the source as well as a single sideband spur at 1.1 GHz that is 20 dB down from the main signal.

 

ANALYSIS

Spec In - This shows the 1 GHz main signal with a sideband spur 20 dB down at 1.1 GHz.

 

Spec Out - This shows the 4 harmonics created by the divider and the respective sideband spurs that grow or shrink at the rate of 20Log(N) where N is net harmonic / division ratio.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the power level of the Spur signal and observe the resulting spectrum.

2. Change the reverse isolation at the graph parameters for the input spectrum to see the effects of the reverse isolation.

Workspace.Name: Freq Divider Basic
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Freq Mult Div\Freq Divider Basic.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Freq Divider Basic Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of a frequency divider output including an input spur. 

 

BACKGROUND

This frequency divider model can be configured for the desired division (DIV) as well as a harmonic parameter (MULT) that can be used to identify the desired harmonic of the division. By default the harmonic parameter is set to 1. The harmonic and division parameters are used to correctly mark the desired output of the frequency divider. There is a conversion gain (CG) parameter. There is also a harmonic level vector (HL) that can be specified to control the level of all the harmonics after the division of the input. This is applied after the conversion gain has been applied. The input power must exceed the input drive level (InDrv) in order to turn on the multiplier. An entry in the harmonic level table must be made for each harmonic of interest. Generally, a reference level of 0 dB will be used for the harmonic of interest. i.e. for a doubler the 2nd entry in the harmonic level vector will be 0. The Maximum Order on the Calculate tab of the system analysis may need to be increased to include all the specified harmonics. All spurious products generated by the frequency multiplier will also appear at the input through the reverse isolation parameter (RISO). When the EnableSSB parameter has been enabled any spurious sideband signals at the input will be processed by the multiplier. These spurious products shrink or grow at the rate of 20Log(M/D) where M is the harmonic number and D is the division number.

 


SETUP

This is a simple frequency divide by 2 that generates 4 harmonics. A main signal at 1 GHz called Main is created in the source as well as a single sideband spur at 1.1 GHz that is 20 dB down from the main signal. The harmonic level table has been configured so the fundamental 1 GHz signal will be 0 dB down, the divide by 2 -10 dB, 3rd harmonic of the divide by 2 -20 dB, and the 4th harmonic of the divide by 2 (2nd harmonic) 50 dB down. Since the input power is 0 dBm and the conversion gain is set to 0 dB then harmonic outputs easily calculated in dBm and are shown on the output spectrum graph.

 

ANALYSIS

Spec In - This shows the 1 GHz main signal with a sideband spur 20 dB down at 1.1 GHz.

 

Spec Out - This shows the 4 harmonics created by the divider and the respective sideband spurs that grow or shrink at the rate of 20Log(M/D) where M is the harmonic number and D is the division number.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the power level of the Spur signal and observe the resulting spectrum.

2. Change the reverse isolation at the graph parameters for the input spectrum to see the effects of the reverse isolation.

Workspace.Description:
Freq Multiplier Basic Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of a frequency multiplier output including an LO spur. 

 

BACKGROUND

This frequency multiplier model can be configured for the desired harmonic order (MULT) as well as the conversion gain (CG). There is also a harmonic level vector (HL) that can be specified to control the level of all the harmonics. This is applied after the conversion gain has been applied. The input power must exceed the input drive level (InDrv) in order to turn on the multiplier. An entry in the harmonic level table must be made for each harmonic of interest. Generally, a reference level of 0 dB will be used for the harmonic of interest. i.e. for a doubler the 2nd entry in the harmonic level vector will be 0. The Maximum Order on the Calculate tab of the system analysis may need to be increased to include all the specified harmonics. All spurious products generated by the frequency multiplier will also appear at the input through the reverse isolation parameter (RISO). When the EnableSSB parameter has been enabled any spurious sideband signals at the input will be processed by the multiplier. These spurious products grow a the rate of 20Log(N) where N is the harmonic number.

 


SETUP

This is a simple frequency doubler that generates 4 harmonics. A main signal at 1 GHz called LO is created in the source as well as a single sideband spur at 1.1 GHz that is 20 dB down from the main signal. The harmonic level table has been configured so the fundamental 1 GHz signal will be 30 dB down, the 2nd harmonic 0 dB, 3rd -40 dB, and the 4th harmonic 50 dB down. Since the input power is 0 dBm and the conversion gain is set to 0 dB then harmonic outputs easily calculated in dBm and are shown on the output spectrum graph.

 

ANALYSIS

Spec In - This shows the 1 GHz LO signal with a sideband spur 20 dB down at 1.1 GHz.

 

Spec Out - This shows the 4 harmonics created by the multiplier and the respective sideband spurs that grow at the rate of 20Log(N) where N is the harmonic number.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the power level of the LOSpur signal and observe the resulting spectrum.

2. Change the reverse isolation at the graph parameters for the input spectrum to see the effects of the reverse isolation.

Workspace.Name: Group Delay Verification
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Group Delay\Group Delay Verification.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Group Delay Verification Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration showing how group delay measurements in the linear analysis engine are the same as Spectrasys. A simple filter will be used as an example.

 

BACKGROUND

"Group Delay measures the differential time delay caused by a filter, i.e., it indicates if certain frequency components will be delayed more than other components and by how much" (Radio Receiver Design, Kevin McClaning and Tom Vito, Noble Publishing, pg 174)

 

Spectrasys has the ability to generate and show group delay results, including frequency translations, by using the 'Quick Sweep' feature in a Spectrasys path. The group delay measurement function will then be applied to system S21 data created by Spectrasys.

 

The path voltage in Spectrasys is equivalent to the voltage gain E21. E21 is converted to a system S21 by using the following formula:

 

Sij = Eij * ( conj( ZPortj ) + ZPortj * Sjj ) / ( ZPorti * sqrt( real( ZPortj ) / real( ZPorti ) ) )

 

If ZPorti = ZPortj = R + j0

 

Then for simplified cases

 

Sij = Eij * ( 1 + Sjj )

or

S21 = E21 * ( 1 + S11 )

 

SETUP

A simple Chebyshev filter is use as the device under test. A linear and system analysis is performed on this device. For Spectrasys a path from the input to the output of the filter must be created. The 'Quick Sweep' function is enabled and 'Group Delay' is selected. Group delay data will appear in the dataset for this path. The group delay measurement function will then be applied to the Spectrasys derived system S21 (SysS21).

 

An equation block is used to create frequency variables to be used by both the linear and system analyzes.

 

ANALYSIS

Group Delay - This graph shows both the linear group delay and the group delay from Spectrasys. Notice that the results are identical.

 

Magnitude (Output Voltage) - This graph shows the magnitude of linear gain (S21) and the desired channel S21 from Spectrasys.

 

Phase (Output Voltage) - This graph shows the phase response of both the linear gain and the phase response of the wide carrier output (SysS21) from Spectrasys.

Workspace.Name: RX System Group Delay
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Group Delay\RX System Group Delay.wsv
Workspace.Description:
RX System Group Delay Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration showing how get Spectrasys group delay measurements.

 

BACKGROUND

"Group Delay measures the differential time delay caused by a filter, i.e., it indicates if certain frequency components will be delayed more than other components and by how much" (Radio Receiver Design, Kevin McClaning and Tom Vito, Noble Publishing, pg 174)

 

Spectrasys has the ability to generate and show group delay results, including frequency translations, by using the 'Quick Sweep' feature in a Spectrasys path. The group delay measurement function will then be applied to system S21 data created by Spectrasys.

 

The path voltage in Spectrasys is equivalent to the voltage gain E21. E21 is converted to a system S21 by using the following formula:

 

Sij = Eij * ( conj( ZPortj ) + ZPortj * Sjj ) / ( ZPorti * sqrt( real( ZPortj ) / real( ZPorti ) ) )

 

If ZPorti = ZPortj = R + j0

 

Then for simplified cases

 

Sij = Eij * ( 1 + Sjj )

or

S21 = E21 * ( 1 + S11 )

 

Steps for Group Delay Creation and Measurement

  1. Add a path to the System Analsysis
  2. Enable 'Quick Sweeps'
  3. Select 'Group Delay' for the type of sweep
  4. Run the simulation
  5. Right click on the output node of the path
  6. Select 'Group Delay' from the submenu in 'Add New Graph / Table'

Note: If the simulation is slower than desired or the file size is too large calculating intermod, harmonics, and noise can be disabled when making group delay measurements.

 

SETUP

A simple receiver is use as the device under test. A Spectrasys path has been created from the input to the IF output. A group delay quick sweep path has been created.

 

ANALYSIS

Group Delay - This graph shows the group delay of the IF output voltage at port 2.

 

Magnitude - This graph shows the magnitude of the IF output voltage.

 

Phase - This graph shows the phase response of the IF output voltage.

Workspace.Name: Amp Mixer Cascaded IP3
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Intermods\Amp Mixer Cascaded IP3.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Amp Mixer Cascaded IP3 Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration that shows the cascaded 3rd order intercept point for an amplifier followed by a mixer yields the expected intercept point. This is due to the fact that coherency for the same intermod combination generated in the amplifier and mixed to the IF frequency is coherent with the same intermod intermod generated internally in the mixer and mixed to the same IF frequency.

 

BACKGROUND

Ignoring compression effects, when the output 3rd order intercept point equals the input 3rd order intercept point for the following stage the overall output cascade intercept point will decrease by half, or 3.01 dB.


SETUP

In this simple example two tones are created at the input. Tone1 at 120 MHz and Tone2 at 140 MHz. Both tones have the same level of -50 dBm. They will produce 3rd order intermods at 100 and 160 MHz. A path has been created to look at the intermods in the 100 MHz channel. The output 3rd order intercept point for the amplifier is set to have the same input intercept point of the mixer which is 0 dBm. The other non-linear parameters have been set in such a way to minimize the effect of compression. This is an unrealistic configuration that doesn't represent the real world but illustrates correct calculation of cascaded intercepts points.

 

ANALYSIS

IF Output Spec - This spectrum plot zooms in on the 10 MHz mixer difference spectrum. There are two individual pieces of intermod spectrum and their totals. One intermod is created in the amplifier and then mixed down to 10 MHz. The other is generated in the mixer and mixed down to 10 MHz. Both intermods contain the same coherency number and therefore are coherent giving a 3.01 dB drop in the cascaded output intercept point.

 

Intercept Data - This table compares the measured cascaded output 3rd order intercept point (OIP3) and traditional equation based cascaded output 3rd order intercept point (EOIP3). In this case they are virtually identical except for the minor compression effects that are included in the real intercept (OIP3) measurement. The compression effects (COMP) are also included in the table.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the power level of the interfering tones and note the effect on the intercept point and compression.

2. Set the non-linear parameters of the mixer and amplifier to more realistic values and note the differences.

Workspace.Name: Basic IP2 and IP3 Measurements
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Intermods\Basic IP2 and IP3 Measurements.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Basic IP2 and IP3 Measurements Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how do perform an IP2 and IP3 measurement on the same circuit at the same time. 

 

BACKGROUND

When two or more tones are injected into a nonlinear circuit they generate intermods. These intermods can be measured along with the tones that created them and use these measured values to determine the intercept power levels.

 

SETUP

A multicarrier source is used to create two tones at 100 and 120 MHz with equal amplitudes. 2nd order intermods will be created at sum an difference frequencies of 20 and 220 MHz. 3rd order intermods will be created at 80 and 140 MHz. Two paths have been created in the system analysis; one for the 2nd order intermod channel and the other for the 3rd order intermod channel. A table for each path has been created showing intermod and interferer power levels along with input and output interecpt points. The interferer (tone) channel frequency (100 MHz) is specified on the 'Calculate' tab of the 'System Analysis'.

 

ANALYSIS

2nd Order Table - The 2nd order channel frequency used in this example is the one at 20 MHz as shown in the table. Only 2nd order intermod products appear in the channel as demonstrated by comparing the 'Total Intermod Power' (TIMP) measurement and the 'Total 2nd Order Channel Power' (TIMCP2) measurement. The interferer (or tone) used to calculate the intercept point is located at 100 MHz as shown by the 'Interferer Channel Frequency' (ICF) measurement. The 'Interferer Channel Power' (ICP) and 'Interferer Cascaded Gain' (ICGAIN) measurements show the power levels of this 100 MHz tone. Both the 'Output 2nd Order Intercept' (OIP2) and 'Input 2nd Order Intercept' (IIP2) measurements are shown in the table and their results are the same as those specified in the amplifier.

 

3rd Order Table - The 3rd order channel frequency used in this example is the one at 80 MHz as shown in the table. Only 3rd order intermod products appear in the channel as demonstrated by comparing the 'Total Intermod Power' (TIMP) measurement and the 'Total 3rd Order Channel Power' (TIMCP3) measurement. The interferer (or tone) used to calculate the intercept point is located at 100 MHz as shown by the 'Interferer Channel Frequency' (ICF) measurement. The 'Interferer Channel Power' (ICP) and 'Interferer Cascaded Gain' (ICGAIN) measurements show the power levels of this 100 MHz tone. Both the 'Output 3rd Order Intercept' (OIP3) and 'Input 3rd Order Intercept' (IIP3) measurements are shown in the table and their results are the same as those specified in the amplifier.

 

EXERCISES

1. Measure the 2nd order intercept point by using the sum 2nd order product of 220 MHz.

 

2. Measure the 3rd order intercept point by using the 3rd order product at 140 MHz.

 

3. Measure the intercept points by using the other interferer tone at 120 MHz.
