Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to perform both in-band and out-of-band intermod analysis. 

 

BACKGROUND

Intermod requirements in the form of intercept points often part of customer specifications. Calculating intercept points in SPECTRASYS  is much like doing so in the lab. Intermod requirements generally fall in to two categories 1) in-band and 2) out-of-band.

 

In-Band - In-band intermod analysis is used when interfering signals are not attenuated through the signal path. A broad band power amplifier is a good example.

 

Out-of-Band - Out-of-band intermod analysis is used when interfering signals are attenuated through the signal path. A good example here is the classic superheterodyne receiver. Receivers generally have a input intercept requirement specifying intermod performance relative to the receiver input. Interfering signals generally come from adjacent transmit bands close to the receive band. The strength of these interfering transmit signals cannot be controlled by the receiver. Furthermore, these interfering signals can create intermods in our own receiver and completely mask weak received signals. Consequently, good receiver designs must deal with strong interfering signals and intermods created by them.


GENERAL SETUP

This workspace contains both an in-band and out-of-band configuration complete with its own System Analysis, Schematic, and Table of data.

 

IN BAND INTERMODS

SETUP

This setup is consists of a two tone source (Intermod source) and attenuator followed by an RF amplifier. The intermod source will generate third order intermods at the specified intermod frequency. The user must specify the intermod and the one interfering tone frequencies. The program will automatically figure out the frequency of the 2nd tone to produce a third order product at the specified frequency.

 

NOTE: A path must also be created whose frequency is the same as the intermod frequency being measured. If the frequency is incorrectly specified the program will measure whatever intermods are found at the specified path frequency. Furthermore, the 'Channel Measurement Bandwdith' must be at least 3 times the bandwidth of the signal source when measuring the 3rd order intermods. However, the bandwidth must be small enough to only include the intermods and NOT the interfering tones!

 

ANALYSIS

In Band Table - This tables shows a summary of the analysis of the 'In Band Sch' schematic. Note that the channel frequency is the same as the intermod frequency specified in the source ... we know that our path measurements will show intermod calculations at this frequency. The total 3rd order intermod power at the output is -153 dBm. The 'Interferer Channel Frequency' is 140 MHz ... the is the frequency of the closest interfering tone. The 'Interfering Channel Power' is -31 dBm at the output. The difference between the interferer and intermod power is 122 dB (-31 dBm - (-153 dBm)). Half of this difference is 61 dB which when added to the interfering tone of -31 dBm will give an output 3rd order intercept point of +30 dBm ... the exact 3rd order intercept point specified in the RF amplifier! The SOIP3 and SIIP3 measurements show intercept values entered by the user for each stage.

 

EXERCISES

1. Examine the spectral output of the RF amplifier to correlate it with path measurements.

2. Change the power level of the interfering tones and examine calculated intercept points.

3. Change the 'Ignore Power Level Below' parameter on the 'System Analysis Options Tab' to higher level like -100 dBm and examine the recalculated analysis. What happened and why?

 

 

OUT OF BAND INTERMODS

SETUP

This setup is consists of a three tone source (RX Intermod source) and filter followed by an RF amplifier. The intermod source will generate third order intermods at the specified intermod frequency. The user must specify the intermod and the one interfering tone frequencies. The program will automatically figure out the frequency of the 2nd tone to produce a third order product at the specified frequency. For out of band intermod measurements the interfering tones are likely to be attenuated in filters so the level of the interfering tone at the output cannot be used to determine intercept points unless the in-band gain can be determined and a virtual interfering tone at the output is created. This is the purpose of the 3rd tone in the RX intermod source. This 3rd tone is a pilot signal created at the intermod frequency, since this frequency will be in-band it is used to determine the in-band cascaded gain used to calculate the virtual interfering tone output. The power level of this pilot tone should be low enough to not effect compression of non-linear stages.

 

NOTE: A path must also be created whose frequency is the same as the intermod frequency being measured. If the frequency is incorrectly specified the program will measure whatever intermods are found at the specified path frequency. Furthermore, the 'Channel Measurement Bandwidth' must be at least 3 times the bandwidth of the signal source when measuring the 3rd order intermods. However, the bandwidth must be small enough to only include the intermods and NOT the interfering tones!

 

ANALYSIS

Out of Band Table - This tables shows a summary of the analysis of the 'Out of Band Sch' schematic. Note that the channel frequency is the same as the intermod frequency specified in the source ... we know that our path measurements will show intermod calculations at this frequency. The total 3rd order intermod power at the output is -180.8 dBm (lower than the In-Band case since interfering tones have been attenuated before reaching the amplifier). The 'Interferer Channel Frequency' is 140 MHz ... the is the frequency of the closest interfering tone. The 'Virtual Tone Channel Power' is -30.98 dBm at the output. The difference between the virtual interferer and intermod power is 149.8 dB (-30.98 dBm - (-180.8 dBm)). Half of this difference is 74.9 dB which when added to the virtual interfering tone of -30.98 dBm will give an output 3rd order intercept point of +43.92 dBm ... higher than the output 3rd order intercept point specified in the RF amplifier! The SOIP3 and SIIP3 measurements show intercept values entered by the user for each stage.

 

EXERCISES

1. Examine the spectral output of the RF amplifier to correlate it with path measurements.

2. Change the frequency of the interfering tones and examine calculated intercept points.

 

 

ANSWERS - IN BAND INTERMODS

3. When the 'Ignore Level Below' was raised to -100 dBm all intermods below this level were thrown away and TIMCP3 was now -300 dBm because there was no 3rd intermod in the channel and the calculated OIP3 was also higher than expected. Caution must be exercised not to set this threshold so high that important data is ignored.

Workspace.Name: IP2 and IP3 vs Freq
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Intermods\IP2 and IP3 vs Freq.wsv
Workspace.Description:
IP2 and IP3 vs Freq Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how do perform an IP2 and IP3 versus frequency measurement on the same circuit at the same time. 

 

BACKGROUND

When two or more tones are injected into a nonlinear circuit they generate intermods. These intermods can be measured along with the tones that created them and use these measured values to determine the intercept power levels. True intercept measurement in Spectrasys is very similar to the process that would be followed on the bench. This process would include setting up two tones in the signal source, combining them together, and then running them through the device under test (DUT). The frequency and power levels would be set for the two tones and a spectrum analyzer would be used to look at the resulting spectrum. The intermod products (2nd or 3rd) would need to be located on the spectrum analyzer and then calculations could be made to determine the intercept points for the given tone frequencies. The process is repeated for all frequencies of interest.

 

SETUP

A multisource is used to create two tones at 1000 and 1010 MHz with equal amplitudes that are specified in the equation block. 2nd order intermods will be created at sum an difference frequencies of 10 and 2010 MHz. 3rd order intermods will be created at 990 and 1020 MHz. Two paths have been created in the system analysis; one for the 2nd order intermod channel and the other for the 3rd order intermod channel. A table for each path has been created showing intermod and interferer power levels along with input and output intercept points. The paths must be configured to locate both the intermod (Channel Frequency) and the Tone Interferer Frequency (Tone 1) (1000 MHz). If these parameters are not configured correctly the measurements results will be incorrect.

 

A sweep has been created to sweep Tone 1 frequency from 500 MHz to 5 GHz in 500 MHz steps. In the equation block Tone 2 frequency is determined from Tone 1 frequency and the two tone spacing.

 

ANALYSIS

2nd Order Table - The 2nd order channel frequency used in this example is the one at 10 MHz as shown in the table. Only 2nd order intermod products appear in the channel as demonstrated by comparing the 'Total Intermod Power' (TIMP) measurement and the 'Total 2nd Order Channel Power' (TIMCP2) measurement. The Tone Interferer Frequency used to calculate the intercept point is located at 1000 MHz as shown by the 'Interferer Channel Frequency' (ICF) measurement. The 'Interferer Channel Power' (ICP) and 'Interferer Cascaded Gain' (ICGAIN) measurements show the power levels of this 1000 MHz tone.

 

3rd Order Table - The 3rd order channel frequency used in this example is the one at 990 MHz as shown in the table. Only 3rd order intermod products appear in the channel as demonstrated by comparing the 'Total Intermod Power' (TIMP) measurement and the 'Total 3rd Order Channel Power' (TIMCP3) measurement. The Tone Interferer Frequency used to calculate the intercept point is located at 1000 MHz as shown by the 'Interferer Channel Frequency' (ICF) measurement. The 'Interferer Channel Power' (ICP) and 'Interferer Cascaded Gain' (ICGAIN) measurements show the power levels of this 1000 MHz tone.

 

EXERCISES

1. Measure the 2nd order intercept point by using the sum 2nd order product of 2010 MHz.

 

2. Measure the 3rd order intercept point by using the 3rd order product at 1020 MHz.

 

3. Measure the intercept points by using the other interferer tone at 1010 MHz.

Workspace.Name: RF Amp 11th Order Intermods
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Intermods\RF Amp 11th Order Intermods.wsv
Workspace.Description:
RF Amp 11th Order Intermods

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: Data must be calculated before it can be displayed.) 

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how the RF Amplifier model simulates intermod products up to the 11th order.

 

BACKGROUND

Internal proprietary algorithms are used to determine the following odd order coefficients: 5th, 7th, 9th, and 11th from P1dB, PSat, and IP3. The even order intercept points due to two tones was determined empirically by measuring several amplifiers and determine the general guidelines as follows:

 

OIP2 is specified by the user in the amplifier

OIP4 = OP1dB +13

OIP6 = OP1dB + 11

OIP8 = OP1dB + 9

OIP10 = OP1dB + 8

The Maximum Order parameter on the Calculate Tab of the System Analysis is used to determine what order of intermod products to simulate in the amplifier.


SETUP

This is a very simple design with a single RF amplifier. Two tones have been created at 975 and 1025 MHz. The power level of each tone is at -12 dBm giving a combined total input power of -9 dBm which is the input P1dB point.

 

ANALYSIS

Spec Out - This graph shows the entire output spectrum of the amplifier including noise, intermods, and harmonics.

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the MaxOrder variable and note the changes in the spectrum.

2. What happens when the order is set to higher than 11? Or less than 3?

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

EXERCISE ANSWERS

2. Only 11 orders are generated by the amplifier. However, the broadband noise simulated will increase with the MaxOrder. For orders less than 3 third and second order intermods will always be simulated.

Workspace.Name: RF Amp Intercept Quick Sweep
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Intermods\RF Amp Intercept Quick Sweep.wsv
Workspace.Description:
RF Amp Intercept Quick Sweep

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how the 2nd and 3rd order intercept points for an RF Amplifier model can be characterized vs swept power or frequency.

 

BACKGROUND

In Spectrasys because we keep track of individuals spectrums and can maintain signals underneath other signals the cascaded 2nd and 3rd order intercept points can be determined with a single tone. The one tone and two tone methods are equivalent under the assumption that when using the two tone method the power levels and phases of the two tones are equal to each other.

 

For the 2nd order intercept point the cascaded 2nd harmonic is used to determine the 2nd order output intercept point. This difference in power levels between the 2nd harmonic and two tone intermod power level of F1+F2 is exactly 20Log10(2) higher than the 2nd harmonic. Therefore with a one tone test we can determine the 2nd order output intercept point.

 

For a one tone simulation a 3rd order product 2F1-F1 = F1 falls at the single tone or F1 frequency. Since this is a 3rd order 2x1 intermod product its amplitude is the same as as the 2F1-F2 or 2F2-F1 intermod product created when doing a two tone analysis. In the two tone method if the amplitudes and phases are equal, which is the common case, then these 3rd order intermod levels are identical and can be used to determine the cascaded output 3rd order intercept point.


SETUP

In this workspace there are two designs.

1) Freq Design: This design uses a single Sys-Parameter amplifier from Analog Devices the ADL5240. Gain, P1dB, Return Loss, and IP3 all vary with frequency. A quick sweep from 100 to 4000 MHz is used to get the swept Gain, OIP2, and OIP3. To have the Gain measurement put into the Quick Sweep dataset the General Measurements have also been enable for that Quick Sweep.

2) Pwr Design: This designs uses a simple RF amplifier. A Quick Sweep is used to calculated the compression curve.

 

For both designs the Intermod Measurements for the Quick Sweep have also been enables so that the one tone OIP3_OneTone and OIP2_OneTone measurements are available.

 

ANALYSIS

Params_vs_Freq - This graph shows the Gain, OIP3, and OIP2 versus frequency. The results correspond with the Sys-Parameter dataset.

 

Params_vs_Pwr - This graph shows the compression curve and OIP3 and OIP2 versus input power. From this graph the intercept points default to 200 dBm at low power levels until the 3rd order intermod and/or 2nd harmonic are higher than the Ignore Below Level specified in the System Analysis. The current ignore value is set to -200 dBm. Notice that the accuracy of the intercept points are fine until we get within about 20 dB of the compression point. At higher power levels the intercept point accuracy decreases as expected.
Workspace.Models: *OUT@RF Design:MultiSource@RF Design:RFAMP@RF Design:RFAMP_IP2@RF Design

Workspace.Name: RF Amp One Tone Intercept Points
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Intermods\RF Amp One Tone Intercept Points.wsv
Workspace.Description:
RF Amp One Tone Intercept Points

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how the one tone intermod results give the identical answer as a two tone test.

 

BACKGROUND

In Spectrasys because we keep track of individuals spectrums and can maintain signals underneath other signals the cascaded 2nd and 3rd order intercept points can be determined with a single tone. The one tone and two tone methods are equivalent under the assumption that when using the two tone method the power levels and phases of the two tones are equal to each other.

 

For the 2nd order intercept point the cascaded 2nd harmonic is used to determine the 2nd order output intercept point. This difference in power levels between the 2nd harmonic and two tone intermod power level of F1+F2 is exactly 20Log10(2) higher than the 2nd harmonic. Therefore with a one tone test we can determine the 2nd order output intercept point.

 

For a one tone simulation a 3rd order product 2F1-F1 = F1 falls at the single tone or F1 frequency. Since this is a 3rd order 2x1 intermod product its amplitude is the same as as the 2F1-F2 or 2F2-F1 intermod product created when doing a two tone analysis. In the two tone method if the amplitudes and phases are equal, which is the common case, then these 3rd order intermod levels are identical and can be used to determine the cascaded output 3rd order intercept point.

 

One tone intermod measurements are much easier to use and are always available in the path dataset as long as there is a single input tone for the path of interest. When more than one tone exists at the path input exists these one tone intercept measurements are not placed in the path dataset.


SETUP

Two cascaded amplifiers were placed in a user model called DualAmpSch. The gain and non linear parameters were picked in such a way that neither one amplifier or the other dominated the intermod performance of the cascade. Two different designs each use the DualAmpSch design. One design has a one tone input at 1 GHz and the other design has two input tones with tones at 990 and 1010 MHz. The PinTotal variable was created so that the total input power in both designs is constant. This value is tunable. For the two tone case the power for each of the tones is 3 dB less so the total input power is equivalent to the single tone case. Three tables of intercept points were created to compare:

 

1. One Tone Intercept Points

2. Two Tone Intercept Points

3. Equation Based Intercept Points

 

For the two tone design the appropriate intermod paths were created to properly track the intermods of interest as Spectrasys needs to know the location of the intermod and interferring tone in order to properly calculate the intercept point.

 

 

ANALYSIS

One Tone Intercept Table - This table shows the total node power and the one tone 2nd and 3rd output intercept points.

 

Two Tone Intercept Table - This table shows the total node power and the two tone 2nd and 3rd output intercept points.

 

Equation Intercept Table - This table shows the total node power and the equation based 2nd and 3rd output intercept points.

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the PinTotal variable and note the intercept changes in the tables.

2. Why doesn't the values in the Equation Intercept Table change with power?

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

EXERCISE ANSWERS

1. Only in the linear range will the one and two tone intercept measurements be equal to the equation based values. The one and two tone measurements are power, frequency, and VSWR dependent just like intermod measurements made in a laboratory. It the responsiblity of the user to correctly pick the linear input power levels to determine the intercept points that are not cluttered by higher power effects. A power level about 20 dB below the compression point will provide answers close to those in the cascaded equations.

2. Cascaded intercept equations ignore power. They do not include frequency or VSWR dependencies.

Workspace.Name: Switch Intermods
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Intermods\Switch Intermods.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Switch Intermods Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a very basic illustration of intermods generated by a nonlinear switch due to signals at multiple ports.

 

BACKGROUND

Nonlinearities are generated only from signals sources arriving on the given pin of the switch. i.e. only signals arriving on pin 2 will generate intermod spectrums that will be propagated to other pins of the switch. This pattern is repeated for all pins of the switch except for the nonlinearities on the common port. The nonlinear block located on the common pin has some additional parameters that allow the user to control the level of signals that will be used as virtual inputs to this nonlinear block. These intermods will be generated and propagated to the other pins on the switch. These intermods will be attenuated by the isolation or insertion loss dependent on the state of the switch. i.e. in this case pin 2 (switch state 1) will use insertion loss whereas pin 3 will use isolation. The parameter that controls the virtual level of signals at the input is called the Reverse Intermod Factor (RevIM). It is specified in dB. 0 dB means that the signal amplitude at the output of the nonlinearity will be the same ampltude that will virtually appear at the input. To control the level of intermods generated by the switch that appear on the common port the Out to In Intermod Isolation (InIMIso) parameter can be used. This is also in dB and specifies the level of isolation between the nonlinear block output and the input. i.e if this was set to 0 dB then the input port intermod amplitudes would be the same as those generated by the nonlinear block on the common port. 

 


SETUP

This is a very basic analysis with a single nonlinear switch. Two signals sources are used.

 

ANALYSIS

RF1 Out Spec - Shows the spectrum on pin 2 (switch state 1) of the switch.

 

RF2 Out Spec - Shows the spectrum on pin 3 of the switch.

 

In Spec - Shows the spectrum on the common pin (1) of the switch.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the RevIM and note the change in the intermod spectrum at output RF1 and RF2.

2. Tune the InIMIso and note the change in the intermod spectrum at the switch input.

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to set up a sweep and examine the performance of a log detector. 

 

BACKGROUND

Log detectors can be used as power sensors. The RF input power, both signal and noise, is converted to a DC signal. If the total RF input power is above the sensitivity of the detector and below its saturation level the DC output voltage will be proportional to the RF input power.


 

SETUP

A multisource is used to create a CW source with a variable input, RFPwrIn, which contains the power of the source that is swept from -120 dBm to +20 dBm. The output of the log detector will be plotted in a table and on a graph.

 

ANALYSIS

Log Output - Shows the swept input power versus the DC output power of the detector.

 

Output Table - Shows in tabular form the swept input power versus the DC output power of the detector.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the 'Output Threshold' on the log detector and notice the affect at the output.

 

2. Change other log detector parameters and notice the affect at the output.

Workspace.Name: Switched Power Measurement
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Log Detector\Switched Power Measurement.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Switched Power Measurement Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of a non-linear switch that has switch state dependent S-parameters.

 

SETUP

A 4 pole switch is used to select 1 of 4 carriers that are fead to an RF detector. The carriers are spaced 1 GHz apart with the first carrier at 1 GHz. A path is created for each carrier. The switch is a SP4T switch from Hititte, HMC241QS16. The S-parameters were downloaded from their site. They provide S-parameters for each state of the switch. The 'SDSwitchN' model is used to take advantage of these S-parameters.

 

A sweep is created that sweeps the state of the switch from 1 to 4. An amplifier is located between the switch output and RF detector input. The detector input and output will be examined versus switch state. Since all carriers have the same power and all couplers have the same coupling the S-parameter variation of the switch is examined.

 

A MATLAB Script equation block is used to create swept variables that look at the total input power and DC output to the RF detector.

 

ANALYSIS

Amp In Spec - This is the input spectrum to the measurement amplifier. Notice the leakage of the other carriers that appear in this spectrum.

 

Amp Out Spec - This shows the spectrum at the amplifier output. Notice that the carriers that leak across the switch isolation create intermods at the amplifier output.

 

Amp Out vs SW State - This graph shows the Total Node Power at the amplifier output (RF detector input) versus the switch state. Notice the frequency rolloff at the higher frequencies. In this case this is the frequency response of the switch.

 

DC Out vs SW State - This graph shows the RF detector output versus the switch state. The DC output is proportional to the RF input power.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the switch model from 'SDSwitch4' to 'SWITCH_NonLinear4' and re-run the simulation and sweeps. Examine graphs, does the new data seem consistent with the change in models?

Workspace.Name: Basic Mixer Compression
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Mixers\Basic Mixer Compression.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Basic Mixer Compression Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how do perform a simple RF power sweep to determine the 1 dB compression point of an RF amplifier.

 

BACKGROUND

As RF amplifiers are driven with more input power they eventually reach a point where their output power is limited which is called the saturation region. Before this occurs a point will be reached where the gain of the amplifier is 1 dB less than the small signal gain. This is referred to as the 1 dB compression point.

 

SETUP

This workspace consists of a multisource set to CW and a basic mixer. The input power is swept from -10 to +14 dBm. The specified 1 dB input compression point of the mixer is +1 dBm and the input saturation level is +2 dBm. This translates to an output 1 dB compression point of -7 dBm and an output saturation level of -6 dBm since the conversion loss is 8 dB. A variable representing input power (RFPwrIn) is created in the equation block associated with the design. This variable is used in the CW source as well as the sweep.

 

The 'Output Equations' block contains the necessary equations to form the swept data in a format that can be used for graphs or tables.

 

ANALYSIS

Power Sweep - This graph contains the swept input power versus the channel output power. A 1 dB compression marker can be placed at +1 dBm input power which yields a linear gain of -8 dB but an actual gain of about  -9 dB. Another marker can be placed at +10 dBm input power highlighting the output saturation power level of the amplifier.

 

Sweep Table - This table shows the numerical results of swept input power, the output power, linear gain, and difference in dB between the linear power and actual power.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the compression and saturation points and rerun the sweep to see the effects.

Workspace.Name: Image Rejection Mixer
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Mixers\Image Rejection Mixer.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Image Rejection Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: The simulation data must be calculated before the data can be displayed)

 

Abstract
This simple workspace illustrates the concept of an image reject mixer.
 
Setup
Three signals are applied to the image reject mixer.  1) RF signal at 1100 MHz, 2) Image signal at 930 MHz, and 3) LO signal at 1000 MHz.
 
Background
Mixer output phase is as follows:
Output Phase = LO Phase + Input Phase (Sum)
Output Phase = LO Phase - Input Phase (Difference for High LO Side Injection )
Output Phase = Input Phase - LO Phase (Difference for Low LO Side Injection )
 
Because of the phase split caused by the hybrid splitter at the input to the mixers and the recombining by the hybrid splitter at mixer output high side RF signals are separated from low side RF signals.  Port 3 contains IF signals less than the LO frequency and Port 4 contains IF signals greater than the LO signal
 
Analysis
Graphs have been created for the output power and phase of both mixers.
 
Example the following graphs:
(RF < LO) Output Power
(RF > LO) Output Power
 
The spectrum analyzer mode has been turned on which will show the total coherent power addition.  Individual signals can still be seen in these graphs since individual spectrum identification has been turned on.  It becomes clear from these pictures which signals are being cancelled and which are not.
 
Exercises
1. Tune the frequency of the image signal and observe the changes.
2. Change the phase and amplitude balance of the splitters and mixer paths while observing the results.

Workspace.Name: Read IMT Data from File
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Mixers\Read IMT Data from File.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Read IMT Mixer Data from File

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

 

Intermod table (IMT) files come in many formats and sizes. The number of LO and RF harmonics in an IMT file is totally arbitrary. Therefore, the Equation2 page should be modified for your specific file. The important variables are:

 

MixerFilename -- set this to your IMT file's path & name.

Num_LO_harmonics -- set this equal to the number of columns (LO harmonics) in your IMT file.

 

Running Equation2 will read the entire file at once into powers. From there, MATLAB Script extracts first the RF and LO power levels (two values that the mixer needs) and then the IMT matrix itself.

 

The textscan() function is used to read the entire file at once because it can skip comment lines and deal with varying delimiter length and other file characteristics.

 

Once textscan() does its thing, it’s relatively easy to read the RF and LO power levels (which the mixer needs for its RFTableInPwr and RFTableLOPwr parameters) from line 1 of the file. The rest of the file, of course, contains the IMT data. When you run Equation2, you’ll see the table IMT_data immediately populate with the data, telling you that it was successful. This is important because the MIXER_TBL model doesn’t show this data. For the IMT file supplied with this example, the resulting matrix will be 16 x 16 (15 harmonics plus DC term for both RF and LO).

 

CAUTION: This method is looking for comment lines that begin with a ‘!’. This can be changed in the call to textscan(). Files with other types of header lines may require a little more work.

Workspace.Name: Simple Table Mixer
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Mixers\Simple Table Mixer.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Simple Table Mixer Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is example will help the user understand table mixer configuration and operation.

 

BACKGROUND (General Table Mixer Basics)

The following equation governs the desired mixer output signals:

 

FIF = FLO +/- FRF (assuming RF is the input port)

 

Both the sum and difference signals are present at the output with equal amplitudes. However, other unwanted spurious combinations to the mixer input and LO signals also appear at the output according to the equation:

 

FIF = | M x FRF +/- N x FLO |

Where M = 0,1,2,... and N = 0,1,2,...

 

A spurious amplitude table can be created for every combination of the input and LO signal that appear at the mixer output. These amplitudes are in dBc and are relative to the desired mixer output which is at 0 dBc. Each column of the table represents a harmonic of the LO and each row represents a harmonic of the mixer input. The first column represents the 0th harmonic of the LO ... or simply a list of all the harmonics of the input signal that appear at the mixer output. The first row represents the 0th harmonic of the mixer input ... or simply a list of all harmonics of the LO that appear at the mixer output. The first entry in the table (1st column and 1st row) is a don't care since there will never be a 0th harmonic of the input and 0th harmonic of the LO that will appear at the mixer output.

 

A simple table could look like:

 

'0    1      2     3      4     5    Harmonic of the LO

99   14   29   23   42   25   ' Input Harmonic 0
20   0     30   12   34   27   ' Input Harmonic 1
52   40   58   43   59   41   ' Input Harmonic 2
46   48   50   49   53   47   ' Input Harmonic 3
73   72   65   62   66   57   ' Input Harmonic 4
77   76   84   63   64   60   ' Input Harmonic 5

Note: The ' is a comment and not part of the actual table data.

 

Notice that the 1 x 1 entry is always 0 dBc since this is the desired mixer output signal and is the reference point for the rest of the data in the table.

 

Caution: Even though the data in the table is all relative to the mixer output power level the user must be very careful to recognize that when examining the spectral output of a table mixer that the table amplitude values will only represent the specified values when the mixer input and LO drive levels correspond with the drive levels used to characterize the mixer. In practice, mixers are generally not flat over frequency and the mixer table should be characterized at the same drive levels and frequencies that will be used in the real system.

 

The mixer table applies equally to both sum and difference products.

 

     Input Drive Level

If the mixer input power level is below the mixer input characterization level of the spurious table then the amplitudes of the spurious mixer output products fall off at rate of M - 1 dB for every dB that the input power is below the mixer input characterization power level, where M is the order of the input signal. For example, 3 x 2 (Input x LO) entry in the table is 50 dBc. If the mixer was characterized with an input power level of -10 dBm and the actual input power level was -11 dBm then the 3 x 2 spur would be 2 dB lower than 50 dBc ... or 52 dBc (the input order is 3 so 3 - 1 = 2 dB drop for every dB drop in input power). Indeed the entire input 3rd harmonic row would drop by 2 dB.

 

BACKGROUND (Specific Table Mixer Implementation)

     A Table for Each Direction

Generally, a mixer table is used to specify the mixer output performance based on mixer input and LO signals. This is a good representation of the output but provides no way to simulate the harmonics of the LO that will appear at the mixer input. Or if the mixer is back driven there will be mixed spectrum in the reverse direction that appears at the mixer input. Consequently, this mixer implementation supports a table for both mixer input and output driving directions through the mixer. However, the table in the reverse direction may only represent the harmonics of the LO that appear at the mixer input.

 

     How to Create a Table

Table entry format is identical to matrix entry.

To begin a table use open bracket followed by values separated by commas. To start a new row in the matrix use a semicolon. To end the table use an end bracket.

 

For example [ 2, 3, 4; 5, 6, 7 ] would be syntax for the following matrix or table

|  2  3  4  |

|  5  6  7  |

 

Tables can be entered directly as a parameter or as a variable in an equation block.

 

     Isolation

All signals appearing at the RF or IF mixer ports will also appear on the LO port. Mixer isolation parameters are determined from the mixer table characterization levels as well as the table values. For example, a mixer is characterized with an input drive level of -20 dBm and an LO drive level of +10 dBm, its conversion gain is -10 dB. Using the example mixer table above we find that the 1st harmonic of the LO is 14 dBc below the output level. The desired mixer output power level is -30 dBm since the mixer input level is -20 dBm with a conversion gain of -10 dB. The LO to output isolation would be +10 dBm (LO Drive ) - 30 dBm (output power ) - 14 dBc (0x1 table entry) = 54 dB. This same process is repeated for the LO to input isolation using the table representing the spurious combinations of the output signal mixed with the LO. The mixer input to output isolation is taken directly off the spurious table and is the 1st harmonic of the input and 0th harmonic of the LO. Using the above table this would be 20 dB.

 

     Linearity

Mixer spur tables do not account for non-linearities in drive level since they are based on single value characterization power levels. Consequently, with these types of models mixer output power always increase linearly with input power. The current implementation of the table mixer uses input P1dB and PSAT to hard limit the output power of the mixer.

 

     Multiple Input Signals

The current implementation of the table mixer applies the spurious table individually to each mixer input signal. There is not enough information contained in the table to determine the non-linearities of the mixer and create the true mixed response for multiple signal inputs

 

     Signals Used for the LO

By default the system analysis uses the peak LO signal found on the LO port. If more than 1 LO signal appears on the LO port the other LO signals are not used in table calculations and mixer output other than propagated through the isolation of the mixer. There is an option on the 'Options' page of the system analysis to use all LO signals within a specified range of the peak LO signal. When this option is selected the mixer table will be applied to each mixer input signal for every LO signal within the given range.

 

     Specifying the Maximum Mixing Order

The maximum mixer order is specified on the 'Calculate' tab of the system analysis. For a high order spurious signal where a mixer table entry has not been specified a default suppression value specified in the mixer will be used.

 

     Impedances

Because the mixer is a non-linear device S parameters cannot be determined across the mixer. Therefore, loading effects of the mixer are not reflected in its conversion gain or isolation. However, mixer port impedances are used to account for mismatches between the mixer and its connected circuitry.

 

     Bandwidths

Bandwidths of the signals are multiplied according the to the harmonic of the mixer input signal. For example, a CW signal has a 1 Hz bandwidth by definition. At the table mixer output the bandwidth of the 2 x 3 ( input x LO ) spurious signal would have a 2 Hz bandwidth. The LO harmonic doesn't affect the mixer spurious output bandwidth.

NOTE: When comparing the table mixer output spectrum to the table values be sure the channel bandwidth is set to a bandwidth greater than or equal to the bandwidth of the signal you are trying to measure.

 

SETUP

This example is a simple illustration of a table mixer. A CW signal (1 Hz bandwidth) is used at the mixer input whose power level is set to the same value at the characterized table. A level +10 mixer is used whose LO power level is also set to the mixer characterization power level. An equation block has been added to the design which has the definition of the table. A simple table was create in the reverse direction (mixer output to input) that simply represents the harmonics of the LO at the input. Note: An LO table has also been specified in the equation block but is not used by the mixer except in the exercises below.

 

ANALYSIS

     'Input Spec' Graph - This graph shows the harmonic spectrum of the LO at the mixer input.

 

     'Output Spec' Graph - This graph shows the output spectrum of the table mixer.

 

EXERCISES

  1. Compare results in the 'Output Spec' graph to the table values. Note: The actual values in the equation block are the same values as those contained above.
  2. Drop the power level of the input signal by 1 dB and verify that the spurious output power falls off at 'input order - 1' dB. Note: Remember when comparing dBc results that the desired output power will also drop by 1 dB.
  3. Use the 'LOTable' defined in the equation block instead of the default table specified in the mixer (Note you must type in 'LOTable' for the 'IF Input Table Data' parameter in the mixer). Examine the 'Input Spec' graph while tuning the amplitude of the entries in the 'LOTable'.

Workspace.Name: BER Estimation Validation
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Modulated RF\BER Estimation Validation.wsv
Workspace.Description:
BER Estimation Validation Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration showing the correlation between theoretically calculated BER curves and those estimated using in-channel signal to noise or interference ratio.

 

BACKGROUND

The relationship between Eb/No (energy per bit to noise power spectral density) and C/N (carrier to noise ratio) is as follows:

 

C/N = ( Eb/No ) * ( R / B )

 

where

R is the channel data rate

B is the channel bandwidth

 

When R = B then C/N = Eb/No. This is the assumption made in the internal estimation equations inside Spectrasys.

 

Note: C/N is used interchangeably with S/N (signal to noise ratio).

 

MATLAB has a function called berawgn that supports specific modulation formats. The user passes in Eb/No, the modulation format, and some other modulation specific information and the function returns the BER for those given conditions. If a vector of Eb/No values are passed in a vector of BER values will be returned. BER theoretical curves are created in this fashion.

 

SETUP

This is a very simple setup where a single amplifier is used to estimate BER performance. This estimated performance can be compared with theoretical data from equations.

 

The gain and noise of the amplifier are known so it is easy to calculate input and output signal to noise ratios. In the Input Equ equations input variables are defined and the input power is calculated based on a tunable signal to noise ratio. A Modulated RF BER Estimation path has been created where the modulation type can be selected by the user. A sweep has been added to sweep SNR of the system analysis from 2 to 15 dB.

 

The estimated BER (measurement called BERE) is a path measurement that is swept by the sweep. In order to look at the estimated BER at a particular node along the path the BERE data will need to be extracted from the swept data for the particular node of interest. The extractsweptdata( Dependent Variable, Independant Variable, Independent Value of Interest) function will be used for this purpose. The dependent variable in this example is BERE. The independent variable is called NodeNames which contains a list of the named nodes along a path. The node name of interest is at the output of the amplifier and is "2". The extractsweptdata function will search through all the BERE values looking for those whose node is named "2". The result will be a vector of BERE data at node "2".

 

The BERAWGN Equ equation block contains MATLAB equations for various modulation formats using Eb/No as a swept variable. The BER Theory graph shows BER as a function of Eb/No that varies from 2 to 15 dB.

 

Swept and theoretical results are shown on the BER Theory vs Est graph.

 

NOTE: The calculations of intermods has been turned off in this example so that it would be easy to identify and control the signal to noise ratio.

 

ANALYSIS

Spec Out - Shows the output spectrum of the amplifier.

 

RF and BER Est Measurements - This table shows BER estimates along with RF simulated performance like Carrier to Noise and Distortion Ratio (CNDR).

 

BER Theory vs Est - This graph shows the BER of the swept RF SNR ratio versus theoretical results.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the modulation type used for BER estimation in the path. Re-run the sweep. How do the results compare with the theoretical?

2. Change the gain or noise figure of the amplifier and re-run the sweep. To the measurements agree with expectations?

3. Enable the calculation of intermods and re-run the sweep. What happened to the BER? Why?

 

 

 

 

ANSWERS TO EXERCISES

1. Answers very close

2. Yes

3. No change in the BER because at low power levels in channel signal to noise ratio is not a factor.

Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Modulated RF\EVM Basic Estimation.wsv
Workspace.Description:
EVM Basic Estimation Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to perform EVM estimation. 

 

BACKGROUND

EVMrms is approximately equal to 1 / sqrt( S/N ). Spectrasys has the ability to simulate in-channel signal to noise ratio, signal to intermod ratio, and signal to phase noise ratio. Therefore Spectrasys can show EVM contributions for each of these categories. Furthermore, algorithms developed by the test and measurement group have been used internally to estimate EVM across the channel due to amplitude and phase distortions. The total EVM is the square root of the sum of the squares of the individual contributions. Measurement values are given in %.

 

Estimation does not need a digital modulation source nor a digital simulation. The entire estimation is achieved with the RF simulation engine.


SETUP

This is a very simple setup consisting of a source, narrowband filter, and amplifier. Contributions to each category can be seen in this example.

 

ANALYSIS

EVM Table- Shows EVM contributions due to noise, intermods, phase noise, and channel flatness.

 

EVM Level Diagram - Shows EVM contributions in level diagram format.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune filter parameters such as ripple, insertion loss, and corner frequencies to determine affects on EVM. Which contributor was affected the most?

2. Enable the phase noise in the simulation and on the source or residual phase noise in the amplifier. What affect does that have on EVM?

3. Increase the input power by 10 dB. What is the dominant contributor to EVM?

Monte Carlo Spur Analysis Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This simple example illustrates how to do a spurious analysis of a receiver using a monte carlo simulation.

 

BACKGROUND

Receivers are typically designed to receive a band of input frequencies. The LO is generally tunable to select any of these input frequencies. To do a thorough spurious analysis all RF input frequencies and all LO frequency must be considered. This would generally imply that a nested sweep analysis is necessary. A monte carlo analysis can be configured to pick any frequency in the RF band as well as any frequency in the LO band. The monte carlo results can be ploted to see the performance of the spectrum avoiding time consuming nested sweeps.

 

SETUP

This is a simple 8.5 to 9.5 GHz receiver. The IF output is at 2 GHz. The RF input frequency FRF and the LO frequency FLO are made tunable and these variables are configured in the Monte Carlo analysis. Their distribution has been configured as uniform whose frequencies cover their entire range. In the case of FRF the range is from 8500 to 9500 MHz. For the LO it is from 6500 to 7500 MHz. The node spectrum has been set as the measurement in the Monte Carlo analysis which is plotted on a few graphs.

 

ANALYSIS

Monte In Spec - This graph shows the spurious response that potentially would be re-radiated by the antenna. The single simulation run of the system is also plotted in a different color.

 

Monte Out Spec - This graph is shows the spurious response at the output of the IF. The single simulation run of the system is also plotted in a different color. 

 

EXERCISES

1. Change filter bandwidths and notice the effect on the spurious.

Workspace.Name: Quick Sweep Monte Carlo
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Monte Carlo\Quick Sweep Monte Carlo.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Quick Sweep Monte Carlo

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration showing how to use Monte Carlo simulation for Spectrasys Quick Sweep Path measurements. A simple filter will be used as an example. A Quick Sweep of Group Delay measurements are used in the Monte Carlo simulation.

 

BACKGROUND

"Group Delay measures the differential time delay caused by a filter, i.e., it indicates if certain frequency components will be delayed more than other components and by how much" (Radio Receiver Design, Kevin McClaning and Tom Vito, Noble Publishing, pg 174)

 

Spectrasys has the ability to generate and show group delay results, including frequency translations, by using the 'Quick Sweep' feature in a Spectrasys path. The group delay measurement function will then be applied to system S21 data created by Spectrasys.

 

The path voltage in Spectrasys is equivalent to the voltage gain E21. E21 is converted to a system S21 by using the following formula:

 

Sij = Eij * ( conj( ZPortj ) + ZPortj * Sjj ) / ( ZPorti * sqrt( real( ZPortj ) / real( ZPorti ) ) )

 

If ZPorti = ZPortj = R + j0

 

Then for simplified cases

 

Sij = Eij * ( 1 + Sjj )

or

S21 = E21 * ( 1 + S11 )

 

SETUP

A simple Chebyshev filter is used as the device under test. A linear and system analysis is performed on this device. For Spectrasys a path from the input to the output of the filter must be created. The 'Quick Sweep' function is enabled and 'Group Delay' is selected. Group delay data will appear in the dataset for this path. The group delay measurement function will then be applied to the Spectrasys derived system S21 (SysS21).

 

An equation block is used to create frequency variables to be used by both the linear and system analyses.

 

ANALYSIS

Group Delay - This graph shows both the linear group delay and the group delay from Spectrasys. Notice that the results are identical.

 

Magnitude (Output Voltage) - This graph shows the magnitude of linear gain (S21) and the desired channel S21 from Spectrasys.

 

Phase (Output Voltage) - This graph shows the phase response of both the linear gain and the phase response of the wide carrier output (SysS21) from Spectrasys.

Antenna Noise Temperature Figure Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to model the effects of antenna noise temperature on a system. 

 

BACKGROUND

This is a simulation of a design example from the book, 'Noise in Receiving Systems' by Raoul Pettai, John Wiley and Sons 1984. pgs 114 - 123, 140 - 143

 

The MultiSource has the ability to create noise sources. This noise source can have temperatures lower than the value specified in the Analysis. A noise source can be added to represent the noise power being received from an antenna.


SETUP

This is a simple receiver that has some of its components specified by noise temperature. Equations are used to convert noise temperature to noise figure used by simulation models. The low antenna temperature is modeled in the signal source. Equations are also used to create the antenna noise input power density based on the antenna temperature.

 

A carrier frequency of 5 GHz is used. A noise source was added whose power was derived from the antenna temperature. The frequency range for this noise was specified from 4.5 to 5.5 GHz.

 

Several equations were written to convert between noise power and temperature parameters.

 

ANALYSIS

Noise Table Data - In this table the channel noise power and cascaded noise figure are shown. The simulated channel noise power is the same as shown in the book on pg 118. The cascaded noise figure is the same as shown on pg 141.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the antenna temperature. What happened to the cascaded noise figure and why?

2. What happens to the input and output channel noise power at the antenna temperature is changed?

3. Disable the noise source in the MultiSource and re-simulate. What happened? Why?

 

 

 

 

ANSWERS TO EXERCISES

1. The cascaded noise figure remains constant since by definition it is measured at 290 K. The cascaded noise figure is independent of the antenna noise temperature.

2. When the antenna noise temperature decreases so does the input and output channel noise power. Likewise the input and output channel noise power increases as the antenna temperature increases.

3. The default noise temperature is 290 K. This default noise source was used since the added noise has been disabled.

Workspace.Name: Attenuator Noise vs Temperature
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Noise\Attenuator Noise vs Temperature.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Attenuator Noise vs Temperature Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how noise is calculated for a simple device like an attenuator for different generator and attenuator temperatures.

 

BACKGROUND

Noise Power is a function of noise temperature. The available total noise power (matched case) is: k*T*B where k is Boltzman's constant, T is Temperature in K, and B is the noise bandwidth. The excess noise temperature is the equivalent input noise temperature for a noiseless circuit. Texcess = (L - 1) * Tphsyical where L is the attenuator loss (linear not dB) and Tphysical is the physical temperature in K of the attenuator. The excess noise temperature is referred to the input so the input noise power can be calculated by k*Texcess*B and then multiplied by the gain of the attenuator to determine the available output noise power. Excess noise power at the output = ( k*B*G ) * (L - 1)*Tphysical. The available generator noise output power is k*Tg*B*G where Tg is the temperature of the generator in K. The total noise available at the output of the attenuator is the sum of the generator noise and excess noise at the output.

Total available output noise = ( k*B*G ) * [ Tg + (L - 1) * Tphysical ].

 

The IRE definition (1952) of noise figure is: F = Output Noise / (Input Noise * G) = Output Noise / (k*To*G) = Output noise / (k*290*G) where 290 K is the defined noise temperature for noise factor measurements. Using these equations F = 1 + (L-1)*(Tphysical / To).

 

H.T. Friis also defined noise figure as the ratio of Signal to Noise at the input versus the Signal to Noise at the output: F = SNRin / SNRout when the generator noise temperature is set to 290K or Tg = 290 K.

 

Spectrasys uses the IRE definition of noise figure. However, both definitions of noise figure give idenitical results when Tg = Tphysical = To = 290 K.

 

Note: The IRE definition of noise figure is independent of the generator noise temperature Tg however the Friis definition of noise figure is dependent on the generator noise temperature.

 

Noise Figure = 10 Log ( Noise Factor )

 

Room temperature has been defined to be 290 K or 16.85 C.


SETUP

A simple cascaded lineup of a source and attenuator are shown in 'Sch1'. Tunable variables have been created for the attenuation value and the generator (source) and physical temperature of the attenuator. A system analysis has been created showing the simulation results of the attenuator. The equation block also calculates noise power at the input and output and the noise figure using both definitions from the IRE and Friis.

 

Individual identification of noise has been enabled on the 'Composite Spectrum Tab' of the System Analysis.

 

 

ANALYSIS

Note: The loss of the attenuator and its noise figure is only identical when the physical temperature of the attenuator (Tphysical) is 290 K. However, the ratio of SNRin / SNRout will only equal the attenuation value when generator noise temperature (Tg) is also 290 K.

 

Spec Out - This graph shows the desired output signal along with the noise components.

 

Data Table - This table shows the simulated channel noise power (CNP) as well as the cascaded noise figure (CNF).

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune generator temperature 'Tg' and note the effects on the total thermal noise power, noise figure and ratio of signal to noise ratio in both the 'Data Table' and calculated equations.

2. Tune the physical temperature of the attenuator 'TPhysical' and note the effects on the total thermal noise power, noise figure and ratio of signal to noise ratio in both the 'Data Table' and calculated equations.

Workspace.Name: Attenuator Noise
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Noise\Attenuator Noise.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Attenuator Noise Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how noise is calculated for a simple device like an attenuator.

 

BACKGROUND

Noise Basic for the simple configuration:

 

Input Port >----- Gain -----> Output Port

 

Noise_OutputPort = Noise_InputPort * Gain + Noise_AddedByGainBlock (1)

 

You can also consider the noise at the output port due to some noise factor multiplied by the gain and input noise:

 

Noise_OutputPort = NoiseFactor * Noise_InputPort * Gain (2)

 

Solving equation (1) for 'Noise_AddedByGainBlock'

 

Noise_AddedByGainBlock = Noise_OutputPort - ( Noise_InputPort * Gain ) (3)

 

Substituting equation (2) into equation (3)

 

Noise_AddedByGainBlock = NoiseFactor * Noise_InputPort * Gain  - ( Noise_InputPort * Gain ) (4)

 

Simplifying (4)

 

Noise_AddedByGainBlock = Noise_InputPort * Gain * ( NoiseFactor  -  1 ) (5)

 

The excess noise or self-noise of the gain device is: ( NoiseFactor - 1 )

 

Noise Figure = 10 Log ( Noise Factor )

 

Room temperature has been defined to be 290 K or 16.85 C.
SETUP

A simple cascaded lineup of a source and attenuator are shown in 'Sch1'. Variables have been created for the attenuation value.

 

An equation block contains all the manual noise calculations for each part as well cascaded noise calculations.

 

Individual identification of noise has been enabled on the 'Composite Spectrum Tab' of the System Analysis.

 

 

ANALYSIS

Spec Out - This graph shows the desired output signal along with the noise components.

 

Data Table - This table shows the simulated channel noise power (CNP) as well as the cascaded noise figure (CNF).

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune 'Atten' and note the effects on the total thermal noise power at the attenuator output.

2. Tune the 'TempC' System Temperature. Are the results consistent with your calculations and expectations?

Workspace.Name: Image Noise
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Noise\Image Noise.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Image Noise Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This simple example illustrates how easy it is to determine the effect of the image noise on receiver sensitivity.  Furthermore, the exact requirements of an image noise rejection filter can be determined.
 
BACKGROUND
Mixer translate their input frequencies to new output frequencies based on the Local Oscillator (LO) frequency. The image frequency is the frequency of a mixer input signal when mixed with the LO frequency will produce the same difference output frequency (IF frequency) as the desired signal when mixed with the same LO.
 
For example, a receiver input band could be from 2110 to 2170 MHz. Let's suppose that the channel bandwidth was 1 MHz and that the IF frequency was 140 MHz. Assuming that the LO frequency is below the RF frequency then an LO tuning range from 1970 to 2030 MHz is needed. If the LO frequency is set to 2000 MHz to receive the 2140 MHz channel then the two basic mixer output frequencies would be the sum of 2140 + 2000 = 4140 MHz and the difference of 2140 - 2000 = 140 MHz. The IF filter would typically be designed filter out the sum frequency.
 
The image frequency is the other RF input frequency that will cause a difference frequency to fall into the IF band. In this case an input frequency of 1860 MHz will also produce and a difference frequency of 140 MHz ( 2000 - 1860 = 140 MHz ).  Consequently, our mixer will receive both the signal at 2140 MHz as well as the 1860 MHz signal unless there is a filter ahead of the mixer to reject the unwanted image. The 1860 MHz frequency is the image of the 2140 MHz signal. 
 
This frequency mixing is not limited to discrete frequencies but also applies to broadband noise. Any noise at the image frequency will also be down converted into the IF band and will increase the cascaded noise figure of the receiver. If no filtering takes place between the LNA and the mixer the cascaded noise figure can be increased by as much as 3 dB!
 
SETUP
This example shows a typical receiver with a low noise amplifier (LNA), attenuator, mixer, and IF filter. Equations have been written such that we can change the RF input frequency and the LO frequency will automatically tune to our desired channel.
 
A quick calculation of the cascaded noise figure can be determined by adding up all the loss up to the first amplifier and then adding the noise figure of the amplifier (assuming the gain of the LNA is large enough). Since we have no loss ahead of the LNA we can just include the noise figure of the LNA which is 2.5 dB.
 
ANALYSIS
Notice in the 'Cascaded NF' graph that the cascaded noise figure jumps up across the mixer by about 3 dB. This can also be seen in the 'RX Table'. This is generally and indication of image noise.
 
EXERCISES
  • To fix the image noise issue we need to add an image reject filter between the output of the LNA and the mixer input.  This can be easily done by dragging the attenuator out of the circuit (you may have to hold down the ALT key so that the wire connections will be broken). Next, drag the image filter located below the main schematic and connect it to the receiver. After a recalculation notice how the cascaded noise figure is now much closer to the expected noise figure.
  • Tune the 'FilterOrder' and notice the affect on the cascaded noise figure.  It's  very easy to see that even a 1 pole filter is sufficient to reject the noise created by the LNA to maintain the desired cascaded noise figure.  However, the upper band should also be checked in this case since the worst case image noise will occur at the highest RF channel frequency.
  • Tune the IF center frequency (place a ? in front of the 140 MHz value in the equation block) if you want to examine the impact of image noise versus IF frequency. As expected when the IF frequency is very low ... about 40 MHz the cascaded noise figure is starting to be effected because of the lack of rejection in the image filter.
CAUTION: Cascaded noise figure equations assume no image noise! In many cases this is a dangerous assumption.
 

SUMMARY

Cascade noise figure equations make some poor assumptions like no image noise. This can be detrimental to the sensitivity of a receiver and lead to a redesign. SPECTRASYS automatically accounts for all the noise in the image channel among many other things giving the user an accurate depiction of the receiver performance before testing in the lab.

Workspace.Name: Mixer Model Noise
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Noise\Mixer Model Noise.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Mixer Model Noise Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how noise is calculated and displayed at each node. Furthermore, it is shown how mixer input and self noise is calculated and how this relates to traditional cascaded equations.

 

BACKGROUND

1. Spectrum Noise - Spectrasys is a broadband noise simulator. The System Analysis specifies a default number of noise points that will be used across the entire simulation bandwidth. Furthermore, a smart noise point insertion algorithm is used to ensure noise points are calculated at signal frequencies. This ensures accurate signal-to-noise ratio measurements even through narrow filters. Each model creates self noise. Each model also propagates noise arriving at each of its terminals. Since each Spectrasys model is bidirectional noise flows in all directions through the model. Spectrums plots at the node will show noise and spectrums traveling in all directions through the node.

 

NOTE: When comparing spectrum noise to cascaded noise calculations the noise traveling in the direction of the path are the only noise spectrums of interest.

 

2. Image Noise - There are 2 aspects of image noise. First, noise arriving at the mixer input at the image frequency will be converted to the mixer output frequency. Image rejection or input noise filtering will attenuate this input noise. Second, noise is generated by the mixer at the desired input frequency as well as at the image frequency. Both of these noise frequencies are amplified by the mixer conversion gain and converted to the mixer output frequency.

 

NOTE: Mixer generated self noise is NOT affected by image rejection nor input noise filtering.

 

3. Traditional Cascaded Noise Calculations - The traditional cascaded noise figure calculations completely ignore both aspects of mixer image noise. Even setting the image rejection in the simulation to a high value will still not give the same noise results as the traditional cascaded noise calculations since these equations also ignore the effects of mixer self noise generated at the image frequency.

 

For additional information on noise please refer to the help file.


SETUP

A simple cascaded lineup of an RF amplifier, mixer, and an IF amplifier are shown in 'Sch1'. Variables have been created for the gain and noise figure for each of these stages as well as the mixer image rejection.

 

An equation block contains all the manual noise calculations for each part as well cascaded noise calculations.

 

 

ANALYSIS

MIxer In Spec - The Source (Port) and RF amplifier self noise can be viewed and compared to the corresponding manually calculated noise given in the equation block.

 

Mixer Out Spec - This graph shows fundamental (desired) and image noise propagated to the mixer output due to mixer input noise consisting of the Source (port) noise as well as the RF amplifier self noise. Furthermore, the mixer generated self noise at the fundamental and image frequencies are also shown. Image rejection is accounted for in both the simulation and manual noise calculations.

 

IF Amp Out Spec - This graph shows the IF amplified Source (port) and RF amplifier self noise propagated through the mixer as well as the amplified mixer self noise.

 

Spectrasys Table - This table shows the simulated channel noise power (CNP) as well as the cascaded noise figure (CNF). Also in this table is the traditional cascaded noise figure calculations (ECNF).

 

NOTE: That regardless of the amount of image rejection the simulated noise is higher than the traditional cascaded noise figure due to the mixer self noise created at the image frequency.

 

Equation Table - This table shows the manually calculated 'CascadedNoisePower' as well as the 'CascadedNF'. Also in this table is the 'CascadedGain' calculations.. These results compare to those in the 'Spectrasys Table'.

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune 'Image Rejection' and note the effects on the cascaded noise figure. Note that the traditional cascaded noise figure measurements are unaffected by changes in image rejection.

2. Enable the tuning of other gain and noise figure parameters by placing a '?' in front of the respective value in the equation block. Tune these variables and compare simulated and manually calculated results.

Workspace.Name: Negative Noise Figure
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Noise\Negative Noise Figure.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Negative Noise Figure Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration showing how cascaded noise figure can be negative through a system.

 

BACKGROUND

The cascaded noise figure of a system is a ratio of the signal-to-noise ratio at the input compared to the signal-to-noise ratio at the output.

 

F = ( S/N )in / ( S/N )out 

 

A negative noise figure can occur when the signal-to-noise ratio at the output is larger than the input. This occurs when noise is measured in a bandwidth that is larger than the signal bandwidth and filters downstream in the chain have bandwidths smaller than noise measurement bandwidth.

 


SETUP

A CW source is created that has a frequency of 140 MHz, which is in the intermediated frequency (IF) range. The source is followed by an amplifier that has a gain of 20 dB and a noise figure of 0 dB, for illustration purposes. The amplifier is followed by an ideal isolator and an 11 pole bandpass filter that has a tunable bandwidth. The default bandwidth for the filter is 100 kHz.

 

A system analysis has been created. The Channel Bandwidth is also tunable and has a default value of 1 MHz.

 

The CW signal power at the input is -50 dBm. Since the Channel Bandwidth is set to 1 MHz the total noise power at the input is -113.975 dBm yielding a ( S/N )in ratio of 63.975 dB. The noise and signal are both amplified by 20 dB by the RF amplifier. The signal at the amplifier output is -30 dBm and the noise -93.975 dBm which still yields a 63.975 dB S/N ratio. When the signal and noise meet the 100 kHz wide bandpass filter much of the noise power in the 1 MHz channel is filtered just leaving the noise in the 100 kHz bandwidth. This noise power drops by about 10 dB while the signal is not attenuated. This gives a  ( S/N )out of -30 dBm / -103.933 dBm = 73.932 dB. The ( S/N )in / ( S/N )out = -9.957 dB showing that the noise figure improved through the system.

 

Note: The reason the noise figure doesn't change by exactly 10 dB is because the filter skirts are not ideal and the noise power spectrum is integrated. Additional noise points have been added to the system analysis to provide noise points in the narrow filter bandwidth.

 

Note: The cascaded noise figure appears to change across the isolator and not the filter. This is because noise at the filter input is attenuated due to the mismatch loss of the filter. The out-of-band input impedance to the filter is NOT 50 ohms!

 

A linear analysis has been created and the noise figure versus frequency is displayed in a plot. Notice that the linear noise figure shows 0 dB in the pass band. This is because a linear analysis has no concept of channel bandwidth and the signal and noise are always measured in the same bandwidth.

 

ANALYSIS

Cascaded NF - This graphs shows that the cascaded noise figure is -10 dB.

 

Linear NF - This graphs shows how the linear noise figure is 0 dB in the passband and high everywhere else.

 

System NF Data - This table shows cascaded system parameters as they travel through the system.

 

Other graphs include the signal spectrum at various nodes.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the channel bandwidth to 1 Hz. What is the cascaded noise figure? How does it compare to the linear analysis?

2. Tune the filter bandwidth to 1 MHz. What is the cascaded noise figure?

3. Reduce the filter bandwidth. What happens to the cascaded noise figure?

 

Note: There is an accuracy limit issue associated with the ratio of the channel bandwidth to the filter bandwith. As the filter becomes really narrow additional noise points must be added within the measurement bandwidth so the integration integrity can be maintained.

Workspace.Name: Noise Wave Power
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Noise\Noise Wave Power.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Noise Wave Power Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This file illustrates how you can obtain noise wave information directly from the linear noise S-Correlation matrix. The diagonal of this matrix represents the noise going out each port (not including ANY port noise), normalized to kT.  This matrix is normalized to the actual port impedances, so no renormalization is necessary to correct for impedance mismatch.

 

To find the total wave going out any port, we simply add the noise power to the noise due to the rest of the ports.  That noise is simply the sum of the magnitudes of all S parameters going to that port (remember, the noise wave power from a matched resistor is always kT, and our correlation power is normalized to kT).  The noise wave is then denormlalized by multiplying by kT.

Workspace.Name: NPR Measurement
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Noise\NPR Measurement.wsv
Workspace.Description:
NPR Measurement Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how do perform noise power ratio (NPR) measurement.

 

BACKGROUND

The NPR measurement in Spectrasys is almost trivial due to the Spectral Propagation and Root Cause Analysis (SPARCA) engine found in Spectrasys. Since SPARCA can keep track of signals separate from intermods and noise a notch in the spectrum is not needed to accurately measure the intermods in the channel.

SETUP

This a simple setup consisting of a 21 carrier source and an RF amplifier. Each carrier is CW with a 1 MHz spacing to represent a continuum of signal spectrum. Each of the 21 carriers has a power level of -30 dBm. A path has been created from the input to output of the amplifier. A special display mode is used to only show signal groups instead of all the individual spectrums.

 

ANALYSIS

Out Spec - The graphs shows the intermod spectrum in one color and the signal spectrum in another. Even though individual 3rd intermods have a much lower power level when they are combined coherently they cause peaks in the spectrum and can be readily seen underneath the signals.

 

Path Table - The table shows the 'Channel Power (CP)' of the signals which are about - 5 dBm at the amplifier output. Also shown is the 3rd and 2nd order intermod power in the same channel as shown in the 'TIMCP3' and 'TIMCP2' measurements respectively. As expected there is no 2nd order intermod power underneath this particular group of carriers. The ratio of the 'CP' to the 'TIMCP3' is the NPR ... or in this case the 'Carrier to Noise and Distortion Ratio' since phase noise and thermal noise are not significant contributors.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the power level and note the change in 'CNDR'.

 

2. Enable the display for individual and total spectrums to see the amount of intermod regrowth within the channel.

Workspace.Name: True Cascaded Noise Figure
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Noise\True Cascaded Noise Figure.wsv
Workspace.Description:
True Cascaded Noise Figure Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how traditional cascaded noise figure will give incorrect answers unless all paths are considered. 

 

BACKGROUND

 

Traditional Cascaded Noise Figure

NFcascade = F1 + (F2 - 1) / G1 + (F3 - 1) / G1G2 + ... + (Fn - 1) / G1G2...Gn-1

 

Note: Traditional cascaded noise figure equations are not used in Spectrasys. The are very restrictive and suffer from the following conditions:

  • Ignore effects of VSWR, frequency, and bandwidth

  • Assume noise contributions are from a single path

  • Ignore mixer image noise

  • Can ignore effects of gain compression

The SPARCA (Spectral Propagation and Root Cause Analysis) technique used Spectrasys does not suffer from these restrictive assumptions. Occasionally users are troubled if Spectrasys simulations give different answers than the traditional approach. Using Spectrasys under the same assumptions as the traditional approach will always yield identical answers. To use Spectrasys under the same assumptions only frequency independent blocks like attenuators and amplifiers must be used. Even so, amplifiers must be used as linear devices with infinite reverse isolation. Filters cannot be used since their impedance varies with frequency. Mixers cannot be used since noise from the image band will be converted into the mixer output. Only 2 port devices must be used because of the single path assumption. Of course the bandwidth must also be very narrow.


SETUP

A 'main' and 'secondary' paths are created in this example. The 'main' path consists of just the passive loss of the splitter which is 3.02 dB. The 'secondary' path is made up of an RF amplifier with a gain of 20 dB and a noise figure of 5 dB. This amplifier drives the other leg of the splitter.

 

A Spectrasys simulation has been create and the cascaded noise figure (CNF) results of both paths are illustrated in the tables. Likewise, a linear analysis has been created also showing the noise figure of both paths.

 

ANALYSIS

Linear NF Table - This table shows the cascaded noise figure for both the 'main' and 'secondary' paths from the linear simulator.

 

Main Path Table - This table shows the cascaded noise figure (CNF) for the 'main' path from a Spectrasys simulation.

 

Secondary Path Table - This table shows the cascaded noise figure (CNF) for the 'secondary' path from a Spectrasys simulation.

 

NOTE: That even though the linear simulator and Spectrasys use completely independent noise simulation techniques they give the same noise figure results. However, once mixers are involved linear simulations have to deal with the frequency translation as well at image noise ... which they don't do!

 

Traditional cascaded noise figure equations would yield a cascaded noise figure of 3.02 dB for the 'main' path ... which is completely wrong ... since this noise figure is 25.0 dB. For the 'secondary' path traditional cascaded noise figure equations would predict a cascaded noise figure of 5.0 dB ... which is correct. Remember, if the gain of the amplifier was much less the thermal noise of the 'main' path would begin to affect the true noise figure of the secondary path.

 

EXERCISES

1. Add a mixer and LO to the output of the splitter. Note that the true cascaded noise figure in Spectrasys shows a cascaded noise figure of greater than 28 dB due to the image noise of the mixer.

 

2. Set the image rejection of the mixer to 100 dB. The noise figure will now improve by about 3 dB. (The image is at 80 MHz so the band below the LO is the image).

 

NOTE: The linear simulator uses the mixer RF to IF isolation since this property provides no frequency translation. The user can 'fake out' the linear simulator by changing the RF to IF isolation to be the same value as the conversion loss. Remember, the linear simulator cannot deal with mixer image noise ... but Spectrasys can!
