Workspace.Name: Base Station RX Front End
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Optimization\Base Station RX Front End.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Base Station RX Front End Yield and Opt Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This workspace shows the how to determine the budgeting tradeoffs between a base station receiver front end and its individual receivers. The front end consists of a single LNA split 12 ways to support 12 receivers. The gain, noise figure, and IP3 requirements will be determined for the LNA and receivers through optimization and the final yield results by a yield analysis.  

 

BACKGROUND

Low noise figure and high input third order intercepts are important performance parameters for most base stations. For multiple receivers it is usually more cost effective to spend extra money on a good single LNA and then split the output to drive several receivers.

 

SETUP

This example is a PCS base station which covers the 1850 to 1910 MHz receive band. A single front end receive filter and LNA are used before a 12 way splitter. RG-214 cable is used between the splitter and receivers. The receivers are represented by amplifiers. Since the gain of the amplifiers are set to zero then output parameters such as IP3 are referred to the input ... which is what we want if we are trying to determine the high level requirements for the receiver. Furthermore, since this gain is zero the cascaded gain from input to output really represents the front end gain. Tables and level diagrams have been added to display the cascaded noise figure, front end gain, and input third order intercept point for our base station.

 

OPTIMIZATION AND YIELD

In order to get the best performance out of our receiver we need to determine what the optimum LNA and receiver parameters are. We will use the optimizer to determine the optimal LNA gain, LNA noise figure, LNA IP3, receiver noise figure, and receiver IIP3.

 

1. LNA and receiver variables must be created in the equation block.

2. These variables need to be substituted back into the respective elements in the schematic.

3. An optimization evaluation is added. Cascaded noise figure and input third order intercept parameters will be optimized. The path needs to be selected and the node location that the goals apply to along the given path. Optimization goals have been set for cascaded noise figure < 3 dB and input third order intercept > 5 dBm. Noise figure has a higher weight in this example.

4. A yield evaluation has been set up in a similar manner to the optimization targets so that we can determine the yield of the final design. The yield goals are cascaded noise figure is < 3.5 dB and input third order intercept > 2.5 dBm.

5. Variable constraints can be entered to limit the range of the variables during the optimization and yield processes. This is done on the 'Variables' tab of the respective optimization and yield evaluations.

 

NOTE: Optimization goals are set higher than yield goals because optimizer performance is much better when goals are harder to achieve.


ANALYSIS

IIP3 - This is the system input third order intercept point for the entire receiver. Note that the intercept point before any optimization is about +2.0 dBm.

 

Noise Figure - This is the system cascaded noise figure for the entire receiver. Note that the cascaded noise figure is about 3.9 dB before optimization.

 

RX Data Table - This table contains some basic receiver parameters including cascaded noise figure and third order intercept point.

 

EXERCISES

1. Run the yield analysis by right clicking on the 'Yield Targets' evaluation and select 'Calculate'. Note that all 10 runs fail the yield goals.

 

2. Start the optimizer by right clicking on the 'NF & IP3 Opt' evaluation and select and optimize routine (i.e. Least Squares, Automatic). After running for a few minutes we see that the noise figure is down to about 3 dB from the initial value of about 3.9 dB. The IIP3 went up from about +2 dBm to about +5 dBm. Click 'Stop' to stop the optimizer.

 

3. Rerun the yield analysis. Notice how the yield analysis is now about 100% for both the cascaded noise figure and third order intercept point.

 

NOTE: Before running the Monte Carlo analysis the user may want to set the LNA and receiver values to the typical values that would be used for the component specifications. The variable constraints may also be adjusted to closely represent the actual specification of the LNA and receiver after the optimization. This will result in a more accurate representation of the expected performance of components that meet their specification. Furthermore, a variable can be created for the cable length and the yield analysis or optimization can be configured for this variable also. Consider using the 'rand()' function to create random cable lengths between two fixed limits for differing cable lengths for all twelve receivers.
Workspace.Models: *OUT@RF Design:BPF_ELLIPTIC@RF Design:MultiSource@RF Design:RFAMP@RF Design:RG214@RF Design:SPLIT3@RF Design:SPLIT4@RF Design

Workspace.Name: Intermod w Optimization
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Optimization\Intermod w Optimization.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Intermods with Optimization Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how do perform an optimization along a path in Spectrasys.

 

BACKGROUND

Non-linear behavior models, like amplifier and mixers, will generate intermods and harmonics in Spectrasys. These intermods will propagate both forward and backwards along all paths. These intermods can be separated by intermod order and processed by path measurements. Spectrum identification information is available for every data point in a spectral plot.

 

Cascaded intermod equations are not used in Spectrasys. These equations make restrictive assumptions like a) frequency response is always flat, b) all stages are perfectly matched, c) intermods come from only one path, d) intermods never travel backwards, e) interfering tones generating intermods are never attenuated through the path, etc.. Instead, Spectrasys uses a SPARCA (Spectral Propagation and Root Cause Analysis) technique to overcome all of these limitations. Non-linear behavioral models create intermods and harmonics which propagate forwards and backwards. Measurements then operate on intermod and harmonic power found within the channel bandwidth.

 

To accomplish this Spectrasys knows the difference between intermods that are generated (GIMCP) in a particular stage versus those conducted (CIMCP) from prior stages. Generated and conducted intermods can be summed together to provide total intermod power (TIMCP) that is conducted to the following stage.

 

Measuring intermods and intercept points in Spectrasys is much like doing so in the lab. Interfering tones must be created at necessary frequencies to generate intermods that fall within the channel being measured.

SETUP

This example uses two cascaded amplifiers amongst other passive stages. A three tone signal source is used to create 2 interfering tones and a third signal used as a pilot to determine the gain of the channel at the same frequency as the third order intermods. The two interfering signals appear at 4100 and 4200 MHz each having a power of -20 dBm. The intermod and pilot frequencies are at 4000 MHz. The pilot signal power level is -100 dBm. The path frequency is also set to 4000 MHz so intermods will appear in the measured channel.

 

The channel measurement bandwidth is set to 10 kHz, which is wide enough to account for the intermod bandwidth but small enough to exclude the interfering tones. Intermods in Spectrasys will have bandwidths according to their intermod order and the bandwidths of the parent signals. For example, a 3rd order intermod with the equation of Fintermod = 2 x F1 - 3 x F2 would have the following bandwidth BWintermod = 2 x BW1 + 3 x BW2. Note: bandwidths never subtract.

 

If the channel measurement bandwidth is set narrower than BWintermod then the full intermod power will not appear in the spectrum plots nor the path measurements.

 

ANALYSIS

Intermod Table - This table shows a summary of intermod measurements. The cascaded gain (CGAIN) measurements show the gain of the channel at 4000 MHz. One interferer channel is shown at 4100 MHz (ICF and ICP). The total third order intermod channel power (TIMCP3) is shown as well at the percent third order intermod power (PRIM3). See the 'Percent IM3' heading for more information.

 

Percent IM3 - This level diagram show the percent contribution of the given stage to the total intermod power. From this graph it is relatively easy to see where the main offending stage is, the first RF amplifier.

 

Also it can be seen that the total percentage from all stages is greater than 100%. This difference is due to coherent addition. The measurement projects what the intermod power would be at the output of the path assuming linear operations. Since coherent addition can cause doubling or canceling the measurement is unable to accurately predict the contribution to the total in these cases. When 'Coherent Addition' is disabled the sum will equal 100%.

 

Intermod Diagram - This level diagram shows 3 basic intermod measurements along the path 1) total third order intermod channel power (TIMCP3), 2) generated third order intermod channel power (GIMCP3), and 3) conducted third order intermod channel power (CIMCP3). A lot of information can be gleaned off of this graph. First, TIMCP3 is equal to GIMCP3 and CIMCP3 ... except for backward propagating intermods ... like those that appear back at the path input. Second, generated intermods in the first RF amplifier stage dominate the intermod performance of the cascade chain.

 

EXERCISES

Redistribute the gain between the first and second amplifiers to lower the total third order intermod power while maintaining a cascaded gain of 10 dB.

 

One solution is to reduce the gain of the first RF amplifier stage from 20 dB to 16 dB and increase the 2nd RF amplifier stage from 10 dB to 14 dB. The cascaded gain will remain the same though the intermod performance improves by over 5 dB.

 

OPTIMIZATION

Any path measurement in Spectrasys can be optimized. To optimize a path measurement the following steps must be taken. 1) Create variables that the optimizer can tune, 2) place these variables in their respective models, and 3) create an optimization for the path using the desired measurements and variables.

 

Variables for gain and 1 dB compression point have been created for each RF amplifier. Intercept points have been tied to their respective compression points. These variables have been placed in their respective models.

 

 An optimization has been created and two measurements have been selected for optimization, cascaded gain (CGAIN) and total third order intermod channel power (TIMCP3). Intermod performance cannot come at the expense of reducing the cascaded gain so a larger weighting will be given to the cascaded gain measurement. The goal will be improve the intermod performance from around -72 dBm to something less than -95 dBm.

 

Tuned variables have been added to the optimization and maximum gain and 1 dB compression limits have been added.

 

OPTIMIZATION EXERCISES

Right click on the 'Intermod Opt' optimization and select 'Optimize: Least Squares, Automatic'. The optimizer will change the gain and compression points of the amplifiers to achieve better intermod performance while maintaining the cascaded gain.

Workspace.Name: Forced Path Frequency
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Paths\Forced Path Frequency.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Forced Path Frequency Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to create a path that changes frequency at a user specified node name.

 

BACKGROUND

The system analysis keeps track of the path frequency even through frequency translation devices such as frequency multipliers, dividers, and mixers. The path frequency is post processed after all spectrum have been propagated throughout the system. Each element in the path determines it desired output frequency. For example, a multiply by 4 multiplier will have a path output frequency that is 4 times that of the input. For a mixer the user selects the desired output, sum or difference. This information is used by the path to determine the intended frequency at the mixer output.

 

There are occasions where the user would like to track a particular frequency through the system. This can be done by associating another frequency with a given node along the path. This is implemented by having path node name and frequency pairs. If only 1 frequency is specified then the system analysis will determine the frequency of the entire path. If a 2nd frequency is specified the path frequency will change frequency at the 2nd node name specified in the path. The user can add as main node name frequency pairs as they would like.


SETUP

This schematic is a simple line up that represents a high frequency LO chain (1.75 to 14 GHz). The chain consists of a 1.75 GHz LO input that is amplified, filtered, and multiplied a total of 8 times to achieve the 14 GHz operating frequency.

 

Two paths have been created. Both start at the LO and end at the output port. The first path has the normal frequency line up.

 

The 2nd or harmonic path is configured to track the 2nd harmonic at the output of 'Amp2' all the way to the output. This path starts out at 1.75 GHz and gets doubled at the output of the first multiplier to become 3.5 GHz. At the output of 'Amp2' we want to track the 7 GHz 2nd harmonic. Normally the path frequency would want to be multiplied by 4 at the output of the 4 times multiplier. To continue to track the 7 GHz signal the frequency is set back to 7 GHz at the output of the 4 times multiplier. The harmonic path definition summary is:

 

Nodes: 1;4;5;2
Frequency: 1.75;7.0;7.0 GHz

 

In summary we see that 1.75 GHz is associated with node 1, 7.0 GHz for node 4, 7.0 GHz at node 5 and through the remainder of the circuit.

ANALYSIS

Out Spec - This graph shows the spectrum of the high frequency LO chain.

 

LO Table - This table shows the basic signals traveling through the LO path. Notice the channel frequency changes through the system (CF measurement).

 

Amp2 2nd Harm Table - This table shows how the path frequency has been forced to 7 GHz at the output of 'Amp2' and remains constant through to the output.

 

EXERCISES

1. Remove the last frequency (7.0 GHz) from the 'HarmPath' and notice the channel frequency (CF) now gets multiplied by 4 at the output of the multiply by 4 multiplier.

Workspace.Name: Switched Filter Bank
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Paths\Switched Filter Bank.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Switched Filter Bank Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates that both the path frequency and path definition track through the state of a switch.

 

BACKGROUND

The complete list of nodes for a path is created during the simulation run. The path is determined by finding the shortest path that contains all the parts or node names specified by the user. When multiple paths exist that have the same path length the first path found by the simulator will be used. This may not be the path intended by the user. This may be especially true when using a switched filter bank. In this case the user would generally like the path to follow the state of the switch.

 

An option is provided in the path setup that forces the path to follow the switch state.

 

Furthermore, a different path frequency may be desired for each of the switched paths.


SETUP

A 5 filter switch bank has been created. The center frequency spacing of the filters is 100 MHz apart. A variable has been created in the equation block to allow setting both switches simultaneously. Five carriers have been created in a multisource also spaced by 100 MHz with the beginning frequency at 2100 MHz. Other variables have also been defined to control other aspects of the created carriers.

 

Five frequency comb carriers have been created in the source and applied to the input of the switch bank. Each carrier power level decreases by 5 dB beginning with the 2nd carrier. The reason for the decrease in power level is to easily show the user that a different carrier is being used for the path calculations when the switch state is changed.

 

A vector of path frequencies is created in the equation block. The switch state is used to pick the actual path frequency from the path frequency vector.

 

ANALYSIS

Output Spec - This graph shows the channel power through the filter bank. When the switch state is changed the appropriate carrier is selected. This carrier power level differs from the other carriers.

 

Chan Pwr - This graph shows the output spectrum of the filter bank followed by an amplifier. As the switch state is changed the user can observe the selected carrier.

 

Channel Table - This table shows a list of the parts for the selected path along with some common path measurements.

 

EXERCISES

1. Disable the 'Force path through Switch state' option on the edit path dialog box and tune the filter state while watching the table and graphs. Notice how the path now remains fixed.

Workspace.Name: Spectrum Phase
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Phase\Spectrum Phase.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Spectrum Phase Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example will show the user how to display the pahse of individual spectral components of an internal node.

 

BACKGROUND

Since SPECTRASYS has a spectral domain engine each spectral component is propagated to every node in the system. After breaking down the spectrum into its individual pieces the user will be able to see the phase of each spectral component, even for internal nodes.

 

SETUP

In this particular example we have two transmission lines that each have a given electrical length in degrees for the specified frequency. Both of these transmission lines are connected together at a common node. Two sources have been created for each of the transmission lines at the same frequency as the electrical delay of those lines. Consequently, if we decompose the spectrum into its individual pieces and then look at the angle of the voltage of the common node we will see that the phase of the spectral components is the same as the respective transmission line electrical delay. To decompose the spectrum the "Show Individual Spectrums" option should be selected on the 'Composite Spectrum' tab of 'System1' simulation. Furthermore, the 'Show Individual Signals' checkbox should be checked on this same tab.

 

OBSERVATIONS

'Output Phase' graph: This is a graph of the phase of the voltage at node (4) where the transmission lines are combined. Markers have been place on each of the two spectral components. The marker phase shows the phase delay of the transmission line as expected. The attenuator was placed in the schematic to show that measuring the phase of internal nodes is very easy.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the phase of the each of the transmission lines and observe how the respective phase of the signal changes.

 

2. Tune the phase of each of the sources and observe that the resultant phase is a sum of both the source phase and phase of the transmission line. Note: To make the source phase tuneable click the 'Tune' checkbox of the 'Phase Shift' parameter in the 'CW Source' dialog box.

Workspace.Name: Phase Noise and Noise Figure
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Phase Noise\Phase Noise and Noise Figure.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phase Noise and Noise Figure Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how phase noise affects the cascaded noise figure.  Two cases are examined. The phase noise introduced 1) in the middle of schematic as with a mixer LO,  2) at the input to a cascade of amplifiers.

 

BACKGROUND

The Noise Factor of a system is ( S/N )in / ( S/N )out. The Noise Figure (dB) = 10Log( Noise Factor ). The Cascaded Noise Figure measurement in Spectrasys includes both thermal and phase noise powers. The phase noise contributes to the total noise power and will cause an increase in the cascaded noise figure. If however phase noise is only added to a system at the input then phase noise will increase proportional to the signal level throughout the system. If the phase noise power is larger than the thermal noise power, which is generally the case, then thermal noise contributions are so small that they may not affect the noise figure. In the case where the phase noise power is significantly larger than the thermal noise power then the cascaded noise figure will be shown as 0 dB since the thermal noise contribution does not affect the overal signal to noise ratio through the cascade.


SETUP

There are two cases that are examined. 1) Two amplifiers in cascade separated by an attenuator where phase noise is added at the source. 2) A simple receiver where the phase noise is added to the system by a mixer LO.

 

The carrier frequency of 1950 MHz is used in both cases. Two system analyzes are created each pointing to the same schematic respectively. One has phase noise calculation enabled and the other does not.

 

ANALYSIS

Amp Noise No Phase Noise - In this table we see the thermal noise power (or Channel Noise Power) CNP and the Phase Noise Channel Power PNCP which has been turned off in its system analysis. Therefore phase noise in this case will have no impact on the cascaded noise figure since it is not calculated. The Carrier to Noise Ratio CNR is also shown which is the difference between DCP and CNP plus PNCP. Since PNCP is off this is really a ratio of DCP and CNP.

 

Amp Noise With Phase Noise - This table is similar to Amp Noise No Phase Noise except that the phase noise has been turned on. Since the Phase Noise Channel Power is > 30 dB higher than the thermal noise the addition of the thermal noise or Channel Noise Power has no effect on the total noise power and the Carrier to Noise Ratio is constant through the system. Because the Carrier to Noise Ratio is constant through the system the Cascaded Noise Figure must be 0 by definition.

 

Mixer Noise No Phase Noise - Since the phase noise calculation is turned off the cascaded noise figure appears to be normal.

 

Mixer Noise With Phase Noise - Phase noise calculations are enabled and the phase noise channel power at the output the mixer increases dramatically causing the Carrier to Noise ratio to decrease. Notice that the phase noise channel power is > 30 dB above the thermal noise power eliminating any contributing affects to the cascaded noise figure result.

 

 

EXERCISES

Mixer Phase Noise

1. Change the phase noise amplitude in the Local Oscillator and predict what the noise figure will be.

2. What power level of LO phase noise is needed to have little affect on the overall noise figure?

 

Cascaded Amp Phase Noise

1. Change the phase noise amplitude in the Multisource and predict what the noise figure will be.

2. What power level of phase noise is needed to have the same noise power as the thermal noise? What happens to the cascaded noise figure in this case?

 

 

 

 

 

 

ANSWERS TO EXERCISES

 

Cascaded Amp Phase Noise

2. The current PNCP value is -140 dBm/Hz and the thermal noise is -173.975 dBm. Hence the current phase noise power at the center of the channel needs to drop by 33.975 dB. The current value of phase noise specified in the Multisource at the lowest offset is -90 dBm/Hz thus the value must be changed to -123.975 dBm/Hz. The values at the other offsets should be lowered accordingly. The cascaded noise figure starts out at 3 dB at the source output since the phase noise channel power and channel noise power are equal.

Workspace.Name: Phase Noise and Ref Clock
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Phase Noise\Phase Noise and Ref Clock.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phase Noise and Ref Clock Workspace

Keysight Technologies Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration showing how to implement a master reference clock in a system that has multiple oscillators using the same reference clock. 

 

BACKGROUND

Phase noise at a mixer output will be added coherently for sum products and subtracted coherently for difference products if both the input signal and LO are tied to the same reference clock. Furthermore, the amplitude of the phase noise for a given oscillator will be multiplied by the difference in frequency between the reference oscillator frequency and the frequency of the source or LO.

 

For example, using a reference oscillator of 10 MHz for a 1000 MHz source the phase noise of the reference oscillator would be multiplied by 20 Log( 1000 / 10 ) = 40 dB. Thus the 1000 MHz source would have phase noise higher than the reference oscillator by 40 dB.

 


SETUP

The phase noise for a reference oscillator has been defined in the equation block. The reference oscillator is chosen to have a reference frequency of 10 MHz. A scale factor is calculated in dB for each of the oscillators that represents the reference oscillator phase noise scalling. The calculated phase noise is used for all signal sources in a double coversion receiver schematic. All sources in the schematic are locked to the same reference clock called 'A'. To unlock one of the reference clocks this name can be changed or left blank.

 

The equation block also calculates what the simulated phase noise should be at the output of Mixer1 and of the system.

 

The dual conversion receiver uses the 1st mixer as an upconversion stage and the 2nd as a down conversion stage.

 

ANALYSIS

Phase Noise Table - This table shows the phase noise in dBc for each source as well as the calculated phase noise for sum and difference products for each mixer.

 

Out Spec - This graph shows the output spectrum of the system. Notice that the output phase noise is lower than the original source phase noise.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the reference clock frequency. What happened to the phase noise shown in the Phase Noise Table?

 

2. Unlock the reference clock to one of the oscillators on the 1st mixer. Can you predict the resultant output phase noise for the system?

Workspace.Name: Phase Noise Cancellation
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Phase Noise\Phase Noise Cancellation.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phase Noise Cancellation Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to cancel the effects of LO phase noise in an RF system. 

 

BACKGROUND

If the same LO (or coherent LOs) is used to down-convert an RF input signal to an IF frequency then up-converted back to the carrier frequency the output phase noise should be cancelled. Of course in order for this technique to work the phase noise of the RF input signal must be smaller than the phase noise of the LO. Furthermore, non-linear distortion in the RF path between the two mixers can also prevent cancellation.


SETUP

A signal source is created at 1 GHz. An LNA precedes the first mixer that down-converts the RF signal down to a 100 MHz IF. This signal is filtered, then up-converted back to 1 GHz.

 

Even though two oscillators are used in this schematic they are phase coherent because there are at the same frequency and have the same reference clock. The user could also choose to use a single oscillator followed by a splitter.

 

ANALYSIS

Data Table - This table gives an overview of the noise performance along the path. The thermal noise (CNP) and phase noise (PNCP) channel powers are shown along with the cascaded noise figure (CNF).

 

Mixer 2 Out Spec - This spectrums shows the cancelled phase noise centered around the carrier at the system output. The filter changes the phase at other phase noise offsets so they are not cancelled.

 

CNF - This level diagram shows the effect of the cancelled phase noise on the noise figure. Of course the reason for the huge noise figure in the first place is because of the poor LO phase noise.

 

EXERCISES

1. Disable the phase noise calculation on the 'Calculate Tab' of the System Analysis. Compare the cascaded noise figure when the phase noise is calculated and when it is not.

2. Change the reference clock in one of the LOs. Notice that there is no cancellation now since the LOs are no longer coherent.

Workspace.Name: Phase Noise Channel Power
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Phase Noise\Phase Noise Channel Power.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phase Noise Channel Power Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a very basic illustration of calculation of phase noise.

 

BACKGROUND

Phase noise looks linear versus frequency on a logarithmic axis. Care must be taken when integrating the area underneath this type of curve because simple linear interpolation will produces errors. In this example, the difference in channel power this this simple phase noise curve is about ~3.8 dB, where the more accurate logarithmic integrations yields the lower power level.


SETUP

This is a very basic analysis with a single RF amplifier. The phase noise in the amplifier model has been enabled as well as the calculation of the phase noise in the system analysis. An equation block specifies the phase noise parameters as well as doing both a simple linear integration approach as well as a more complicated logarithmic integration method.

 

ANALYSIS

Spec Out - We see the output spectrum of the amplifier and notice that residual phase noise has been created on the desired amplifier output spectrum. The residual phase noise does not appear on intermods and harmonics.

 

Main Equ - This equation block  integrates the phase noise in a simple linear fashion (TrapezoidPNPwr_dBm = -46.541 dBm) and in a logarithmic fashion (LogPNPwr_dBm = -50.31 dBm).

 

Data Table - This table shows the phase noise channel power (PNCP) calculation which simulates the phase noise power to be -50.311 dBm at the amplifier output. This is the same as the calculated out.

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the number of Bins in the equation block and observe the changes in the calculated LogPNPwr_dBm.

2. Change the residual phase noise values in the equation block and notice the effect.

Workspace.Name: Phase Noise Plot from Dataset
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Phase Noise\Phase Noise Plot from Dataset.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Phase Noise Plot from Dataset Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This workspace shows how to extract and plot the SSB phase noise from an RF carrier. 

 

BACKGROUND

Spectrasys has the ability to separate different types of spectrum along a path. One of these path spectrum types is phase noise. These path spectrum groups can be added to the path dataset by checking the 'Power, Voltage, and Impedances' option in the path. Then using some simple math the phase noise can be extracted from the desired carrier. This phase noise can then be shifted down to baseband to be plotted.

 

The steps are as follows:

  1. Create a path and enable 'Power, Voltages, and Impedances' along the path.
  2. Extract the phase noise vector at the carrier of interest.
  3. Extract the frequency offset vector that corresponds to the phase noise vector.
  4. Shift the frequency offset vector down to baseband.
  5. Set the independent variable of the new phase noise variable.


SETUP

A very simple transmitter is constructed from a signal source, a mixer, and local oscillator. The input IF frequency is 300 MHz with a 1 GHz LO frequency. The phase noise for the LO is created in the equation block. The equation block is also used for post processing to extract out the phase noise from the 1300 MHz carrier.

 

ANALYSIS

Defined Phase Noise - This is a plot of the phase noise defined in the equation block.

 

Full Output Spectrum - This graph shows the full spectrum at the mixer output.

 

Output Spectrum Groups - This graph show only the phase noise and desired spectrum groups at the mixer output. This illustrates different types of spectrum groups along a path.

 

Output Phase Noise - This graph show final post processed SSB phase noise extracted from the 1300 MHz carrier.

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the phase noise variable 'PN1' and notice the change in the phase noise plots.

Workspace.Name: RF Amp Residual Phase Noise
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Phase Noise\RF Amp Residual Phase Noise.wsv
Workspace.Description:
RF Amp Residual Phase Noise Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a very basic illustration of residual phase noise in an RF amplifier. 

 

BACKGROUND

Residual (additive) phase noise is the self phase noise of a model that adds to an existing signal that passes through the model. Residual phase noise does and will affect the cascaded noise figure. It may become more dominant than thermal noise.


SETUP

This is a very basic analysis with a single RF amplifier. The phase noise in the amplifier model has been enabled as well as the calculation of the phase noise in the system analysis.

 

ANALYSIS

Spec Out - We see the output spectrum of the amplfier and notice that residual phase noise has been created on the desired amplifier output spectrum. The residual phase noise does not appear on intermods and harmonics.

 

Noise Level Diagram - This graphs shows the thermal noise channel power (CNP), the phase noise channel power (PNCP), and the cascaded noise figure (CNF).

 

EXERCISES

1. Disable the residual phase noise in the amplifier model. What is the effect on the cascaded noise figure?

2. Change the residual phase noise values in the amplifier model and notice the effect.

Workspace.Name: RX Blocking
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Phase Noise\RX Blocking.wsv
Workspace.Description:
RX Blocking Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to perform a receiver blocking simulation to detemine the required receiver phase noise to meet a given carrier-to-noise ratio. 

 

BACKGROUND

1. Reciprocal Mixing - When a strong out-of-band signal feeds the receiver mixer, it can heterodyne noise sidebands of the receiver synthesizer or local oscillator into the IF band.  This process is known as reciprocal mixing.  For example, let's assume there are two input signals driving a mixer input.  One of them is the desired signal with a power level equivalent to the receiver sensitivity threshold.  The second is an undesired signal with much higher power.  If the power of the local oscillator is sufficiently strong at the frequency offset, equivalent to the spacing of the desired and undesired signals, the undesired signal will be converted into the IF band decreasing the desired signal-to-noise ratio.

 

2. Phase Noise - The blocking signal will 'inherit' the phase noise of the local oscillator which also may have sufficient power at a frequency offset that falls within the converted IF channel. The phase noise of the local oscillator can become the limiting factor in determining the power levels and frequency offset of receiver blocking signals.


SETUP

A simple receiver has been created with a mixer followed by an IF filter.  Two signals are applied to the mixer input.  One is desired and the other undesired.  The desired signal is a GSM signal with a power level of -100 dBm.  Whereas the interfering signal, or blocking signal, is located at a -1 MHz offset from the center frequency of the GSM signal.  The power level of the interfering signal can be tuned by the user.

An LO with phase noise is applied to the mixer LO port. 

 

Equations and variables have been created to tie all of these frequencies and power levels together to make it easier to determine the phase noise requirements of the receiver.

 

The IF filter is centered at 220 MHz and has a 2 MHz bandwidth.

 

ANALYSIS

IF Out Spec - We can see the noise pedestal of our IF filter along with other signals.  One signal is the desired GSM signal the other is the interferer signal that has inherited the LO phase noise. The phase noise is shown on spectrum plots in 'dBm/Hz'. Their is a channel power for phase noise called PNCP (Phase Noise Channel Power) which includes the effects of the bandwidth (in this case 200 kHz or 53 dB). This information is also available by placing the mouse over the phase nosie curve.

 

CNDR - This shows a level diagram of the Carrier to Noise and Distortion Ratio. This measurement is a ratio of the carrier power to the channel noise power + channel phase noise power + channel intermod power.

 

Chan Powers - This level diagram shows individual channel power measurements used to derive the CNDR measurement.

 

EXERCISES

2. Tune the offset frequency , which is the 'FOffset' variable and note the carrier-to-noise ratio changes.

Workspace.Name: RX SFDR
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Receivers\RX SFDR.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Rx SFDR Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration shows verification of the Spurious Free Dynamic Range (SFDR) measurement used by Spectrasys with a manual calculation of the same.

 

BACKGROUND

The spurious free dynamic range of a receiver is the power range of input signals where 3rd order intermods are less than or equal to the noise floor.

 

 

The minimum detectable signal (MDS) is the thermal noise level plus the cascaded noise figure. When the 3rd order intermod power is equivalent to the minimum detectable signal then the maximum spurious free drive level has been reached.

 

The equation for SFDR is:

SFDR[n] = 2/3 [ IIP3[n] - MDS[n] ] (dB), where n = stage number

 

The equation for MDS is:

MDS[n] =  CNP[0] + CNF[n] (dBm), where n = stage number

 

 

 

SETUP

A simple receiver has been created with a front end filter and LNA. The 1800 MHz signal is down converted to a 500 MHz IF. An in-band SFDR measurements is being made so an interferer signal of 1801 MHz is used. It is also assumed that there is no image noise created in this example so mixer provides rejection at the image frequency.

 

 

ANALYSIS

RX Table - This table contains all the information to make a manual spurious free dynamic range calculation. The channel noise power at the output of our cascade is about -105 dBm. The interferer signal (1801 MHz) is adjusted until the third order intermod channel power is equivalent to -105 dBm. This occurs with an input interferer power level of -48 dBm. Due to the cascaded gain the interferer power is about -31 dBm at the output. This can be seen in the interferer channel power (ICP) measurement. The difference between the output interferer power level of -31 dBm and output channel noise power of -105 dBm is the spurious free dynamic range which is about 74 dB. Just as shown by the SFDR measurement in the table.

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Remove the image rejection from the mixer and note the degradation in the spurious free dynamic range. 

 

 

See Example 7.2 pgs 648-649 in "Radio Receiver Design", Kevin McClanning and Tom Vito, Noble Publishing

Workspace.Name: Spreadsheet_Template
Workspace.Description:
Spreadsheet_Template Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

ABSTRACT

This workspace is used in conjunction with the Import Excel RF System Chain tool. The tool will extract cascaded parameters off of an Excel spreadsheet and write them into the appropriate part located in this workspace. NOTE: the Import Tool is designed to be run once. If multiple imports are needed, please restart the tool each time.

BACKGROUND

Traditional cascaded equations have serious limitations. Some of the main issues are:


• Scalar calculations
• No frequency response
• No mismatch loss
• No compression effects
• No intermod generation
• No spurious analysis
• Limited to two ports
• Single path analysis
• No leakage paths
• No broadband noise analysis
• Amplifiers noise figure ignores source impedance
• No mixer image noise


For these reasons it becomes trivial to model a cascaded analysis in a spreadsheet with attenuators and amplifiers. Since there is no such thing as frequency response a spreadsheet filter must be modeled as an attenuator. Attenuators have constant attenuation and matched at all frequencies. Amplifiers are needed to calculated intercept and compression points. However, in the simulator the amplifier models generate intermods and can go into compression. Be careful about drive level when comparing Spectrasys results to those in the spreadsheet unless you are only using equation based measurements.


Spectrasys has Stage, Equation and Simulation based measurements. Stage based measurements are just the values entered by the user. They are prefixed with an S. Equation based measurements do not use simulation results. They are the equivalent of cascaded analysis found in spreadsheets. They are prefixed with an E. For example, cascaded gain analysis in a spreadsheet is independent of the input power to the system. A high input power will give the same cascaded gain result as a low input power because compression effects are ignored. Equation based measurements do the same thing. They only use values typed in by users' not simulated values.


SETUP

This is a simple cascaded lineup of attenuators that have an alternate amplifier model. The source frequency and power level are defined in the equation block.

ANALYSIS

Cascaded Equ Table - Most the measurements in this table are equation and stage based. These are calculated just like cascaded equations.

Spec Out - Shows the spectrum at the cascaded output.

Cascaded Gain - This level diagram cascaded gain through the system.

TRANSITIONING FROM SPREADSHEETS TO SIMULATION

To account for all the effects that cascaded analysis ignores the following steps must be taken to convert the spreadsheet design into a real simulation design:

  • Replace appropriate attenuators with real filter models
  • Replace other attenuators with respective passive models such as splitters, couplers, isolators, etc.
  • Replace amplifiers with real mixer models. An LO must also be added
  • Use Simulation based measurements (remove the E from the measurement prefix)

Workspace.Name: Amplifier Power Sweep w Harmonics
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Sweeps\Amplifier Power Sweep w Harmonics.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Amplifier Power Sweep w Harmonics

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

How to sweep the input power and obtain the fundamental, 2nd and 3rd harmonics at the output of a circuit.

 

BACKGROUND

A nonlinear device such as an amplifier generates harmonics as well as the fundamental. We can sweep the input power and track the power levels of these signals to create the classic 'intercept graph'.

 

SETUP

A single-tone 100 MHz CW source drives the amplifier input. If we want to track the harmonics, we have to inform RF System to track the 2nd and 3rd harmonics as desired signals. This is done on the Paths tab of the System1 analysis in pairs of nodes and frequencies:

 

Path2nd - Defined as 'Source,Out' with [100, 200] as the desired, trackable amplifier output frequency at each node. This means that the desired output signal at the'Source' node is 100 MHz, and at the 'Out' node is changed to 200 MHz.

 

Path3rd - Defined as 'Source,Out' with [100, 300] as the desired, trackable amplifier output frequency at each node. This means that the desired output signal at the 'Out' node is 300 MHz, or the 3rd harmonic.

 

NOTE: When configuring a system with more notes there is a certain path syntax and format that must be used to properly track harmonics at the desired location in the path. Please refer to the 'Forced Path Frequency' shipping example for additional information.

 

ANALYSIS

Run Sweep1 and watch both the Output Spectrum graph and the Power Sweep graph.

 

The graph is obtained by plotting Desired Channel Power (DCP) for the fundamental and Channel Power (CP) for the others.

 

NOTE: Since harmonics are undesired signals then the Channel Power (CP) measurements must be used for undesired signals.

 

The slope of the red 2nd harmonic is twice that of the black fundamental graph. This is true for all 2nd order products, whether harmonic or intermod.

 

The slope of the blue 3rd harmonic is three times that of the fundamental graph, which is true for all 3rd order products.

 

This technique of specifying the desired frequency by node can be used in any circuit, any time you want to track an arbitrary frequency other than the "usual" one.

Workspace.Name: Block Up Converter Spur Analysis
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Sweeps\Block Up Converter Spur Analysis.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Block Up Converter Spur Analysis Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: Swept data must be calculated before it can be displayed.) 

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates a swept spectrum graph on a 2 to 10 GHz block up converter. The results are displayed similar to WhatIF instead of the spectrum comb that is traditionally seen.

 

BACKGROUND

WhatIF is a frequency planning tool used to help locate spurious free regions or analyze spurious performance for a single agile conversion stage. The graphical output is unique since each spurious product is represented as a horizontal bar whose length tracks the spur across the entire frequency range of the system. The height of these bars on the graph represents the amplitudes of the spurs.

 

The upside is that WhatIF is extremely fast, has small workspaces, can analyze the performance of every IF both in up and down conversion cases. The downside is that it only handles a single agile mixer stage. To overcome this limitation and help users visualize spur performance of arbitrary topologies a 'sweepplot()' function has been created.

 

This 'sweepplot()' function points to sweep spectrum data. The swept data is resorted and organized in a fashion where traces are created from each piece of spectrum. These pieces of spectrums are tracked across the sweep range and then plotted as a frequency response bar. The height of the bar corresponds to the amplitude of the spur at that particular sweep frequency.

 

SETUP

There are three sections in this workspace. Each is stored in its own folder. Spurious analysis will take place up to 5th order. It is assumed there are 6 RF blocks each having a 250 MHz bandwidth for a total of 1500 MHz.

 

1) A WhatIF analysis of a 2 to 10 GHz block up-converter. The default configuration is using the summing process between the IF input and mixer LO.

 

2) A Spectrasys sweep that contains a single mixer was created to compare the 'sweepplot()' to the plots in WhatIF. 

 

3) A complete block up converter with front end IF filter and variable gain control. Also included are some post mixer filtering along with amplification and coupling.

 

A variable called 'LOInjection' was created to compare a 'IF + LO = RF' and a 'LO - IF = RF' response. A '0' corresponds to the sum configuration and a '1' the high side LO configuration.

 

ANALYSIS

FreqPlan1 Graph - This graph is an analysis of the block up-converter created by WhatIF. To toggle between the sum and difference configurations change the 'Desired Output Frequency' on the 'Inputs' tab from 'Sum' to 'Difference Show Hi Side LO, LO > RF'. Notice an in-band '3 x 2' response exists in the 'Sum' configuration.

 

Sweep Plot - This graph is similar to the 'FreqPlan1 Graph' created by WhatIF except that this uses the 'sweepplot()' function.

 

NOTE: When comparing graphs between WhatIF and the 'sweepplot()' the spurious bandwidths are slightly different because the 'sweepplot()' function only tracks the center of the spectrum and doesn't take into consideration the bandwidth of the carrier. Also, WhatIF graphs are displayed in 'dBc'. The '0 dBc' reference point in this example = - 20 dBm.

 

Full Tx Sweep Plot - This graph shows the true spurious response due to the entire block up-converter. This graph can be compared with the 'FreqPlan1 Graph' and 'Sweep Plot' graphs to see the effects the additional stages have on the spurious responses.

 

EXERCISES

1. Which mixer configuration (sum or difference, high side LO) has the best in-band spurious performance?

 

2. For the 'Full Tx Sweep Plot' who creates the positive sloped spurs located between 14 and 20 GHz?

 

3. Tune the variable gain amplifier bias and notice the affects of the intermod spectrum.

 

ANSWERS TO EXERCISES

1. The high side LO in a difference configuration gives better in-band spurious performance.

 

2. These positive sloped spurs are created by the 'TxAmp'.

Workspace.Name: Quick Sweep - Freq and Ampl
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\Sweeps\Quick Sweep - Freq and Ampl.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Simple Freq and Amp Quick Sweep Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to perform a quick sweep on an architecture to determine the fundamental frequency and amplitude response.

 

BACKGROUND

A Quick Sweep is a feature that estimates the compression point and bandwidth of the system to determine an optimum vector of amplitudes and frequencies that are swept. An optimum amplitude vector includes the cascaded 1 dB compression point as well as the cascaded saturation point. An optimum frequency vector is based on the source center frequency and channel measurement bandwidth.

 

Users can select whether to create a Quick Sweep for:

  • Amplitude
  • Frequency
  • Amplitude and Frequency

They also can change the number of points used for the sweep by changing the fidelity.

 

By default the Desired Channel Power (DCP) and Desired Channel Phase (DCPH) are always placed in the dataset. Other path measurements may be swept. These measurements can be added to the Quick Sweep by choosing the appropriate categories on the edit path dialog box. The help file identifies which measurements belong to given categories.


SETUP

This is very simple system used to illustrate Quick Sweeps. The architecture consists of an attenuator, amplifier, and filter. The filter has a 60 MHz bandwidth. The channel measurement bandwidth is set to 10 MHz.

 

Three paths have been defined:

To create a Quick Sweep graph just right click on the output node and select the appropriate graph from the Add New Table / Graph submenu.

Workspace.Description:
Quick Sweep of Dual Amp w Filter Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to perform several quick sweeps to characterize the system performance with respect to spurs, compression, and group delay.

 

BACKGROUND

A Quick Sweep is used to Spectrasys to generate input signals for a path and collect the associated swept data. During a quick sweep any schematic sources appearing at the input of the path are disabled and the appropriate quick sweep source is created. The source will be swept across the range of frequencies and amplitudes as determined by the quick sweep parameters. The swept data will be stored in the respective path dataset.

 

They have several advantages over traditional sweeps. They are:

  • Can be quickly created by adding a *path* to a system analysis and enabling the quick sweep feature
  • Default graphs are quickly created by right clicking on the output node of the path and selecting the graph of interest
  • Compression sweeps are highly optimized since the path had a good estimate of where the compression knee occurs
  • They are non-invasive. The user doesn't have to disconnect / connect specific schematic sources to do a particular test
  • Simulation speed will be faster since it is embedded in the system analysis
  • File size is smaller because swept data is only kept for the path, not the entire schematic

SETUP

This system consists of identical cascaded amplifiers separated by a bandpass filter. A total of six paths will be created as follows:

  1. Regular
  2. Compression Curve
  3. Frequency Response
  4. Spectrum Sweep
  5. Amplitude Sweep
  6. Group Delay

Paths 2 - 6 are quick sweeps.

 

ANALYSIS

Compression - The compression curve for our system.

 

Freq Response - This is a default frequency response curve for our path.

 

Spec Sweep - This is a unique graph of swept input spectrum. The characteristics of various intermod products are easily identified as they vary with input frequency.

 

Amp Sweep - This is a refined amplitude sweep around the compression knee of our system.

 

Group Delay - This is the group delay of the system using default settings.

 

Sys S21 Mag - This is the magnitude of the System S21 using default settings.

 

Sys S21 Phase - This is the phase of the System S21 using default settings.

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the non-linear aspects of the two amplifiers and observe changes in output responses.

2. Tune filter characteristics and observe changes in output responses.

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to assign temperature coefficients to parameters and create temperature sweeps.

 

BACKGROUND

Spectrasys has a feature called 'Quick Sweeps' that will run a power or frequency sweep on a selected path. When adding a path the user has the ability to select either a 'Normal' or 'Quick Sweep' path. A single system analysis can contain combinations of 'Normal' and 'Quick Sweep' paths.

 

For additional information on 'Quick Sweeps' see the 'Add / Edit Path Dialog' box reference in the help file.

 

SETUP

Two paths have been added to the System Analysis. One of them is a power sweep and the other a normal path.

 

A temperature sweep has been created that sweeps the system analysis at three temperatures: -40, +25, and +85 C. At each of these temperatures the system analysis will run which includes the quick sweeps. Thus a Power Out vs Power In sweep will be created for each of the three temperatures.

 

The 'OutEquations' block has been configured to extract the desired swept data. This requires some post processing to extract the 3 temperature curves from this data.

 

ANALYSIS

Pout vs Temp - This graph contains the Power Out vs Power In for each temperature.

 

CGAIN CNF vs Temp - This graph shows the Cascaded Gain and Cascaded Noise Figure vs Temperature. This is measured at the output of the receiver.

 

 

EXERCISES

Tower Top Receiver Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 (NOTE: Sweep data must be calculated before it can be displayed.) 

 

 

ABSTRACT

This example shows how different parts of a system can be simulated with different temperatures. Furthermore, power supply requirements will be determined for this design.

 

BACKGROUND

The physical device temperature affects the performance of both active and passive devices. Active and passive devices are affected in different ways.

 

     Active - Behavioral affects from the physical device temperature cannot be predicted. Parameters that are typically affected by temperature are Gain, Noise Figure, 1 dB compression, and intercept points. A circuit simulator can be used to simulate these parameters versus temperature or they can be measured in the lab versus temperature. Since parameter performance cannot be predicted therefore these parameters will not change as the temperature is changed unless equations are used to specify the relationship between them.

 

     Passive - For passive devices losses are thought of as resistive. A resistor generates noise proportional to its temperature. Therefore for passive devices the noise figure will be a function of temperature. Noise figure is defined by IEEE to be measured at 290 K (16.85 C). Because of this the noise figure of the passive device will only equal the insertion loss when the physical temperature of the device is at 290 K.

 


SETUP

This design contains a tower top set of electronics that include some filtering, amplification, biasing, and bypass operation. All devices in the tower top unit are modelled at the same temperature. The tower top temperature has been defined in the equation block. Furthermore, equations have been created for the gain and noise figure of the tower top LNA as a function of temperature.

 

A sweep has been created to sweep the system analysis accross the three temperatures of -30, +25, and +60 degrees C.

 

 

ANALYSIS

Rx Table Data - This table contains some of the common receiver performance data.

 

DC Supply Data - This table contains all of the DC power supply requirements for the design.

 

Temperature Perform - This graph shows the noise figure and cascaded gain performance of the entire system versus temperature.

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Enable the LNA bypass state by changing the state of the tower top switch state. Notice the change in system performance.

 

2. Change the DC power supply parameters and notice the effect on the DC supply measurements.

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of a diversity transmitter with a hybrid amplifier. Two IS95 carriers are created at 1955 and 1965 MHz. 

 

SETUP

Two transmitters drive a dual hybrid power amplifier to deliver power to two different antennas. Each transmitter consists of an IF chain at 220 MHz and is then upconverted to an on channel signal in the 1900 MHz band. An IS95 carrier is driving each IF input. The IF frequency is filtered and amplified before being upconverted to the carrier frequency. A hybrid power amplifier is a common redundant amplifier architecture that amplifies both carriers and phases them properly to drive one antenna from TX1 and the other from TX2. Should one of the power amplifiers fail both carriers will still appear at the output even though the total power output will be reduced.

 

NOTE: The in the schematic TX1 is in the upper left however the antenna for TX1 is in the lower right due to the phasing of the hybrid couplers. Likewise for TX2.

 

ANALYSIS

TX1 Out Spec - Output spectrum of TX1 showing only the total spectrum. Notice the degree of cancellation of the carrier at 1965 MHz.

 

TX2 Out Spec - Output spectrum of TX2 showing only the total spectrum. Notice the degree of cancellation of the carrier at 1955 MHz.

 

TX1 Path - A sample level diagram with a few measurements along TX1 path.

 

TX2 Path - A sample level diagram with a few measurements along TX2 path.

 

LO1 Table - A table showing the drive level of LO1 to Mixer1 LO port.

 

LO2 Table - A table showing the drive level of LO2 to Mixer2 LO port.

 

TX1 Table - A table showing some basic measurements along TX1 path.

 

TX2 Table - A table showing some basic measurements along TX2 path.

 

 

EXERCISES

1. Drop the gain of one of the power amplifiers to 0 dB and observe that both carriers are still being transmitted by their respective antennas.

 

2. Enable the individual spectrums and the signal, intermod, and noise spectrums. Observe the individual power levels of each of the carriers and notice that one of the carriers is out of phase and is being cancelled and the other one is in phase and is increasing in power.

 

3. Enable the noise and observe the noise pedestal at the transmitter output.

 

4. Tune the carrier frequencies and IF input powers and observe the performances changes to the system.

Workspace.Description:
Reverse TX Intermods Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: System1 must be calculated before the data can be displayed)

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how reverse intermod simulation can be performed in Spectrasys. 

 

BACKGROUND

Intermods that are created from desired forward traveling input signals and from undesired signals back driving a non-linear device are called reverse intermods. These reverse intermods can be radiated by a transmitter causing emissions compliance failures or may create other interference in the system.

 

Two tone measurements systems must be especially careful with the level of reverse intermod creation to avoid inaccurate measurements due to the reverse intermods created in the test setup.

 

The 'NonLin' models in Spectrasys have a reverse intermod factor parameter which is nothing more than the amount of attenuation of a back driven signal before appearing at the input. This reverse intermod input signal will be used with other forward traveling input signals during the intermod creation process. The signals that have been processed by the reverse intermod factor are different than the regular reverse isolation signals that will continue to propagate backwards through the system since they don't propagate past the input to the non linear block model. These special reverse intermod signal sources are identified by the 'RevIM' text if the spectrum identification string.

 


SETUP

A simple two transmitter schematic has been created.  The transmitters have been coupled together through 2 antennas. The 'NonLin' non-linear block model is used to represent the transmitter non-linear behavior. The reverse intermod factor for each transmitter has been set to 50 dB. Thus the back driven spectrum from the other transmitter will be 50 dB lower at the input than the output. These reverse intermod source spectrum will be combined with the forward traveling input spectrum and re-radiated by the antennas. The input spectrums are GSM signals at 1850 and 1860 MHz for TX1 and TX2 respectively. The transmit output power is 40 dBm.

 

ANALYSIS

TX1 Output - This graph shows the 1850 MHz main GSM carrier along with the backwards traveling TX2 spectrum at 1860 MHz and the intermods created by these two signals that appear at the transmitter 1 input. Spectrum identification at 1840 and 1870 MHz show the method by which the intermod was created.

 

TX2 Output - This graph shows the 1860 MHz main GSM carrier along with the backwards traveling TX1 spectrum at 1850 MHz and the intermods created by these two signals that appear at the transmitter 2 input. Spectrum identification at 1840 and 1870 MHz show the method by which the intermod was created.

 

TX1 Input - This graph show what the spectrum looks like at the transmitter input. Notice that he reverse isolation spectrum (TX2 at 1860 MHz) is around -20 dBm and the reverse intermod source spectrum is about -70 dBm also at 1860 MHz.

 

TX2 Input - This graph show what the spectrum looks like at the transmitter input. Notice that he reverse isolation spectrum (TX1 at 1850 MHz) is around -20 dBm and the reverse intermod source spectrum is about -70 dBm also at 1850 MHz.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the power level of the reverse intermod factor and observe the corresponding changes in the spectrum.

2. Disable the reverse intermod factor and observe the resulting spectrum.

BACKGROUND

At times a user may like to create a custom model with their own custom parameters.

 

Follow these steps to create a user model:

1. Select 'Action' the 'Design Wizard'.
2. Set the design name to 'NL_Butter'.

4. Click the 'Next' button.

2. Click the 'Add Parameter' button.
3. Type in the parameter information: 
        Name: IL, Description: Insertion Loss, Default Value: 1, Units: Relative Power dB, Show: Checked, Validation: Warn if negative

           Type       Input Stopband Impedance        None                 1                   -             -                       X                        Warn if negative

           IPSAT     Input Saturation Power               dBm                 63                  -             -                       X                        Warn if negative

Workspace.Name: Transfer Switch
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\User Models\Transfer Switch.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Transfer Switch Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to create a transfer switch with a user model that includes a dynamic schematic symbol that changes with the switch state.

 

BACKGROUND

A transfer switch is a special type of switch that has four ports. Port 1 to 2 and 3 to 4 are connected in switch state 1 and Port 1 to 3 and 2 to 4 are connected for switch state 2. There is also an off state where no switch connections are made. This switch will be created using three 4 port S Parameter files. One for each switch state (0, 1, and 2).

 

A user model is created using a 4 port S Parameter Dataset model called 'NPOD4'. The Dataset name for this model will be a variable that is changed in the user model equation block. As the switch state is changed the S parameter dataset name will be updated.

 

Parameters are created that represent the switch state, S parameters for each of the switch states, and the reference impedance.

 

The name of the user model is 'SDTransSwitch'.

 

A schematic symbol must be created for each switch state and named such that they end with the same number that represents the switch state. i.e. TransSw0 is the name of the schematic symbol that represents the switch when at State = 0, or the off position.

 

A part is created by dragging the user model (SDTransSwitch) from the workspace tree to the schematic. At this point the schematic symbol must be set. Double click the part then click the 'Advanced Options..' button, click on the 'Symbol' tab and change the 'Symbol:' to 'TransSw+State+'. This special syntax is used to tell the part to build the symbol name by cascading the 'TransSw' text with the text value of the 'State' parameter.

 

NOTE: It is very important when building a user model to match port names in the schematic of the electrical model with the port names used on the schematic symbol. i.e. 'Port_1' in the schematic of the user model will map to 'Port_1' used in the schematic symbol. Careless port naming can cause unexpected behavior.


SETUP

Two signal generators have been created each with a different frequency but having the same power level. The transfer switch part has been created and the two sources are connected to switch ports 1 and 4. Graphs have been created at the other two ports 2 and 3. Three 4 port S parameter files have been imported and the data is saved on the workspace tree. The 'State' variable has been made tunable. The State can be tuned and the change in the schematic symbol and graphs can be observed.

 

ANALYSIS

Port 3 Out Spec - Shows both signal spectrums at Port 3. One signal goes through the main path and the other through the leakage path.

 

Port 4 Out Spec - Shows both signal spectrums at Port 4. One signal goes through the main path and the other through the leakage path

 

EXERCISES

1. Tune the the 'State' parameter and observe the changes in the output spectrum.

Workspace.Name: 5 GHz VSWR Detector
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\VSWR\5 GHz VSWR Detector.wsv
Workspace.Description:
3 Sector 5.8 GHz TX Power / VSWR Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple example of a 3 sector 5.8 GHz receiver that can be used as a TX power
meter or VSWR tester.  This example will show the importance or RF architecture work
and how many design parameters can be confidently selected using an RF architecture
design tool.

 

DESIGN REQUIREMENTS

  1. Frequency band: 5.725  to 5.850 GHz
  2. TX Power Range: +10 to +30 dBm
  3. Measure absolute power across TX power range
  4. Measure antenna return loss across TX power range
  5. Conducted emissions below -80 dBm in a 30 kHz bandwidth

Design Parameters to be Determined

  1. Overall Architecture
  2. Switch Isolation
  3. Filtering Requirements


 

BACKGROUND

Three coupled antennas have been connected through a virtual node that represents the antenna to antenna isolation.  Consequently, multiple carriers can be driven into each antenna where the 5.8 GHz receiver will be able to see all transmitted carriers through all paths.

 

Equations have been written to determine the complex impedance of the antenna based on VSWR and the reflection coefficient angle.  This impedance has been substituted into all antennas.  A six position switch is used to select which antenna and the direction of power flow to be examined by the receiver.  The user will be able to see the return loss and the given antenna impedance from the 'Variable1' output.  The return loss can be verified by comparing the forward and reverse traveling power.

 

Two IF outputs have been used for this design.  IF #1 is at 450 MHz and has no AGC.  On the other hand IF #2 is at 70 MHz and has an AGC amplifier.  Perhaps IF #2 could be used for demodulation of some other receiver functions and IF #1 output could be used to drive a power detector.

 

SETUP

CW LO signals have been created and applied to each mixer LO port.  A modulated signal has been created with a file source and has been applied to each transmitter output each at a different frequency.  As mentioned earlier a six position switch is used to select the which antenna and the direction of power flow, either toward the antenna or away from it.  In order to minimize cost for this design low pass filters are used as much as possible and an inexpensive passive splitter is also used. Several equations have been written that control the frequency of the RF carriers as well as the IF and LO frequencies.

 

Two paths have been create from TX1 input through IF1 and IF2.  These paths are used to place various RF measurements in a table and on level diagrams.

Initial Conditions: 'Switch.State' : 1, 'Equation.TX_Pwr' : 20 dBm, and 'Equation.ReturnLoss' : 10 dB

 

ANALYSIS

The three main parameters that we want to tune in this example are 'Equation.TX_Pwr' (transmit power, all three carriers are tied to this same power level), 'Switch.State' (control which antenna and direction of power flow we are looking at), and 'Equation.ReturnLoss' (from this parameter the actual antenna impedance will be determined)

 

Coupler In Spec - This is a graph of the transmitter output spectrum that will drive our antennas.  This is a file source representing WLAN DQPSK modulation.

 

Emissions - This graph shows the conducted emissions at the antenna of TX1.  Our design objective is to have all out of band conducted emissions to be below -80 dBm in a 30 kHz bandwidth.  We can see that we have 2 issues at 5300 MHz and 5680 MHz which both are above this limit.  By placing the mouse over these two signals we can identify their origin and the path they took to arrive at the antenna.  From this information we can determine the best architecture solution to the problem.

 

Chan Pwr IF1 - This level diagram show the Total Node Power (TNP) and the Channel Power (CP) along the respective paths.  Note that since we intend to use this circuitry as a power detector as a designer we want to ensure that the total node power is larger than the channel power.  These level diagrams show that if IF1 output is used as a power meter we would have a serious problem since the total node power is larger than the channel power when we look at the reflected power (Switch.State = 2) and our input power is at the bottom end of the requirements at +10 dBm.  An architecture change is required to make this correction.

 

Spec IF1 Out - This spectral plot of the IF output identify many design issues.  From this graph we can identify all of the intermods, harmonics, noise and junk that appears at the output.  We can immediately see that we have a serious LO leakage problem that is getting into our output (this is the tallest CW signal in the spectrum).  Once again we can use the mouse to identify that this CW signal is 'LO2' at 380 MHz.  Which is actually the 2nd LO that came through the mixer, across the splitter, through the filter, amplifier, and attenuator to arrive at IF1 output.  This information will help a choose the best architectural solution to this problem.  Furthermore, on this same spectral plot we can identify the effect of the switch isolation.  Since all TX signals have the same power level their forward traveling power will all be at the same level when they arrive at the switch.  The switch has a fixed amount of isolation.  So once again we can identify the largest modulated signals in this spectrum will by using the mouse and find the path of the spectrum and we will find that the weakest link in this chain for other carriers is through the switch.  Another to identify this spectrum is to flip the switch to the respective carrier and watch the power change.

 

Dyna Range IF1 - This level diagram show the amount of signal headroom along the path.  From this graph we can see that RFAmp2 is the weak link in the chain.  Furthermore, we know from the 'Chan Pwr IF1' level diagram that the total node power is higher than the channel power with just compounds the problem.

 

Pwr Table IF1 - This table contains tabular measurement results of some the RF measurements along their paths.

 

ACP IF1 - This level diagrams show the channel power along the defined path as well as the power of both upper and lower adjacent channels.

 

EXERCISES

1. Verify Return Loss Measurements:
Verify the channel power is about 0 dBm at IF #1 Output.  Set the 'Switch.State' to 2 and the channel power should drop by 10 dB which is the return loss to about -10 dBm.  Change the 'Equation.ReturnLoss' to 15 dB and verify that the channel power is -15 dBm.

 

2. Verify Headroom or Dynamic Range:
Set 'Switch.State' back to 1 and 'Equation.TX_Pwr' to max power which is +30 dBm.  Notice on level diagram 'Dyna Range IF1' that RFAmp2 is orange and that there is no headroom in this amplifier.  An orange part means a warning and by right clicking on the amplifier in the schematic the user can see what the warning is.  It's apparent that our power meter will not have enough dynamic range at the top end so we will need to increase the 1 dB compression point.  We can do this by simply clicking on RFAmp2 on the level diagram and bring up the amplifier properties.  Lets increase the OP1dB, OPSAT, and OIP3 by 3 dB to +13, +16, and +23 dBm respectively.  Notice now that we have about 1 dB of headroom and that the return loss performance at the top end is not as good than at lower power levels because of the amplifier compression.

 

3. Verify Lowest Power Performance:
Set 'Equation.TX_Pwr' to the lowest power which is +10 dBm and the Switch.State = 2 for reflected power and notice how the total node power is much higher than the channel power.  This can be observed in the 'Pwr Table IF1' and in the 'Chan Pwr IF1' level diagram and 'Spec IF1 Out' graph.  We can see that the worst offender is 'LO2' which is the 2nd LO signal at 380 MHz.  Since we can identify the path that this offender took by placing the mouse of this spectrum we know that the signal came through the LO leakage of the mixer then went through the passive splitter, filter, amplifier, attenuator, and to the output.  We can fix this problem in one of three ways:

 

1) Better LO to RF Isolation on Mixer2
2) Better Isolation in the Splitter (i.e. use of a Wilkinson instead of a resistive)
3) Change Filter3 to a bandpass filter (i.e Filter5 is available)

 

Experiment with all these types of changes.  Notice that any one of these architecture changes can be implemented to solve the problem.  However, there are many tradeoffs
that would need to considered to select the best solution.  Notice that the bandpass
filter solution provides the cleanest spectrum at IF1 output.

 

4. Verify Conducted Emissions Performance:
Change the Channel Measurement bandwidth in 'System1' system analysis from 22 MHz to 0.03 MHz (or 30 kHz).  Examine the spectrum contained in the 'Emissions' graph and change the 'Switch.State' between 1 and 2 and notice that the we exceed our performance of -80 dBm when we are in 'Switch.State' 2 or we are looking at the reflected power.  Once again we can use the mouse to determine the origin and traveled path of the spectrum and we find that are conducted emissions problems are related to LO leakage.  It is left as an exercise to for the user to determine the best solution with may include better filtering, better LO to RF leakage performance of the mixers, lower LO drive, or a combination of all of the above.

Workspace.Name: Basic Return Loss
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\VSWR\Basic Return Loss.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Basic Return Loss Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

(NOTE: Swept data must be calculated before it can be displayed)

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration that shows how to sweep the load across a constant VSWR circle and examine the performance output. 

 

BACKGROUND

Functions can be created in this product to assist in simulating parameters like VSWR, Return Loss, and Reflection Coefficient in Spectrasys.

 

These functions are:

 

Zload = gammatoz( Z0, Gamma ) - This function will return the complex load impedance given the characteristic impedance Z0 and the reflection coefficient Gamma

 

Zload = rltoz( Z0, RL, Ang ) - This function will return the complex load impedance given the characteristic impedance Z0, return loss in dB, and the return loss ang in radians.

 

Gamma = rltogamma( Z0, RL, Ang ) - This function will return the reflection coefficient given the return loss in dB, and the return loss ang in radians.

 

Swept path data contains path measurements at every node along the path. There is a special variable in the path dataset called NodeNames which indicates the name of the node along the path. There is a function called extractsweptdata( ) that is used to extract measurement data for a particular node from swept data. For example, if we wanted to examine the cascaded gain at the node named '2' the syntax would be:

 

extractsweptdata( CGAIN, NodeNames, '2' )

 

We can examine the data at any node in the path.

 

SETUP

A function has been created relating VSWR to Return Loss. The user enters the VSWR and the load impedance angle and the internal rltoz function is used to determine the complex load impedance. This complex load impedance is used in the schematic on the load port.

 

The LoadAng has been made tunable and a sweep of this angle has been created from 0 to 360 degrees.

 

The swept results of the path are then plotted and can be examined.

 

The VSWR Block of equations shows how to build a VSWR vector along the path.

 

ANALYSIS

Swept Output - This graph shows the cascaded gain and cascaded noise figure at the output versus the swept load angle.

 

NF Histogram - This graph shows a histogram of the cascaded noise figure at the output as the phase is rotated from 0 to 360 degrees.

 

VSWR Table - This table shows the VSWR along the path.

 

EXERCISES

1. Change the VSWR value and compare results from different sweeps
