Workspace.Name: Wideband Carrier VSWR
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\VSWR\Wideband Carrier VSWR.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Wideband Carrier VSWR Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This is a simple illustration of how to determine the VSWR input of a cascade for a wide carrier. 

 

BACKGROUND

VSWR is defined by  ( 1 + | Gamma | )  /  ( 1 - | Gamma | ) where Gamma is the complex reflection coefficient. The reflection coefficient (Gamma) is defined as ( Zload - Zo ) / ( Zload + Zo ).

 

Spectrasys has the ability to break down pieces of the path spectrum into appropriate spectrum types used for path measurements. These types are:

  • Desired
  • Noise
  • Total
  • Various Intermod Groups

Variables are created for Power, Voltage, and Impedance at every node in the system. These groups of signals can be used for post processing. These variables don't automatically appear in the path dataset. This must be enabled by checking 'Add Powers, Voltages, and Impedances to Path Dataset' on the 'Path' tab of the system analysis.

 

By default wideband carriers are represented with 2 data points. To get good VSWR resolution more data points are needed. This must be enabled by checking 'Minimum source data points' and increasing the number of source data points on the 'General' tab of the system analysis.

 

Once the data is available simple equations are used to determine the VSWR.

 

NOTE: With this technique it becomes trivial to get the VSWR at any internal node in the system.


SETUP

A simple cascade has been created with VSWR across the channel. A wide 500 MHz carrier is used being represented by 50 source data points. Powers, voltages, and impedances are enabled for the path dataset.

 

A reflection coefficient (gamma) function has been written in the equation block. The vswr function has been created on the workspace tree.

 

ANALYSIS

Input Spectrum - This is the spectrum seen looking into the cascade.

 

In VSWR - This graph shows a plot of the 'InVSWR' equation on the left axis and the input impedance on the right. It's clear to see the VSWR increase near the band edges of the filter.

 

EXERCISES

1. Disable the filter with a short (double click the part, select the 'Simulation' tab, select 'Disable part for all simulations (Short Circuit ALL terminals together)' ). Recalculate the simulation and examine the VSWR and input impedance.

 

2. Tune the corner frequency of the filters and observe the changes to the VSWR and input impedance.

Workspace.Name: Multitone Volterra
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\X Parameters\Multitone Volterra.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Multitone Volterra Workspace 

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example uses simple multi-tone tests to show how nonlinear PA results can be calculated two different ways, with reasonable confidence in the reliability of the modeling (and the RFLINK technique):

  1. SPECTRASYS: local RF system spectral simulation, using a Volterra technique on X-parameter devices
  2. DATAFLOW: system-level DF transient simulation, using DSP tones through an RFLINK model

It also shows how multi-tone results can be approximated from single-tone X-parameters.

 

This example creates a series of (2) or (10) CW tones in either RF Spectrasys or Dataflow.  Both the Spectrasys and Dataflow-on-top-of-Spectrasys (RFLINK) techniques yield valid, self-consistent results for behavioral RF memoryless amplifiers.  The lowest-level RF devices are X-parameters generated by the Keysight ADS software, having a known result. Based on these spectral regrowth results, a designer can be confident in vector-modulated systems.

 

DO THIS:

Tune Ptotal from -25dBm to 0 dBm, when the amplifier goes in compression. Observe how fast Volterra simulates the RF spectrum, comparing with DF analysis, and how the results agree.

Workspace.Name: QPSK_Xparam_RFLink
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\X Parameters\QPSK_Xparam_RFLink.wsv
Workspace.Description:
QPSK_Xparam_RFLink Example

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

What you need to know before executing this example

        How to create and execute a Data Flow simulation in SystemVue.

 

What does this example do

        This example contains two Data Flow simulation schematics, namely, QPSK and QPSK_VSA.  Both of them demonstrate how to bring an actual RF device (in this example, an RF Amplifier) into a system level simulation in SystemVue through the X-parameters characterization of the RF device ("AMP_XParams.mdf" file in this example). 

       Observe the simulation results of constellation in the two plots: DF1_S_Orig, DF1_S_RFLink, and the measured EVM values: RF_LINK_EVM_RMS, REF_EVM_RMS (values are in %) in DF1_Data.

 

        Please note that the only difference bewteen the two schematics is that the QPSK_VSA design relies on Keysight 89600 VSA software to perform the QPSK demodulation and EVM computation, hence it requires the installation of Keysight 89600 VSA software on your computer.  The "QPSK_EVM.set" setup file is used to set up the VSA.

Theory of Operation

    Both schematics generate QPSK modulated RF signal as testing stimulus.  This RF signal will be demodulated directly along one path; while along the other path, it is demodulated after passing through an RF_Link that embodies an "RF amplifier" via its X-parameters profile.  The amplifier is intentionally pushed into compression, hence its impact on the EVM and constellation of the QPSK signal is clearly observable in the two constellation plots: DF1_S_Orig and DF1_S_RFLink, and the two EVM measured values: RF_LINK_EVM_RMS, REF_EVM_RMS (values are in %) in DF1_Data. 

   

Further Exploration

In the following, we will show you step-by-step how to create a Data Flow schematic that uses X-parameters profile of an RF device.

 

We will also show you how to generate a Spectrasys simulation to analyze RF device characteristics in the frequency domain (i.e. harmonics, mixing terms, etc.). 

 

The X-parameters profile can be extracted either in ADS from its design or through Keysight network analyzers that supports X-parameters measurement.

 

1. Create a Data Flow schematic that incorporates the X-parameters profile of an RF device

          Note that you can create your Data Flow schematic before the sub-network that embodies the X-parameter.

  • Create an sub-network that embodies the X-parameters profile
    1. Mouse right click on the "Designs" folder and Add -> Designs ->Add Sub-Network Model ... and give it a meaningful name. 
    2. Go to the "Part Selector A" window and select "RF Design" as "Current Library:", leave "Category:" at its default "<All>". Now at almost the bottom of the list of the parts, you will see "X-parameters" part, click it and then click any where in the sub-network empty design schematic.  An X-parameters part will be dropped into the design schematic.
    3. Double click the dropped part and use the "Browse..." button next to the "Filename (data source):" field to provide the X-parameters file.  Click OK and the appropriate number of connection pins/ports will be available now. (Optional: if there is a need to connect the Ground of the part, check the "Show Reference Ground on Symbol" checkbox).
    4. If any of the pins/ports are DC bias pins/ports, you can add the DC bias here too. You can use either Signal Ground part or Source(DC Volt) part to provide DC bias.  You can also add R, L, C components in this sub-network.
    5. Add Input and Output parts to the desired pins/ports to provide input and output interfaces for this sub-network design.  Feel free to use meaningful names for these Input and Output parts.
  • Create a Data Flow schematic
  • Bring the sub-network into the Data Flow schematic
    • Drag the sub-network icon from the workspace tree into the Data Flow schematic, notice a RF_Link part is automatically created for you as a access interface for the underlying sub-network design.  Double click on this RF_Link part to see how it wraps around the sub-network you just created.
  • Now create a Data Flow simulation controller, i.e. Data Flow Analysis, and configure it to simulate the Data Flow schematic you just completed.

2. Create a Spectrasys simulation to analyze the RF device characteristics in the frequency domain

  • Create a sub-network that embodies the X-parameters profile
  • Create a Spectrasys design schematic
    1. Mouse right click on the "Designs" folder and Add -> Designs ->Add Schematic... to add a new design schematic
    2. Bring in an RF signals source into the design schematic by dragging a "Source (Multi)" part from the "Part Selector A" window with "RF Design" selected as "Current Library:" - Note: always bring in some RF Design parts before step 4 below. 
    3. Double click the placed "Source (Multi)" part and set it up.
    4. Drag the sub-network design icon from the workspace tree into this schematic and connect its input to the place "Source (Multi)" (Optional: To remove the Ground pin/port from the placed part, double click on the part and click the "Advanced Options..." button, under the "Symbol" tab change the content in the "Symbol:" field from "2-PORT" to "2-PORTNOGND").
    5. Add an "Output" part to the output of the placed sub-network part
  • Add a Spectrasys simulation controller
    1. Mouse right click on the "Designs" folder and Add ->Analyses -> Add RF System Analysis...
    2. Select the appropriate design for the "Design to Simulate:" field
    3. Click the "Calculate Now" button.
  • Analyze the simulation results
    • Go to the RF design schematic you just simulated, mouse right click on the "Output" part, Add New Graph/Table -> ... New Power Plot ... This will create a spectral lines plot.  Now move the mouse around those spectral lines and you can see their values.

For your convenience, a complete Spectrasys simulation has been created (see System1 analysis under Analyses folder and DCP_vs_Pin and System1_PWR_at_Node_2 graphs in the Graphs folder).

Workspace.Name: XParameter Balanced Amp Noise Power Ratio
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\X Parameters\XParameter Balanced Amp Noise Power Ratio.wsv
Workspace.Description:
XParameter Balanced Amp Noise Power Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates several items of interest.

  • A balanced RF amplifier configuration, at the system level
  • Use of X-parameter data in an analog configuration, with the possibility of mutual impedance loading
  • Volterra improvements to multi-tone evaluation of single-tone X-parameter data
  • Noise Power Ratio (NPR) as a measurement.

Balanced Amplifier Operation

This a parallel amplifier configuration that cancels both 2nd and 3rd order intermod and harmonic products.  The complete amplifier consists of 4 individual amplifiers paralleled in such a way to suppress both 2nd and 3rd order products.  Two identical amplifier banks are paralleled and fed 90 degrees apart giving cancellation of 3rd order products.  Each amplifier bank consists of 2 amplifiers that are fed 180 degrees apart giving cancellation of 2nd order products. Balanced amplifiers also have higher operational reliability, since the system still operates with the failure of any individual component.

 

The X-parameters amplifiers are defined by 1-tone X-parameters files. Spectrasys runs 1-tone Harmonic Balance analysis, and exctracts the a Volterra  polynomial model which enables the prediction of 2-tone intermod distortions.  The option "Use Fast Volterra Simulation" on the 'Circuit_Link' component must be enabled.

 

TRY THIS

  1. Noise Power Ratio (NPR) : Observe the difference in dBm between the top of the spectral lines, vs. the depth of the notch.  NPR is usually pessimistic in terms of predicting power handling for communications signals., but is an easy physical measurement to make.
  2. Tune the "Pcarrier" variable to values of -40, -20, and 0 dBm.  Note the values.  How many dB does the notch rise for each 1dB increase in input power? YOUR ANSWER: ________
    What is the small-signal power gain of this PA?  YOUR ANSWER: _______
  3. Tune the "Iso" parameter from an ideal value of 90dB to 50dB to 10dB.  ("Iso" is used in each of the RF splitters.)  What happens to the distortion-cancelling properties of the balanced PA?
  4. Now simulate a partial failure by de-activating one of the four X-parameter devices to an open circuit, so that only three remain active.  Re-do the measurements from Step 1. 
    What is the new gain? _______  What is the new depth of the notch?______

XParameter Balanced Amp Volterra Workspace

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates a parallel amplifier configuration that cancels both 2nd and 3rd order intermod and harmonic products.  The complete amplifier consists of 4 individual amplifiers paralleled in such a way to suppress both 2nd and 3rd order products.  Two identical amplifier banks are paralleled and fed 90 degrees apart giving cancellation of 3rd order products.  Each amplifier bank consists of 2 amplifiers that are fed 180 degrees apart giving cancellation of 2nd order products.

 

The X-parameters amplifiers are defined by 1-tone X-parameters files. Spectrasys runs a 1-tone Harmonic Balance analysis behind the scenes and exctracts the amplifier Volterra  polynomial model which supports the prediction of 2-tone intermod distortions.

Workspace.Name: XParameter Compression
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\X Parameters\XParameter Compression.wsv
Workspace.Description:
XParameter Compression Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

This example plots the gain compression of an X-parameter file so that you can verify the response of the part before applying it in a system simulation.  This tutorial also shows how to set up a simple simulation.

 

The set-up has already been completed for you, and only needs to be re-simulated.  The procedure below is simply an explanation to guide you through the process for yourself.

 

If you want to re-use this workspace as a template, use the "Save As" feature, and copy to your own working directory.


Full procedure:

  1. First, create a new schematic ( a "model") containing the X-parameter part and any DC bias sources, other RF analog components, and ports.  This schematic is called "Xamp" in the workspace tree.  When you first insert the X-parameter part from the RF DESIGN parts selector, it has no pins.  When you point to an external X-parameter file, the part is fully instantiated with additional information, including the right number of ports and internal variables.  Afterward, everything in this subnetwork will be simulated using a dedicated nonlinear circuit simulator to present a single, accurate, self-consistent result back up to the RF system simulator.  This encapulates harmonics and mutual loading in the most authentic, accurate method possible to take full advantage of X-parameter capabilities.
  2. Now create a RF system schematic (here called "RF") for simulation using Spectrasys.  In that RF system schematic, place a Circuit_Link part and any other elements of your system.  (In this workspace, our trivial "RF system" only consists of a MultiSource and Circuit_Link.)  Configure the Circuit_Link part to refer to the X-parameter subnetwork, called "XAmp."  Configure any necessary nonlinear simulation convergence parameters on the Circuit_link part, such the number of harmonics, or convergence tolerances. For very high power levels, simulator convergence may be slower and take more internal iterations.
  3. Now set up the master Spectrasys RF system simulation controller and its output measurements.  (This simulator is documented more fully elsewhere.) 
    If you want to use the RF system ("RF") in an even higher-level Dataflow DSP simulation, you can stop at this point, and drag & drop your RF system directly into the Dataflow schematic using the "RF_link" feature.  However, we will stay in the RF domain, and add one more level of RF simulation in this workspace, to finish this tutorial.
  4. Now, set up the PowerSweep controller, which steps the variable called "RFSystem_power" from -30 to +10 dBm input power, invoking Spectrasys at each point.  (The sweep controller is under "Evaluations" in the workspace menus. ) During the sweep, Spectrasys further invokes the nonlinear Circuit_link simulator underneath it to evaluate all nonlinear devices in that subnetwork.  You may have many Circuit_link networks in one RF system, but they each function independently and do not load each other, or interact in any way.
  5. When the power sweep is complete (possibly a couple minutes), you can plot the data from the dataset using Spectrasys measurements and syntax.  Here, the DCP function calculates the integrated channel power in a Spectrasys analysis bandwidth.  The Input and Output powers are ratio'ed to calculate the gain, and then normalized to give the gain compression. 

The "RFSystem_power" and "RFSystem_freq" variables are initiated in the VarEqn block.

Workspace.Name: XParameter Mixer
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\X Parameters\XParameter Mixer.wsv
Workspace.Description:
XParameter Mixer Workspace

KeysightTechnologies Example Workspace

 

This example shows an RF downconverter built around an X-parameter device from of a commercial off-the-shelf mixer.  The data sheet conversion gain of the mixer is about -5 dB in a 50 ohm environment.  This value changes, depending on whether the mixer and its isolation terms are are loaded in 50 ohms, or with the complex frequency-dependent input impedance of the filters and other components. The LO-IF, LO-RF, and RF-IF isolation terms are each approx 12-25 dB.

 

The RF power spectrums at various nodes are presented, along with level Diagrams for Channel Power (CP) and the Stage Dynamic Range (SDR) at each point along the signal path.  


TRY THIS

  1. POWER DEPENDENCE.
    • Change the input RF power "PRF" from -35 to -25.  By how many dB does the 60MHz IF increase? 
    • Change the LO drive power "PLO" to 10 dB above and below the nominal value.  How much does the conversion gain change?
  2. LOAD DEPENDENCE. 
    • Most system tools and spreadsheets assume 50 ohm loads for all components.  X-parameters allow for nonlinear complex loading, even of harmonics and intermods. 
    • Note the Channel Power values before and after the mixer.  (Hover your mouse over the Level Diagram to see the values)  Subtract them.  What is the conversion gain?
      Complex ZL Conversion Gain = ________
    • Select all 3 filters in the system.  De-activate them to SHORT.  Re-simulate.  Re-measure the conversion gain.  What is the new conversion gain with simple 50 ohm loading?
      50-ohm Conversion Gain = ________________
      Datasheet Conversion Gain (above) = ________
    • Re-enable the filters, and change the variable "ZFILTER" from 50 to 75 or 25 ohms.  What is the conversion gain now?
  3. OVERALL DYNAMIC RANGE.  The final IF amplifier is voltage-controlled, at 10dB/Volt.   (2V= 20dB gain)
    • Try changing the AGC_V voltage to 6 volts.

Workspace.Name: XParameters and Circuit Link
Workspace.Path: RF Architecture Design\RF Design Kit\X Parameters\XParameters and Circuit Link.wsv
Workspace.Description:
XParameters and Circuit Link Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

ABSTRACT

This example illustrates the purpose of the Circuit Link component that is used to simulate accurate results when cascading circuit level components.

 

BACKGROUND

Simulating individual RF subcircuits and cascading the results generally does not give the same results as a single simulation for the entire cascade of RF subcircuits. This is only true when the boundaries between subcircuits is well defined and are well matched like circuits with 50 ohm inputs and outputs.

 

SETUP

The circuit under consideration consists of two cascaded X parameter amplifier separated by a lumped element network. Two cases are considered, one using a Circuit Link component and the other not.

 

A data flow simulation has also been created using a Circuit Link component.

 

ANALYSIS

No Circuit Link Spec Out- This graph shows the RF output spectrum from the cascaded amplifier / lumped components that are not using a Circuit Link component.

 

Circuit Link Spec Out- This graph shows the RF output spectrum from the cascaded amplifier / lumped components that are using a Circuit Link component.

 

Xparams and Circuit Link Workspace

Keysight Technologies Example Workspace

 

 

What does this example do

        This example contains Spectrasys simulations to show how CIrcuit_link should be used when cascading non-linear parts such as X-parameters part.

        The RF_Circuit design uses a Circuit_link part to bring the CascSubNet into top level Spectrasys design for simulation. The RF_CascSubnet design contains a top level design that is equivalent to the CascSubNet. Note the warning messages about cascading non-linear parts in top Spectrasys design when simulating the RF_CascSubnet.  

 

Theory of Operation

    .   Typically, when non-linear parts are cascaded directly in a design, they need to be put into a Circuit_Link part so that a single Harmonic Balance is performed over the complete circuitry, which will provide realistic results.

 

         As a matter of fact, in this example, instead of using XAmp and Lumps subnets to build the CascSubNet subnet, we can also use an equivalent single subnet that uses 2 X-parameters part with the lumped components in between. The reason we choose to use the XAmp and Lumps subnets topology is to emphasize what happens in a more realistic multi-team work environment.

   

Further Exploration

1. Create a Spectrasys simulation using Circuit_Link

  • Create subnets that use non-linear circuits and/or lumped components (e.g. XAmp and Lumps subnets in this example).
  • Create a subnet that will cascade the subnets generated above (e.g. CascSubNet subnet in this example).(Optional: To remove the Ground pin/port from a drag-dropped sub-network part, double click on the placed part and click the "Advanced Options..." button, under the "Symbol" tab change the content in the "Symbol:" field from "2-PORT" to "2-PORTNOGND").
  • Create an RF design schematic that uses a Circuit_Link part (e.g. the RF_CircuitLink design in this example) and pick the desired subnet for the Schematic (Design): field under the "Circuit Link Parameters" tab of the placed Circuit_link part.
  • Add ->Analyses -> Add RF System Analysis... to add an RF/Spectrasys simulation controller (e.g. the System1 in this example) and simulate.

2. Create a Data Flow schematic that uses Circuit_Link

  • As shown in the example under the Data Flow folder on the workspace tree, a CircuitLinkWrapper subnet is used to provide the needed Circuit_Link for the cascaded non-linear parts subnet.  This CircuitLinkWrapper subnet in turn is used in the data flow design through the RF_Link part.

Workspace.Name: ModulatorPowerCalibration
Workspace.Description:
ModulatorPowerCalibration

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates how to calibrate the power at the output of the Modulator model. Refer to the documentation of the Modulator model for details on the expressions used in this workspace.

 

For each of the designs in this workspace you first need to run the simulation and read the ModIn__RMS value in the generated dataset. This value is computed by the RMS_Meter model (defined in the Models folder) that is connected to the I/Q inputs (or the Amp input) of the modulator. This RMS value is used to set the modulator amplitude sensitivity (in the design equations) to achieve a desired output power level. For this example and for the types of signals connected to the modulator inputs, the simulation stop time is set long enough to get an accurate estimate of the input signal RMS value. If you are using this calibration process in your own design make sure you run the simulation long enough to capture an accurate estimate of the RMS value of the input signal. Otherwise, this calibration process will not be successful.

 

After you read the ModIn__RMS value from the corresponding dataset, go to the design equations and set the ModInRMS variable to the value you read. In addition, you can set other system parameters such as the desired output power, the LO power if an external LO is used, etc.

 

After you run the simulation a second time, go to the OutputEqns equations page and observe the measured power results. Power is measured in two ways: summing the power in the spectrum (ModOutPwr<N> variable) and integrating the time domain signal using the PowerMeter model defined in the Models folder (ModOutPwr<N>_PowerMeter variable). <N> is 1, 2, 3, 4 and corresponds to the simulation results of Design<N>. The values of these variables should match (for the same value of N) and they should also match the desired output power level Pout set in the design equations of the corresponding design.

Design1 shows how to calibrate the modulator output power when there is no external oscillator and the modulator is used as an I/Q one.

 

Design2 shows how to calibrate the modulator output power when there is an external oscillator and the modulator is used as an I/Q one.

 

Design3 shows how to calibrate the modulator output power when there is no external oscillator and the modulator is used as an Amp/Phase one. The process for an Amp/Freq modulator is the same.

 

Design4 shows how to calibrate the modulator output power when there is an external oscillator and the modulator is used as an Amp/Phase one. The process for an Amp/Freq modulator is the same.

Workspace.Name: PowerMeter_calculations
Workspace.Description:
Estimating Average Signal Power

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Tutorial Workspace

 

This workspace explores a few ways to estimate the total signal power occurring at a node.  Knowing the absolute signal power is useful for comparing responses that involve RF nonlinearities, including transmitter EVM and ACLR, and also Digital Pre-Distortion.  The key assumption for all these methods is that the complex envelope values in the dataflow simuation are analogous to a peak carrier voltage, into a certain impedance (say, 50 ohms), with a given timestep.  Another key calculation is a normalization to either the number of points, or the timestep.  Just integrating the values gives you Energy which keeps increasing with more points, but to get Power, you need to account for the absolute time interval. Some of these factors are already taken into account with different methods, so you have to be careful.

 

The power estimation methods are:

  1. Time Sink - sum the "power waveform" in the time domain
  2. Spectrum Sink - sum the spectral lines in the freq domain
  3. Subnetwork probe - create a network that does these calculations during the simulation, and outputs dynamic values
  4. 89600 VSA software - use the integrated bandwidth markers in the instrument software (if installed) to give a dynamic calculation.

Method 1 - Time Sink

Using the relationship Power = V^2/R, you can use the mean(x) function to sum the power and normalize at the same time, as long as the time step is uniform. Only gives 1 average value for the whole simulation. 

 

Method 2 - Spectrum Sink

By using the linear spectrum magnitude, you can sum to get the total power.  Be sure to set the Spectrum sink to the "Power/Phase" mode, and do the summation in linear watts before taking the dbm(x) function.

 

Method 3 - Subnetwork

By doing the calculations on the fly in the time domain with real DSP, you can output dynamic values during the simulation itself, for control, etc.  You can also get average and instanteous peak values, for a picture of PAPR or Crest Factor. Note that this is not a moving average; the most accurate value is always the last point. 

 

Method 4 - 89600 VSA software

If you have the 89600 VSA software, you can use the integrated bandwidth power marker function to see a dynamic bandpass power value during the simulation.  The results for this default waveform are provided as a reference.

Workspace.Name: Spectrum Analysis
Workspace.Description:
Spectrum Analysis

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates the use of the Spectrum Analyzer sink.

 

In the first example schematic (Baseband), a random bit source generates a bit stream of 10 kbps sampled at 10 kHz. The bit stream is converted to an NRZ waveform using a BitFormatter. This waveform is filtered by a low pass square root raised cosine filter with 0.5 roll-off factor. The filter also upsamples the signal by a factor of 10. The signal at the output of the filter is distorted by the addition of AWGN (Additive White Gaussian Noise). In order to reduce the distortion caused by noise, the noisy signal is filtered with another low pass square root raised cosine filter with 0.5 roll-off factor. The two graphs "Baseband Signals" and "Baseband Spectra" show the time domain waveforms and the spectra of the signals at the output of the first filter (Signal), after adding the noise (SignalPlusNoise), and at the output of the second filter (SignalPlusNoiseFitlered). In order to get smoother spectra, the SpectrumAnalyzer sinks average the spectra of 100 segments each 10 msec long.

 

In the second example schematic (RF), two random bit sources generate two bit streams of 10 kbps sampled at 10 kHz. The bit streams are converted to NRZ waveforms using a BitFormatter. These waveforms are filtered by low pass square root raised cosine filters with 0.5 roll-off factor. The filters also upsample the signals by a factor of 10. The two filtered signals are then used to modulate the I and Q inputs of an I/Q modulator with carrier frequency of 200 kHz. The signal at the output of the modulator is distorted by the addition of AWGN (Additive White Gaussian Noise). In order to reduce the distortion caused by noise, the noisy signal is filtered with a band pass square root raised cosine filter centered at 200 kHz and having a roll-off factor of 0.5. The two graphs "RF Signals" and "RF Spectra" show the time domain waveforms and the spectra of the signals at the output of the modulator (Signal), after adding the noise (SignalPlusNoise), and at the output of the band pass filter (SignalPlusNoiseFitlered). In the "RF Signals" graph only the in-phase (I) envelopes of the modulated signals are shown. In order to get smoother spectra, the SpectrumAnalyzer sinks average the spectra of 100 segments each 10 msec long.

Workspace.Name: Dithering Quant Errors
Workspace.Description:
Dithering Quantization Errors

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

Dithering

This shows the effect of quantization on spurs in the frequency domain.  By adding a bit of AWGN to dither quantization errors, energy in the spurs is spread out, increasing the Spur Free Dynamic Range.  SFDR is observed in the Spectrum graph window.

 

Try this

1. Use the slider bars to find the optimum value of added dither, and note the maximum spur level for each of these settings:

  • Numbits=4, NDensity= -90, -60, -50, -45, -42, -40, -30
  • Numbits=8, NDensity= -100, -80, -70, -65, -60, -50, -40

2. Now type values in the manual Tune Window controls (left-hand panel), pressing "Enter"

  • Numbits=1, NDensity= -30,  -20, -15, -10

3. Finally, vary the "number of samples" in the DF1 dataflow simulation from 1001 to 1000 and 10001 pts.  Also, vary the signal Frequency from 9,10,11 Hz.  Notice how the spectrum changes with interactions among these parameters.

 

Hints:

If the spurs are too closely spaced to see easily, increase the Frequency to 20Hz.

 

About the Measurement Equations

 

This workspace has math measurements to post-process the Spur-Free Dynamic Range (SFDR) and the Signal to Noise And Distortion (SINAD). 

  • SFDR ratios the 2 highest peaks in the spectrum plot, assuming that the highest peak is the desired signal and the next-highest peak is a spur.  There is a "trace_aperature" variable that specifies the width of the spectrum window to exclude around the peak value, expressed as a percentage of the total x-axis.  "trace-aperature=2%" means the algorithm finds the peak value, then removes the trace data +/- 1% of this along the x-axis, then finds the next peak value (spur).  For high-dynamic range signals, you may want to adjust this width.
  • SINAD integrates the power inside the spectrum window, vs. outside the spectrum window, and accounts for all noise and distortion/spur terms added together. 
  • THD+N is expressed here as the percentage of integrated power outside the signal window, to the total power.  This is typical of audio signal processing.

Workspace.Name: 3GPP_LTE_DL_Tx
Workspace.Description:
3GPP_LTE_DL_TX

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example workspace demonstrates SystemVue-ADS-VSA links for LTE_DL_Tx.

 

1. The folder containing this example workspace also contains a subfolder ADS with a corresponding ADS workspace ADS_SV_LTE_wrk.7zads. Unarchive ADS_SV_LTE_wrk.7zads using ADS.

  • If you are using an older version of ADS the unarchived project path may not be allowed to contain spaces.

2. Open ADS_SV_LTE.dsn under ADS_SV_LTE_wrk.

3. Start simulation for ADS_SV_LTE.dsn in ADS.

4. Then start simulation for this workspace, 3GPP_LTE_DL_Tx, in SystemVue.

  • "InvokeADS" parameter should be set to NO.

5. Data will transfer from SystemVue to ADS and back to SystemVue using the ADSCosimBlockEnv model in SytemVue.

6. For more details, please refer to application note http://edadocs.software.keysight.com/display/eesofkcsysvue/SystemVue+ADS+link+bidirectional+cosim+3-in-1+example+LTE+HD+WPAN+ZigBee

Using the steps above, you can design and verify your cosimulation schematic in ADS. After verification, you can use the following steps to further streamline the SV-ADS cosimulation without opening ADS.

7. In ADS, use "Simulate > Generate Netlist" to generate cosimulation netlist from ADS schematic design.

8. In SystemVue, double click the ADS cosimulation part on schematic to bring up part properties dialog.

  • Set "InvokeADS" parameter to YES.
  • Set "Netlist" parameter to the path of the ADS cosimulation netlist.
  • Set "HPEESOF_DIR" parameter to the ADS installation directory.

9. Start simulation in SystemVue. SystemVue will automatically invoke ADS hpeesofsim process to simulate the netlist. No need to open ADS and start simulation in ADS manually.

Workspace.Name: RFAmp
Workspace.Description:
RFAmp

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Template Workspace

 

This workspace demonstrates how to use SystemVue and SystemVue Engine to add RF impairments to a signal generated in MATLAB and have that signal available back in MATLAB to do further processing.

 

Make sure you add the folder <SystemVue Installation Dir>\Baseband_Link to your MATLAB search path.

 

Copy this workspace and the two MATLAB scripts (RF_ImpairmentsTwoTones.m, RF_Impairments16QAM.m) located in the same folder as this workspace to a directory where you have write access to.

 

Design1_TwoTones and Design2_16QAM have been simulated in SystemVue and the behavioral data for the RF system has been extracted and saved in the workspace (one set of data for each design). This data is valid ONLY for the SampleRate and FCarrier values used in the simulation. If SampleRate or FCarrier changes, the data will NOT be valid anymore and you will have to double click on the RF_Link part, press the Clear Behavioral Data button, and resimulate with the new values of SampleRate and FCarrier. The same is true if you change anything in the RFSch design, e.g. any parameters of the RFAMP model.

 

Exercises/Experiments for design Design1_TwoTones

  1. Open design Design1_TwoTones and read the note inside the yellow box at the top to understand how it is setup to be simulated in both SystemVue and from MATLAB.
  2. Press the Run Analysis (green triangle) button and observe the input and output spectra in graph DF1_Spectra.
  3. Open the script RF_ImpairmentsTwoTones.m in MATLAB and read the code and comments to understand the flow.
  4. Run the script. The first time you run the script, SystemVue Engine starts and there is some one-time initialization delay. Next time you run the script it should run faster.
  5. A plot should appear showing the input and output spectra. Compare the spectra to the ones in the SystemVue DF1_Spectra graph.
  6. In SystemVue, in the Equations tab of the design change ToneAmp to 0.25.
  7. Run the simulation and observe the input and output spectra again. The intermod levels should have increased relative to the two mai tones.
  8. In MATLAB, change ToneAmp variable in the RF_ImpairmentsTwoTones.m to 0.25.
  9. Run the script and compare the spectra again.
  10. In MATLAB, change BlockSize variable in the RF_ImpairmentsTwoTones.m from 10 to 1, 100, 1000.
  11. Run the script for each of these values and notice any simulation speed improvement/degradation.
  12. BlockSize is passed from MATLAB to the SystemVue Engine analysis, through the call

    analysis.param('BlockSize').value = BlockSize;

    This sets the BlockSize parameter in the Parameters tab of the Design1_TwoTones design, which is then used in the two Baseband_Link blocks to control the number of data points transferred between SystemVue Engine and MATLAB each time they communicate with each other. The larger the BlockSize the fewer the times SystemVue Engine and MATLAB will communicate with each other resulting in lower communicated overhead and faster overall simulation.

  13. In the Parameters tab of the Design1_TwoTones design, change FCarrier parameter to 200e6.

  14. Open the RFSch design and notice that the RFAMP has different non-linear proeprties at 200 MHz compared to 100 MHz.

  15. Go back to the Design1_TwoTones design, double click the RF_Link part, press the Clear Behavioral Data button, and resimulate.

  16. In MATLAB, change FCarrier variable to 200e6, run the script, and compare the spectra again.

 

Exercises/Experiments for design Design2_16QAM

  1. Open design Design2_16QAM and read the note inside the yellow box at the top to understand how it is setup to be simulated in both SystemVue and from MATLAB.
  2. Press the Run Analysis (green triangle) button and observe the input and output spectra in graph DF2_Spectra and the EVM in the yellow text box next to the EVM block on the schematic.
  3. Open the script RF_Impairments16QAM.m in MATLAB and read the code and comments to understand the flow.
  4. Run the script.
  5. A plot should appear showing the input and output spectra. Compare the spectra to the ones in the SystemVue DF2_Spectra graph.
  6. The spectra will not be identical as in the case of the Two Tone example, since the random bit sequence generated in SystemVue and in MATLAB are different. In addition, there could also be differences in the mapping of the bits to the 16-QAM symbols. However, the spectra should be statistically equivalent and show the same distortion (spectral regrowth) in a qualitative sense.
  7. Compare the EVM values reported by SystemVue (yellow text box on the schematic) with the EVM value computed in MATLAB (EVMrms and EVMrmsManual variables). They will not be identical due to reasons explained above but they should be fairly close.
  8. In MATLAB, change BlockSize variable in the RF_ImpairmentsTwoTones.m from 10 to 1, 100, 1000, run the script and observe any simulation performance speed up or slow down.
  9. In MATLAB, change the BackOff_dB value passed to SystemVue from 10 to 5.

    analysis.param('BackOff_dB').value = 5;

  10. This will drive the RFAMP more into compression. Run the simulation and observe the input and output spectra again. The spectral regrowth should have increased. EVM should also increase.
  11. If you want to compare again with the SystemVue results, set the BackOff_dB parameter in the Parameters tab of the design to 5 and simulate.

 

To be able to impair a MATLAB generated signal with RF impairments from a SystemVue RF model you DO NOT need to set up designs similar to Design1_TwoTones and Design2_16QAM where you generate an equivalent signal inside SystemVue. These designs were set up to demonstrate that the RF imprairments added through RF_Link are the same regardless of whether the signal is generated in SystemVue or "streamed" from MATLAB. The design you need to create in SystemVue is much simpler as shown in Design3_Baseband_Link_Template. All you need to do in the SystemVue simulation is to extract the RF system behavioral data over the bandwidth of interest. This can easily be done by simply connecting an Oscillator model to the RF_Link input. The Frequency and SampleRate parameters of the Oscillator control the bandwidth over which the behavioral data extraction is done, [ Frequency - SampleRate/2, Frequency + SampleRate/2 ]. You do not even have to set up complicated sinks at the output of RF_Link. Since the behavioral data extraction happens during simulation initialization, all you need is the Sink model set up to collect a single sample (see RF_Link_Out Sink in Design3_Baseband_Link_Template).

Workspace.Name: NR_DL_Tx
Workspace.Description:
3GPP NR DownLink Example of SVE Baseband Link

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

 

Make sure you add the folder <SystemVue Installation Dir>\Baseband_Link to your MATLAB search path.

Copy this workspace and the two MATLAB scripts (NR_DL_Tx.m, NR_DL_Tx_Functions.m) located in the same folder as this workspace to a directory where you have write access to.

  1. Open each design and read the note inside the yellow box at the top to understand how it is setup to be simulated in both SystemVue and from MATLAB.
  2. For each time MATLAB starts, SystemVue Engine path might need to be specified by executing the command in MATLAB command window: SystemVue.config.setEnginePath('<SystemVue Installation Dir>\Bin'); where Bin contains the SystemVueEngine.exe.
  3. Press the Run Analysis (green triangle) button and observe spectra, CCDF, ACLR and the EVM results in corresponding figures, tables and dataset in the design folder.
  4. Open the script NR_DL_Tx.m in MATLAB and read the code and comments to understand the flow.
  5. Run the script.
  6. Plots and results should appear showing spectra, CCDF, ACLR and EVM.

 

 

 

This example workspace provides a SVE Baseband Link test bench demonstration to measure spectrum, constellation, EVM, ACLR and CCDF for NR downlink. There are three designs located in three folders.

Folder: DL_Tx. This NR_DL_Tx design provides a NR downlink source example to enable users to get NR DL source data generated by SystemVue in MATLAB through SVE Baseband Link.

Folder: DL_Rx. This NR_DL_Rx design provides a NR downlink receiver example. The design will receive NR DL signal from MATLAB and analyze quality of the received signal.

Folder: DL_TxRx. This NR_DL_TxRx design includes both NR downlink source generation and signal reception in SystemVue. Users can get NR DL source data generated by this SystemVue design in MATLAB and then perform digital signal processing to the data in MATLAB. After that, the signal can be transferred back to SystemVue for further reception analysis.

 

Overall the followings are the features supported in the example.

1. NR transmitter signal generation according to Test Models defined in 3GPP TS 38.141 V15.3.0 (2019-09)  or user defined downlink parameter configuration. 

2. Spectrum, constellation, EVM, ACLR and CCDF measurements are available in MATALB after simulation.

 

 

Test Models

Test Models of (0:NR-FR1-TM1.1; 1:NR-FR1-TM1.2; 2:NR-FR1-TM2; 3:NR-FR1-TM2a; 4:NR-FR1-TM3.1; 5:NR-FR1-TM3.1a; 6:NR-FR1-TM3.2; 7:NR-FR1-TM3.3; 8:NR-FR2-TM1.1; 9:NR-FR2-TM2; 10:NR-FR2-TM3.1) are supported for FR1 FDD / TDD mode and for FR2 TDD mode in this workspace.

Set UseTestModel to YES, then you can select TestModel and Bandwidth to configure different test models. 

When UseTestModel is set to YES, SSB is not enabled for test models.

When UseTestModel is set to NO. NR signal is configured by other parameters. In this case, there is no SSB for Numerology 2 (60kHz) according to the specification. And SSB for 240kHz is not supported for now. When the Numerology is set 2 and 4, SSB should be disabled. BWP is defined occupy the whole bandwidth of component carrier. Frequency location of SSB in component carrier are defined by SSB_RBOffset. It is defined with the reference to the beginning of component carrier. SSB_RBOffset is defined based on 15kHz for Numerology 0 and Numerology1, and 60kHz for Numerology 3 as defined in 3GPP TS 38.211. PDSCH_RBOffset and PDSCH_NumRBs define the frequency location of PDSCH in BWP. PDSCH RB offset is defined with the reference to the beginning of BWP. Please make sure BWP and SSB is in the bandwidht and PDSCH is in the BWP. Either SSB or PDSCH can be disabled by setting SSB_Enable or PDSCH_Enable to NO when UseTestModel is set to NO. But the workspace will not work if both of SSB and PDSCH are disabled. Please make sure at least one of them is enabled. Users need to specify modulation for PDSCH by setting Modulation.

 

 

3GPP NR EVM measurement

The EVM measurement in SystemVue is based on EVM model. In this example, one frame signal is used to do demodulation and get EVM result.

Filter is added in EVM model before demodulating the signal if EnableRxFilter is set to YES. Bandwidth of this filter is set as the same bandwidth of the component carrier.

There is also a Bandpass Filter before EVM measurement in both NR_DL_Rx and NR_DL_TxRx design. The filter will influence EVM measurement in noise free scenario. But this little influence can be neglected in noisy scenario.

 

 

ACLR measurement

ACLR is calculate by function NR_ACLR_Measurement which is based on TS 38.104 (v15.3.0). Basically, ACLR of both first and second adjacent bandwidth will be calculated automatically once simulation is over. ACLR is valid for first adjacent bandwidth when OversamplingOption is no less than 2 (Ratio 4) and ACLR is valid for first and second adjacent bandwidth when OversamplingOption is no less than 3 (Ratio 8).

 

 

Notes

SignalPower is defined as the power of PDSCH. If SSB is in the location of PDSCH, SignalPower equals to the power of the transmitter. If SSB is outside PDSCH, signal power of transmitter will be a little stronger than SignalPower when UseTestModel is set to No. When UseTestModel is set to YES, number of RBs of PDSCH is obtained according to TestModel, Bandwidth and Numerology. PDCCH and PDSCH is not overlapped in time domain, the SignalPower may not be accurate when PDCCH is transmitted.

 

Signal distortions added in transmitter modulator can be set up by parameters GainImbalance, PhaseImbalance, etc. 

 

Tx and Rx RF link can be turned on/off by parameter EnableTxRFLink and EnableRxRFLink.

In Tx RF link, a RF power amplifier is included, where amplier gain and noise figure can be set by parameter TxRF_AmpGain and TxRF_AmpNF. 

In Rx RF link, a RF power amplifier and a frequency downconversion to Intermediate frequency are included, where power amplier gain and noise figure can be set by parameter RxRF_LNAGain and RxRF_LNANF and output intermediate frequency frequency and phase noise list of the oscillator can be set by parameter RxRF_IFCarrier and RxRF_IFOSFOPN 

Note Tx and Rx RF link only work for FR1. For FR2 simulation,they should remain to disabled.

 

When OversamplingOption is more than 1 (Ratio 2), the signal will be down sampled to Ratio 2 with a bandpass filter and send to EVM model to perform demodulation.

 

Frequency range of source and EVM model are defined by FCarrier.

 

The number of simulated subframes for EVM measurements should be no less than 15 and be multiples of 5 in this workspace for complete demodulation of EVM based on NR radio frame.

 

The ideal low pass filter for spectrum shaping can be turned on/off by parameter EnableTxFilter. The filter taps number can be set by FIR_Taps. If EnableTxFilter is set to NO, no spectrum shaping would be applied.

 

This SVE Baseband Link example is based on SystemVue 2020.

 

Try to change the parameters, run the analysis and check the simulation results.

  • ACLR shows ACLR results when OversamplingOption is set to no less than Ratio 4
  • Graph CCDF shows the Complementary Cumulative Distribution Function of the transmitted or received signals
  • Graph Constellation shows the constellation of each physical channel and signal when SaveConstellation is set to YES. The constellation of PDSCH, PBCH, PSS and SSS are shown when UseTestModel is set to NO. PDSCH DMRS is shown alongside PDSCH channel and PBCH DMRS is shown in PBCH. Constellation of PDSCH and PDCCH are shown when UseTestModel is set to YES
  • Table Error Summary shows average EVM, peak EVM, frequency errors and other measured results of each frame from EVM model
  • Table Error lists EVM of each enabled physical channel
  • Graph Spectrum shows the spectrum of NR downlink signal
  • All the measurement results and plot figures contain the impact of Tx_RFLink and Rx_RFLink if they are enabled

Exercises/Experiments for design PhaseArray_Radar

  1. Open the script PhaseArray_Radar.m in MATLAB and read the code and comments to understand the flow.

Workspace.Name: RF_Radar
Workspace.Description:
RF_Radar

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Template Workspace

 

This workspace demonstrates how to use SystemVue and SystemVue Engine to add RF impairments to Radar channel in MATLAB and have that signal available back in MATLAB to do further processing.

 

Make sure you add the folder <SystemVue Installation Dir>\Baseband_Link to your MATLAB search path.

 

Copy this workspace and the MATLAB scripts (RF_Radar.m) located in the same folder as this workspace to a directory where you have write access to.

 

There is 3 designs in the the workspace, the designs are TxChannel, RxChannel and RxChannel+SignalProcessing. The RxChannel+SignalProcessing have build-in model RADAR_PulseCompression and RADAR_MTD campared with RxChannel.

 

Exercises/Experiments for design RF_Radar

  1. Open the script RF_Radar.m in MATLAB and read the code and comments to understand the flow.
  2. Run the script. The first time you run the script, SystemVue Engine starts and there is some one-time initialization delay. Next time you run the script it should run faster.
  3. In the matlab, the simulation process is 1. Specify parameters ->2.Run the TxChannel analysis and generate the transmitting signal ->3. Plot the Tx channel waveform and spectum on different nodes -> 4. Generate the target echo in the matlab -> 5. Run the RxChannel analysis and generate the baseband signal -> 6. Plot the Rx channel waveform and spectum on different nodes -> 7. Collect the baseband signal and do the signal processing, complete pulse compression and Doppler processing in matlab, and plot the Range-Velocity map.
  4. In Step 5, if we specify the parameter NameOfRxAnalysis = 'RxChannelSignalProcessingAnalysis' , in the step 7, pulse compression and Doppler processing will be done using radar library built-in model.

Workspace.Name: PostProcessingSimulationData
Workspace.Description:
Post-Processing

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Tutorial Workspace

 

This example workspace explores post-processing simulation data in SystemVue.  Detailed descriptions of the designs in this workspace can be found in the Tutorials > Algorithm Design > Working with MATLAB Script section of the documentation.

 

Please visit this documentation section, and follow the instructions provided under the three subsections titled

  1. Time Domain Power Measurements
  2. Histogram
  3. Spectrum Averaging

 

using( 'Design1_Data' );

Power = abs( ModOut ).^2 / ( 2.0 * 50.0 );
MeanPower = mean( Power );
MaxPower = max( Power );
PeakToAverageRatio = 10 * log10( MaxPower / MeanPower );

Idx = find( Power == MaxPower );
MaxPowerTime = ModOut_Time( Idx );

PercentOfTimeAboveMeanPowerPlus3dB = 100 * length( find( Power > MeanPower*2 ) ) / length( Power );

using( 'Design2_Data' );

x = histogram( S1, 11 );

DataMin = min( S1 );
DataMax = max( S1 );

bins = linspace( DataMin, DataMax, 12 );
y = zeros( 11, 1 );

for i = 1:length( y );
 indices = find( bins(i) <= S1 & S1 < bins(i+1) );
 y(i) = length( indices );
end

indices = find( S1 == bins(i+1) );
y(i) = y(i) + length( indices );

setindep( 'y', 'bins' );

using( 'Design3_Data' );

N = 1;

BlockSize = floor( length( ModOut ) / N );

MySpec = zeros( BlockSize, 1 );

for i = 1:N
 ModOutI = ModOut( (i-1)*BlockSize+1 : i*BlockSize );
 TimeVecI = ModOut_Time( (i-1)*BlockSize+1 : i*BlockSize );
 [MySpecI, MyFreq] = MySpectrumAnalyzer( ModOutI, TimeVecI );
 MySpec = MySpec + MySpecI;
end

MySpec = MySpec / N;
MyFreq = MyFreq + ModOut_Fc;

setindep( 'MySpec', 'MyFreq' );
setdisplayunit( 'MySpec', 'dBm' );
setdisplayunit( 'MyFreq', 'Hz' );

Workspace.Name: FixedPointParameters
Workspace.Description:
This tutorial is comprised of three folders:

 

1- Bit Manipolation: Explore the functionalities of different bit handling parts [SerToPar, ParToSer, BitMerge, and Extract]

2- OverFlow : Explore the differences between different overflow modes

3- Quantization: Explore the differences between different quantization modes

 

Below are the steps of this tutorial:

 

1-Bit Manipulation:

- Right click on the Bit_Manipulation_Analysis and select Run

- Note the updated values on the text box beside the sinks.

- Try different values and fixed point parameters and explore the functionalities of these bit manipulation blocks

 

2- OverFlow:

- Right click on OverFlow_Analysis and select Run

- Open the OVRFLW_MODES graph and note the difference between different over flow modes. The x axis represents the floating point values. The y axis represents different overflow modes.

- Go to the equation tab of the OverFlow_Design, change the value of SignFlag from 1 to 0. SignFlag variable is used for all the FloatToFxp converters (except for the WRAP_SM as this overflow mode is not defined for unsigned numbers). By changing this variable to zero, all the converted fixed point values are unsigned.

- Run the analysis again

- Open the OVRFLW_MODES graph

- Double click on the graph and check the "hide" option for the WRAP_SM variable.

- Note that the dynamic range of the fixed point values have changed from the rang [-4, 3 ] to the range [0, 7].

 

3- Quantization:

- Right click on Quantization_Analysis and select Run

- Open the RND_MODES graph and note the difference between different rounding modes. The x axis represents the floating point values. The y axis represents different rounding modes.

- Open the TRN_MODES graph and note the difference between different truncation modes as compared to the rounding mode RND. The x axis represents the floating point values. The y axis represents different truncation modes.

Workspace.Name: HDL_CODE_GEN
Workspace.Description:
HDL Code Generation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Tutorial Workspace

 

The purpose of this tutorial is to introduce the HDL code generation

 

Pre-requisite: Modelsim SE from Mentor Graphic. For the supported versions of these products, review the System Requirements page at Getting Started  > Installation Guide .

 

This tutorial has four folders:

 

1- DFF_Design: This is a code generation example of a synchronous element

2- FFT_Design: This is a code generation example of a synchronous digital processing system

3- Gain_Design: This is a code generation example of an asynchronous element

4- MAC_Design: This is a code generation example of a simple digital design

 

For each of these folders, follow the steps below:

 

1- Run the Analysis of the design

 

2- Check the results on the corresponding graph

 

3- Open the HDL code generation of that design. Add the Code_Gen_SubSys to the code generation list.

 

4- Make sure that the option "Automatically add generated model to Part model list" is asserted.

 

5- Run the HDL code generation by clicking "Generate"

 

6- Switch the model of the Code_Gen_SubSys part to the code generated model : <Model_Name> (ModelSim) (HDL@Data Flow Models), where <Model_Name> can be DFF_Design, FFT_Design, Gain_Design, MAC_Design.

 

7- Run the Analysis again.

 

8- Make sure that the diff_value at the data set is zero.

 

9- Review the generated HDL files in <Model_Name>_HDL folder.

 

For detailed information about this tutorial. Refer to the Tutorials > Hardware Design > HDL Code Generatiion (Hardware Design)

Workspace.Name: CustomHDL_workspace
Workspace.Description:
Custom HDL Co-Simulation

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Tutorial Workspace

 

Tutorial Objective: Introducing the HDL cosimulation for custom HDL code 

 

This tutorial demonstrates how to cosimulate imported/custom HDL code using ModelSim. Two types of digital designs are considered:

Workspace.Name: Dynamic Plots QAM16 Demod
Workspace.Path: Tutorials\Plotting and Visualization\Dynamic Plots QAM16 Demod.wsv
Workspace.Description:
Dynamic plots

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

This example illustrates the concept of "dynamic plots" with the continuous, run-time tuning feature.  Two different plotting utilities are shown: A) SystemVue's built-in sinks, and B) the external 89600 VSA software (which requires its own license).

 

Key points:

  • Normally a dataflow simulation has a stop & stop time configured on the analysis controller, or mandated by the data collection "sinks" (eg - BER).  In this case, setting the parameter "CONTINUOUS=YES" on any sink changes the simulation behavior to continue indefinitely.  The data is then streamed to a dynamic plot, instead of silently going to the dataset. 
  • You'll notice that the set-up information about your dynamic plots is stored in an external .adx file.  Next time you run your simulation, it will remember your window arrangement.
  • Sliders are "annotation" objects that can update the values of variables, even during a simulation.  Don't over-use them during a simulation, because updating the variables a lot slows down the simulation.  Just make simple changes, and watch for the effect.

Notes on Dynamic Sinks

  • 89600 VSA
    • The 89600 VSA software is a professional signal analysis program used by many Keysight instruments.  If you want to compare exactly the same EVM, ACLR, etc between SystemVue vs. a true hardware measurement, then use the real instrument software for both.  It offers ultimate consistency.  Note that it read an external set-up file ".setx" to configure the demodulation.
  • DigitalDemod_Env
    • As a convenience, SystemVue also includes some basic built-in receiver IP in the "EVM_Env" and "DigitalDemod_Env" sinks.  This IP can do some synchronization and filtering to clean up the signal, then measure the EVM, Constellation, Eye, and other quantities.  For a limited set of QAM-type modulation formats, the results are very comparable to the 89600 VSA, and don't require an additional license or memeory, so they pop up instantly.
    • TIP: IIt turns out that if you pre-set the demodulation format to 256-QAM, it will also successfully demodulate lower-order formats like 64QAM, 16 QAM, and QPSK.  This allows you to change the signal type quickly, without re-configuring the de-modulation.
  • Other Sinks
    • The DigitalDemod_Env part has many functions built in.  It provides a complete report.  Whereas the smaller sinks only have individual functions:  Eye, Constellation, Sink, and SpectrumAnalyzer.  They also do not include synchronization and filtering, since they are "just plots".  Nevertheless, they are still helpful for debugging and require less set-up; they are just not as quantitative.

Notes on Run-time tuning

Not all schematic parameters are run-time tunable during an ongoing simulation.  Some part parameters are read once at the beginning of the simulation, and then are not updated.  This is particularly true of things that affect the simulation timestep, and nonlinear parameters on Timed Envelope (RF) parts.  There are couple ways to work around this.

    • Sometimes, you can express your variable as a signal, and use other dataflow parts (like multipliers, adders, etc) to manipulate that signal to achieve amplitude, phase shift, Doppler offset, IQ imbalance, etc. 
    • In the case of tuning the Modulation format, this does change the number of bits/symbol.  Therefore this schematic is set up to stream a constant number of symbols (ie - 1xN matrixes) into the special Mapper_M part, not a constant number of samples.  This approach is often used for "frame" based signals like LTE, which can change format in each frame.  Refer to the documentation on Dynamic Data Flow for more on this topic.

Workspace.Name: MultiStandardRadio
Workspace.Description:
Multi-Standard Radio (MSR)

Keysight Technologies SystemVue Example Workspace

 

NOTE: This example is the same as the one in the \Examples\Comms directory, except that this one enables built-in, dynamic spectrum sinks, instead of relying on an external license for the 89600 VSA software.

---

 

This example demonstrates Multi-Standard Radio (MSR) signal generation using SignalCombiner. The resulting MSR signal combines 2 LTE, 2 WCDMA, 2 GSM, and 2 EDGE signals at different input sample rates and carrier frequencies.

 

For the SignalCombiner part, users specify the Sample Rate (SR), Carrier Frequency (Characterization Frequency, Fc), and Bandwidth (BW) of each individual input signal. Users also specify the desired output characterization frequency and can either specify the output sample rate or let SignalCombiner to compute the minimum output sample rate that can fully capture the entire spectrum and is a multiple of a base sample rate.

During simulation, SignalCombiner resamples and recharacterizes the input signals at the output sample rate and output characterization frequency, synchronizes the resampled signals (due to different input sample rates) and combines them into one signal at the "combined" output port. Users can also evaluate each resampled / recharacterized signal at the "output" multi-port. For further information, please refer to SignalCombiner model document.

 

In this example, eight wireless standard signals are combined at Fc = 1e9 Hz. Here is the list of the source signals and their respective Carrier Frequency (Characterization Frequency, Fc), Bandwidth (BW), and Sample Rate (SR):

  • LTE1: Fc 1e9+2.5e6, BW 5e6, SR 15.36e6, FDD
  • LTE2: Fc 1e9+7.5e6, BW 5e6, SR 15.36e6, FDD
  • WCDMA1: Fc 1e9-2.6e6, BW 5e6, SR 30.72e6
  • WCDMA2: Fc 1e9-7.6e6, BW 5e6, SR 30.72e6
  • GSM1: Fc 1e9-11.6e6, BW 0.6e6, SR 3.25e6
  • GSM2: Fc 1e9-12.2e6, BW 0.6e6, SR 3.25e6
  • EDGE1: Fc 1e9+11.6e6, BW 0.6e6, SR 3.25e6
  • EDGE2: Fc 1e9+12.2e6, BW 0.6e6, SR 3.25e6

 

The Equations tab of Design1 specifies the Fc, BW, and SR information of the above signals in the order of LTE1, LTE2, WCDMA1, WCDMA2, GSM1, GSM2, EDGE1, EDGE2. The order of input signals MSR(1:8) of the SignalCombiner need to match the order of SampleRate, Fc, and Bandwidth parameters.

 

In this example, the two LTE signals are generated from the "LTE" subnetwork using LTE_DL_Src @ LTE 8.9 library. The two WCDMA signals are generated from the "WCDMA" subnetwork using 3GPPFDD_DL_Source @ 3GPPFDD library. The carrier frequencies of these signals are exposes from the subnetwork models and can be set from the "Design1" schematic. The sample rate information of the LTE and WCDMA sources can be obtained from the "SamplingRate" variable defined inside the Equations tab of the "LTE" and "WCDMA" subnetwork respectively. The bandwidth information of the LTE and WCDMA sources can be obtained from the document.

 

The GSM and EDGE signals in this example are generated from the built-in SignalStudio files. If the SamplerRateOption the ReadSignalStudioFile sources ("GSM1", "GSM2, "EDGE1", "EDGE2" ) is set to "Timed from source data", the sample rate from these built-in files are 1.083333e6 Hz, which is the truncated version of infinite decimal 3.25e6 / 3. In data flow simulation, the ratio of the integer-valued data flow rates must match the ratio of the sample rates. To prevent extremely high multirate behavior introduced into the system due to infinite decimal or truncated version of infinite decimal sample rates, the ReadSignalStudioFile sources ("GSM1", "GSM2, "EDGE1", "EDGE2" ) use "Timed from sample rate" option and use the internal interpolator to resample the built-in SignalStudio GSM and EDGE files to 3.25 Mhz.

 

The spectrum graph "MSR_spec_Power" shows the combined spectrum. The spectrum graph "MSR_spec_Power with individual spectrums" shows the combined spectrum along with individual standard spectrum.

 

The graphs inside "Time Domain Graphs" folder compare input and output signals after resampling. For the purpose of comparison, the input signals are delayed in time and the output signals are recharecterized back to the input characterization frequencies.

 

In general, to use SignalCombiner for arbitrary signal sources, users can turn on "Display Data Flow Information" in the Data Flow Analysis Options tab to obtain the sample rate information from Data Flow Information Table and can use Sink to record characterization frequency in dataset and use SpectrumAnalyzer to measure bandwidth.

 

TRY THIS:

  1. Adjust the sliders to view amplitude changes to individual WCDMA and LTE signals.  Resimulate each time.  Also watch the CCDF change, since the peak-to-average ratio of the composite signal is a function of all the underlying signals being summed.
  2. Lower the P1DB power of the amplifier from +30dBm to +10dBm, and resimulate.  Do you see the notches filling in?
  3. Activate the 89600 VSA sink, and interactively tune the sliders, and watch the spectrum and CCDF change while you tune.  (you may need to retrigger some of the measurements inside the VSA software, in order to get that software to update a completed trace)

Workspace.Name: QPSK_FixedP
Workspace.Description:
QPSK Transceiver with symbol timing recovery

 

This example workspace demonstrates a QPSK transmitter and receiver system built entirely from parts in the Hardware Design library. This makes it possible to generate HDL code for the entire system, so that it can be implemented on an FPGA.

 

This QPSK transmitter/receiver system consists of:

 

a)  Bit_Source

It can generate pseudo-random bit sequence. The bit sequence is obtained by performing an XOR operation between a PN15_Bits and a PN9_Bits sequences. Both PN15_Bits and PN_9Bits are generated using an LFSR (Linear Feedback Shift Register). Their primitive ploynomials are:

 

PN15_Bits

p(x)=x^15 + x + 1

PN9_Bits

p(x)=x^9 + x^4 + 1

 

b) Tx

It is a QPSK modulator. After QPSK mapping, the signal is upsampled by 4 and goes through a square root raise cosine filter with a roll-off factor 0.5.

 

c) PN_AWGN

It is an approximation of an AWGN noise generator. According to the law of large number, eight pseudo-random integer generators are added together to approximate AWGN noise.

The eight pseudo-random integer generators are all implemented using LFSRs (a SerToPara part is used to convert 8 bits to an integer). The primitive polynomials for the LFSRs are:

PN9

p(x) = x^9 + x^4 + 1

PN10

p(x) = x^10 + x^3 + 1

PN11

p(x) = x^11 + x^2 + 1

PN12

p(x) = x^12 + x^6 + x^4 + x + 1

PN13

p(x) = x^13 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1

PN14

p(x) = x^14 + x^10 + x^6 + x + 1

PN15

p(x) = x^15 + x + 1

PN16

p(x) = x^16 + x^12 + x^3 + x + 1

   

In "Design1 (Schematic)" Equation tab, there is a variable SNR, which can be used to control the power of AWGN. Only positive values are valid for this variable.set.

 

d) Rx

It consist of a matched filter, symbol timing synchronization with Gardner algorithm, and QPSK demodulator. It uses a polyphase filter to get 16 samples per symbol and adjust the sampling position according to the detected result of the Gardner detector.

 

The Gardner detector result is:

Er = YI(r-1/2) * [YI(r) - YI(r-1)] + YQ(r-1/2) * [YQ(r) - YQ(r-1)]

where YI(r) is the sample in I path and YI(r-1/2) is the sample half symbol behind YI(r); YQ(r) is the sample in Q path and YQ(r-1/2) is the sample half symbol behind YQ(r).

When Er is less than 0, the current sampling position is leading the optimal sampling position; otherwise, when Er is larger than 0, the current sampling position is lagging the optimal sampling position.

 

The detected Er value goes through a loop filter and is fed back to the polyphase filter to select the sampling position. In "loop_filter" model, the detected Er values are accumulated. When the accumulated value is larger than the parameter "loop_threshold" (specified in equation tab of "loop_filter" model), the sampling position is adjusted accordingly.

 

e) BER

This model is used to compare Tx and Rx bit streams. It outputs "err_num" and "total_num" to represent the numbers of error bits and total bits. Then BER ratio can be calculated. This model can also be implemented in FPGA, and "err_num" and "total_num" are output from FPGA for BER ratio calculation.

 

Note

Make sure to remove the sinks in qpsk_demod model before running the HDL Code Generation because the sinks are not supported in HDL code generation.

Workspace.Name: QPSK_FloatingPoint
Workspace.Description:
QPSK Transceiver with symbol timing recovery

 

This example workspace demonstrates a QPSK transmitter and receiver system built entirely from parts that are supported by C++ code generation in the Algorithm Design library. This makes it possible to generate C++ code for the entire system.

 

This QPSK transmitter/receiver system consists of:

 

a)  Bit_Source

It can generate pseudo-random bit sequence. The bit sequence is obtained by performing an XOR operation between a PN15_Bits and a PN9_Bits sequences. Both PN15_Bits and PN_9Bits are generated using an LFSR (Linear Feedback Shift Register). Their primitive ploynomials are:

 

PN15_Bits

p(x)=x^15 + x + 1

PN9_Bits

p(x)=x^9 + x^4 + 1

 

b) Tx

It is a QPSK modulator. After QPSK mapping, the signal is upsampled by 4 and goes through a square root raise cosine filter with a roll-off factor 0.5.

 

c) PN_AWGN

It is an approximation of an AWGN noise generator. According to the law of large number, eight pseudo-random integer generators are added together to approximate AWGN noise.

The eight pseudo-random integer generators are all implemented using LFSRs (a SerToPara part is used to convert 8 bits to an integer). The primitive polynomials for the LFSRs are:

PN9

p(x) = x^9 + x^4 + 1

PN10

p(x) = x^10 + x^3 + 1

PN11

p(x) = x^11 + x^2 + 1

PN12

p(x) = x^12 + x^6 + x^4 + x + 1

PN13

p(x) = x^13 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1

PN14

p(x) = x^14 + x^10 + x^6 + x + 1

PN15

p(x) = x^15 + x + 1

PN16

p(x) = x^16 + x^12 + x^3 + x + 1

   

In "Design1 (Schematic)" Equation tab, there is a variable SNR, which can be used to control the power of AWGN. Only positive values are valid for this variable.set.

 

d) Rx

It consist of a matched filter, symbol timing synchronization with Gardner algorithm, and QPSK demodulator. It uses a polyphase filter to get 16 samples per symbol and adjust the sampling position according to the detected result of the Gardner detector.

 

The Gardner detector result is:

Er = YI(r-1/2) * [YI(r) - YI(r-1)] + YQ(r-1/2) * [YQ(r) - YQ(r-1)]

where YI(r) is the sample in I path and YI(r-1/2) is the sample half symbol behind YI(r); YQ(r) is the sample in Q path and YQ(r-1/2) is the sample half symbol behind YQ(r).

When Er is less than 0, the current sampling position is leading the optimal sampling position; otherwise, when Er is larger than 0, the current sampling position is lagging the optimal sampling position.

 

The detected Er value goes through a loop filter and is fed back to the polyphase filter to select the sampling position. In "loop_filter" model, the detected Er values are accumulated. When the accumulated value is larger than the parameter "loop_threshold" (specified in equation tab of "loop_filter" model), the sampling position is adjusted accordingly.

 

e) BER

This model is used to compare Tx and Rx bit streams. It outputs "err_num" and "total_num" to represent the numbers of error bits and total bits. Then BER ratio can be calculated.

 

Header File Contents

 

#pragma once
#include "SystemVue/ModelBuilder.h"

class GAD_timing : public SystemVueModelBuilder::DFModel
{
public:
 // This Macro is required for all classes derived from DFModel
 DECLARE_MODEL_INTERFACE( GAD_timing );

 

 // Constructor to initialize parameters
 GAD_timing();
 
 //-------- Function Overloads --------
 virtual bool Run();
 virtual bool Initialize();

 

 // Ports
 SystemVueModelBuilder::CircularBuffer< double > input, output;
 
 // persistent y;
 double y[3];
};

 

 

Source File Contents

 

#include "GAD_timing.h"

 

#ifndef SV_CODE_GEN
DEFINE_MODEL_INTERFACE ( GAD_timing )
{ 
 ADD_MODEL_INPUT( input );
 ADD_MODEL_OUTPUT( output );
 return true;
}
#endif

 

GAD_timing::GAD_timing()
{
}

 

bool GAD_timing::Initialize()
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i)
        y[i] = 0;

    return true;
}

 

//-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Run
//  Here we do the math
//-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
bool GAD_timing::Run()
{
    y[2] = y[1];
    y[1] = y[0];
    y[0] = input[0];

    output[0] = y[2 - 1] * (y[1 - 1] - y[3 - 1]);
    return true;
}
